name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota attorney general urges beefed-up consumer protection after $53 million Meta settlement
description: State lawmakers should decide how to spend the largest consumer protection settlement with a single company in South Dakota history, Attorney General Marty Jackley said. But he’d like to see them put at least some of the money toward consumer protection. Jackley’s office has two lawyers and six investigators in its consumer protection division, handling […]
text:
South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley speaks during a press conference on Dec. 19, 2025, in Sioux Falls. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)State lawmakers should decide how to spend the largest consumer protection settlement with a single company in South Dakota history, Attorney General Marty Jackley said.
But he’d like to see them put at least some of the money toward consumer protection.
Jackley’s office has two lawyers and six investigators in its consumer protection division, handling upwards of 82,000 consumer complaints a year.
That team was part of the work that led to Wednesday’s $17.1 billion settlement offer from Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, in a multi-state lawsuit to which South Dakota was a party. The 29 states alleged that the social media platforms are addictive and harm children.
Meta to pay 47 states up to $17.1B in landmark child safety settlement

South Dakota is in line for $52.6 million of that money from Meta, which could rise to $73.4 million if the other defendants in the case — the owners of YouTube, TikTok and Snapchat — also offer separate monetary settlements.
South Dakota’s share of the money is 11% higher than it would’ve been had the state not signed on as one of the 29 plaintiffs in the initial lawsuit in 2023, Jackley said during a Wednesday press conference in Pierre. South Dakota’s $52.6 million share includes $4.5 million to resolve the state’s claims that Meta had shared nonpublic information about its users during the 2016 election cycle with a company called Cambridge Analytica.
“As part of the conversation,” on how to spend the money, Jackley said, he thinks “adding a lawyer or two to work on these significant cases” in consumer protection would be wise.
“When you’re bringing in upwards of $73.6 million, I think it justifies building up the team,” said Jackley, who asked for and received funding from lawmakers last year for an outreach worker in consumer protection.
The money would be deposited initially into the consumer protection fund, and continue to flow to the state over the course of 10 years. Jackley’s spokesman, Tony Mangan, told South Dakota Searchlight that the Attorney General’s Office can’t spend money from the consumer fund without legislative approval.
Under the terms of the settlement, at least 50% of the money needs to be used to address “the concerns raised” by the lawsuit, Jackley said. Beyond that, Jackley said, he hopes lawmakers consider “guardrails” on how to invest the remaining dollars that make sure the money benefits children.
$10 million settlement over online gaming child exploitation will fund safety, after-school efforts

The dollar amount from Facebook is “the record” for the state’s largest settlement with a single company, Jackley said. Collections from tobacco and opioid settlements have been larger overall, but the money in those instances came from multiple companies. 
Because of ongoing negotiations, Jackley said he “has to be careful” when discussing how much money the owners of YouTube, TikTok or Snapchat might offer to resolve claims of harm to children. He said, however, that he’d expect it to “be somewhat consistent” with the Facebook figure.
Wednesday’s settlement addresses the lawsuit against Meta from the state of South Dakota and other states, the trial for which began Aug. 12. Several other lawsuits of a similar nature against the company and other social media businesses are ongoing in other state and federal courts.
Among them are cases filed separately by the Standing Rock, Cheyenne River, Oglala and Sisseton-Wahpeton tribes, each of which have lands entirely or partially located within the borders of South Dakota.
Tim Purdon, of the law firm Robins Kaplan, represents those four tribes, as well as others, in ongoing cases against Meta, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube. The Wednesday settlement, Purdon told South Dakota Searchlight, does not resolve those tribal cases.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC to receive upwards of $247M in Meta settlement over child safety on social media
description: Meta settled a 47-state lawsuit and vowed to make its social media platforms safer for children. South Carolina’s share is at least $247M.
text:
Meta settled a 47-state lawsuit and vowed to make its social media platforms safer for children. South Carolina’s share is at least $247M.(Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)COLUMBIA — Facebook parent company Meta settled a 47-state lawsuit for up to $17.1 billion and vowed to make its social media platforms safer for children.
South Carolina’s share of the settlement will be at least $247 million, and perhaps as much as $350 million, state Attorney General Alan Wilson announced Wednesday.
The court must still sign off on the agreement, and the payments will be in yearly installments over the next decade, with the first payment due 30 days after the judge’s order.
The trial began in California last week and had been expected to last six to eight weeks. Attorneys general from California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey led the case.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
South Carolina, along with 25 other states, Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands were also part of the lawsuit.
The states claimed Meta’s Instagram and Facebook features were designed to drive compulsive use by children and teens while also claiming the platforms were safe for young users.
Immediate changes Meta must implement as part of the settlement include:

Time limits and “Productive Pauses” for children: for its two platforms, Instagram and Facebook, a combined two-hour daily time limit with mandatory pauses after 15 minutes of continuous use and again at 60 and 90 minutes to interrupt endless scrolling.
“Nighttime blocks” restricting children’s access from 12:00 a.m. to 6:00 a.m.
Limited school-time access for children, eliminating push notifications on weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. during the school year.
Robust age assurance measures to more effectively verify the age of young users.
Safer, age-appropriate content controls, including stronger safeguards against bullying, content promoting eating disorders, and content related to suicide and self-harm.
Stronger, more user-friendly parental controls.

An independent auditor will regularly review the platforms to ensure compliance over a 10-year period.
State Rep. Brandon Guffey, who has championed measures to improve online safety for children since the death of his son four years ago, said it’s less about the dollar amount and more about “how many parents can still tuck their children in at night.”
The Rock Hill Republican’s 17-year-old son Gavin committed suicide in 2022 after a 24-year-old Nigerian man posed as a young woman on Instagram to coerce the teen, as well as several other people, into sending him explicit photos.
Nigerian man faces life in a US prison for sextortion that led to death of SC legislator’s son

The man, Hassanbunhussein Abolore Lawal, then threatened to leak those photos unless Gavin Guffey continued to send him money, federal prosecutors said in court in January 2025.
After Gavin Guffey’s death, Lawal kept demanding money from other family members, including Brandon Guffey. The case against Lawal is still pending in federal court. Lawal’s attorney declined to comment on the case.
Wilson, a Republican, called the agreement “one of the largest state consumer protection settlements in history outside the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.”
“As a dad to two teenagers who’ve grown up in the digital age, protecting children from Big Tech is personal to me,” he said in a statement. “This settlement doesn’t undo the damage that has been caused, but it’s a strong step in preventing the harms caused by social media to future generations of young people.”
According to the agreement, states may use the funds for a wide variety of preventative measures, such as:

phone and text-based suicide and crisis hotlines
after school or summer programs, such as sports, literacy, dance, and other indoor and outdoor activities
public health advertising
a public digital education fund
youth mental health programming
phone-free school zones
digital literacy counselors
training for medical providers on body dysmorphia.

States may also use a portion of the settlement to cover attorneys’ fees and other investigation and litigation costs.
For South Carolina in particular, the agreement said payments will be allocated at the state attorney general’s “sole discretion and in accordance with any and all obligations imposed by law.” The agreement specifically states the money will go into a “consumer protection enforcement fund, consumer education fund, consumer litigation fund, consumer aid fund or revolving fund.”
South Carolina has set up similar settlement funds for doling out grants related to opioid addiction.
Care for opioid-addicted mothers and infants is one way SC is spending opioid settlement dollars

Brandon Guffey would most like to see the money spent on increased mental health care access, especially for teens.
“South Carolina has dropped the ball over the past two decades when it comes to mental health,” he said. “That’s why we have homelessness and overcrowding in jails.”
Guffey also wants to see more money going to educate youth about the potential harms of social media.
He said the success of this or any future lawsuit will be based on whether companies are actually forced to implement changes.
The South Carolina Legislature passed Gavin’s Law, named after Guffey’s son, in 2023, which bans sexual extortion, or “sextortion.”
And this year, it passed a pair of social media laws. One requires companies to estimate the age of users and deactivate any accounts believed to be held by someone age 15 or younger, unless parental consent has been granted and privacy controls are put in place. The other sets design standards for social media platforms in an attempt to make them less addictive to minors.
At the federal level, President Donald Trump in 2025 signed a law requiring social media platforms to remove falsified intimate images and so-called “revenge porn.” Guffey testified in Congress in favor of the legislation.
“I can’t save Gavin but can keep fighting to save another child,” he said.
US bill with backing from SC legislator heads to president’s desk

As part of Wednesday’s Meta settlement, South Carolina also will receive $8 million from Meta within 30 days for investigations related to Cambridge Analytica. Ahead of the 2016 election, Meta shared nonpublic information about its users with third parties, including the political consulting and data analytics firm, the states allege.
In addition to the guaranteed amounts, South Carolina could be eligible for 10 more installment payments of $10.3 million each. That would bring the grand total to $350 million, but those dollars are contingent upon all other major social media platforms, with annual profits above $10 billion, implementing similar protections for youth.
“Now that Meta has stepped up, TikTok, Snapchat and Google all have to follow,” Guffey said. “It’s time to prioritize protecting children over profits.”
In a statement, Meta called on TikTok and YouTube to join them in making these changes.
“While this is an important step, the fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day,” the statement said. “All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place, because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another.”
Wilson also said this problem for youth safety extends well beyond one company and credited Meta for being the first major platform to reach an agreement.
“I appreciate Meta’s recognition of the harms caused by their platform design and working with attorneys general across the country to reach this historic settlement,” he said in a statement. “Advancements in technology, like social media, connect the world but also come with huge responsibility, and the changes Meta has agreed to make to their platform reflect that.”

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Instagram’s parent company to pay Idaho up to $127M to settle social media addiction lawsuit
description: Idaho could receive more than $100 million under a settlement in a child social media addiction lawsuit by the tech giant Meta, which runs Facebook and Instagram. The settlement, announced Wednesday, was reached in the midst of a lawsuit trial that 47 states and D.C. are parties to, the Idaho Attorney General’s Office announced. Idaho’s […]
text:
In this photo illustration, social media apps are seen on a mobile phone. (Chris McGrath/Getty Images)Idaho could receive more than $100 million under a settlement in a child social media addiction lawsuit by the tech giant Meta, which runs Facebook and Instagram.
The settlement, announced Wednesday, was reached in the midst of a lawsuit trial that 47 states and D.C. are parties to, the Idaho Attorney General’s Office announced.
Idaho’s share of the $17.1 billion multi-state settlement with Meta is between $89.2 million and $127.7 million, the state’s legal agency said. The settlement payments are set to be doled out over the next decade, National Public Radio reported. 
Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador participates in a May 2026 National Police Week roundtable at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C., alongside Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel and other officials. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Attorney General’s Office)
“Protecting children in Idaho is one of the most critical responsibilities of my office,” Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador said in a written statement. “Intentionally engineering any product to addict children is unconscionable. Meta’s design was a cynical attempt to create a lifetime user, regardless of the psychological damage and harm our children were exposed to. When this trial began, I said we would hold Meta accountable and today I’ve kept that promise.”  
The settlement also requires Meta to implement several changes intended to protect children on Facebook and Instagram, such as:

Limiting app use daily for up to two hours, and requiring mandatory pauses after long sessions. The changes must remain for five years.
Blocks to children’s access to the apps at night between midnight and 6 a.m.
Halting push notifications on weekdays, when children are in school
Age verification for young users
And other limits, such as better parental controls and limits on “social comparison features,” such as visible counts of likes on posts and beauty filters

In a statement obtained by NPR, Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney called on other social media platforms, such as TikTok and YouTube, to follow “Meta’s lead.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Former ISU track athlete sues NCAA over denial of eligibility
description: A former Iowa State University athlete is suing the National Collegiate Athletic Association over her inability to compete in indoor track during the 2026-27 school year. Jenna James, a 23-year-old 2026 graduate of ISU, says a recent class-action lawsuit related to a change in NCAA rules should result in her ability to compete in the […]
text:
(Stock photo by Tom Werner/Getty Images)A former Iowa State University athlete is suing the National Collegiate Athletic Association over her inability to compete in indoor track during the 2026-27 school year.
Jenna James, a 23-year-old 2026 graduate of ISU, says a recent class-action lawsuit related to a change in NCAA rules should result in her ability to compete in the upcoming year, despite the NCAA’s denial of eligibility.
According to James’ lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa, the NCAA, when calculating seasons of competition, treated indoor and outdoor track and field as entirely separate sports during her college years.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
She alleges she completed indoor track events during four seasons, from 2022 through 2026. In June 2026, the NCAA adopted a new policy that allowed Division 1 athletes up to five years of eligibility and participation. That new policy, however, provided no additional year of eligibility for athletes who had just completed their fourth season in 2026, as James had.
A class action lawsuit initiated in Colorado then resulted in a preliminary ruling blocking the NCAA from enforcing that exclusion on athletes whose collegiate participation began in 2022-23 and who had completed their fourth season in the 2025-26 school year.
James’ lawsuit alleges that ISU then informed her that it didn’t believe the ruling would make her eligible to compete in indoor track during the upcoming school year since her participation in outdoor track events during the spring of 2022 meant her participation began in the 2021-22 school year.
In her lawsuit, James argues that for purposes of determining her current eligibility for indoor track, the NCAA should look at her first year of competing in indoor track, rather than outdoor track.
The current stance of the NCAA, James argues in her court filings, “uses her earlier participation in a different sport — outdoor track — to leave her excluded from a fifth season.
Noting that the 2027 NCAA Division 1 Indoor Track and Field Championships are scheduled for March 12-13, 2027, James’ lawsuit seeks eligibility through that period.
James, the lawsuit argues, is “a proven impact athlete within Division 1. She has individually qualified for the NCAA championship in the 400-meter hurdles, earned NCAA All-America honors, competed internationally, and scored at Big 12 conference championship meets. Her third-place relay finish at the 2026 indoor championships further demonstrates that she can contribute at the national level.”
Court records indicate that after graduating from ISU this year, James left Iowa and returned home to Canada because she is awaiting employment authorization to work in the United States now that she’s no longer a student.
James told the Iowa Capital Dispatch this week that should the court rule in her favor, she’d like to compete for ISU but understands that she may have to go elsewhere if there’s no room for her in the track program. Her concern, she said, is that at least a preliminary decision is needed within the next several weeks.
“Once we start getting into November and December, then it’s too late because if I want a scholarship to any other school, by then that money is already dedicated or committed for the next semester,” she said. “I’d love to come back to Iowa State, but at the same time, I’m not going to, you know, pressure them to hold a spot for me or hold back any money for me. I know that’s not realistic. But if I got a call from my coach to say, ‘I have some scholarship money for you, and I have a spot for you,’ well, then, yes, I would love to come back to ISU.”
The NCAA has yet to file a response to the lawsuit. ISU is not named as a defendant in the case.

title: Oklahoma voters oust two incumbent Senate Republicans. Third lawmaker member barely advances
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Two of the three incumbent Oklahoma lawmakers on the ballot Tuesday were voted out of office by Oklahomans.  Sens. Dana Prieto, R-Tulsa, and Jack Stewart, R-Yukon, lost their bids for reelection in their respective primary runoffs. A third incumbent, Rep. David Smith, R-Arpelar, narrowly won his party’s nomination by about 100 votes.  […]
text:
Sen. Dana Prieto, R-Tulsa, speaks at an Oklahoma Freedom Caucus news conference April 7, 2026, at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City. (Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Two of the three incumbent Oklahoma lawmakers on the ballot Tuesday were voted out of office by Oklahomans. 
Sens. Dana Prieto, R-Tulsa, and Jack Stewart, R-Yukon, lost their bids for reelection in their respective primary runoffs. A third incumbent, Rep. David Smith, R-Arpelar, narrowly won his party’s nomination by about 100 votes. 
Prieto was part of the group of Republican lawmakers that launched the Oklahoma Freedom Caucus in September 2024. 
The Freedom Caucus, a group of far-right lawmakers, has often challenged the priorities of Senate leadership and, alongside Senate Democrats, blocked some proposed state questions from being added to the August ballot this past session. 
Constituents in Senate District 34, which encompasses part of Tulsa County, soundly rejected another four-year term for Prieto. With over 5,200 votes cast, 65% of voters supported his opponent, Aaron Forst who will face Democrat Amy Hossain in November. 
Prieto did not immediately return a phone call requesting comment Wednesday and did not appear to post a statement on social media. 
Sen. Jack Stewart, R-Yukon, attends a Senate Appropriations Committee meeting on Oct. 3, 2023. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)
Stewart represents Senate District 18, which includes parts of Oklahoma City, Yukon and Canadian County. Only 45% of the nearly 8,000 votes were for Stewart, pushing his opponent, Tyler Herring, forward to the general election to face Democrat Meredith McGinnis. 
In a statement posted to Facebook, Stewart wrote that while the outcome was not what he wanted, he was glad to have met so many constituents during the campaign. 
“It will take me some time of reflection to consider how we can do better at getting the truth out to people and not allow lies to be so influencing,” he wrote. “But for now, I want to say a heartfelt thank you to you all for allowing me to serve as your state senator for four years. It was a joy and an honor.”
Stewart’s votes often aligned with known members of the caucus, but he denied being a member, according to reporting from NonDoc. The Freedom Caucus never publicly listed its membership. 
Voters in June ousted another Senate incumbent. Sen. Dusty Deevers, R-Elgin, came third in his Lawton-area district. Deevers was also a founding member of the state’s Freedom Caucus.
Nine other legislative races will advance to the general election after Tuesday’s partisan runoff. The winners of the Republican nomination in their respective races include: 

Jon Painter in Senate District 24; 
Curtis Erwin in Senate District 32; 
Justin Wood in Senate District 17; 
Chris White in House District 1; 
Scotty Stokes in House District 9; 
Madison Bolay in House District 38; 
Toby Thompson in House District 47; 
Troy Talley in House District 81; and
Roberto Seda in House District 91. 

The only Democratic runoff for the state Legislature was in House District 99 where Herschel Brown had a decisive victory. Brown faces Republican opponent Melvin Latham in November. 
Republican Jessica Winegeart won the runoff in Senate District 26. No challengers from another party filed in the race, making her the next state senator for the district. 
Michael Brittingham also won the Republican runoff election in House District 19 but faces no other opponents in November.

title: Oklahoma sees uptick in voter turnout for 2026 runoff elections
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Major races for statewide offices, plus two state questions, attracted higher-than-usual voter turnout for Tuesday’s runoff elections.  More than 371,000 Republicans cast ballots in the GOP primary runoff for governor between the winner Mike Mazzei and Attorney General Gentner Drummond, according to Tuesday’s election results. That represents[...]
text:
A sign directs voters into the Oklahoma County Election Board on Aug. 20 in Oklahoma City to vote in the primary runoff elections. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — Major races for statewide offices, plus two state questions, attracted higher-than-usual voter turnout for Tuesday’s runoff elections. 
More than 371,000 Republicans cast ballots in the GOP primary runoff for governor between the winner Mike Mazzei and Attorney General Gentner Drummond, according to Tuesday’s election results. That represents about 29% of the 1.29 million registered Republicans in Oklahoma.
The last time Oklahoma saw a gubernatorial race go to a runoff was in 2018, when over 302,000 Republican voters decided between eventual Gov. Kevin Stitt and Mick Cornett.
More than 360,600 people voted in Tuesday’s GOP runoff for state superintendent, which Robert Franklin won. That’s far more than the previous two times Republican superintendent candidates went to runoffs in 2022 and 2018.
Nonpartisan state questions, open to voters of any party, received the greatest number of votes Tuesday.
Over 535,500 Oklahomans voted on State Question 846, which enshrines voter identification requirements in the state Constitution. The measure passed with about 55% of the vote.
About 7,000 fewer people voted on State Question 844, but those that did overwhelmingly rejected it by 74%. The ballot measure would have allowed state lawmakers to change how much they reimburse public schools and local governments for a manufacturing tax break.
August elections typically attract fewer voters than more well-known dates in June and November. That trend continued.
In June, more than 630,400 voters decided on an unsuccessful state question that sought to raise Oklahoma’s minimum wage.
The nine-candidate Republican primary for governor drew 403,000 votes in the June election.
Although runoff turnout was elevated this year, it still represents a fraction of the total number of registered voters in Oklahoma.
About 22% of the state’s 2.4 million registered voters cast ballots on the measure enshrining voter identification in the state Constitution.
Democrats had an even lower turnout rate, only 21%, for their sole partisan statewide primary, a U.S. Senate race between the eventual winner N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas and Jim Priest. About 616,000 Oklahomans are registered as Democrats, according to the state Election Board.
Independents and Libertarians were barred from voting in the partisan primary races, as neither Republicans nor Democrats opened their elections to them.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: New poll shows tight races for Iowa governor, U.S. Senate in 2026
description: Though Iowa has seen major Republican victories in the last several election cycles, a poll from Suffolk University Political Research Center published Wednesday found the races for U.S. Senate and governor are shaping up to be highly competitive. In the Senate race between Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek, a Democrat, Hinson […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek will compete in the Nov. 3, 2026 election to become Iowa's next U.S. senator. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Though Iowa has seen major Republican victories in the last several election cycles, a poll from Suffolk University Political Research Center published Wednesday found the races for U.S. Senate and governor are shaping up to be highly competitive.
In the Senate race between Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek, a Democrat, Hinson leads with 45% to 41% among likely voters, according to the poll. Libertarian candidate Thomas Laehn was the top choice for 4% of respondents.
Democratic State Auditor Rob Sand led in the poll for the gubernatorial race with 48% to Republican nominee Zach Lahn’s 44%. The poll of 500 likely midterm voters, conducted between Aug. 20 and 23, has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.4 percentage points — meaning both races fall within the statistical margin of error.
These results were reflected in a 300-person “bellwether” poll also conducted by Suffolk University in Muscatine County with 300 likely voters conducted Aug. 17-19. That sample has a margin of error of plus or minus 5.6 percentage points. In the Muscatine County poll, Hinson led Turek 44% to 40%, and Sand led Lahn 48% to 44%.
In a news release, David Paleologos, director of the Suffolk University Political Research Center, said these results are important to note because of how decisively President Donald Trump and other Republicans have won in previous election cycles.
“Keep in mind this is a state that Donald Trump won by more than 13 points in 2024,” Paleologos said. “The fact that both of these races are within the statistical margin of error in a survey where the same voters selected Trump by double digits speaks volumes about where these races stand right now.”
Trump won Iowa in the past three presidential election cycles. Iowa also currently has an all-Republican federal delegation, as well as a GOP trifecta at the Statehouse. Sand is the only Democrat to currently hold statewide elected office.
The Suffolk University poll is not the only indicator that Iowa’s elections are expected to be more competitive this cycle. The Cook Political Report, an election forecaster,  recently shifted ratings for the Iowa Senate race from “leans Republican” to a “toss up,” and the gubernatorial race from a “toss up” to “leans Democrat.”
Jessica Taylor, U.S. Senate and Governors Editor for Cook Political Report, similarly noted “even though, on paper, it should be extraordinarily difficult for Democrats to flip seats that President Donald Trump won by more than 13 points, it’s increasingly hard to ignore both public and private polling showing both races to be more competitive than the Lean category reflects,” while shifting the ratings in both Iowa and Texas Senate and governor’s races.
Rising costs and dissatisfaction with the political climate were some issues brought up by likely Iowa voters in the Suffolk University poll that may account for the shift toward Democrats.
Polltakers, who participated through live telephone interviews, were asked about their “primary motivation for voting in the midterm election” in 2026. The largest group of respondents, 40%, said they planned to vote because it was fulfilling their “civic duty” as a U.S. citizen. But the second most common reason why people planned to vote was to express “dissatisfaction with the current national political climate,” at 30%.
These responses were much more common than supporting a specific candidate’s vision, which 11% of poll respondents said motivated them to vote, or to weigh in on key local ballot issues at 16%.
When asked about household costs, gas and fuel prices, as well as grocery prices, were the top two issues poll respondents said have the highest impact on their household budgets at 28%. Healthcare costs came in third at 22%, while only 8% of Iowans responded that housing or rent expenses impact their budget the most, and 7% answered with utility bills as a top economic issue.

The last week of August is designated as “National Park Week,” and includes multiple themed days, according to the National Park Service. In addition to offering a f[...]
text:
Steamboat Geyser erupts  in the Norris Geyser Basin of Yellowstone National Park on September 17, 2018. (Photo by Jacob W. Frank/National Park Service)Montana U.S. Sen. Steve Daines, chairman of the chamber’s National Parks Subcommittee, cosponsored a resolution this week celebrating the National Park Service’s 110-year anniversary on Aug. 25.
The last week of August is designated as “National Park Week,” and includes multiple themed days, according to the National Park Service. In addition to offering a fee free day at National Park Service sites on Tuesday, the celebration includes Watch Wildlife Wednesday, Thankful Thursday, Freedom Friday, Staff Saturday and Junior Ranger Day on Sunday, Aug. 30.
Many NPS locations will hold special programming during the week.
“America’s national parks are true national treasures worth protecting,” Daines, a Republican, said in a statement. “These parks are America’s crown jewels, and we will cherish them for generations to come.”
Maine independent Sen. Angus King cosponsored the resolution with Daines, and 64 senators signed on, including Montana Sen. Tim Sheehy, a Republican.
“From the rocky coasts of Acadia to the breathtaking canyons of Zion, America’s national parks hold some of our nation’s most treasured landscapes and inspire people from around the world by the majesty and vision of America’s best idea,” King said in a statement. “As our parks continue to face serious staffing and funding challenges, National Park Week is an important reminder of our responsibility to protect these special places and support the dedicated employees who care for them.”
To find out what your closest NPS site is doing to celebrating the week, visit the National Park Week page online.

title: A by-the-numbers look at Darline Graham’s runoff win
description: COLUMBIA — U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won the GOP nomination for the next six-year Senate term with wide support over all but one swath of the state, according to unofficial state Election Commission results. The final tally Tuesday night showed Graham with 52.5% of the nearly 369,000 total votes cast. The 5 percentage-point lead over […]
text:
U.S. Sen. Darline Graham speaks to supporters at her election watch party Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026, in Columbia, South Carolina, after she's declared the GOP nominee for the next six-year Senate term. Behind her are her husband, Larry Nordone, Gov. Henry McMaster, first lady Peggy McMaster, U.S. Rep. William Timmons of Greenville County, and Cody Simpson, GOP nominee for state agriculture commissioner. (Photo by John A. Carlos II/Special to the SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — U.S. Sen. Darline Graham won the GOP nomination for the next six-year Senate term with wide support over all but one swath of the state, according to unofficial state Election Commission results.
The final tally Tuesday night showed Graham with 52.5% of the nearly 369,000 total votes cast. The 5 percentage-point lead over U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman represented more than 18,000 people.
The younger sister of the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham led in 34 of the state’s 46 counties, while Norman won 12 adjoining counties in the deeply red northwest corner.
That’s two more than he won in the Aug. 11 primary, adding to his concentration in the Upstate. But Graham picked up all eight counties in the 7th District won two weeks ago by its congressman, U.S. Rep. Russell Fry, who endorsed her after placing third.
Norman did best, by far, in Greenville County, both in the number (nearly 33,000 people) and percentage of votes cast for him. He led there with 67.5% of the votes, a whopping 35-point lead in the state’s most populous county. In his home county of York, the 5th District congressman took 64% of the votes, but that represented much fewer people (about 14,000).
Norman won half of the 10th counties in the U.S. House district he’s represented since 2017.
Meanwhile, Graham’s biggest win came in Horry County, the anchor of the 7th District, suggesting President Donald Trump’s rally Friday in Myrtle Beach helped with turnout. Others on stage supporting her included Fry.
She was the pick for 73% of voters in the ruby red coastal county, giving her about 26,500 votes there. Her biggest win by percentage was in rural Williamsburg County, but that 78% meant less than 750 votes.
She won her home county of Lexington with about 60% of the ballots, or 14,300 votes.
The runoff brought out more voters than in the primary two weeks earlier, when 10 candidates were competing. On Aug. 11, 11% of South Carolina’s registered voters participated. Turnout bumped up to 12% in the runoff.
Graham will face Democrat Annie Andrews, a Lowcountry pediatrician, in November.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Kanawha County Schools disagrees with AGs letter, says Hope Scholarship policy follows the law
description: Kanawha County Schools issued a defense in response to Attorney General JB McCuskey’s stern letter about the county’s protocol regarding the Hope Scholarship and students with disabilities. The school system argued they’re operating in accordance with federal and state law.
text:
The Hope Scholarship is West Virginia's education saving account program. (Courtesy photo)Kanawha County Schools issued a defense in response to Attorney General JB McCuskey’s stern letter about the county’s protocol regarding the Hope Scholarship and students with disabilities. The school system argued they’re operating in accordance with federal and state law.
McCuskey has taken issue with a letter from KCS to parents that said students with disabilities would have to be reevaluated if they choose to reenter public schools after leaving to use the Hope Scholarship. 
The Hope Scholarship is West Virginia’s education voucher program, and it gives students around $5,400 each school year to pay for education outside of public schools.
McCuskey recently sent a letter to state school officials saying that the KCS decision did not square with state and federal disabilities laws. He worried local school officials might try to withhold disability-related services or subject the child to disciplinary action without their disability protections. 
The AG’s letter was not sent to KCS.
Chris Williams, KCS director of communications, said that they’re now reviewing the letter that they sent out to parents who file a notice of intent to leave public education and making necessary changes to the wording.
“However, the purpose of the letter will remain the same, which is to alert parents of students with (Individualized Education Plans) that at the time of their withdrawal from public school, they will no longer have an IEP. This is a required notice and in accordance with federal and state law,” Williams said.
“Furthermore, the letter does and will continue to state that should the student return to public education, their student’s IEP will not automatically be reinstated as it was at the time of the withdrawal. This is also in accordance with Federal and State law,” he continued. 

KCS does not have specific policy addressing this issue, according to Williams.
“We developed this letter to accompany the required Prior Written Notice sent to parents who are withdrawing from public school, based on guidance that the WVDE issued in 2018, long before the HOPE Scholarship existed,” Williams explained. “This letter has accompanied the required PWNs since 2024 and was written due to parent confusion regarding the status of their students’ prior IEP upon re-enrollment. Further, the information is consistent with information contained on the State Treasurer’s website that is publicly available.”
Williams concludes the statement by saying, “McCuskey’s letter to the WVDE does appear thorough, however, it leaves out pivotal points of the law that make the difference in the legal analysis and that is unfortunate.”
Local school leaders have reported that their counties are millions of dollars in debt due to special education costs; in some counties, special education students account for a quarter of all students enrolled. The current school funding model mostly doesn’t account for the high cost of providing special education services.
McCuskey has asked State School Board President Paul Hardesty to intervene in the situation at KCS and identify students who were denied services or reentry because of the county’s decision.
Blatt and Hardesty were also asked to respond to several questions, including if any other county had issued similar letters to parents of students with disabilities. 
There are more than 25,000 students using the Hope Scholarship this school year. The education voucher has opened up to all West Virginia students for the first time since it launched five years ago.

name: VTDigger
title: Antisemitism isn’t a shield for Israel’s human rights record
description:
Criticism of Israel's actions in Gaza and Lebanon is not the same thing as antisemitism, and conflating the two undermines the fight against real hatred.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Antisemitism isn’t a shield for Israel’s human rights record.
text:
Dear Editor, 
In my recent letter to VTDigger, I expressed my concerns over the United States’ continued support of Israel despite the country’s genocidal actions against Palestinian and Lebanese people. Mark Treinkman’s letter in response, signed by members of the Vermont Friends of Israel, claims that my strong opinions must stem from a lack of Holocaust education and antisemitism in Vermont. 
This is not true. What is true is that the tragedies of the Holocaust should not be repeated anywhere. Genocide is something that should never be taken lightly, and the hateful, destructive actions in Nazi Germany against Jewish people should never be forgotten. However, focusing on and educating about just one genocide, one group of people, is a questionable tactic. It is important to be educated on the Holocaust, but it shouldn’t be viewed as more tragic or more worthy of knowledge and respect than atrocities committed against other groups of people. 
Just as we should not forget the Holocaust, we must not continue to ignore the annihilation of innocent civilians in Gaza. While Treinkman and other members of the Vermont Friends of Israel may question the depth of my education and that of other Vermont students, if there is one thing I’ve always been taught, it is that we learn history to ensure it does not repeat itself. 
When talking about the conflicts between Israel and Gaza, the topic of antisemitism is bound to come up. What is so difficult about that conversation is the way that criticism of Israel is often conflated with prejudice against Jewish people. Falsely equating human rights advocacy for Palestinian and Lebanese people to antisemitism discredits and undermines the real, vicious and persistent problem of antisemitism when it arises in Vermont and around the world. There has been a rise in anti-Jewish violence over the past few years, and it is something that we must strongly condemn. But it is not acceptable to use the label of antisemitism as a tool to protect problematic governments from ever facing criticism. As a young person, it is my responsibility to uphold my values and standards for the future, and this cannot be done if we continue to protect the most problematic behavior of governments with our silence. 

READ MORE

While the topic of the Israel-Hamas war is complex and something that should not be underestimated, I stand by my belief that the United States is lawfully obliged to stop providing Israel with weapons and military support. Under the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, the United States is prohibited from providing security assistance, including weapons sales, to any government that engages in a consistent pattern of gross violations of human rights. 
The Israeli government’s actions toward Palestinians have given cause for utmost humanitarian concern, and to many, including the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry, it is unquestionably considered genocide. Attacks by the Israeli government on medical facilities, open firings on those trying to access food — claims denied by Israel — and bombings of civilian areas, including refugee camps and schools, have led to devastating destruction and a staggering number of deaths. According to the Palestinian Health Ministry, the Palestinian death toll in the Gaza Strip stands near 73,400 since Oct. 7, 2023, with many bodies likely unaccounted for in the rubble. 
The systematic expulsion of people from their homes, the denial of medical services, the deprivation of food, forced displacement and creating circumstances that would lead to a slow death — such as a lack of proper housing, clothing or hygiene — are all indicators of the genocide crime of deliberately inflicting conditions of life calculated to bring about a group’s physical destruction, although again many of these claims have been denied by Israel. However, there is no way to deny the desolation that the Israeli government has caused among Palestinians. 
This is why I must reiterate the importance of Senate Resolution 797, introduced by Sen. Peter Welch, D-Vt., which requests an investigation of Israel’s human rights practices. He should push this privileged resolution to a floor vote.
From the Holocaust to apartheid to the situation in Gaza and Lebanon today, genocide is woven into the history of our species. It is up to us to foster a better future, and that begins with refusing to enable the catastrophic actions of those in power. 
Zoya BianchiWaterbury, Vt.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Antisemitism isn’t a shield for Israel’s human rights record.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Gov. Stein announces funding for housing in Western NC
description: This week, Gov. Josh Stein announced federal awards of more than $69 million to bring affordable rental housing to Western North Carolina. In 2024, the region lost thousands of rentals in the wake of Hurricane Helene. Stein also announced the availability of $53.4 million in competitive federal grants to develop workforce housing units for homeownership […]
text:
Workers build the frame of a new housing project. (Getty Images/Ryan Lane) This week, Gov. Josh Stein announced federal awards of more than $69 million to bring affordable rental housing to Western North Carolina. In 2024, the region lost thousands of rentals in the wake of Hurricane Helene.
Stein also announced the availability of $53.4 million in competitive federal grants to develop workforce housing units for homeownership across Western North Carolina, bringing total housing investments announced this week to more than $120 million.
The awards for rental units will go to 10 developers in 10 counties to provide more than 828 affordable units. The awards range from $1.7 million to $13.5 million. The money will help fund projects in Ashe, Buncombe, Burke, Caldwell, Cleveland, Haywood, Henderson, Rutherford, Transylvania, and Watauga counties.
“Getting families back into safe housing that they can afford is critical to the recovery from Hurricane Helene,” Stein said in a press release. “This program will ensure these 828 apartments remain financially accessible to people living in the 828 area code for the next 30 years.”
The money comes from more than $69 million in Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery funds administered and monitored by the state Department of Commerce and the N.C. Housing Finance Agency.
Award recipients must comply with income limits, rent restrictions, and other program requirements for a minimum 30-year affordability period. The state Department of Commerce will monitor projects throughout the affordability period to ensure compliance with federal requirements and confirm that units serve eligible low- and moderate-income households.
Margaret Fenton Lebeck (Courtesy photo)
Margaret Fenton Lebeck, CEO of the Housing Assistance Corporation (HAC) in Hendersonville, told NC Newsline that the federal dollars will go a long way toward providing rentals in areas devastated by Hurricane Helene.
“We had an immense housing crunch before in the counties that our organization works in,” Fenton Lebeck said. “We were at 99.3% occupancy before the hurricane, and so to lose any housing at all just made finding housing that people could afford so much harder.”
Meanwhile, funding for the competitive workforce housing grants will come from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and be administered by the Renew NC Workforce Housing for Ownership (WHFO) Program to provide homeowner opportunities in areas most “impacted and distressed” by Hurricane Helene. Workforce housing refers to households earning up to 80% of the area median income.
Eligible counties include Ashe, Avery, Buncombe, Burke, Caldwell, Cleveland, Haywood, Henderson, Madison, McDowell, Mitchell, Polk, Rutherford, Transylvania, Watauga, and Yancey counties.
“This $53 million investment will expand access to affordable housing across western North Carolina as the region continues to recover from Hurricane Helene,” Gov. Josh Stein said in a statement. “It’s a critical step toward helping our neighbors rebuild in the places they call home.”
Eligible applicants include for-profit housing developers, non-profit housing developers, Community Land Trusts (CLTs) and public housing authorities and counties and municipalities among others.
Award amounts will range from $2 million to $5 million per project.
“Retaining a strong workforce depends on access to affordable housing,” said N.C. Commerce Secretary Lee Lilley. “Through the Workforce Housing for Ownership Program, we will help increase the supply of housing available to working families and foster more resilient local economies as communities recover from Helene.”
The application window opened Tuesday and closes at 5:00 p.m. on December 13, 2026. The eligibility criteria, scoring details, and application materials can be found at commercerecovery.nc.gov.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Gianforte appoints former commissioner to PSC
description: Gov. Greg Gianforte appointed Kirk Bushman to the Montana Public Service Commission during the suspension of Commissioner Brad Molnar. Bushman, a Republican on the PSC from 2013 through 2016, is tapped to serve a temporary appointment on the regulatory board through July 8, 2027. “Kirk brings decades of engineering experience and a strong understanding of […[...]
text:
(Screenshot from a PSC social media page.)Gov. Greg Gianforte appointed Kirk Bushman to the Montana Public Service Commission during the suspension of Commissioner Brad Molnar.
Bushman, a Republican on the PSC from 2013 through 2016, is tapped to serve a temporary appointment on the regulatory board through July 8, 2027.
“Kirk brings decades of engineering experience and a strong understanding of the important work of the Public Service Commission,” Gianforte said in a statement. “Having previously served on the commission, Kirk understands the responsibility of ensuring Montanans have access to reliable, affordable utility services.”
In July, Gianforte suspended Molnar after an investigation into allegations of professional misconduct including sexual harassment. 
Molnar is fighting the suspension in Lewis and Clark District Court. His lawyer, Matthew Monforton, said Bushman lost the last three Republican primaries for the seat, including against Molnar in 2024.
“Judge (Mike) Menahan is still deciding whether the governor had any authority to suspend an elected commissioner in the first place — and still deciding whether to block any appointment to this seat,” Monforton said. “The governor didn’t wait for the judge. He decided the judge was optional.”
Any plans to swear in Bushman at the PSC were not immediately clear. A PSC spokesperson said Wednesday “it’s a highly fluid situation and we are seeking clarity.”
The PSC regulates monopoly utilities in Montana including NorthWestern Energy, the state’s largest public utility.
Bushman is a graduate of Montana State University and has a degree in mechanical engineering technology, according to the news release from the Governor’s Office. It said he has more than 30 years of experience in industrial engineering.
The PSC is made up of five commissioners elected by district.
If seated, Bushman will represent District 2, which includes Carbon, Park and Stillwater counties and parts of Big Horn, Gallatin, Rosebud, Sweet Grass and Yellowstone counties, the news release said.
He was among five candidates who applied for the position and the only former commissioner to do so.
“I look forward to his service on behalf of Montana ratepayers,” Gianforte said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis: Only police officers should issue tickets
description: Amid the growing public and political backlash against Flock cameras, add Gov. Ron DeSantis to the list of skeptics about their use. The governor said Wednesday that roadside cameras that use artificial intelligence to photograph and log vehicle data are useful tools for law enforcement agencies and that the Florida Highway Patrol uses automated license […]
text:
Flock automated license reader as captured don Aug. 5, 2026. (Photo by Valentin Termite/Idaho Capital Sun)Amid the growing public and political backlash against Flock cameras, add Gov. Ron DeSantis to the list of skeptics about their use.
The governor said Wednesday that roadside cameras that use artificial intelligence to photograph and log vehicle data are useful tools for law enforcement agencies and that the Florida Highway Patrol uses automated license plate recognition in its work. 
But the governor draws the line there.
“Now, I’ve never supported the automatic tickets being sent if you’re speeding. I think a human being has to do that, and so I’ve never, I’ve never embraced that,” DeSantis told reporters during a Wednesday morning press event at Florida International University.
He added: “I’m all about having law enforcement have tools to be able to hold criminals accountable. I think that’s important that we do that. And no one’s been stronger on law enforcement than me. But I don’t want to have this become a surveillance state.”
The website DeFlock reports there are 7,169 such cameras in Florida. The state ranks 10th in the number per capita and sixth in the number per road mile, according to the site.
The governor, who will be term-limited out of office in January, reiterated that he championed an artificial  intelligence “Bill of Rights” during the 2026 session. He claimed the proposal would have offered protections to residents had the Legislature agreed to pass it. He took a shot at the Republican-controlled House of Representatives for refusing to pass his bill.
The governor warned, “It’s going to get a lot worse unless we have some protections for the people in Florida.” Noting the cameras are being approved at the county and municipal levels, DeSantis said, “The only way it could be dealt with is legislatively.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee to receive $750M of $17B Facebook, Instagram settlement
description: Tennessee will receive over $750 million as part of a nationwide $17.1 billion settlement by Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. The company agreed to settle claims that it improperly collected data on minors and that its platforms are designed to addict children. In the settlement, Meta also agreed to impose daily […]
text:
Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti announced that Tennessee will receive $750 million as part of nationwide settlement with Meta Platforms, the owner of Facebook and Instagram. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)

Tennessee will receive over $750 million as part of a nationwide $17.1 billion settlement by Meta Platforms, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram.
The company agreed to settle claims that it improperly collected data on minors and that its platforms are designed to addict children. In the settlement, Meta also agreed to impose daily time limits on children and prevent minors from using its platforms from midnight to 6 a.m., among several other provisions. 
“We took Meta to trial because Instagram was hurting kids and misleading parents,” said Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti in a news release. “Now we’re ending the trial with a settlement that imposes unprecedented protections for kids.”
The money will go into a special fund managed by state officials called the Children’s Digital Protection Fund. The money can be used to fund research and treatment for children’s mental health and law enforcement-related activity to protecting minors. 
The agreement comes as Meta’s trial with Tennessee in Nashville neared its end. Tennessee’s suit is part of a broader set of litigation by nearly every state, and this settlement also ends a separate federal trial against the company. 
Meta is one of the largest publicly traded companies in the United States. It generated over $200 billion in revenue in 2025 and reported a net income of $60 billion. 
C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a news release that the company was happy to reach an agreement with a bipartisan group of state attorneys general. 
“The framework we’ve negotiated will empower parents to easily manage how their children access our platforms,” Mahoney said. “Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution. We therefore call on our industry peers, TikTok and YouTube, to implement this new framework, right away.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas would receive $172M under proposed multistate settlement with Meta
description: Arkansas is set to receive at least $172 million under a multistate settlement proposed with Meta to end lawsuits regarding child safety on social media, Attorney General Tim Griffin’s office said Wednesday. The parent company of Facebook and Instagram agreed to settle with Arkansas and 50 other attorneys general for $17.1 billion, the largest ever […]
text:
MENLO PARK, CALIFORNIA - JANUARY 29: Visitors take pictures by a sign posted in front of Meta headquarters on January 29, 2025 in Menlo Park, California. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Arkansas is set to receive at least $172 million under a multistate settlement proposed with Meta to end lawsuits regarding child safety on social media, Attorney General Tim Griffin’s office said Wednesday.
The parent company of Facebook and Instagram agreed to settle with Arkansas and 50 other attorneys general for $17.1 billion, the largest ever with a Big Tech firm. The proposed agreement is still subject to court approval.
Arkansas sued Meta in 2023, accusing the company of violating the state’s deceptive trade practices act and misleading minors and parents about the addictive nature of its platforms’ algorithms. 
Meta to pay 47 states up to $17.1B in landmark child safety settlement

Griffin, a Republican who took office in 2023, called the settlement announcement a “proud day for Arkansas.”
“For years, Meta represented that its platforms posed no risk to the mental health of young people, all while knowing that its algorithms were designed to get kids hooked and to keep them online for as long as possible, with well-documented adverse mental health consequences,” Griffin said in a statement.
As part of the settlement, Meta agreed to new safety features including “nighttime blocks” restricting children’s access from 12 a.m. to 6 a.m. and stronger safeguards against bullying, content promoting eating disorders and content related to suicide and self-harm.
Meta urged TikTok and YouTube to join and put the same safety measures in place.
“Ensuring teens have a safe and productive experience on our platforms is an absolute imperative for Meta,” Meta said in a statement on its website. “We want to get this right for parents and teens, and that’s why we partnered with state attorneys general to set a new industry standard.”
Arkansas has filed several lawsuits against social media and gaming platforms, including Roblox, Snapchat and Tiktok, over child safety concerns. 
Arkansas files lawsuit against Snapchat parent company

Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has also pushed for more restrictions on minors’ social media access. 
A federal judge in April blocked the enforcement of a 2025 law Sanders signed that would have required age verification to create new social media accounts. A 2023 version of the law had been struck down as unconstitutional.
“This historic settlement is a testament to the hard work of states like Arkansas that led on this fight to protect kids online,” Sanders said in a statement. “We will continue to hold Big Tech accountable, and I am hopeful other social media companies will follow Meta’s lead accepting responsibility for the harm their platforms have done to kids and begin to right this wrong.” 
The Meta settlement would be one of the biggest Arkansas has received in recent years. Arkansas has received nearly $1.5 billion through a 1998 settlement with tobacco companies and is set to receive at least $216 million through a 2021 settlement with three opioid distributors.

name: National
title: Meta to pay 47 states up to $17.1B in landmark child safety settlement
description: Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, on Wednesday agreed to pay 47 states, the District of Columbia, and a handful of U.S. territories, up to $17.1 billion in penalties over claims that its social media platforms are addictive and a danger to children. As part of the settlement, Meta also pledged to make changes […]
text:
Facebook owner Meta agreed to pay nearly $18 billion to an array of U.S. states over claims its platforms intentionally addicted teens. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, on Wednesday agreed to pay 47 states, the District of Columbia, and a handful of U.S. territories, up to $17.1 billion in penalties over claims that its social media platforms are addictive and a danger to children.
As part of the settlement, Meta also pledged to make changes to Instagram and Facebook that are designed to reduce young people’s use of the platforms.
“Meta intentionally exploited kids for profit and then lied about it, claiming its products were safe when its own internal research confirmed the platforms were addictive and harmful,” said Washington, D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb, a Democrat, in a statement announcing the settlement.
“The physical, mental and emotional harms that intentionally addictive social media inflict on youth — and particularly teenage girls — are widespread across the tech industry, and this successful, coordinated multistage litigation has resulted in Meta being the first platform to come to the table and agree to such comprehensive reforms,” he said.
“It will not be the last.”
The settlement ended a high-stakes, landmark case, filed in 2023, in which states said Meta purposely designed its social media platforms with addictive features, that Meta knew it was exposing children to serious mental harms, and that it intentionally misled the public about the safety of those platforms.


New protections for teens, controls for parents included in Meta settlement
Time Limit: A default two-hour daily time limit that can only be turned off with a parent’s permission. Time spent scrolling on Facebook and Instagram counts toward the total.
Night mode: A default block from Meta apps between midnight and 6 a.m.
School Mode: Notifications will be muted by default between 8 a.m. and 3 p.m. During those hours, young people will no longer receive push notifications, except for direct messages and alerts about their account security or safety.
Regular Prompts: Young users will receive prompts after every 15 minutes of continuous screen time on Facebook and Instagram.
Algorithmic Feed Control: Young users will be able to choose a non-algorithmic feed — one that isn’t personalized by Meta’s recommendation system.
Autoplay Control: Young users will be able to turn off autoplay, so that content no longer automatically plays.
Hidden Likes: Young people won’t see the number of likes and reactions on posts — both their own and those from others — by default.
Disabling cosmetic surgery and extreme makeup filters: Young users will not be able to use extreme makeup filters.
Direct messaging features will be excluded from Night Mode, Time Limit and School Mode restrictions.


Meta has not admitted wrongdoing.
The federal trial began last week in Oakland, California, led by a bipartisan group of attorneys general from California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey.
State officials are calling the settlement the biggest consumer protection win since the Big Tobacco settlements of the 1990s.
Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman, a Republican, said in a statement Wednesday that the lawsuit was “never just about the money.”
“Kids deserve a childhood that isn’t measured in likes and followers,” he said. “The online protections delivered by this settlement will bring a generational change that will make social media platforms safer for Kentucky families.”
In addition to the financial settlement, Meta agreed to make major changes to its Instagram and Facebook features for young users, including a daily time limit, automatic pauses, nighttime blocks that restrict access from midnight to 6 a.m., and stronger safeguards against bullying and harmful content. Most of the updates must be in place for at least a decade.
Meta is trying to drag its competitors along with it. The company agreed to further restrict daily time limits for teens only if TikTok and YouTube agree to adopt comparable measures.
Under the settlement terms, Meta will pay out just 70% (about $12.7 billion) to states unless TikTok and Alphabet-owned YouTube also agree to set one-hour daily time limits for young users, as well as night mode and age assurance measures.
Meta will pay the remaining 30% — $5.3 billion — if the other two companies agree to the new measures and each agrees to pay states about $5.3 billion.
C.J. Mahoney, chief legal officer at Meta, said in a statement that the changes needed to be made across the social media landscape to have an impact.
“Our new Time Limit commitments, Night Mode features and usage limits during school hours set the right path forward for our whole industry, but this framework will only work if all our peers join us,” Mahoney said.
“Because teens move fluidly across dozens of apps, we need an industry-wide solution.”
Settlement money will be paid out to the participating states and territories annually over a decade, based on their populations.
Just three states, Florida, New Mexico and Texas, aren’t part of the settlement. New Mexico won its own lawsuit against Meta earlier this year, when a jury ordered Meta to pay $375 million in damages for violating the state’s consumer protection laws. Texas negotiated its own settlement with Meta that includes a $1 billion payout and a promise of more safety features for children.
While state officials lauded the changes coming to Instagram and Facebook as wins for child safety, some free speech advocates expressed concern over broader implications of the new restrictions.
Kate Ruane, director of the Free Expression Project at the Center for Democracy & Technology, a civil rights organization said in a statement that safe and age-appropriate online experiences for children are critical.
“But we also see the potential for significant risks to everyone’s privacy and free expression rights online, especially in the ways this settlement will subject all users to invasive age assurance and limit all kids’ access to content and services regardless of their individual needs,” Ruane said.
Meta and other social media platforms still face thousands of ongoing lawsuits from individuals and school districts across the nation that accuse them of targeting young users with addictive algorithms and inadequate safety measures.
One of those is a lawsuit against Instagram filed by South Carolina state Rep. Brandon Guffey, whose 17-year-old son Gavin died by suicide in 2022. His family said they later learned he was a victim of sexual extortion after being targeted by a scammer on Instagram.
“Scammers put immense pressure and sometimes even a countdown on these teens,” Guffey said in an emailed statement after the settlement announcement. “Gavin didn’t deserve to have less than two hours before he took his life. He deserved to have a parent that was aware of this.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Mail ballots will go out as normal despite Supreme Court ruling, Colorado election officials say
description: Colorado election officials expect the November election to proceed without interruption despite attempts from the Trump administration to change how states use mail ballots.  ​The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed to move forward an executive order from President Donald Trump that would upend mail voting, saying a lower court issued an injunction prematu[...]
text:
Volunteers at the Denver Clerk and Recorder's office atrium check and organize primary ballots on June 30, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Fraieli/Colorado Newsline)Colorado election officials expect the November election to proceed without interruption despite attempts from the Trump administration to change how states use mail ballots. 
​The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday allowed to move forward an executive order from President Donald Trump that would upend mail voting, saying a lower court issued an injunction prematurely. The injunction had come in a lawsuit filed by 23 Democratic-led states, including Colorado, and Washington, D.C., but another injunction that blocks implementation of the order ahead of November remains in place. That order, which applies nationwide, stemmed from a lawsuit filed by several voter advocacy organizations.  
Matt Crane, executive director of the Colorado County Clerks Association, said the Supreme Court ruling is largely procedural because the lower-court judge issued a ruling before any party was harmed, and it will not result in any immediate changes to Colorado’s election system. 
“The most important thing voters should know is that the decision (Monday) doesn’t change anything for November,” Crane said. “It’s my expectation that the election this year coming up in November will be as it always has been in Colorado with the current model.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold, a Democrat running for attorney general, said in a statement Monday that she’s disappointed with the Supreme Court’s decision but that Colorado and other states will “fight back” when the federal government tries to implement the executive order. Her office did not respond to questions from Newsline Tuesday about what that means or any preparations for possible federal interference with mail ballots in Colorado. 
The Supreme Court’s conservative majority did not rule on the constitutionality of Trump’s executive order. The order called on the Postal Service to create a rule that requires states to notify the agency if they intend to send ballots through the mail. States would have to submit a list of voters planning to vote by mail. The Postal Service would not deliver ballots in states that refuse to submit a list. It would also require that ballot envelopes have a unique barcode that allows the Postal Service to identify which voter mailed the ballot. 
The Postal Service issued a final rule Friday detailing how the process would be carried out. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani of Massachusetts said in an order that the Postal Service publishing the rule runs contrary to her Aug. 11 nationwide injunction. The rule states that none of its provisions will be implemented for the 2026 election as long as Talwani’s injunction remains in effect. 



Quotation







Colorado voters should know that nothing has changed about their ability to vote in November.


– Steve Schleiker, El Paso County clerk 


Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, a Democrat running for governor, on Wednesday joined other Democrat states in a new lawsuit challenging the Postal Service rule. 
“States determine the time, place and manner of elections — not the president,” Weiser said in a statement. “And Congress has never given the USPS authority to regulate mail ballots.”
Colorado is one of eight universal mail-in ballot states — every voter receives a ballot in the mail — and the vast majority of residents choose to vote by mail. Implementation of the executive order and the Postal Service rule ahead of the midterm elections would upend Colorado’s ability to conduct elections, but election experts don’t expect that to happen. 
No guidance
El Paso County Clerk Steve Schleiker, a Republican, said counties have received no direction from the secretary of state’s office related to Trump’s order or the Postal Service rule. Guidance from the state has consistently said that state election laws and rules remain in effect and counties should prepare to run their elections under those provisions, Schleiker said. 
The clerk’s office and county attorney staff have been closely monitoring the legal developments around the executive order, Schleiker said, and he anticipates no impact to his county’s administration of the November election. 
“Colorado voters should know that nothing has changed about their ability to vote in November,” Schleiker said in a statement. “Voters do not need to complete any new federal process, enroll with USPS, or take any additional steps. All existing Colorado verification, security, and audit procedures remain unchanged.”
El Paso County’s elections staff have conducted “internal scenario-planning” to determine how the order and the Postal Service rule would affect their ability to conduct elections if implemented. The biggest lift would be the rule’s requirement that election offices upload voter names, mailing addresses and envelope barcodes. 
“For a county our size, that verification step, repeated for every mailing batch, would be a significant operational consideration,” Schleiker said.
Denver Clerk Paul López agreed that the Supreme Court ruling had to do with the timing of the lower court decision and not the legality of Trump’s executive order, which he said is the “latest in a string of baseless claims” intended to undermine confidence in elections, instill fear and confuse voters. 
“I know when you see the headlines and you see people say, ‘Trump is getting closer to his mail in voting restrictions,’ that tends to freak people out, and you know what? That’s what it’s intended to do, is to try to put a chilling effect on people’s participation in an election,” López said. 
Colorado Secretary of State Jena Griswold and Denver Clerk and Recorder Paul López address members of the news media during a press conference at the Denver Elections Division on Super Tuesday in Denver, March 5, 2024. (Photo by Kevin Mohatt for Colorado Newsline)
Trump’s attacks on mail ballots are “absolutely hypocritical coming from a president who also votes by mail,” López said. Trump voted by mail in Florida’s GOP primary this year. 
Local election officials and other agencies in Denver always come together to consider what they need to prepare for going into an election, considering possible scenarios like a blizzard, a power outage, federal troops showing up at polls and problems with the Postal Service, López said. 
“I can tell you that this team that we run here in my office is more than ready. We’ve been ready. We’re the pros at this,” López said. 
Crane said he expects Trump’s executive order ultimately to be deemed unconstitutional. Election officials in Colorado are focused on preparing for the November election and mailing out ballots in the coming weeks. 
“The expectation that we can change all of these processes and procedures for this election, it’s just nuts to think that we can do that and not have it impact both people’s ability to access the ballot and our ability to secure the process,” Crane said. “Changes like this at the last minute will introduce opportunities for error, and so anybody concerned about election integrity would not want changes like this this close to the election.”
Colorado voters can request mail ballots for the November election from their county clerks starting Sept. 19. That’s also the last day clerks can mail ballots to military and overseas voters. Clerks can begin to mail ballots as early as Oct. 2. Election Day is Nov. 3.
