name: Source New Mexico
title: US Rep. Vasquez backs 2 federal data center bills as developments come under scrutiny in New Mexico
description: U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) on Tuesday announced he had co-sponsored two federal bills aimed at data center transparency.
text:
U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) on Aug. 25, 2026, announced he signed on as a co-sponsor to two federal bills aimed at placing guardrails around data center developments nationwide. (Courtesy photo)U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) on Tuesday announced he had co-sponsored two federal bills aimed at data center transparency.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Vasquez signed on as a co-sponsor to the FAIR Data Act, sponsored by Rep. Josh Riley (D-N.Y.), and the Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act of 2026, sponsored by Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-IL).
The FAIR Data Act would shield residential electric customers and small businesses from shouldering increased energy costs related to large data centers. The Data Center Water and Energy Transparency Act of 2026 would require developers to provide state and local governments that have data centers, or are considering them, with information pertaining to energy and water consumption. Companies that don’t comply would face fines of up to $20,000 per day.
“New Mexico’s water, air and resources belong to us, not to billionaires from coastal states who see an opportunity to extract profit from our land,” Vasquez said in a statement. “I’ve been appalled at the backroom deals, silencing of dissenting voices, shady NDAs and shell companies, and the overall lack of transparency from those who seek to do business in our state.”
Vasquez’s announcement came one day after his cCongressional colleague U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) sent a letter to several state agencies demanding detailed information about water usage for Project Jupiter, the Oracle and OpenAI data center under construction in southern New Mexico, which lies in the 2nd Congressional District Vasquez represents.
The only direct mention of Project Jupiter in Vasquez’s announcement was a reference to his July condemnation of a security guard’s use of physical force at a Doña Ana County meeting where residents protested against the development.
Earlier this year, Vasquez called on elected officials in a small New Mexico county to adopt a data center moratorium as a Canadian tech CEO sought to build a massive data center and solar array in their community.
Source NM reported that neither Green Data nor its CEO, Jason Bak, had ever successfully built a data center. Yet Bak’s company sought to build on 10,000 acres in partnership with New Mexico Tech, the local university.
County commissioners ultimately adopted the moratorium and New Mexico Tech nixed the deal, in large part because it didn’t have enough contiguous land to host the development.
“New Mexico should absolutely compete for the jobs and technology of the future, but we are not going to sell out our water, our clean air or our way of life to do it,” Vasquez said in his Tuesday statement. “If you want to do business here, you need to be transparent, listen to local residents, and most importantly, prove to New Mexicans that projects will serve, not steal from, our communities.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Brinks says Senate won’t vote on Money Out of Politics measure, leaving voters to decide
description: The Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot proposal seeking to bar political contributions from major utility companies and government contractors is headed for the November ballot, after Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) said the chamber will not take up a version of the proposal in the Legislature.  Under Michigan law, after a […[...]
text:
Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks, D-Grand Rapids, speaks to reporters at the Michigan Capitol in Lansing, Mich., after Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer's eighth and final State of the State address on Feb. 25, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)The Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot proposal seeking to bar political contributions from major utility companies and government contractors is headed for the November ballot, after Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) said the chamber will not take up a version of the proposal in the Legislature. 
Under Michigan law, after a referendum is approved for the ballot by the Board of State Canvassers, the Legislature has 40 days to take up and pass the measure or the proposal goes to the voters in the general election. 
“MMOP has successfully gathered more than half a million signatures and the message from Michiganders is clear: They want this on the ballot in November. Senate Democrats already agree that there is too much dark money in politics, and we are eager to hear what voters have to say on this issue,” Brinks told the Detroit Free Press on Tuesday. “In that spirit, we will not be subverting the will of the voters, taking it up legislatively.”
Brinks, who was recently named the running mate of Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson, made her statement shortly after a version of the proposal passed through the Republican-controlled Michigan House of Representatives with bipartisan support in the chamber. Votes in favor from the Democratic side included House Minority Leader Ranjeev Puri (D-Canton), while the only Republican to vote against the proposal was Rep. Jim DeSana (R-Carleton). 
House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) celebrated his chamber’s passage of the legislation, saying that they were trying to stop large corporations from “screwing the people” in campaign finance contributions. 
Hall said in a press conference Tuesday afternoon that the proposal for which the group gathered signatures was intended to put it before the Legislature.
“I’ve heard the argument that there’s an attempt to put this on the ballot. I would just say this: if that was the purpose, they could go and do a constitutional amendment,” Hall said. “And a constitutional amendment would go on the ballot. That’s not what we have here. What we have here is one of the processes that the purpose of this is to put it before the Legislature.” 
He was critical of Brinks’ intention not to vote on the legislation throughout the press conference, calling it a “mistake” not to bring the Senate into session to vote on the proposal. 
“I think we took a big step today, so my hope is that Winnie Brinks now will bring the Senate back and do their job and take a vote,” he said. “We can make it a guarantee, we can do it right now. This thing might not pass.”
House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Twp.) presents on proposed cuts within Michigan’s FY27 budget at a press conference. April 16, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.
However, throughout the process of gathering signatures, organizers for the proposal have focused their efforts on getting the proposal on the ballot for general election voters as opposed to passing it through the legislature. 
Michiganders for Money Out of Politics leaders celebrated Brinks’ decision not to take up the proposal, saying that Hall “should be ashamed of himself.”
“Leader Brinks gets it. Michiganders are fed up with out-of-control corporate political spending and are ready to change our political system this November. We thank her for respecting the will of over half of million voters who made it clear they want to vote on this measure in November, said Maura Cowley, campaign manager for Michiganders for Money Out of Politics. “Don’t be fooled – what we saw from Hall today was nothing more than political gamesmanship. He never had any intention of getting money out of politics. If he did, he wouldn’t have let common-sense, bipartisan policies to root out corruption in politics sit in committee time and time again.”  
Attempts by Republican lawmakers to adopt the legislation to keep it off the November ballot could have made it easier to amend or overturn later, Michigan Reps. Carrie Rheingans (D-Ann Arbor) and Betsy Coffia (D-Traverse City) told Planet Detroit prior to the vote in the House.
“The thousands of Michiganders who organized, collected signatures, and successfully qualified this initiative for the ballot deserve the opportunity to vote on it this November,” Rep. Emily Dievendorf (D-Lansing) posted on Facebook to explain why they voted against the proposal in the House. “The question before us today was not whether every legislator agrees with every provision. It was whether we trust Michigan voters to have their say.”
A vote in the Legislature was one of two final hurdles that the proposal faced before going to the voters in November, along with a lawsuit filed by Protect MI Free Speech, a group in opposition to the proposal. As of Aug. 20, no oral arguments had been scheduled on that lawsuit, according to Planet Detroit.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. gives schools a playbook for ICE at the door
authors: Colin A. Young I State House News Service
description: The governor's office shared new guidance for how Massachusetts schools and child care centers should handle federal immigration enforcement.
text:
AS SCHOOLS ACROSS MASSACHUSETTS prepare to welcome students back and adjust to new responsibilities under the state’s recent immigrant protection law, the governor’s office Tuesday shared new guidance for handling situations that involve immigration enforcement at schools and child care centers.
The state guidelines provide “clear steps to follow if ICE agents arrive on site or request access to a student, child or their information,” the administration said, and touches on considerations like designating staff points of contact, reviewing and responding to requests, involving legal counsel when appropriate, documenting interactions, notifying families and protecting confidential information.
The immigrant protection law that Gov. Maura Healey signed August 5 expanded protections against warrantless civil immigration arrests to courthouses, public schools, child care centers and health care facilities. It also required schools and state-funded or licensed child care programs to adopt policies governing interactions with civil law enforcement – and have them in effect by September 1 or the first day of the 2026–2027 school year, whichever is earlier. 
“As families prepare for the new school year, every child should feel safe walking into their classroom and every parent should feel confident dropping them off,” Healey said in a statement. “The PROTECT Act makes clear that schools and child care programs are places for children to learn and grow, not places for ICE to target families. These resources give educators and providers the clear guidance they need to put those protections into practice.”
The Department of Elementary and Secondary Education released model policies and procedures for school districts, charter schools and educational collaboratives on Tuesday. The administration’s suggestions “also provide procedures for alerting school communities when civil law enforcement agents are confirmed on school grounds while protecting individual privacy” and for updating student emergency contacts.
Policies and guidance for licensed and state-funded child care centers, family child care homes, school-aged child care programs and group care facilities came from the Department of Early Education and Care. EEC also partnered with the Massachusetts Office for Refugees and Immigrants to provide “Know Your Rights” training for the early education and care sector, including information about immigrant and refugee rights, available legal resources and interactions with immigration and law enforcement officers.
When Healey signed the law in Chelsea, the city’s manager said it offered relief to many in the community who have been afraid to go to work, school and other locations over fears of running into ICE agents. Chelsea has among the highest foreign-born populations in Massachusetts, with US Census numbers showing about 46 percent of the city’s residents are immigrants.
“We in the city have seen the cost of that fear: empty classroom seats, neighbors who have left the state, businesses that have shuttered, and trust broken between residents and our institutions that are meant to protect them,” Fidel Maltez, Chelsea’s city manager, said.
House Speaker Ron Mariano, a former teacher, said “dangerous and illegal actions taken by federal immigration agents have immigrants in Massachusetts living in fear as they go about their daily lives, including when they bring their children to school.” He said the new law and the guidance for schools “are about ensuring that the Commonwealth is doing everything it can to preserve schools as safe spaces for learning, rather than allowing them to become opportunities for warrantless harassment and detainment.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Absentee ballot requests begin in Iowa for Nov. 3 election
description: Iowans were able to begin requesting absentee ballots for the 2026 general election on Tuesday, even as the Trump administration continues to fight in court for changes in the process of voting by mail. Tuesday was officially 70 days before the Nov. 3 election, which means Iowans can begin submitting Absentee Ballot Request Forms to […]
text:
The Dallas County absentee and special precinct board met in Adel Tuesday, Nov. 12 to count absentee and provisional ballots submitted in the 2024 general election. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Iowans were able to begin requesting absentee ballots for the 2026 general election on Tuesday, even as the Trump administration continues to fight in court for changes in the process of voting by mail.
Tuesday was officially 70 days before the Nov. 3 election, which means Iowans can begin submitting Absentee Ballot Request Forms to their local county auditor’s office in order to receive a mailed absentee ballot for the election. The deadline for submitting an absentee ballot request form is 5 p.m. Oct. 19 — 15 days before the election.
The written application doesn’t need to be notarized or witnessed, but must include information that verifies the voter’s identity, such as a person’s Iowa driver’s license or non-operator ID number, or the PIN number on an Iowa Voter ID Card.
Iowa county auditors can begin mailing out absentee ballots Oct. 14. The ballots must be received by the county auditor by 8 p.m. on Nov. 3, Election Day, in order to be counted. If a person is not able to return their absentee ballot to their county auditor’s office on Election Day, there are still options to vote — voters can surrender their voted absentee ballot at a polling location and cast a regular ballot, or vote using a provisional ballot if they cannot surrender the absentee ballot.
The process of beginning absentee ballot requests comes in 2026 one day after the U.S. Supreme Court issued an unsigned emergency docket opinion finding 23 Democratic-led states do not have standing to stop his executive order related to mail-in ballot processing by the U.S. Postal Service.
Trump executive order still in court
Trump signed an executive order in March that directed the U.S. Department of Homeland Security and the Social Security Administration to compile a list of voting-age American citizens in each state and share it with state election officials. It also required the U.S. Postal Service to only send and receive ballots that include tracking barcodes.
Despite the Monday ruling, another U.S. District Court decision blocking the USPS from carrying out parts of the executive order in a case filed by the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts and several other voting rights groups, remains in place.
A spokesperson for Iowa Secretary of State’s office said in an email the state office overseeing elections expects “no direct impacts on Iowans as a result of this ruling.” Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate, a Republican, told reporters at the Iowa State Fair earlier in August he was opposed to the federal government’s recent approach to regulating mail-in ballots.
“Iowans really lean into being able to vote in the mail,” Pate said. “We have a very high percentage of that. We’ve done it right in the state. And I caution the White House and anybody who wants to listen to us in D.C. (to) come out and look at us in Iowa. I feel pretty good about how we do it here. So take a couple of pages from our playbook, and you’ll be maybe feel more comfortable. I understand where some of their frustration might come from, where some of their passion. But let’s not lose sight that — my humble opinion — the Constitution says elections are run by the states. And with all due respect to the president, I hope he’ll trust Iowans to run our elections.”

title: Montana Republican Party hires Debbie Churchill as new GOP executive director
description: Debbie Churchill has been selected as the next executive director for the Montana Republican Party. She replaces former party executive director Andrew Pierce, who held the position for about a year. Churchill is a fifth-generation Montanan from a ranching family south of Chinook. A graduate of the University of Montana school of law, Churchill is […]
text:
Montana GOP Headquarters in Helena, MT. Credit: Keith SchubertDebbie Churchill has been selected as the next executive director for the Montana Republican Party.
She replaces former party executive director Andrew Pierce, who held the position for about a year. Churchill is a fifth-generation Montanan from a ranching family south of Chinook. A graduate of the University of Montana school of law, Churchill is a retired real estate planning attorney.
She’s volunteered since 2019 for the state Republican Party and was the state party’s first Grassroots Director, a press release from the Montana Republicans said.
“This party isn’t built in Helena. It’s built in county central committee meetings and at kitchen tables from Chinook to Miles City,” Churchill said. “My job is to make sure every one of those Republican volunteers has what they need to win.”
She currently is also involved with the Jefferson County Republican Central Committee.
“Debbie has spent years building the MTGOP from the grassroots up, and she knows this party county by county,” Montana Republican Party Chairman Art Wittich said. “Her leadership, organizational experience, and commitment to Montana Republicans make her the right person to lead our staff into the general election.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Higher education in Louisiana, short $800M, appears headed for a funding overhaul
description: A legislative task force is staring at a growing problem with higher education in Louisiana: How to fund a system with more demands than ever before while state and federal dollars are on the decline.  Louisiana uses a outcomes-based formula to fund its colleges and universities. The bulk of the money provided, 70%, is considered […]
text:
Graduates stand at the end of University of Louisiana at Lafayette commencement exercises May 16, 2025, at the Cajun Dome. (Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)A legislative task force is staring at a growing problem with higher education in Louisiana: How to fund a system with more demands than ever before while state and federal dollars are on the decline. 
Louisiana uses a outcomes-based formula to fund its colleges and universities. The bulk of the money provided, 70%, is considered base funding to cover their operational expenses. The remaining 30% rewards schools for reaching benchmarks, such as student retention, and meeting state priorities like workforce needs. 
Questions about the formula were first raised earlier this year when some conservative lawmakers became aware of an old metric that incentivized universities to graduate already-enrolled minority students. Though it had already been removed from the formula, this metric became the topic of a U.S. Department of Education investigation. 
The task force, which held its first meeting Tuesday, comes together at a time when higher education financing in Louisiana faces myriad challenges. They include schools being asked to do more to promote workforce development as Louisiana launches a series of major industrial projects. 
Louisiana’s higher education funding problems are not new ones, although they have become more acute. During Gov. Bobby Jindal’s tenure from 2008-16, the state was in a self-inflicted fiscal crisis, with the governor choosing to use single-year budget surpluses to fund ongoing state government expenses. Higher education was on the chopping block annually to balance the budget, leading colleges and universities to switch from being primarily state-funded to student tuition-supported. 
Since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic, inflation has created additional constraints across state government. Gov. Jeff Landry has kept higher education spending at a standstill since he took office in 2024. 
Elizabeth Bentley-Smith, the Landry administration’s deputy commissioner of higher education for finance and administration, told the task force that Louisiana’s public colleges and universities are underfunded by more than $800 million. 
Increased costs for college athletics have been amplified over the past few years with the advent of revenue sharing and name, image and likeness payments. Schools are now diverting money from other items previously covered through philanthropy, such as facility upkeep, to keep their team rosters intact, university officials said. 
Louisiana’s college sports programs are losing money. Can sales taxes save them?

As a result, nearly every athletic department at Louisiana’s Division I schools operates at a deficit, adding additional budget pressure to their universities.
These factors, plus declining enrollment at several institutions, have created budget crises at schools, including the University of New Orleans (now LSU New Orleans) and the University of Louisiana at Lafayette. 
UNO faced a $30 million budget shortfall and implemented a spending freeze, layoffs and staff furloughs in an attempt to make ends meet. Due to the budget crunch, the school was transferred from the University of Louisiana System to the LSU System, with legislators approving more than $20 million to pay for the move.
UL Lafayette faced an approximately $50 million shortfall and implemented similar austerity measures. 
The problem is likely to compound moving forward, with college enrollment anticipated to fall and the federal policy landscape uncertain. 
Louisiana’s population is shrinking and its birth rate is declining. The state is projected to see a 7.5% to 15% decrease in students who attend college by 2029, the Public Affairs Research Council detailed three years ago in a report on falling enrollment in Louisiana. 
That’s a problem because Louisiana’s colleges and universities have become increasingly dependent on student tuition dollars. 
“This is a potential harbinger of things to come,” PAR President Steven Procopio told the task force. 
On top of the state-level problems, federal policy could also lead to challenges for higher education, two analysts from the State Higher Education Executive Officers Association told the panel. 
The Pell Grant program, which provides funding for low-income students to attend college, is already operating at a shortfall, which is projected to continually increase. Tom Harnisch, SHEEO’s vice president for government relations, said Congress either needs to provide more Pell funds, restrict who’s eligible or reduce award amounts. 
The latter two options would be a problem for Louisiana, where 42% of college students get the award compared with 32% nationwide. 
In addition, changes in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act reduced federal loan opportunities for graduate school students and could eliminate financial aid opportunities entirely for some programs if they fail the “do no harm” standard. It means graduates from those programs earn no more compared with those without that level of education. 
Higher Education Commissioner Kim Hunter Reed said the Board of Regents is examining these changes to estimate their impact to Louisiana’s college and university budgets. 
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act will also reduce Medicaid funding over the next 10 years, which will cut hard in Louisiana, one of four states facing the largest decreases. Historically, higher education has absorbed the brunt of major budget cuts in Louisiana. 
As these costs pile up, Kristine Strickland, chancellor of Fletcher Technical Community College in Terrebonne Parish, said so do the expectations. 
The governor has announced a series of major economic development projects throughout the state, each with their own specialized workforce needs. Many of these companies have made donations to the community colleges and universities that will train the students they intend to hire, but the brunt of funding these new programs falls on the schools themselves. 
“We’re being called upon more and more to be responsive in an immediate time frame,” Strickland said at the task force meeting. “We do know that standing up new programs is a more expensive venture than maintaining current programs, and then taking those to scale is even more expensive.” 
Sen. Mike Reese, R-Leesville, who chairs the task force, said it will meet at least three more times and hear budget presentations from campus leaders as well as state economic development and labor officials. 
Reese, who became McNeese State University president on July 1, said he wasn’t sure if the committee’s report, which must be submitted to the Legislature by February, would overhaul the state’s higher education formula or just recommend tweaks.

name: VTDigger
title: UVM president says school’s budget deficit is closed despite declining enrollment
description:
Just before the fall semester begins at the University of Vermont, President Marlene Tromp delivered a “State of the University” address. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  UVM president says school’s budget deficit is closed despite declining enrollment.
text:
University of Vermont President Marlene Tromp delivers her State of the University address in Burlington on Tuesday, August 25, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
BURLINGTON — The University of Vermont has closed its $12 million projected budget deficit, President Marlene Tromp reported just days before first-year students are set to arrive on campus. 
Tromp delivered the first “State of the University” address to trustees and hundreds of staff Tuesday with one resounding message: “We will not be daunted in the face of the challenges before us.” 
Her declaration of the university’s resiliency comes after the school warned in March that it projected a 15% decline in freshman undergraduate students this fall compared with last year and a 7% decrease across all undergraduate enrollment. 
In Tromp’s presentation, she reported that about 10,800 students are currently enrolled at the university this fall. And, as expected, freshman enrollment is down. 
Still, the university has been able to fully close its projected budget deficit by eliminating vacant staff positions and “operational inefficiencies,” Tromp said in an interview Tuesday. 

READ MORE

Along with declining enrollment, the university is facing a combination of “serious challenges,” including cuts to federal funding for research and a difficulty recruiting students from Vermont, Tromp said during her address. 
Colleges and universities across the country have long anticipated that enrollment would decline as they face a phenomenon dubbed the “demographic cliff.” Fewer people are projected to attend college in part because Americans started having fewer babies around the start of the Great Recession in late 2007. 
Universities, especially those in New England, have been hit the hardest, Tromp said, as they’re forced to compete for students. 
“We are building a three-year planning process so we can think ahead, and instead of being reactive, we can be proactive in the face of the changes that are before us,” Tromp said. 
About 2,600 first-year students are enrolled this fall, according to Adam White, a spokesperson for the university. UVM usually aims to enroll about 3,000, he said. 
Vermont has its own demographic struggles. With fewer young people in the state and a small overall population, there are limited ways that residents can support the university, which increases UVM’s tuition compared with other public universities, Tromp said. 
Amid sweeping cuts to federal grant funding for scientific research, Tromp said that UVM received $222.6 million in research funding for the 2026 fiscal year — an “extraordinary outcome” given the headwinds in the federal funding landscape. 
“Some universities were really struck hard by those cuts, and we were very fortunate that we didn’t face as many as a lot of other universities did,” Tromp said in the interview. 
In some cases, the university was able to provide short-term funds to keep research projects afloat while grants were paused, she said.
In her speech, Tromp highlighted one professor who lost grant funding for a project that sent graduate counseling and social work students to work in rural schools. After losing her national grant funding, the professor crowdsourced money to keep the project going.  
The university is also set to launch an aggressive fundraising campaign through the UVM Foundation, Tromp said, which raises money for the university’s endowment. 
“I’m really excited about it because that will help us weather a lot of storms,” she said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: One Kansan gets her driver’s license back as cases challenging anti-trans law head to trial
description: TOPEKA — One transgender Kansan had her driving privileges reinstated after challenging a state law that regulates gender markers on driver’s licenses. But only Jamie Miller’s license was returned while hundreds of other trans Kansans await a final decision in her case, which could determine the standing of the state law that has faced scrutiny […]
text:
Douglas County District Court Judge James McCabria talks with attorneys during a March 6, 2026, hearing on the Kansas law that restricts transgender individuals to using their biological sex at birth on documents and which bathrooms they use in government buildings. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — One transgender Kansan had her driving privileges reinstated after challenging a state law that regulates gender markers on driver’s licenses.
But only Jamie Miller’s license was returned while hundreds of other trans Kansans await a final decision in her case, which could determine the standing of the state law that has faced scrutiny from the jump for the restrictions it imposes on trans people.
Douglas County District Judge James McCabria issued on Aug. 17 a nine-page decision that set aside the Kansas Department of Revenue’s invalidation of Miller’s license earlier this year. The department oversees the state’s division of motor vehicles, which issues all driver’s licenses and was responsible for invalidating trans Kansans’ licenses after Republican lawmakers passed Senate Bill 244. 
The law instituted a pair of anti-trans measures, restricting bathroom use in publicly owned facilities and mandating driver’s licenses gender markers align with a person’s sex assigned at birth. Miller sued the state and Attorney General Kris Kobach in an attempt to block the driver’s license portion of the law from going into effect. McCabria denied that request in March.
The law codified in February the Kansas legislative majority’s anti-trans rhetoric, sparking protests and incurring multiple lawsuits.
McCabria’s recent decision didn’t answer whether Miller’s gender marker should reflect male or female.
“That is not the subject of this decision,” he wrote. “This decision is about the process, not the subject matter of the underlying dispute.”
Miller has had a driver’s license that reflects her gender since 2017. On Feb. 24, she received notice that her driver’s license would be invalidated in two days. The Revenue Department’s letter didn’t mention an option to appeal, but state statute allows for a monthlong appeal window.
The attorney general agreed to a grace period, delaying enforcement of the law until March 26. Miller received another letter on March 24 with information on the grace period and notification her license would be invalidated two days later. The deadline for an appeal moved to April 21. 
The Revenue Department sent yet another letter on April 7, notifying Miller her license was invalidated because she didn’t make any changes to her license. Miller called and emailed the department to request an appeal, which was met with a generic response. She sued on April 27.
McCabria concluded that the Revenue Department violated Miller’s due process when it provided unclear guidance about an appeal process and offered conflicting information about the validity of her driver’s license.
McCabria characterized the department’s notices as follows: “ ‘your license will be invalid in two days, you can appeal, no, wait, your license isn’t invalid yet, you can appeal, no, wait, your license has been invalidated because you didn’t do anything to appeal but if you want to appeal, call us.’ ”
The department didn’t provide “meaningful notice,” McCabria said, and Miller was never given a “meaningful opportunity” to be heard before or after her license was invalidated.
McCabria, in the same decision, consolidated Miller’s case with another challenging the same law, so they will be heard at the same trial, which is scheduled for four days beginning Sept. 29. The other case disputes both provisions of the law. 
In addition to the driver’s license restrictions, it challenges the constitutionality of the law’s bathroom ban, which bars people from using public restrooms that don’t align with their sex assigned at birth. Public institutions could face penalties for failing to ensure proper bathroom use, with fines beginning at $25,000 and escalating to $125,000 for subsequent offenses. The law’s supporters said it would make restrooms safer for cisgender women while critics say it accomplishes the exact opposite of what lawmakers seek. That’s because the law requires transgender men, who look and sound like men, to use the women’s bathroom, and vice versa.
Under the law, individuals may be fined $1,000 and charged with a misdemeanor for repeatedly using a bathroom in violation of the law. And an individual who feels “aggrieved” by a trans person’s bathroom use can pursue a private right of action for $1,000.
The case, which is also in Douglas County Court, involves two trans men who are arguing the law violates their rights to due process, privacy, equality and expression. McCabria denied a request for a temporary injunction in that case, allowing the law to remain in effect.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Nitrogen soil sampling project expands to Des Moines, Cedar Rapids watersheds
description: Farmers in the Greater Des Moines Watershed and parts of the Middle Cedar Watershed can participate in a free nitrogen soil sampling project that could help refine fertilizer application rates and contribute to water quality improvements. The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship announced Tuesday it had expanded the Nitrogen Soil Sampling Proj[...]
text:
Iowa farmers in 26 counties can participate in a free nitrogen soil sampling project. (Photo by Catherine Ulitsky/ USDA-NRCS )Farmers in the Greater Des Moines Watershed and parts of the Middle Cedar Watershed can participate in a free nitrogen soil sampling project that could help refine fertilizer application rates and contribute to water quality improvements.
The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship announced Tuesday it had expanded the Nitrogen Soil Sampling Project, with the Iowa Nutrient Research & Education Council, or INREC, to include all 22 counties in the Greater Des Moines Watershed and four counties in the Middle Cedar Watershed. 
Farmers who enroll in the program are expected to share information on nitrogen management, crop rotation, manure application, cover crop history and post-harvest information over the three-year program. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Data collected from the program, according to an IDALS news release, will be shared anonymously with Iowa State University researchers to help “refine” the Iowa Nitrogen Initiative N-Fact tool which helps farmers nail down nitrogen application rates. 
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said a soil sample represents a “snapshot in time.” The multi-year project is meant to “track patterns” to better understand how variability in weather and growing season conditions impacts residual soil nitrogen. 
“When the soil sampling data is coupled with the N-FACT tool, farmers can make more informed fertilizer management decisions to minimize costs while maintaining yields and delivering water quality benefits,” Naig said in the release. 
The program initially launched in April and “filled up quickly,” according to IDALS. The Tuesday announcement doubles the project capacity for fall, which INREC Executive Director Ben Gleason said is a “crucial window” for soil testing.
“Field data from this program helps farmers assess their nitrogen management and informs decisions when planning for next year’s crop is underway,” Gleason said in the news release. 
A more accurate measure of soil nitrogen helps farmers apply the right amount of fertilizer to their fields, which in turn helps to reduce the amount of excess nitrogen that runs off of the field and down a watershed. The targeted watersheds are upstream of the Des Moines and Cedar Rapids metro areas. 
According to the news release, the goal of the free program is to collect samples from 250 farm fields. Eligible counties include: Audubon, Benton, Black Hawk, Boone, Buena Vista, Calhoun, Carroll, Clay, Dallas, Dickinson, Emmet, Greene, Grundy, Guthrie, Hamilton, Hancock, Humboldt, Kossuth, Palo Alto, Pocahontas, Polk, Sac, Tama, Webster, Winnebago and Wright.
Farmers can enroll in the project online ahead of the fall soil sampling season.

title: Nebraska AG says Lincoln must forward charter amendments to Nov. 3 ballot if signature goals are met
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska attorney general has waded into a fight in Lincoln over three proposed city charter amendments, opining that if a measure has enough valid signatures, Lincolnites must be given a chance to weigh in this November. Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, in a nonbinding seven-page opinion Monday, said Lincoln officials have a “ministeria[...]
text:
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers. June 30, 2023. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska attorney general has waded into a fight in Lincoln over three proposed city charter amendments, opining that if a measure has enough valid signatures, Lincolnites must be given a chance to weigh in this November.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers, in a nonbinding seven-page opinion Monday, said Lincoln officials have a “ministerial duty” to certify otherwise compliant petitioned charter amendments for the ballot and have “no discretion” to implement efforts to exclude them. As an example: multiple rounds of meetings before a final vote to forward the issues to voters.
“While the City of Lincoln may be a home-rule charter city, this does not give city officials license to disobey a direct command of the State Constitution,” Hilgers wrote.
Lincoln City Attorney Yohance Christie during a hearing where the Nebraska Attorney General’s Office is challenging a Lincoln city ordinance enacted in response to a new state minimum wage law at the Lancaster County Courthouse on Thursday, July 2, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Kenneth Ferriera-Pool/Lincoln Journal Star)
The Nebraska Supreme Court has said Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen, who oversees statewide petitions, also has certain limits on his authority to reject or certify those issues.
Garret Swanson, a spokesperson for Lincoln, said City Attorney Yohance Christie will meet with city councilors over the next two days to discuss the steps to get an amendment on the ballot.
“After these meetings, City Attorney Christie will make an announcement,” Swanson said.
Good Government Lincoln campaign
Nebraska Constitution Article XI, Section 4, outlines how municipal voters can amend their city charters by petition. This includes signature requirements and a mandate that governing bodies submit qualified amendments at the next general or special election “not held within thirty days after such a petition is filed.” The 30-day buffer is the first weekend of October this year.
However, state law sets slightly different deadlines around certifying issues and the ballot itself.
The seven-member Lincoln City Council. Top row, from left, Sändra Washington, Justin P. Carlson, Tom Beckius and James Michael Bowers. Bottom row, from left, Tom Duden (vice chair), Brodey Weber (chair) and Bennie Shobe. (Photo courtesy of City of Lincoln)
A political subdivision must certify an issue for inclusion on the November ballot by Sept. 1, which is next Tuesday. Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen must certify the ballot by Sept. 11. Certified ballots must be sent to military and overseas voters no later than Sept. 18.
A spokesperson for Hilgers’ office declined to comment on a request to clarify the deadlines.
The Lincoln City Council meets on Mondays. That gives one more chance for officials to certify the issues to go before voters next week, assuming the Sept. 1 deadline.
At center are Good Government Lincoln and its three proposed amendments to the Lincoln City Charter. The issues would limit future Lincoln City Council members to two consecutive four-year terms, move the dates of city elections from odd years to even years and let certain residents within a 3-mile buffer around Lincoln city limits vote in municipal elections, excluding bonds.
‘City may slow-walk the certification’
State Sen. Beau Ballard of Lincoln requested Hilgers’ latest opinion. Ballard previously worked for Hilgers in the Legislature and assisted his 2022 campaign for attorney general. After that, Gov. Jim Pillen appointed Ballard to Hilgers’ Legislative District 21, beginning in January 2023.
Ballard also proposed a law to expand Lincoln election borders this spring. It did not pass.
State Sen. Beau Ballard of Lincoln, right, listens to State Sen. John Fredrickson of Omaha. April 7, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Ballard told the Nebraska Examiner in a text Tuesday that he hasn’t yet read Hilgers’ opinion but had requested it because of concerns that Lincoln officials might try to block the measures.
“The city may slow-walk the certification process and not give enough time for the amendments to get on the ballot,” Ballard wrote.
This isn’t the first time that Hilgers has been asked to weigh in on Lincoln action this year. State Sen. Jane Raybould, a Democrat and former Lincoln city councilor, and Ballard asked whether officials could impose a different minimum wage. Hilgers said they can’t. That issue is now in court.
‘Do the right thing’
Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird has been a chief opponent to the proposed amendments, and Lincoln City Council Chair Brodey Weber has also criticized the campaign. Both are Democrats. Weber ran against Hilgers for Legislature in 2020.
Lincoln City Councilman Brodey Weber during a news conference in Lincoln on Aug. 13, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Weber told the Examiner that a briefing by the city attorney is the appropriate next step when the state attorney general issues an advisory opinion regarding potential city council action.
As a city councilor, Weber described his role as working with Christie’s office and ensuring “we follow the right steps and we have an appropriate procedure.” He said what now appears as a “rushed process” is because of a lack of “basic safeguards” to prevent alleged fraud the first time petitioners gathered signatures.
“Just because they [Good Government Lincoln] did not handle this situation with the level of care that it required doesn’t mean that the city has to act in a similar fashion,” Weber said. “We are going to do the right thing, and we’re going to follow the process to make sure that we’re upholding the law.”
Campaign sponsors have said they were unaware of any alleged criminal activity and that they support investigation and prosecution of all actors, at every level, who may have been involved.
Ongoing fraud investigation
Good Government Lincoln turned in an initial batch of signatures July 20, but on Aug. 5, the Lancaster County Election Commission said no issue had enough valid signatures. More than 65% of signatures were rejected, a supermajority of those flagged as possibly fraudulent.
Each petition needs at least 4,981 valid signatures to qualify for the ballot.
Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen, left, gives Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen a tour of the Lancaster County Election Commission office on April 24, 2026. (Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Law enforcement arrested six out-of-state circulators and is searching for a seventh, the Lancaster County Sheriff’s Office said last week. The first defendant appeared in court Monday. The county fraud investigation has expanded to all statewide ballot measures, too.
Good Government Lincoln submitted more signatures Aug. 19. No valid signatures from before will count toward the campaign’s restarted valid signature count.
Axiom Strategies, a multistate consulting firm that some of the highest-ranking Republicans in Nebraska hire to run their campaigns, including Hilgers, is assisting Good Government Lincoln.
A spokesperson for Hilgers’ office told 10/11 News in Lincoln earlier this month that at the beginning of the investigation, the chief and chief deputy of the office’s criminal bureau “were given full decision-making authority and operational oversight over the Lincoln investigation.”
Signature verification
Lancaster County Election Commissioner Todd Wiltgen confirmed Monday that the city council term-limits measure has enough valid signatures. Of 8,082 petition lines reviewed, 5,628 signatures were valid. That’s a validity rate of 69.6%.
Petition pages reviewed by local county election officials and returned to the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office sit in the office for public inspection at the office’s Elections Division in downtown Lincoln on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
An additional 116 petition pages, which could contain as many as 2,320 signatures, were not reviewed. Verification ended early once the campaign exceeded 110% of its signature goal.
Wiltgen’s office is continuing signature verification for the measure to change municipal election dates and then the measure to expand municipal election boundaries.
In a statement Monday, former state Sen. Tony Fulton, a sponsor of the Lincoln petitions, said his group was “pleased” the first charter amendment has qualified for the ballot.
“Voters are excited for a say on these initiatives in November,” said Fulton, who was tax commissioner under former Gov. Pete Ricketts. “Thank you to the Lancaster County election commissioner for the quick work in verifying the signatures.”
The general election is Nov. 3.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee’s Dolly Parton dies at 80 after a life of music and giving
description: Dolly Parton, the personification of Tennessee music, died Tuesday at age 80 after decades of entertaining the world. Parton’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, delivered the news of her death in a video for the family, sparking mourning from her birthplace of Locust Ridge in the mountains of East Tennessee across the state to Nashville, where she […]
text:
Dolly Parton on stage in Nashville, Tennessee, on March 20, 2025, at the premiere of "Dolly Parton’s Threads: My Songs in Symphony." Hailing from East Tennessee, Parton’s songwriting, savvy, charm and philanthropy made her a beloved figure globally. (Photo by Jason Kempin/Getty Images)Dolly Parton, the personification of Tennessee music, died Tuesday at age 80 after decades of entertaining the world.
Parton’s nephew, Bryan Seaver, delivered the news of her death in a video for the family, sparking mourning from her birthplace of Locust Ridge in the mountains of East Tennessee across the state to Nashville, where she found fame, and around the world, where her name brought people happiness in her deeds and passion for life.
“Sadness lies with us, but not with Dolly. Dolly has lived in the light, and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by (husband) Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed for her to meet them in the heavens,” said Seaver, who led her security detail for a decade.
Parton opened doors for generations of singers and songwriters from all walks of life, giving people hope that “anything was possible,” Seaver said. “She never saw a door she couldn’t open, and the doors she opened made and changed history.”
The daughter of a sharecropper and farmer, Parton asked that she be buried in a field of cotton, he said, “because after a life wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest.”
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee called her “Tennessee’s favorite daughter” after learning of her death.
“Dolly Parton was one of a kind, who loved people, her work, her family, and her Lord. Tennessee has forever been changed — enhanced — by her, and will never be quite the same without Dolly,” Lee said in a statement.
Through her business network, Parton has an estimated net worth of $650 million and used her considerable wealth for philanthropic causes. 
“I’m kind of addicted to the feeling of giving,” she told People magazine in 2021, “knowing that I’m doing something good for someone else.”
The Dollywood Foundation created Dolly’s Imagination Library in 1995, which donates some 10 million books to children each year to bolster literacy.
“They call me the Book Lady,” she said in a 2006 interview with The Washington Post.
She started The Buddy Program in the 1990s, offering $500 to Sevier County middle school students to stay in school and graduate in Tennessee, eventually lowering the dropout rate. The foundation also offers $15,000 scholarships annually to five Sevier County High School seniors “who have a dream they wish to pursue and who can successfully communicate their plan and commitment to realize their dreams.”
Parton raised $12.5 million to help the victims of a 2016 wildfire in the Great Smoky Mountains National Park that devastated cities such as Gatlinburg and $1 million in response to Hurricane Helene in the East Tennessee mountains. She also gave $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center during the COVID-19 pandemic to support development of the Moderna vaccine and filmed herself receiving a shot to encourage people to get vaccinated.
Parton received the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy in 2022 for years of charitable work, which included putting together a team to help her support favorite causes, such as the Imagination Library.
Early this year, officials renamed the East Tennessee Children’s Hospital in her honor after she made a donation described as “generational and transformational.”
Dolly Parton performs in 1974, about a year after she wrote her smash hit songs “Jolene” and “I Will Always Love You.” Her time in the spotlight spanned over six decades. (Photo by Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)
The fourth of 12 children, the country music icon debuted on the Grand Ole Opry at age 13 after growing up singing in church. 
She moved to Nashville and broke in with Porter Wagoner on his show in the 1960s, then went out on her own and recorded hits such as “Joshua,” “Jolene,” “I Will Always Love You,” “Here You Come Again,” “9 to 5,” and “Islands in the Stream.” Her songwriting skills and unmistakable voice enabled her to win 10 Grammys and earn a place in the Country Music Hall of Fame in 1999.
Parton starred in movies such as “9 to 5,” “The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas” and “Steel Magnolias” before opening Dollywood theme park in Sevierville, which led to the creation of a network of theme parks.
Early in her career, Parton’s appearance caught people’s attention, but she also displayed a business acumen that led her to an RCA contract and the decision to protect the publishing rights to her song catalogue, allowing her to collect millions of dollars in royalties over the years.
Parton opened Dollywood in 1986, saying in her biography, “I always thought that if I made it big or got successful at what I had started out to do, I wanted to come back to my part of the country and do something great, something that would bring a lot of jobs into this area.”
The Dollywood Company has multiple parks, including Dollywood’s Splash Country, Dolly Parton’s Stampede, the Dream More Resort and Spa, and her 50% share of the company was believed to be worth $165 million, Forbes reported in 2021.
In addition to the Country Music Hall of Fame, Parton was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2001 and the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, an honor she turned down at first because she didn’t think she “earned that right” but then relented after finding out that musicians outside the rock genre received the recognition.
Parton was a member of the Grand Ole Opry for more than half a century and Time magazine named her to its list of 100 most influential people five years ago.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania AG Dave Sunday is suing another social media platform alleging harm to kids
description: Sunday’s lawsuit against Snap details claims the company used deceptive tactics to build a user base for Snapchat of tens of thousands of teenagers.
text:
Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday speaks at a news conference Tuesday, August 25, 2026, where he announced a lawsuit against the social media company Snap Inc. alleging its Snapchat app is harmful for children. (Screenshot/Commonwealth Media Services)Announcing a lawsuit alleging Snapchat’s 13+ age rating misleads parents and that the platform is designed to be addictive, Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday called on the social media company to take steps to protect young users. 
Fresh off an announcement earlier this month that his office is suing TikTok over claimed violations of the commonwealth’s consumer protection laws, Sunday said the action against Snap Inc. seeks honesty in how it markets its product.
“This lawsuit and our previous actions are not about taking on the role of parents,” Sunday said in a news conference Tuesday. “It’s about empowering parents with the tools … to make decisions for their children. If apps are misleading parents about how those very apps work, how can they make sound decisions for their children?”
Snap said in a statement the lawsuit’s allegations fundamentally misrepresent the platform and the company’s approach to teen safety.
“We share the attorney general’s commitment to protecting young people online and are disappointed they have chosen litigation rather than working with us toward that shared goal,” the California-based company said. 
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The company noted the Snapchat app was designed differently than other social media platforms by focusing on “self-expression and authentic connection with friends.” The first thing users see is their device’s camera, not a feed of other people’s content.
It notes that it has continued to improve and add to its safety tools, including deeper insights for parents into how their teens use Snapchat. It also released a refreshed version of its Family Safety Hub, with an interactive safety program for teens.
The Snapchat suit, filed in the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas, comes as a coalition of state attorneys general, including Sunday, pursue claims in a California court against Facebook and Instagram’s parent company Meta. 
In what’s expected to be a multi-week trial that started last week, the states claim Meta used harmful features to cultivate compulsive use of its apps by children and teens while advertising they are safe for young users.
Sunday’s lawsuit against Snap details claims the company used similar deceptive tactics to build a user base of tens of thousands of teenagers. It seeks a judgment in favor of the commonwealth against Snap, a declaratory judgment that the company violated the state’s Unfair Trade Practices and Consumer Protection Law, monetary penalties and court costs and fees.
It alleges Snap knowingly downplayed the amount of adult material depicting drug use, suicidal ideation, sexual content and other mature themes that appear on the platform.
Snapchat’s AI Assistant feature is pictured on Monday, June 30, 2025. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)
And it claims that once young people start using Snapchat, the app itself fosters compulsive use by rewarding frequent users and penalizing those who take breaks or use it infrequently. Sunday noted the app includes a “streak feature” with a flame signifying the number of consecutive days that a user has sent messages or images to a friend. 
“If you take a day off, that fire goes out, and to a teenager, that is not good,” he said, adding that it plays on adolescents’ insecurities about friendships and acceptance. “We allege this streak feature puts a tangible value on friendships and influences a child’s feelings of self-worth.” 
Snapchat’s secret weapon, Sunday said, is the fleeting nature of posts on the app. When a user sends a message or an image, it disappears after it has been viewed or after a day. 
“This ephemeral component is extremely alluring and can lead to compulsive use. Yet it’s Snapchat’s biggest draw for youth. The result: about half of Americans’ teens use Snapchat every single day,” he said.
The disappearing posts may also lure some teens into a false sense of security, leading them to post things they might not typically share on social media, such as a revealing selfie.
“We all know that once something is sent or posted on the internet, it is never truly gone. But do our kids know that? And if they do, can they fully grasp the ramifications of that?” Sunday asked, adding, “A simple screenshot can turn what they thought was a temporary photo into a permanent nightmare.”
Sunday said the suit alleges that the sense of security for young Snapchat users emboldens online predators to be more aggressive in contacting and grooming children. 
“I can’t think of anything more concerning than predators having access to kids in arenas where they feel even more free to act deviantly,” he said, adding that it could also encourage cyber bullies, knowing that their abusive posts will disappear.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Sen. Tracy Pennycuick (R-Montgomery), who chairs the Senate Communications and Technology Committee, joined Sunday and said tech companies need to be held accountable when they mislead families. 
“Parents should not have to reverse engineer an algorithm to understand what a company is putting in front of their children,” she said.
Pennycuick introduced a resolution passed in the Senate to create a Task Force on Child Protection in the Digital Age. The group, chaired by Sunday, is charged with reviewing the state’s existing statutes, assessing emerging technologies and identifying gaps in the law that could expose children to harm.
She noted the General Assembly created a similar task force to review and recommend updates to the commonwealth’s laws on child pornography. It resulted in the passage of laws criminalizing sexual deepfakes and AI-generated child sexual abuse material and classifying malicious deepfakes as forgeries.
Earlier this year, Sunday’s office pursued charges against two Lancaster County teens, who admitted they used artificial intelligence to create fake nude images of classmates at Lancaster Country Day School.
“I sat across from victims whose images had been manipulated … where we saw the real harm that can be done,” Pennycuick said, adding, “Innovation does not come with a license to exploit children … Technology moves really fast, but Pennsylvania is going to move faster.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: ACLU asks Bellmawr to investigate citations given to protesters
description: The ACLU of New Jersey says Bellmawr police may be improperly giving citations to protesters in violation of the First Amendment.
text:
The ACLU of New Jersey says Bellmawr police may be improperly giving citations to protesters in violation of the First Amendment. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The state branch of the American Civil Liberties Union on Tuesday asked Bellmawr to investigate whether its police officers were improperly issuing citations to punish political expression at roadside protests in the Camden County town.
In the letter, Rebecca Uwakwe, the group’s criminal law reform advocacy director, said the organization had been contacted by members of South Jersey progressive group Cooper River Indivisible who said they had been issued criminal or traffic citations during antifascism rallies on Sundays in Bellmawr.
“If Bellmawr officers are targeting participants and supporters of lawful protests with citations, Bellmawr is interfering with their constitutionally protected activities and violating their civil rights,” Uwakwe said in the letter.
Officers had issued citations to protesters for jaywalking, honking, and other offenses, Uwakwe wrote, adding the government could only impose content-neutral restrictions on speech in public forums like sidewalks. Those protections generally bar penalties for political expression.
It’s not clear how many protesters or passersby were cited by Bellmawr Police.
The ACLU was still conducting interviews and is not representing every person issued a citation, Uwakwe said, but citations were issued to attendees of multiple protests occurring on different days.
“We really want to bring it to their attention in hopes that this stops,” she told the New Jersey Monitor, adding, “We’re looking forward to a response. We’re looking forward to a discussion. We want people to feel protected as they exercise their First Amendment rights.”
Cooper River Indivisible’s weekend protests generally draw a crowd of between 20 and 30 people, Uwakwe said.
Guidance issued by the New Jersey attorney general instructs police to avoid enforcing every violation when dealing with conduct protected by the First Amendment unless the officer has no other way of maintaining public safety, guarding themselves, or protecting property.
As its single example, that section of the 2021 guidance lists “obstructing a sidewalk” as a violation that might not be enforced if doing so would implicate First Amendment rights.
The circumstances of the citations are unclear. The ACLU-NJ did not immediately respond to a request for further comment, nor did Cooper River Indivisible.
An employee of the Bellmawr Police Department on Tuesday afternoon relayed that its chief, Keith Williams, had not yet seen the letter. The department did not immediately return an emailed request for comment.

name: VTDigger
title: As Trump tries to curtail mail-in voting, Vermont officials clean up errors on state voter rolls
description:
Nearly 900 people who did not want to be registered to vote were on the state’s list to receive mail-in ballots until this week, officials said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  As Trump tries to curtail mail-in voting, Vermont officials clean up errors on state voter rolls.
text:
Gov. Phil Scott and Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas announce that 900 people who were wrongly registered to vote have been cut from Vermont’s voter rolls on Tuesday. Photo by Shaun Robinson/VTDigger

MONTPELIER — Vermont officials have removed just shy of 900 people from the state’s voter rolls who they said were wrongly registered to vote due to human error at the state Department of Motor Vehicles.
None of those 900 people actually cast a ballot and the state wrongly registered them at various points over the past 25 years, Gov. Phil Scott and Secretary of State Sarah Copeland Hanzas said at a press conference Tuesday. Some of those people were likely ineligible to vote, possibly because they aren’t U.S. citizens; Copeland Hanzas said she could not provide a breakdown of how many were eligible voters. 
The announcement came a day after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling put fresh focus on President Donald Trump’s attempts to curtail mail-in voting nationwide ahead of this fall’s midterm elections. In Vermont, everyone who is registered to vote — which until Monday included those 900 people — gets mailed a ballot for general elections. 
The justices overturned a lower court ruling that blocked an executive order Trump signed in March attempting to create federally-managed lists of eligible voters and order the U.S. Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to people who are on those lists. 
Monday’s ruling did not decide whether Trump’s order is legal, only finding that the states who challenged it, which include Vermont, lacked the legal right to do so. The order hasn’t taken effect and additional hurdles remain that could make it challenging to implement.
Scott and Copeland Hanzas said they wanted to be upfront about the state’s error to show they’re trying to make Vermont’s voter rolls as accurate as possible before the state mails out general election ballots next month. Both of them said they were strong supporters of voting by mail and criticized the White House’s efforts to undermine the practice.  
Scott, a Republican, also called the Supreme Court’s ruling “misguided.” 
“The federal government has no business encroaching on the states on how we administer free and fair elections,” he said. “Mail-in ballots work well in Vermont, and I remain committed to defending our system from federal overreach.”
How did the error happen?
The error stemmed from the process by which voter registration data is shared between the DMV and the Secretary of State’s Office. Under a 2016 state law, eligible voters who use a DMV service — such as renewing their driver’s license — are automatically registered to vote unless they tell the DMV they do not want to be registered. 
Before that, people could still register to vote at the DMV but they had to opt-in, rather than opt-out.
The 900 people in question chose not to get registered, prior to the 2016 law or after the process became automatic. But DMV staff sent their information to the Secretary of State to register them, anyway, said Andrew Collier, the department’s commissioner. Copeland Hanzas, a Democrat, said most of the errors occurred over the course of several years after the law took effect. Some happened even more recently when the DMV transferred data into a new information technology system.
Far more people have elected not to be registered to vote at the DMV over the past 25 years, Copeland Hanzas said. She estimated 20,000 had declined to do so since the process became automatic. But of all those people, officials found only about 900 who never made an effort to register to vote elsewhere, such as by visiting their local clerk’s office. The goal, Copeland Hanzas told reporters, was to purge names of people who had shown no desire to register at any point.
State officials used an artificial intelligence tool to help determine which people to remove, Denise Reilly-Hughes, secretary of the state Agency of Digital Services, said at the press conference. 
The error was first brought to the Secretary of State’s attention last winter by “a regular Vermonter” who said they were registered to vote despite intending not to be. Copeland Hanzas’ office did not immediately take action based on the complaint.
But an announcement last month by officials in New Jersey that thousands of non-citizens there were wrongly registered to vote because of a software glitch in the state Motor Vehicle Commission’s voter registration system prompted Copeland Hanzas to take a deeper look, she said. Vermont does not use the same system as New Jersey, she said.
“When the New Jersey news hit, I said, ‘Now is the time,’” she told reporters. “I wanted to be sure that we could say with a straight face that we did everything we could.”
Collier said Vermont’s DMV has since taken steps to prevent data from being shared incorrectly between the two agencies in the future. The department bolstered its quality checks and increased the amount of training its staff receives, he said. 
“This is not a one-time fix,” Collier told reporters. “We will continue monitoring, auditing and improving to ensure voter intent is respected — and the data we transmit is reliable.”
