name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: No issues reported as DOJ conducts monitoring of GOP Senate runoff in Charleston County
description: Two teams of federal election observers are in Charleston County for routine monitoring of the special GOP primary runoff for U.S. Senate.
text:
Voting machines set up in 2023 in Charleston County. (File photo provided by Charleston County Board of Voter Registration and Elections)Two teams of federal election observers came to Charleston County as part of routine monitoring of polling places amid the special Republican primary runoff for U.S. Senate.
Charleston County election officials reported no polling place issues as of Tuesday afternoon in the runoff between U.S. Sen. Darline Graham and U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham as the GOP nominee.
It is unclear why Charleston was the only county selected for observation out of the state’s 46 counties, especially given the heavier concentration of Republican voters in the Upstate and Grand Strand.
In the June primaries, when Lindsey Graham was on the GOP ballot for re-election, more Democrats than Republicans participated in Charleston County: About 29,700 people voted in the GOP primary, compared to 36,500 people who voted a Democratic ballot, according to results from the state Election Commission.
Two weeks ago, Charleston County ranked fifth in the number of people voting in the 10-candidate GOP primary. Greenville County topped the list, followed by Horry, Lexington, and Spartanburg counties, according to state election data.
This is the second time in two election cycles the county has had federal observers. The last time was in November 2024 under the Biden administration.
Isaac Cramer, executive director of the Charleston County Board of Voter Registration and Elections, said federal officials assured the county its selection was not because of any wrongdoing.
“South Carolina is the next stop in our ongoing effort to ensure election transparency,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon of the U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division said in a statement.
The state Election Commission said it is the purview of the DOJ to decide when and where it wants to send observers. The agency is not aware of any requests from state officials for the DOJ to observe polling places.
“It’s a fairly common occurrence for us, and we welcome them as observers,” spokesman Chris Whitmire said.
The two teams of observers consist of a total of four DOJ attorneys, one assistant U.S. attorney from the South Carolina district office and one other South Carolina U.S. Attorney’s Office employee, according to the DOJ.
Some of the polling places the observers stopped by included the Hazel Parker Playground, the International Longshoremen’s Association building, the North Charleston Sports Complex, the Arthur W. Christopher Community Center, Morris Brown AME Church, Joseph Floyd Manor, and Harborview Elementary School, according to the county election office.
“Observers are a routine and well‑established part of the election process,” a statement from the county Board of Voter Registration and Elections reads. “They must follow specific rules while at any of our polling locations. Our election workers receive training on poll watchers and observers, so they understand the conduct guidelines outlined in state law and are prepared to manage these visits appropriately.”
According to the state Election Commission handbook, observers must stay within a designated area inside each polling location. They can’t take pictures or video, touch equipment, view confidential voter information, speak to voters inside the polling place, or tell a poll manager how to conduct an election.
The Department of Justice also recently conducted similar visits in other states, including Florida and Wyoming.
“Thus far the DOJ has deployed over 80 monitors across seven states and over 200 polling locations this primary season,” according to a statement by the federal agency. “By comparison, during the 2022 midterms the DOJ sent monitors to nine states during the primary season.”
Dhillon, the head of the DOJ Civil Rights Division, recently told Bloomberg News the agency plans to deploy 1,000 observers across the country for the midterm elections.
By comparison, during the Biden administration, the DOJ sent monitors to 86 cities and counties in 27 states for the 2024 presidential election and 64 cities and counties in 24 states, including Horry County in South Carolina, for the 2022 midterm elections.
During President Donald Trump’s first term, the department sent monitors to 44 cities and counties in 18 states, including Richland County in South Carolina, for the 2020 presidential election, according to news releases at the time.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Group behind whites-only community sues Arkansas, federal agencies
description: The founders of a whites-only community in northeast Arkansas have filed a lawsuit against several state and federal agencies claiming their constitutional rights are being violated by investigations into the housing development. Return to the Land, a white nationalist organization that describes itself as a “private membership association” promoting “Europe[...]
text:
People attend an afternoon rally against racism on February 2, 2019 in Atlanta, Georgia. Alt-right and white supremacist groups had planned to hold a rally at Stone Mountain, a park celebrating confederate history, but backed out after officials closed the park with a heavy police presence. Atlanta is hosting Super Bowl LII between the Los Angeles Rams and New England Patriots on Sunday. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)The founders of a whites-only community in northeast Arkansas have filed a lawsuit against several state and federal agencies claiming their constitutional rights are being violated by investigations into the housing development.
Return to the Land, a white nationalist organization that describes itself as a “private membership association” promoting “European heritage communities” and “traditional views,” filed the lawsuit in federal court in Arkansas on Friday. 
A company affiliated with the group owns 160 acres of land near Ravenden for a housing settlement that’s only open to whites, Christians and heterosexuals.
The community has been widely criticized by elected officials in Arkansas and Missouri, and its planned development received international attention last year. It’s also the subject of a federal discrimination lawsuit filed earlier this year.
The group’s lawsuit accuses several agencies, including the U.S. Justice Department and Arkansas’ attorney general, of retaliation by opening investigations into the community.
“Whether through explicit coordination or convergent animus, the defendants have engaged in a campaign to punish the plaintiffs for their protected speech and association through the mechanism of government investigation itself,” the lawsuit said.
Jeff LeMaster, spokesperson for Attorney General Tim Griffin’s office, said the lawsuit’s claims “are meritless.”
“We look forward to demonstrating that in court,” he said.
The Justice Department and the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, which is also a defendant in the suit, did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday morning.
Plaintiffs in the case include Eric Orwoll and Peter Csere, co-founders of Return to the Land. The lawsuit claims the group is being unfairly targeted because its membership criteria includes European heritage.
“The government would not subject a Black, Hispanic, Jewish or Muslim intentional community to the same multi-agency campaign,” the lawsuit said. 
Missouri resident Michelle Walker filed a federal lawsuit in May accusing Return to the Land of violating housing and civil rights laws by rejecting her application. Walker’s application included questions about her ancestry and religion, according to her complaint.
Walker is a white Christian woman who has Jewish ancestry, a Black husband and biracial children, according to the complaint. The Return to the Land online application portal deemed Walker’s family “not an ideal fit” for the organization.
The land for the Arkansas development is owned by Wisdom Woods, a limited liability company that was formed by Return to the Land members and is also a plaintiff in the lawsuit filed Friday.
Return to the Land this month asked a judge to dismiss Walker’s lawsuit, arguing she didn’t have standing. Walker’s application to Return to the Land membership was rejected but she hadn’t made an offer to buy land, the group’s filing said.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Ballard unveils prototype for state-issued, precinct-level voter guides
description: Independent Secretary of State candidate Greg Ballard on Tuesday released a prototype of what he called the first state-sponsored voter's guide personalized down to the precinct level.
text:
Greg Ballard, an independent candidate for secretary of state, shows reporters a demo of a personalized voter guide he said the state would send to every registered voter were he elected to office, on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026 at the Indiana Statehouse. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Lincoln Party Secretary of State candidate Greg Ballard on Tuesday debuted a prototype of what he called the first state-sponsored voter’s guide personalized down to the precinct level. 
“No Hoosier should ever walk into the voting booth feeling unprepared to cast their ballot, and no one should stay home because they didn’t have time to learn who or what would be on that ballot,” said Ballard, a former Republican mayor of Indianapolis.
“When I’m secretary of state, that won’t happen,” he said during a news conference at the Statehouse. “Each registered voter would receive a printed voter’s guide mailed to their home for each general election, with customized information for all of the races on their ballot.”
Ballard’s campaign, under the nascent Lincoln Party banner, has created a unique four-candidate race for the office that oversees statewide election and voting policies.
The voter’s guide would include a sample ballot, candidate information, ballot questions or constitutional amendment guidance, polling locations, calendar reminders for early voting or Election Day and more, according to Ballard.
The prototype, available on his campaign website, uses data from his own precinct in Boone County.
A stack of prototypes for a personalized voter guide proposed by Greg Ballard on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026 at the Indiana Statehouse. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)
Ballard assured reporters that the guide would be nonpartisan, with brief descriptions of each elected office’s responsibilities and blurbs submitted by candidates themselves. Those would be limited to 150 words and could not include attacks on other candidates.
Voters would also be able to use an app with similar functionalities.
Ballard said his team had completed a “very detailed cost analysis” showing the voter guides would cost an estimated $2.5 million to $3 million.
That’s “a penny for every $100 the state spends,” he said. “It’s also about six, seven, eight days of interest that the state makes on a daily basis. So, you give me six, seven, eight days, it pays for this also.”
Ballard would seek to create and mail the voter guides within the office’s existing budget, but said an additional appropriation “would be helpful.”
“This is going to be given to you,” he said of the voter’s guide. “… You don’t have to go find it. It’ll be pushed out to you. That’s a big change.”
His election opponents, however, panned the plan.
“Greg Ballard is making promises the Secretary of State doesn’t have the budget or authority to keep,” Republican candidate Max Engling’s campaign said. “There is no funding for his proposed voter guide, and instead of partnering with nonprofits already doing this work across the country, Ballard wants to grow state government and stick taxpayers with the bill.”
Democrat Beau Bayh’s campaign manager, Jack Tormoehlen, said Bayh “believes providing information about voting to Hoosiers is important and plans to do just that” — but that “the millions of dollars of taxpayer resources required to mail a 32-page booklet, that many people will discard upon receiving, can be better spent elsewhere.”
Libertarian Lauri Shillings noted the cost as well as technology-based shifts in constituent habits.
IndianaVoters.IN.gov already hosts “most of this information,” she said, and “could easily be updated to provide more information on each candidate, if those candidates wish to submit it.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Louisiana lets ankle monitor companies off the hook for accountability
description: Louisiana fixed the corruption it could identify within court ankle monitoring programs but left the supervision problem exactly where it found it — in the shadows.
text:
Stock photo by Darren Klimek/Getty ImagesAshtin Ursin was already a convicted felon and already facing a second-degree murder accusation when Baton Rouge Police arrested him Jan. 25, 2025, on charges including possession of a firearm by a convicted felon, handling of machine guns, unlawful use of body armor and possession with intent to distribute. 
He posted $45,700 bail and walked out three days later, WBRZ-TV reported. 
On July 30, 2025, Ursin was arrested again on new gun and drug charges. The judge revoked his bond from the arrest earlier in the year. But earlier this year, a judge let him out. Ursin posted $180,100, was released from jail Feb. 20 and placed on house arrest with an ankle monitor.
During the bond review on March 31, the court changed Ursin’s 24-hour house arrest to a curfew starting at 8 p.m., allowing exceptions for medical visits, court appearances, church and a recording studio. 
Ursin, a rapper, performs as MMY ASH. He is set to stand trial for the 2023 shooting death of Jasper Dorsey Jr. in Ascension Parish.  
Between Feb. 20 and April 29 this year, according to a motion from East Baton Rouge District Attorney Hillar Moore, GPS reports from Home Bound Monitoring, the company paid to watch him, show Ursin violated his release conditions between 967 and 1,181 times, according to WBRZ. His unapproved itinerary included a trip to Houston with roughly 92 stops and visits to TopGolf and a casino. At one point, his ankle monitor clocked a vehicle he was in traveling at 119 mph, WAFB-TV reported. 
Home Bound Monitoring did not report any of this. It later submitted a report stating Ursin was not in violation because he had communicated with their office. According to WBRZ, text messages Ursin posted publicly appear to show an Home Bound Monitoring employee approving his requests to leave. One referenced a “full day of partying,” while another told him he was on 24-hour house arrest but simply needed to “communicate.” 
Prosecutors say the exceptions the Home Bound claimed were never part of the bond conditions set in court, and that the company provided incomplete or disputed responses to several items in a court-ordered subpoena, including its communications with Ursin.
On April 28, an investigator from the DA’s office requested Ursin’s location report, The Advocate reported. A Home Bound employee texted Ursin that same day, telling him to stay put. 
Which employee okayed trips that no judge approved? Does that person still work there? No one has had to answer because no one has been made to ask.
Home Bound has not responded to questions from journalists.
Prosecutors moved May 4 to revoke Ursin’s bond. By then, federal authorities had already taken him into custody. 
Ask yourself an honest question: What about Ursin’s prior record suggests that he would comply with a stay-at-home order? The prosecutor who witnessed the violations had no power to end them. The judge with that power did not use it. The company holding the data had no reason to hand it over.
Louisiana has seen where this ends. 
In West Feliciana Parish, Marshall Rayburn breached the exclusion zone around his estranged wife’s home five times in four days, triggering notifications to American Electronic Monitoring, WAFB reported. The company never alerted law enforcement. On Sept. 20, 2021, Rayburn killed Peggy Beasley Rayburn, shot a neighbor who ran toward the screaming and then killed himself. 
American Electronic Monitoring and its employees “have blood on their hands,” District Attorney Sam D’Aquilla said. A grand jury indicted the company owner and an employee with negligent homicide, but the case still has not gone to trial four years later.
In New Orleans, Court Watch NOLA found that Judge Paul Bonin sent defendants to one company, ETOH Monitoring, in 23 cases in a single year. One of ETOH’s principals is a former law partner of Bonin who contributed more than $9,000 to his campaigns, according to the Institute for Justice.
The Louisiana Legislature responded to this incident. Act 746, effective January 2025, bars any judge, sheriff or district attorney from holding a financial interest in a monitoring vendor and requires home confinement violations be reported within one day.
Ursin’s monitor was installed after the law took effect, and no one has alleged a conflict of interest in his case. 
Act 746 fixed the corruption it could identify and left the supervision problem exactly where it found it — in the shadows.
“Electronic monitoring can provide significant cost advantages over incarceration when it actually substitutes for a custodial prison place,” said Abiodun Raufu, a Southern University criminal justice professor. 
Raufu points to England and Wales, where the National Audit Office reported monitoring costs of roughly £9 per person ($12) per day compared with about £142 ($194) for a prison space, though he notes the £9 figure excludes probation and police supervision. However, he cautions against reading anything into those findings too quickly. Unlike England’s centralized system, American programs run across federal, state and local jurisdictions, and many push the cost onto the monitored themselves.
Moore, the East Baton Rouge DA, said it best.
“These monitors are the next best option to jail as long as someone is watching the monitor,” he told WAFB.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Dolly Parton, music star, actor and beloved figure who spanned generations, has died at 80
description: Dolly Parton performs at a United Way of America convention in Detroit, Friday, May 15, 2009.
text:
Dolly Parton, the country music icon whose soaring vibrato vocals, poignant songwriting and sparkling costumes defined her rise from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to the height of stardom and acclaim, has died. She was 80 years old.
Parton died peacefully Tuesday in Nashville, Tennessee, her publicist said in a statement.
Known for her curvy physique, massive blonde wigs and skin-tight outfits that served her self-deprecating wit, she was among the most beloved personalities in music and beyond — the rare celebrity whose appeal transcended generations, geography and politics.
She wrote hundreds of songs, including classics like “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors” and “I Will Always Love You,” that totaled more than 100 million worldwide sales and more than 1 billion online streams. Parton, who plucked bejeweled banjos, guitar and dulcimers with her long fingernails during performances, was a generous philanthropist and successful businesswoman whose projects included a theme park in the Smoky Mountain foothills near her birthplace.
Dolly Parton appears at Dollywood’s Season Passholder and Media Day in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., March 8, 2024.  Credit: AP Photo/Amy Harris
Her career was forever influenced by her upbringing as one of 12 children born into what she called a “dirt poor” Tennessee family. She started her education nonprofit, Imagination Library, to send free books to children in Tennessee because her father, who quit school to work on the farm, struggled to learn to read.
Parton’s first musical performances were in church, where her grandfather was a preacher. By age 10, she was learning guitar and singing on local television shows. At 13, she appeared on the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, where Johnny Cash introduced her as “a little girl here from up in East Tennessee.”
With a suitcase of songs, she followed her uncle, Bill Owens, also a songwriter, to Nashville after graduating high school in 1964. Fred Foster, who produced Roy Orbison, Willie Nelson and more, saw her potential and got her songs cut by other artists, as well as recording and releasing Parton singing her own material. By the mid-1970s, Parton was a Nashville queen.
A key collaboration with Porter Wagoner
Parton’s partnership with Porter Wagoner, a pencil-thin pompadoured star with flashy rhinestone outfits, was key to her career. She honed her acting skills on his syndicated TV show and he advocated for her to get a record deal at RCA. Their first duet, “The Last Thing On My Mind,” was released in 1967, the same year she started her own publishing company.
While their duets were often big radio hits, Parton’s solo singles didn’t chart as high at first. With Wagoner as a co-producer, she began to adjust her country warble to a more polished, pop-leaning style.
She got her first No. 1 solo single with “Joshua,” and reached the Top 5 with the ballad “Coat of Many Colors,” about how her mother sewed together scraps of clothes to make a coat Parton wore “so proudly” even as her peers mocked her for being poor. The song, with its Biblical references and ode to maternal love, was later made into a children’s book and a TV movie.
Dolly Parton appears at Dollywood’s Season Passholder and Media Day in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., March 8, 2024.  Credit: AP Photo/Amy Harris
In 1973, she had the hit that made her career — “Jolene,” a country music standard with its steady, churning rhythm and Parton’s repeated delivery of the title as she pleads for the woman not to steal her man.
The song topped the country charts, crossing over to pop and later being released internationally, opening up new audiences for Parton. “Jolene” is one of her most covered compositions, including by Miley Cyrus (Parton’s goddaughter), Olivia Newton-John and The White Stripes.
She left Wagoner’s show in 1974, amid reports of squabbling between the two, although they continued to record together and Wagoner stayed her producer for years after that. But the relationship turned litigious when Wagoner sued her in 1979 for millions in management fees and royalties.
A pop crossover star
She followed “Jolene” with a huge hit in 1974, “I Will Always Love You,” an ode and farewell to Wagoner that helped her win the Country Music Association’s female vocalist of the year back-to-back in 1975 and 1976. She famously turned down Elvis Presley, who wanted to record it, because she would not share publishing rights.
Decades later, Whitney Houston’s version of “I Will Always Love You” became a smash for the soundtrack of her 1992 film “The Bodyguard,” and broke sales records. Houston won a Grammy for her performance in 1994, presented to her by Parton.
“Here You Come Again,” a pop crossover hit and one of the few she didn’t write, further established Parton as a multi-genre entertainer and brought her first Grammy Award in 1979.
“A lot of people thought I had totally lost my mind,” she told The Associated Press in 1979 of changing her singing style. “But I had no fear of change. I expected success, but I was braced for failure. I didn’t care if people thought I was wrong. In my own heart, I knew I was doing the right thing.”
Dolly Parton, left, Lily Tomlin, center, and Jan Fonda arrive for the premiere of their film “9 To 5” in New York on Dec. 14, 1980.  Credit: AP Photo/Richard Drew
Parton’s other crossover hits included the title song from “9 to 5,” the 1980 comedy starring Parton, Jane Fonda and Lily Tomlin; and her duet with longtime friend Kenny Rogers, “Islands in the Stream,” written by brothers Barry, Maurice and Robin Gibb of the Bee Gees. In 1987, she collaborated with Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris on the million-selling “Trio” album.
Down home charm
For millions of fans, she was simply “Dolly,” a mixture of Southern charm, humor and glamour. But she was also considered a feminist role model for holding the reins of her own career, writing her own songs, owning her content and looking after her finances in an entertainment world dominated by men.
Parton was open to making fun of herself; when she hosted “Saturday Night Live” in 1989 she told the writers that her only restrictions were she wouldn’t curse and she wouldn’t make fun of Jesus. She regularly joked about her breasts or her dumb blonde appearance, but with a wink that she was the one controlling the laughs. In the memoir “My Life So Far,” Fonda remembered Parton’s way with a wisecrack, “usually high raunch,” and a laugh that was “somewhere between a girl’s giggle, an explosive shriek, and a cascade of little bells.”
Dolly Parton reads her book “Coat of Many Colors,” at the Library of Congress in Washington on Feb. 27, 2018. Credit: AP Photo/Andrew Harnik
After her gown split down the front when she won CMA’s entertainer of the year in 1978, Parton quipped: “My Daddy said that’s what I got for putting 50 pounds of mud in a five-pound bag.”
Throughout her career, she embraced her glamorous style, often wearing custom curve-hugging rhinestone dresses and bodysuits even if they drew tsk-tsks from others in the industry. Her look was always a part of her larger musical business plan.
“I knew my songs were good even if I had been ugly as sin,” she told the AP in 2014. “So I thought, ‘Well, I would have probably chose to look this way even if I had been a waitress.’ I mean, this is my look. I mean, I like a lot of makeup. I like a lot of hair. I like flashy clothes. I like to show it off. But that’s just who I am.”
She married Carl Dean, an asphalt paving contractor, in the mid-1960s; they were together until his death in 2025 at the age of 82. Though rarely seen in public, he was an influence on her career. She told NPR that she wrote “Jolene” about a flirty bank teller who seemed to take an interest in Dean.
‘9 to 5’ to Hollywood and Broadway
In her first major film role, Parton played alongside Fonda and Tomlin as office workers who rebel against their tyrannical boss in “9 to 5.” Critic Roger Ebert called her a “natural-born movie star” and the title song earned her two Grammy Awards and a ranking of 78 on the American Film Institute’s list of top 100 movie songs. Starring roles in the “The Best Little Whorehouse In Texas” and “Steel Magnolias” followed.
“I never thought of myself as a movie star,” she told AP’s Bob Thomas in 1979. “I knew I’d be a star, but as a singer or as a writer of songs or books or poetry. I wanted to be a famous performer and wear flashy clothes, but singing in movies was not one of my ambitions. My family lived in the mountains and we didn’t see movies.”
Her love affair with TV and film continued for decades, with appearances alongside Cyrus on “Hannah Montana” and adaptions of her music for Christmas specials, films and streaming series. She also became an author, her books ranging from the memoir “Dolly” to a bestselling novel co-authored by James Patterson, “Run, Rose, Run,”
The stage adaptation “9 to 5: The Musical” debuted in 2009, and “DOLLY: A True Original Musical” had been set to open in December 2026.
United States of Dolly
Beyond her music, Parton’s most lasting legacy might be her generosity and broad appeal.
When a deadly wildfire swept through the Smokies in 2016, she held an all-star telethon and set up a foundation that sent monthly checks to residents whose homes were damaged or destroyed.
Dolly Parton poses at the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy Ceremony in New York, on Oct. 13, 2022.  Credit: AP Photo/Andres Kudacki
She opened up her Dollywood theme park in East Tennessee, a major economic driver in Appalachia that draws tourists from around the country, and established the Dollywood Foundation. She wrote books and memoirs, was inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame and was given a lifetime achievement award by the Recording Academy. She was selected for the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award from the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences in 2025.
With 55 Grammy nominations and 10 wins, Parton is the third-most nominated woman in Grammy history, only behind Beyoncé and Taylor Swift.
Parton spanned social and political divides, through multiple generations of fans, urban and rural and in between. In tumultuous election years, it wasn’t uncommon to see “Dolly for President” shirts. But she was strict in not voicing her own political beliefs, often turning aside questions about presidents, candidates, policies and other controversies.
“I don’t do politics,” Parton told host Jad Abumrad on his hit podcast “Dolly Parton’s America.”
“I have too many fans on both sides of the fence. Of course, I have my opinion about everything, but I learned years ago to keep your mouth shut about things.”
When the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Foundation sent out a ballot in 2022 with her name on it, though she said she felt she hadn’t earned it, the voters answered with a “Hello, Dolly.” Parton showed up to the induction ceremony, performed and then put out a rock album.
___
Associated Press writer Hillel Italie contributed.

name: Michigan Advance
title: El-Sayed, Moss stress opposition to Rogers amid dispute over Piker comments
description: U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, speaking at a “Hate Has No Home in Michigan” event at a Dearborn church Tuesday, would not say whether he wants state Sen. Jeremy Moss’ endorsement amid concerns about Jewish support for El-Sayed’s Senate campaign and backlash over controversial statements from an El-Sayed ally about the possibility of violence against [[...]
text:
Left to right front: Abdul El-Sayed, Democratic U.S. Senate nominee; Halim Shukair, Christ Episcopal & Mother of the Savior Church in Dearborn and Sayed Saleh Qazwini, Imam of the Muslim Educational Community Center of America in Canton. Left to right back: Abbas Alawieh, Democratic nominee for Michigan's 2nd Senate District; Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud and Democratic attorney general nominee Eli Savit, at a "Hate Has No Home in Michigan" event at Christ Episcopal & Mother of the Savior Church in Dearborn to address “the recent rise in hateful rhetoric targeting Michigan communities," on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance)U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, speaking at a “Hate Has No Home in Michigan” event at a Dearborn church Tuesday, would not say whether he wants state Sen. Jeremy Moss’ endorsement amid concerns about Jewish support for El-Sayed’s Senate campaign and backlash over controversial statements from an El-Sayed ally about the possibility of violence against members of the Jewish community who vocally support Israel.
“I’m not going to sugarcoat that we have our disagreements, especially when it comes to foreign policy and the best use of our tax dollars, and the plurality of Michigan Democratic Primary voters nominated me to be the Democratic nominee,” El-Sayed said when asked by Michigan Advance whether he wanted Moss’ endorsement.
El-Sayed’s statement came after Moss, the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 11th Congressional District, condemned comments made by El-Sayed ally and Twitch streamer Hasan Piker about the possibility of violence against Jews who vocally support Israel. Piker campaigned with El-Sayed in Michigan and was present at his primary victory party.
During an Aug. 20 stream, while showing an image of Moss, Piker said “If pro-Israel Jews keep putting this idea out there that they’re singularly invested in Israel, eventually somebody’s going to come around and take action, not against the State of Israel but against American Jews.”
Abdul El-Sayed, Democratic U.S. Senate nominee, speaks at a “Hate Has No Home in Michigan” event at Christ Episcopal & Mother of the Savior Church in Dearborn to address “the recent rise in hateful rhetoric targeting Michigan communities,” on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance)
In a statement on X, Moss said that Jews “won’t be gaslit that we’re responsible for the antisemitic harm upon us. The attempted murder of Jewish children in West Bloomfield has no justification,” referencing the March 12, 2026 attack at Temple Israel in West Bloomfield Township. 
The attack was carried out by a Lebanese-born U.S. citizen of Dearborn Heights who authorities say was “motivated and inspired” by the Hezbollah terrorist group’s militant ideology and followed ongoing military strikes on Lebanon by Israel.
While Moss has not endorsed El-Sayed, he has also not criticized him directly as has U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten (D-Grand Rapids), who told POLITICO she would not, “campaign with someone who continues to associate with Hasan Piker,” noting that El-Sayed “had a prime opportunity to cut ties with Piker and directly disavow his words, but he did not. There is a lot of work left to do to unite the party.”
Former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-White Lake), the GOP candidate for U.S. Senate, has also used El-Sayed’s connection to Piker as political fodder — even calling him El-Sayed’s “running mate” at the state Republican Party’s nominating convention on Saturday. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a Tuesday statement about Piker’s comments regarding Moss, El-Sayed said “I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without the fear of violence … But I want to be crystal clear, nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.”
Tuesday’s event was held at Christ Episcopal & Mother of the Savior Church in Dearborn to address “the recent rise in hateful rhetoric targeting Michigan communities,” including a Christian nationalist rally held in Dearborn last week, organized in part by a member of Rogers’ Faith Coalition Leadership Team. Following the rally, flyers promoting recruitment for the Ku Klux Klan were also found on residential streets in nearby Dearborn Heights and Melvindale.
El-Sayed was joined by several fellow Democrats, including Lt. Gov. Garlin Gilchrist, the Democratic nominee for secretary of state, and Washtenaw County Prosecutor Eli Savit, the Democratic nominee for attorney general, as well as Christian, Muslim and Jewish faith leaders. Speakers not only condemned hateful actions but also emphasized the community’s strength.
Abdul El-Sayed, Democratic U.S. Senate nominee (left) and Abbas Alawieh, Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 2nd Senate District (left), at a “Hate Has No Home in Michigan” event at Christ Episcopal & Mother of the Savior Church in Dearborn to address “the recent rise in hateful rhetoric targeting Michigan communities,” on Aug. 25, 2026. (Photo by Tyler Scott/Michigan Advance)
“This is also the place where the assembly line was built.  Where people came together despite differences, building a thing together. That is the best metaphor for America. People coming together to build a thing together,” El-Sayed said.
El-Sayed also said that while he and Moss will continue their dialogue on the issue of U.S. policy toward Israel, they are aligned in wanting to make sure that Rogers doesn’t win in November.
“I think all of us agree that the things that divide us are so much smaller than the things that unite us against somebody like Mike Rogers,” El-Sayed said. “Don’t forget that Mike Rogers questioned the outcome of his 2024 election against a Jewish American Senate candidate, and now-U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin. Don’t forget that Donald Trump, the chief surrogate for Mike Rogers, wined and dined Nick Fuentes. Don’t forget that we deserve union rights and guaranteed healthcare and opportunity for schools. Those are all things that Jeremy and I agree on.”
That viewpoint was also reflected by Moss in the statement he posted on X.
“As a Democrat and a believer in our Constitution, I will never agree with Mike Rogers’ dangerous election denial, backing of ICE’s cruelty, and obedience to Donald Trump and his future court picks that will erode our rights. Let me be clear: I’m not supporting Rogers,” Moss said.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: FBI arrests Ohio man on charges of threatening to kill Rep. Fine, his family
description: A 26-year-old Ohio man was in custody after threatening to kill U.S. Rep. Randy Fine and his family, according to the congressman and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. The FBI determined there was probable cause to arrest Alex Miller of Columbus after investigators tracked his identity to an email address that sent a message with […]
text:
Sen. Randy Fine talks to reporters at the Capitol on Jan. 28, 2025, during a special session on immigration. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)A 26-year-old Ohio man was in custody after threatening to kill U.S. Rep. Randy Fine and his family, according to the congressman and the Federal Bureau of Investigation.
The FBI determined there was probable cause to arrest Alex Miller of Columbus after investigators tracked his identity to an email address that sent a message with a threat involving “hanging” Fine’s head “from the rooftops of the White House.”
Miller’s alleged threats, spelled out in the FBI complaint, were made last week, on primary election day, with the email subject line, “Can’t wait to snipe your head off your shoulders!! :)”
“I unfortunately have learned what the difference is between a nasty message and a death threat, and this clearly was a death threat,” Fine told Fox News, adding that he does not know Miller’s motive or anything about him.
According to Fine, this is the fourth person arrested for making death threats to him in the past 10 years.
“If they think this will make me afraid, they are wrong. There is no place in our political system for this. And those who make these threats — whether to a Republican or Democrat — will go to prison for a very long time,” Fine posted on social media Tuesday.
The FBI, Brevard County Sheriff’s Office, U.S. Capitol Police, and U.S. Secret Service investigated the threats, according to Fine’s press release.
The maximum possible sentence for Miller would be five years, according to the arrest announcement.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Eastern Kentucky group urges Rep. Rogers to support bill boosting black lung benefits
description: A Kentucky group representing miners with black lung is urging U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers to support a bill significantly boosting the federal disability benefits these miners receive.  In a Tuesday letter, the Black Lung Association of Southeastern Kentucky to Rogers urged him to sign on as a co-sponsor of the Support Our Miners Act, a bill […]
text:
X-rays of a patient with black lung disease. (National Archives at College Park photo)A Kentucky group representing miners with black lung is urging U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers to support a bill significantly boosting the federal disability benefits these miners receive. 
In a Tuesday letter, the Black Lung Association of Southeastern Kentucky to Rogers urged him to sign on as a co-sponsor of the Support Our Miners Act, a bill introduced by Democrats in Congress earlier this summer that seeks to increase monthly black lung disability benefits back to the same funding level, relative to inflation, as miners received in 1969. 
The association wrote the monthly benefits miners receive has eroded over several decades of inflation, and the amount of benefits haven’t kept up with the cost of living to pay for gas, groceries and utilities. 
“We need something done, we have to help our miners and the widows. We need you to recognize that coal miners need your help now and are asking for your support,” the group wrote. “Disabled coal miners need this raise to help ease the constraints of the difficult positions they face daily while living with this disease.”
The association also referenced how in recent years “miners have been forced to leave the mines at younger ages due to more severe forms of the disease caused by exposure to silica dust.” Earlier this month, Public Health Watch, Kentucky Public Radio and NPR reported that the rate of black lung disease among veteran underground coal miners in Central Appalachia is at its highest level in nearly 50 years, driven by exposure to toxic silica dust. 
A spokesperson for Rogers did not immediately provide a response to an emailed request for comment Tuesday afternoon, telling the Lantern that Rogers and staff were traveling to events in Eastern Kentucky. 
An analysis from the Letcher County-based nonprofit Appalachian Citizens’ Law Center and the nonprofit Appalachian Voices found that the benefits received, as of 2023, are 30% less compared to what recipients were receiving in 1969. 
The Kentucky Lantern reported in July that increasing black lung disability benefits has bipartisan support among local elected officials in Kentucky, but such consensus in Congress hasn’t yet emerged. Republicans in Congress have previously expressed concerns over increasing benefits from the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund amid worries about the fund’s solvency. 
The trust fund pays out benefits when a responsible coal operator isn’t identified in a black lung case or the identified operator doesn’t pay. The fund receives revenue from a tax on mined coal and has taken on hundreds of millions of dollars of benefit liabilities because of coal mine bankruptcies, coinciding with the significant decline of the state’s coal mining industry.  
In an emailed statement last month, Rogers, 88, told the Lantern the trust fund needs “significant reform to ensure that our coal miners get their hard-earned benefits before this painful disease robs them from seeing a dime.” 
The association wrote it also cares about the trust fund’s solvency but that “the fund’s debt is a legacy of decades past when the benefits being paid were higher than the revenues.” 
“That is no longer the case and we ask that you not allow historic issues to act as a barrier to helping us today,” the association wrote. “Representative Rogers, we are just trying to survive. There is nothing more noble than taking care of the miners that built this country.”
This story may be updated.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Private sales among Indigenous homeowners could reduce tribal housing shortage, advocate says
description: An advocate for tribal homeownership told state lawmakers this week that establishing a private market on tribal lands could help address the long reservation waitlist for homes.
text:
Christopher Billey, executive director of the Tribal Homeownership Coalition of the Southwest, told lawmakers on Aug. 24, 2026, that enabling private sales between tribal members could help Indigenous governments reduce tribal housing shortages. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)An advocate for tribal homeownership told state lawmakers this week that establishing a private market on tribal lands could help address the long reservation waitlist for homes.
Tribal-run housing authorities oversee most of the housing stock on tribal lands. But approximately 10% of tribal housing stock belongs to individuals or families, according to Christopher Billey, executive director of the Tribal Homeownership Coalition of the Southwest.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Those homeowners largely do not realize that their homes are assets that grow in value and often sell them for less than they are worth, or even abandon them.
That’s because of a “missing link” for private sales on tribal lands, Billey told state lawmakers on the state Legislature’s Mortgage Finance Authority Oversight Committee during a Monday meeting. 
“Then we see the houses boarded up,” he said. “There’s no clear cut process for this.”
Meanwhile, waitlists for tribal housing continue to grow.
Billey said Monday that a survey his organization conducted over the last two years of more than 300 tribal members in Arizona and New Mexico shows that growing demand exists among Indigenous working professionals and others willing to pay fair-market rates. Nearly three-quarters of them said they want to buy homes in their tribal communities, he said. 
Billey’s organization, which began as a subsidiary of the New Mexico Mortgage Finance Authority, is working with homeowners, as well as tribal governments and local and state agencies, to establish a housing market similar to the one that exists off the reservation. 
That means helping tribal homeowners acquire clear titles to their properties and navigate other legal hurdles. He pointed to a case study his organization conducted regarding a home on the Navajo Nation in Lechee, Arizona, that owners wanted to sell after the Navajo Generating Station closed. 
That house would have sold, informally, for roughly $30,000, but Billey’s organization helped homeowners list Arizona’s Multiple Listing Service, which enabled it to be advertised on sites like Zillow or Realtor.com. 
In response, multiple Navajo prospective homebuyers —  a “park ranger, teachers, working professionals, and returning college students” — inquired about buying the home. Ultimately, in January of 2025, the home sold for $170,000 to a business owner, and county and state officials recorded the sale, providing a data point for comparable sales analyses in the area going forward. 
About two months ago, Billey’s organization helped facilitate a similar sale on the Jemez Pueblo in New Mexico, marking what he said is the state’s first-ever, market-rate sale outside of a housing authority between tribal members.
Officials from Jemez Pueblo did not immediately respond to Source NM’s request for comment Tuesday about the transaction.
He said he hopes the transaction will spur the creation of a housing market and spur related economic growth from housing-related industries like construction, inspections and licensing. 
Billey told Source NM after the meeting that creating a private housing market on tribal land also represents a “double-edged sword,” offering both the benefits and drawbacks of a housing market that suffers booms and busts and speculation. 
But tribal sovereignty means governments have an opportunity to design markets that reflect their values, he said, and take into account the failures of the housing market outside of tribal lands. 
“It cuts both ways, right? We have seen a number of folks who have been taken advantage of, but at the same time, we’re also trying to notify the tribal legislators and the tribal executives , saying, “Hey, this is already happening at this level. Can we create policies and regulations that helped protect buyers, sellers, and homeowners?”

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont could save Brattleboro’s birthing center — if it does the math
description:
New Hampshire saved rural maternity care with a Medicaid multiplier. Vermont should at least run the numbers.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont could save Brattleboro’s birthing center — if it does the math.
text:
This commentary is by Lucas Farrell, a farmer and writer in Townshend. He is the treasurer of the board of Grace Cottage Family Health and Hospital. These views are his own.
Defenders of Brattleboro Memorial Hospital’s birthing center need to say this out loud, because our case is worthless without it: The hospital’s finances were catastrophically mismanaged, and the community deserves to be angry.
The record is in BMH’s own filings: nine years of losses — $33.6 million since 2017 — plus bond default, provider-tax arrears, reserves drained for payroll. Its own audit found “all internal and external reporting was unhelpful and inaccurate in most cases.” The audit that finally measured it quadrupled the known shortfall.
I’m a neighboring hospital board’s treasurer, with no patience for excusing this and no interest in rescues rewarding it. The physicians now leading BMH sat on that board through those years; to their credit, they stepped into the vacuum, named the failures and spent 10 months cleaning up. The cleanup is real; the record is still the record.
But a birthing center will close Dec. 31 on a logical error: “They mismanaged” and “the state shouldn’t pay” run together as if one followed from the other. It doesn’t.
Mismanagement explains BMH’s larger hole, but not why the birthing center loses money. Small obstetric units have brutal economics, even when competently run: They’re staffed around the clock whether one baby comes or five. Medicaid covers roughly 40% of BMH’s births and, leaders testified, hasn’t raised rates in five or six years, “and it was woefully inadequate then.” BMH sees perhaps $500,000 in improvements; a $4.5 million annual subsidy remains. Asked about negotiating higher rates, its consultant called extracting $20,000 more per birth from insurers “an insane negotiation.” 
Brattleboro isn’t alone. Northwestern Medical Center in St. Albans stabilized its birth center’s staffing; it remains the largest money-loser, at $3.25 million a year. An obstetrician who helped save it put it plainly: “If Medicaid doesn’t come up on their obstetrical fees, I don’t exactly know how this is going to work.”

READ MORE

New Hampshire answered her: When maternity care reached this cliff in the north country, it amended its Medicaid rules. Coos County hospitals are paid for labor and delivery “as a separate peer group at an enhanced rate,” a 300% multiplier, for one federally approved reason: access. A category, a multiplier — and that county’s last delivery room is open today.
Vermont needn’t copy the number, but it can do something less controversial: Run it. Show us what 200%, 250% and 300% multipliers do. Publish the payment, the remaining deficit and the state’s share.
Vermont would also receive more federal help paying for this than New Hampshire did. The federal government covers 57.76% of Vermont’s Medicaid costs next year, compared with just 50% for New Hampshire — so for every extra dollar Vermont spent raising reimbursement rates, Washington would cover about 58 cents of it. Maybe the state runs the numbers, and the cost still doesn’t pencil out. Fine — then say so, and show the math. But right now, nobody has.
At its budget hearing, BMH told regulators $3.8 million would carry the service for one more year; enough time, leaders said, for Vermont to fix reimbursement. The bridge has a price; the multiplier is its far side.
BMH is right about a second problem: workforce. The hospital has just one employed obstetrician and no pediatricians on staff. Leaders testified that a single gap in coverage can force the hospital to divert patients elsewhere. Money cannot deliver a baby, but finances and workforce are not separate problems. Compare the recruiting pitches: a service the hospital says it may close, or one Vermont has designated as essential infrastructure, durably reimbursed; these are different jobs to recruit for. A service everyone expects to die becomes hard to staff; the staffing trouble becomes the evidence it must die. Vermont must not mistake a death spiral for a diagnosis.
This doesn’t mean signing a blank check. Tie the payment to obligations, maintain the service, rebuild coverage and report transparently. If, after a real attempt, BMH truly can’t, the service should outlive the service line. Act 19 licenses freestanding birth centers starting in 2027. The natural place to prove that model is the region losing its only delivery room. Make the $3.8 million a bridge to reformed rates if BMH can carry the unit, or to a licensed successor if it cannot.
Closure has costs that Vermont has barely counted. A birth decides where a family’s healthcare lives; deliver in Keene, New Hampshire, or Greenfield, Massachusetts, and pediatrics, imaging and years of care follow. BMH acknowledged that ending obstetrics will cut its ultrasound, operating room and lab volume. We still pay for the births; closing a delivery room changes where the check goes. Leaders conceded they lack confirmation that Medicaid patients could deliver at Baystate without prior authorization. We are eliminating the service before finishing the replacement plan.
Asked why maternity wasn’t its “hill to die on,” BMH answered honestly: “Our hill to die on is keeping the hospital open and solvent.” Fair enough. The state’s hill is different: deciding whether rural maternity access is infrastructure worth paying for, instead of having strained hospitals subsidize it until they can’t. New Hampshire decided.
Hold everyone implicated by the record accountable. But don’t confuse accountability with abandonment. The question isn’t whether Vermont can make rural obstetrics profitable; it’s whether Vermont will price keeping it available. Before we close the door, run the numbers.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont could save Brattleboro’s birthing center — if it does the math.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: New court filings reveal more details of undercover agents’ surveillance of anti-ICE protesters
description: A court filing Tuesday morning in the federal case against 15 anti-ICE protesters contained more than 200 pages of undercover agents’ notes and photos from the Department of Homeland Security’s widespread surveillance operation during Operation Metro Surge.  The documents reveal new information about groups and events targeted by the agents — and contain doz[...]
text:
Alec Stewart, one of the 15 people federally indicted for conspiracy to impede or injure federal officers, speaks during a press conference condemning federal surveillance Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)A court filing Tuesday morning in the federal case against 15 anti-ICE protesters contained more than 200 pages of undercover agents’ notes and photos from the Department of Homeland Security’s widespread surveillance operation during Operation Metro Surge. 
The documents reveal new information about groups and events targeted by the agents — and contain dozens of photos of cars of people who trailed immigration agents in their cars.
The exhibits were submitted to the court by attorney Kevin Riach, who is defending Isaac Sant, one of the 15 Minnesotans charged with conspiracy to assault or impede federal agents. All 15 pleaded not guilty to the charges.
The documents further underscore the feds’ use of intelligence tactics — including the use of undercover agents and electronic surveillance — as a frustrated Trump administration sought to tamp down the widespread resistance to the immigration crackdown, which wound up ensnaring many legal residents and led to the killings of two Americans. 
Riach previously submitted another batch of undercover agents’ reports and other surveillance-related documents — including administrative subpoenas for unions’ financial records — in a motion requesting that the judge order DHS to release even more information on the surveillance campaign. 
A hearing on that motion is scheduled for Thursday. (The federal government asked U.S. District Judge David Schultz to postpone the hearing until next week, citing staffing shortages. Schultz denied that request on Monday.)
The new documents describe the efforts agents undertook to identify the individuals behind the websites defend612.com and melttheicemn.com, the website for an event in February that convened hundreds of activists from around the country to learn from members about the Minnesota anti-ICE movement. Agents subpoenaed the websites’ registrars and payment processors to confirm the identities of the website creators. 
Agents also used a “chat capturing software” to record the contents of Signal group chats, according to an undercover agents’ report, though the software isn’t named.
The new documents also contain dozens of photos of cars with redacted license plate numbers, presumably of cars that followed ICE — known as “patrollers” — and attendees at meetings of anti-ICE organizations. Previously-released internal DHS documents described undercover agents noting the license plate numbers of cars in the parking lots of such meetings, including at churches. 
Some of the photos capture daily life in the Twin Cities during the federal operation: anti-ICE graffiti on stop signs and buildings; posters of Renee Good and Alex Pretti with the message “MURDERED BY ICE”; a person in a “FCK ICE” button writing “chinga la migra” in chalk on a sidewalk; a table with pizza and coffee outside of the Whipple Federal Building.
There are several photos of mourners gathered at Alex Pretti’s memorial site. 
Prosecutors have said they have 20 terabytes of data in their possession, though not all of it is directly related to the defendants in the conspiracy case.
“I’m inferring that not every bit of evidence was necessarily gathered pursuant to a warrant,” Schultz said in an earlier hearing in the case.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: New court filings reveal more details of undercover agents’ surveillance of anti-ICE protesters
description: A court filing Tuesday morning in the federal case against 15 anti-ICE protesters contained more than 200 pages of undercover agents’ notes and photos from the Department of Homeland Security’s widespread surveillance operation during Operation Metro Surge.  The documents reveal new information about groups and events targeted by the agents — and contain doz[...]
text:
Alec Stewart, one of the 15 people federally indicted for conspiracy to impede or injure federal officers, speaks during a press conference condemning federal surveillance Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)A court filing Tuesday morning in the federal case against 15 anti-ICE protesters contained more than 200 pages of undercover agents’ notes and photos from the Department of Homeland Security’s widespread surveillance operation during Operation Metro Surge. 
The documents reveal new information about groups and events targeted by the agents — and contain dozens of photos of cars of people who trailed immigration agents in their cars.
The exhibits were submitted to the court by attorney Kevin Riach, who is defending Isaac Sant, one of the 15 Minnesotans charged with conspiracy to assault or impede federal agents. All 15 pleaded not guilty to the charges.
The documents further underscore the feds’ use of intelligence tactics — including the use of undercover agents and electronic surveillance — as a frustrated Trump administration sought to tamp down the widespread resistance to the immigration crackdown, which wound up ensnaring many legal residents and led to the killings of two Americans. 
Riach previously submitted another batch of undercover agents’ reports and other surveillance-related documents — including administrative subpoenas for unions’ financial records — in a motion requesting that the judge order DHS to release even more information on the surveillance campaign. 
A hearing on that motion is scheduled for Thursday. (The federal government asked U.S. District Judge David Schultz to postpone the hearing until next week, citing staffing shortages. Schultz denied that request on Monday.)
The new documents describe the efforts agents undertook to identify the individuals behind the websites defend612.com and melttheicemn.com, the website for an event in February that convened hundreds of activists from around the country to learn from members about the Minnesota anti-ICE movement. Agents subpoenaed the websites’ registrars and payment processors to confirm the identities of the website creators. 
Agents also used a “chat capturing software” to record the contents of Signal group chats, according to an undercover agents’ report, though the software isn’t named.
The new documents also contain dozens of photos of cars with redacted license plate numbers, presumably of cars that followed ICE — known as “patrollers” — and attendees at meetings of anti-ICE organizations. Previously-released internal DHS documents described undercover agents noting the license plate numbers of cars in the parking lots of such meetings, including at churches. 
Some of the photos capture daily life in the Twin Cities during the federal operation: anti-ICE graffiti on stop signs and buildings; posters of Renee Good and Alex Pretti with the message “MURDERED BY ICE”; a person in a “FCK ICE” button writing “chinga la migra” in chalk on a sidewalk; a table with pizza and coffee outside of the Whipple Federal Building.
There are several photos of mourners gathered at Alex Pretti’s memorial site. 
Prosecutors have said they have 20 terabytes of data in their possession, though not all of it is directly related to the defendants in the conspiracy case.
“I’m inferring that not every bit of evidence was necessarily gathered pursuant to a warrant,” Schultz said in an earlier hearing in the case.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Minnesota set to fight in Texas courtroom to extradite ICE agent charged in Minneapolis shooting
description: An attorney from the office of Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison is set to appear in federal court in Texas on Tuesday to argue for the extradition of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent charged with shooting a Venezuelan man during Operation Metro surge.  ICE agent Christian Castro is charged with four counts of […]
text:
Residents confront federal agents following a shooting incident on Jan. 14, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)An attorney from the office of Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison is set to appear in federal court in Texas on Tuesday to argue for the extradition of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent charged with shooting a Venezuelan man during Operation Metro surge. 
ICE agent Christian Castro is charged with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime in the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in north Minneapolis in January. Castro has been in a Texas county jail since May 29, when he was arrested by the Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency. He has not entered a plea in the case, and court records do not list an attorney to speak on his behalf.
A federal law prohibits law enforcement agencies from detaining fugitives awaiting extradition for longer than 90 days. That means Castro could be released from custody as soon as Thursday. Minnesota authorities allege that he is in a relationship with a woman in Mexico, who is living in a home Castro owns — making him a potential flight risk.
But Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a Republican, has so far refused to sign the paperwork to facilitate the extradition. Last week, he said he would not sign the papers until the administration of Democratic Gov. Tim Walz acknowledges “their fault in the fraud that took place, and they fully repay the United States of America for the fraud they committed.”
Republicans in Minnesota and beyond have seized on Minnesota’s wide-ranging investigations of fraud in social safety net programs, going back years.
In a legal filing submitted to the court Monday, Abbott’s office said the governor last month ordered his Secretary of State to investigate “whether Mr. Castro is a fugitive based on public reports and a preliminary investigation indicating he may have been ordered to return to Texas by ICE.” Castro may not be a “fugitive,” the state of Texas argued, because he didn’t flee from Minnesota — he was reassigned to Texas by ICE.
This investigation was news to Minnesota law enforcement officials, who replied in a brief Tuesday arguing that the Supreme Court has made it clear that the Constitution affords “no discretion to the executive officers of the asylum State.” 
The U.S. Department of Justice filed a “statement of interest” in the case, confirming some of the facts underpinning Abbott’s argument. ICE ordered Castro to return to Texas after the shooting over concerns for his safety, given that protesters were “following ICE officers and using aggressive and sometimes violent tactics, including doxxing, to interfere with officers carrying out their duties,” according to an affidavit from an ICE field office director. 
Minnesota reiterated its request that the judge order Texas officials to facilitate the extradition — or, at least, order that Castro remain in jail until the extradition matter is settled. 
Castro is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a Minneapolis home, hitting Sosa-Celis in the leg. Three other people were inside the house, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said, and one of the bullets was found embedded in the wall of a child’s bedroom. 
Castro is also charged with falsely reporting a crime because he accused Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan immigrant of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel before Castro opened fire. The U.S. Department of Justice charged the two immigrant men with assaulting a federal agent, but the charges were dropped after surveillance footage disproved Castro’s claims.

title: Northeast Iowa Community College to launch sterile processing technician program
description: Northeast Iowa Community College has created a new certificate program to help fill necessary roles in ensuring the health and safety of patients undergoing surgery. The Calmar-based community college announced in a news release it is launching a new sterile processing technician career pathway certificate program, with its first classes set to begin Oct. 20[...]
text:
Northeast Iowa Community College will offer the first courses in its new sterile processing technician career pathway certificate this fall. (Photo courtesy of Northeast Iowa Community College)Northeast Iowa Community College has created a new certificate program to help fill necessary roles in ensuring the health and safety of patients undergoing surgery.
The Calmar-based community college announced in a news release it is launching a new sterile processing technician career pathway certificate program, with its first classes set to begin Oct. 20. Students will have one in-person lab day as part of the 14-week program, with the rest of instruction and training taking place online.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to the release, students who complete the program will then be able to move further toward earning their Certified Registered Central Service Technician designation, which requires further hands-on training and passage of a test from the Healthcare Sterile Processing Association. The pathway costs $2,399, the release stated.
The new program works for both new students and professionals returning to further their education, the release stated, as the certification can supplement other medical credentials. Students can also use the pathway as a stepping stone to surgical technician training, offered to Northeast Iowa Community College students through an academic partnership with Kirkwood Community College.
“Our mission has always been to provide high-quality education that leads directly to meaningful employment,” said Northeast Iowa Community College Health Program Developer Kelly Deeney in the release. “By expanding our accessible healthcare pathways to include Sterile Processing, we’re opening doors to rewarding careers and directly supporting the local healthcare workforce our community relies on.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Wanda Geter-Pataky, Alfredo Castillo opt for jury trials in ballot cases
description: Two Democratic officials in Bridgeport, accused of crimes related to absentee ballots, rejected plea offers Tuesday and opted to go to trial.
text:
Two Democratic officials in Bridgeport rejected plea offers in court on Tuesday and chose to put their fate into the hands of Connecticut jurors who will decide whether they are guilty of repeated election-related crimes in recent years.
Connecticut’s Chief State’s Attorney offered Wanda Geter-Pataky, the former vice chair of Bridgeport’s Democratic Party, a plea deal that would have required her to spend at least three years in state prison to resolve the dozens of criminal charges that she faces.
The state prosecutors also extended to Alfredo Castillo, a sitting city councilman in Bridgeport, a similar offer that would have required him to serve two and a half years in prison for allegedly manipulating Connecticut’s absentee voting system and corrupting the results of several recent mayoral elections in the city.
But the two defendants rejected those plea deals and informed a state Superior Court judge in Bridgeport that they intended to defend themselves at trial.
The judge reminded Geter-Pataky and Castillo that the crimes they are accused of could carry far more serious criminal penalties if a jury convicts them.

Alfredo Castillo appeared in Bridgeport Superior Court for a hearing in a case related to absentee ballot abuse on Sept. 9, 2025. Credit: Shahrzad Rasekh / CT Mirror

The 33 felonies that Castillo is accused of committing, which include illegally taking possession of multiple voters’ absentee ballots and registering a non-U.S. citizen to vote, could carry a maximum sentence of 165 years behind bars. Geter-Pataky is facing 96 counts including conspiracy charges, absentee ballot crimes and witness tampering that could equate to a maximum sentence of more than 500 years in prison.
A judge is unlikely to hand down a sentence anywhere close to that, but those calculations drove home the point of what the two defendants are facing as they prepare for their trials.
Both of them are accused of violating the law during multiple election cycles, including city Democratic primaries in 2019 and 2023, and some of those crimes were allegedly committed even after prosecutors initially charged them in court.
Castillo quickly left the courthouse after he rejected the plea deal, and Geter-Pataky declined to comment in the hallway outside the courtroom, where she was surrounded by supporters. 
Frank Riccio, Castillo’s defense attorney, previously told the CT Mirror that he had pressed state prosecutors for a deal that would have allowed his client to avoid prison time, but state prosecutors made it clear they were unwilling to extend such an offer on Tuesday.

Wanda Geter-Pataky appeared in Bridgeport Superior Court for a hearing in a case related to absentee ballot abuse on Sept. 9, 2025. Credit: Shahrzad Rasekh / CT Mirror

John Gulash, Geter-Pataky’s defense attorney, said it would be inappropriate for him to comment on his client’s ongoing case, but he said he will prepare for a trial, which has yet to be scheduled.
Castillo and Geter-Pataky are just the latest Bridgeport residents who have had to make the decision of whether to plead guilty to a host of election-related crimes or face jury of their peers. 
Nine other Bridgeport residents were also criminally charged in recent years for misrepresenting when people could vote via mail-in ballot, for illegally taking possession of other voters’ ballots and for being present when the voters filled out those ballots.
Five of those defendants have already pleaded guilty in court and received sentences that allowed them to avoid prison time. Two other defendants opted for criminal trials. And another, former city councilwoman Jazmarie Melendez, was allowed to enter a diversionary program that will allow her charges to be dismissed.
Melendez was charged exclusively with misrepresenting when people were eligible to vote via absentee ballot, which is no longer a crime in Connecticut since the state adopted no-excuse absentee voting. 
The only remaining defendant who has not made the choice of whether to accept a plea offer or opt for a trial is Bridgeport city councilwoman Maria Pereira. She will likely need to make that decision later this fall.

name: Delaware
title: Jesse Garron Brings Elvis’ Music and Showmanship to The Queen
description: The veteran tribute artist will recreate the excitement of an Elvis concert Friday in the historic Main Hall in downtown Wilmington. WILMINGTON — The music, movement and unmistakable stage presence of Elvis Presley will return to downtown Wilmington when Jesse Garron’s Tribute to Elvis performs Friday, Aug. 28, at The Queen. The all-ages show begins at 8 p.m[...]
text:
For longtime fans, the evening offers an opportunity to revisit music connected to their lives. For younger guests, it provides something recordings and movie clips cannot fully reproduce: the communal excitement of hearing the songs performed by a live band in a historic theater.
The veteran tribute artist will recreate the excitement of an Elvis concert Friday in the historic Main Hall in downtown Wilmington.
WILMINGTON — The music, movement and unmistakable stage presence of Elvis Presley will return to downtown Wilmington when Jesse Garron’s Tribute to Elvis performs Friday, Aug. 28, at The Queen.
The all-ages show begins at 8 p.m., with doors opening at 7 p.m. in The Queen’s Main Hall.
Garron has performed his tribute since 1997, developing a full concert experience supported by live musicians and female backup vocalists. His show focuses heavily on Presley’s concert years, complete with period-inspired costumes, audience interaction and the scarf serenades associated with Elvis’ Las Vegas performances.
It is designed to be more than a collection of familiar songs. Garron attempts to recreate the energy and emotional connection that made an Elvis concert an event.
Known professionally as “The Closest Thing to the King,” Garron was inducted into the International Elvis Tribute Artist Hall of Fame in 2019. His stage name also carries a personal connection to Presley: Jesse Garon Presley was Elvis’ twin brother, who was stillborn.
A performer inspired by Elvis
Garron became interested in Presley at age 4 and first performed an Elvis tribute during a high school talent show at 17, according to his biography.
He later moved from performing with prerecorded tracks to leading a professional touring production. The current show features a live band, backup singers and arrangements intended to capture the sound and scale of Presley’s later concerts.
Garron has performed across the country and was invited to appear for the U.S. Embassy in Algiers. His tribute has also shared bills with performers including Wayne Newton, The Commodores, Little Big Town and Bret Michaels.
The show reaches across Presley’s catalog, drawing from rock ’n’ roll, pop, country, gospel and traditional ballads. Songs featured in Garron’s repertoire include “Burning Love,” “Always on My Mind,” “In the Ghetto,” “Moody Blue” and “You Gave Me a Mountain.”
More information about Garron and samples of his performances are available on the performer’s official website.
Why Elvis continues to matter
Nearly 50 years after Presley’s death, his music continues to find listeners who were not alive during his career.
Older fans may connect Elvis with personal memories of his recordings, films and television appearances. Younger listeners often encounter him through movies, streaming services, social media and the artists he influenced.
Presley’s lasting importance also comes from the range of his music. His performances brought together elements of country, blues, gospel and rhythm and blues during a transformative period in American popular culture. His voice, clothing, movement and command of an audience helped establish a model for the modern music superstar.
His career remains part of a more complicated conversation about the Black artists and musical traditions that helped shape rock ’n’ roll. That history does not diminish Presley’s impact, but it provides important context for understanding the cultural moment in which he became famous.
For tribute performers such as Garron, the goal is to keep the live experience accessible while acknowledging that there was only one Elvis.
A fitting room for a larger-than-life show
The Queen offers an appropriate setting for that experience. Its Main Hall combines a classical balcony, carved pillars and a historic pipe organ with contemporary lighting, sound and a full-size stage.
The building became a movie theater in 1916, when Presley was still decades away from becoming a film star himself. It closed as a theater in 1959 and remained dark for more than 50 years before reopening as a live entertainment venue in 2011.
That combination of restored history and modern concert production gives Garron’s performance a sense of occasion. The room is intimate enough for his audience interaction but large and theatrical enough to support the costumes, vocals and spectacle associated with Elvis’ concert years.
For longtime fans, the evening offers an opportunity to revisit music connected to their lives. For younger guests, it provides something recordings and movie clips cannot fully reproduce: the communal excitement of hearing the songs performed by a live band in a historic theater.
To Go

What: Jesse Garron’s Tribute to Elvis
When: Friday, Aug. 28, at 8 p.m.; doors open at 7 p.m.
Where: The Queen, Main Hall, 500 N. Market St., Wilmington
Admission: All ages; ticket prices and availability are listed on The Queen’s event page.
Box office: Open Wednesdays from 2 to 6 p.m. and 30 minutes before performances
Parking: Street parking is generally free after 5 p.m. The Renaissance Centre Garage is located nearby on East Fifth Street between Market and King streets.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Investigators: Owner of home that exploded cut propane line accidentally
description: The owner of the Cape St. Claire home that explosed last week accidentally cut a propane line while working on the HVAC system, investigators announced Monday, triggering a blast that left one woman dead and the homeowner in “serious condition” in the hospital.
text:
Investigators say an accidentally cut propane line may have led to the explosion that destroyed a Cape St. Claire home last week, killing one person and seriously injuring another. (Photo by Alixandria Chen/Stock.adobe.com0By Thomas Robertson
The owner of the Cape St. Claire home where an explosion occurred last week accidentally cut a propane line while working on the HVAC system, investigators announced Monday.
The explosion Wednesday afternoon left one woman dead and the homeowner, a man, in what investigators Monday called “serious condition” in the hospital.
Cutting the line allowed propane gas to leak and accumulate inside the home without the homeowner realizing it. Family members told investigators he has a diminished sense of smell, which may have affected his ability to detect the odor of the leaking propane.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While continuing to work, the homeowner started using a metal grinder, which ignited the propane, causing the explosion, investigators determined.
The explosion caused the second floor of the home in the 1100 block of Green Holly Drive to collapse onto the first floor.
Linda Synowczynski, 76, suffered from cardiac arrest and died at the scene. The homeowner was rescued from the debris suffering from significant burns and was taken to the hospital in critical condition. Investigators said Monday he was still hospitalized in “serious condition.”
An Anne Arundel County police officer also suffered non-life-threatening injuries and was taken to a hospital.
Investigators reiterated that a propane company’s visit to the home earlier that day did not contribute to the explosion.
Officials with the Anne Arundel County Fire Department reminded individuals that if they smell gas or suspect a leak, they should leave the area immediately and not attempt to locate or repair a gas leak.
