Kennedy Jr. visited New Hampshire in May, former Portsmouth City Councilor Stefany Shaheen stood outside the Concord press conference to let voters know it was his anti-science policies that convinced her to run for Congress.
Hampton Selectwoman Carleigh Beriont, the leading progressive in the race, has been pitching a single-payer Medicare for All system
Christian Urrutia, on the other hand, held a press conference in Manchester last week where he listed all the reasons why he believes he’s the only true Medicare for All candidate in the race.
Maura Sullivan counters them with “Medicare for all who want it.”
Sarah Chadzynski chastised the Medicare for All proponents for focusing on an issue she doesn’t believe is viable in a divided Congress, instead opting for piecemeal solutions.
Shaheen, Beriont, Urrutia, Sullivan, and Chadzynski are five of the eight Democratic candidates running in New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District primary. Rounding out the ballot are Matthew Emerson, Bill Conlin, and Sarah Bella Spinosa. On Monday, state Rep. Heath Howard dropped out of the race and threw his support behind Beriont.
Throughout the campaign, healthcare has proven to be a key focus as candidates in a crowded primary field attempt to stand out in the eyes of voters. Sullivan, who holds a slight lead over Shaheen at the top of the most recent poll from St. Anselm College, called healthcare affordability her no. 1 issue.
Stefany Shaheen, former Portsmouth city councilor and daughter of a former governor and U.S. senator, speaks to reporters after filing her own campaign for Congress on June 11, 2026, in the New Hampshire Secretary of State’s office. She’s running as a Democrat in the 1st Congressional District and told the Bulletin she supports Medicare for All. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Competing calls for Medicare for All
At the heart of the election’s healthcare debate has been expanding Medicare, the country’s public health coverage program, which mainly covers seniors over age 65. 
Five of the candidates are calling for Medicare for All in some form.
Sullivan proposed a “Medicare for all who want it” system. That means offering access to Medicare to everyone but allowing those who don’t want Medicare to keep their private insurance.
“I hear from folks all around our state that they’re just getting crushed for costs, and some want Medicare for All,” she said. “Others are worried about the government running their health care, and with the government the way it is right now, can you really blame them? And Medicare for all who want it gets that public option and the real competition that we desperately need.”
The other four Medicare for All proponents — Shaheen, Beriont, Urrutia, and Chadzynski — are proposing single-payer systems in which the private insurers are replaced by Medicare and governmental programs.
“I want to address what I believe is one of the great moral questions of this election today,” Urrutia said at a press conference on the banks of the Merrimack River last Tuesday. “And the question is, in the richest country on earth, are we prepared to deny life-saving health care to people because they can’t afford it?”
Urrutia said his plan would be paid for with a tax increase on employers and employees to pay for it but that it would be dwarfed by the savings people get from ditching insurance premiums.
Shaheen said she supports a single-payer system that eliminates private insurers, but she acknowledged that, if she couldn’t get single-payer, she would support a public option system like Sullivan’s.
Beriont echoed that sentiment, saying “I am somebody who would absolutely co-sponsor the Medicare for All legislation that’s been proposed right now, and also won’t necessarily say no to anything that would help provide better care for people in the Granite State as soon as humanly possible.”
Emerson, a former Democratic Party volunteer, had a more unique proposal. He doesn’t support immediate expansion of Medicare or Medicaid. He said he wants to create a third public health program that’s available to everyone, but is not Medicare or Medicaid.
“The goal is competition,” he said. “That is the No. 1 goal.”
But who’s the one who can actually make it happen?
In a race filled with Medicare for All advocates, some candidates have struggled to articulate to voters why they are the best candidate to turn the idea into law.
Shaheen pointed to her experience in the biotech industry as an executive for the Manchester-based biomanufacturer ARMI and founder of Good Measures, a company seeking to help people with chronic illnesses find support.
State Rep. Heath Howard gives a speech on the House floor in Concord Aug. 19, 2026. The young progressive suspended his campaign Monday and endorsed Carleigh Beriont. (Photo by Ethan DeWitt/New Hampshire Bulletin)
“I know how hard and complicated the system is,” she said. “I know the kinds of things we can do near-term, and the kinds of things we need to be prioritizing to deliver relief for people. And I think that experience will come through to the voters and make it very clear from my understanding the very complicated network of what it means to be a licensed provider in 50 different states.”
Shaheen is also the mother of a type 1 diabetic, something she has repeatedly said gives her an understanding of the stakes.
Sullivan said her proposal is designed to be viable. She argued her opponents’ plans would be nonstarters for their would-be colleagues in Congress.
“Folks can say all the great ideas they want, but if you can’t get them done, then Granite Staters are still hurting,” she said. “If I had a single term in Congress, what am I going to tell Granite Staters that I’m going to get done for them? This is something I think we can get done in a divided Congress, Medicare for all who want it.”
Still, Sullivan said her plan could be a first step in the path to a single-payer system in later years.
“I know how hard healthcare reform is,” she said. “And so I’m being very thoughtful about what I can get done and what I can deliver.”
Sullivan, a former Obama administration official and Marine Corps veteran, also said she’d capitalize on the camaraderie she holds with Republicans who also served in the military to work across the aisle.
For her part, Beriont said she’s the candidate to get it done “because I can explain clearly and directly to everybody how we can use that type of legislation along with fully funding our public schools to lower our property taxes here in New Hampshire; because I’m an organizer and I serve locally, and I am good at reaching consensus and bringing around to my point of view; and because I’ve just heard enough stories from enough people that I think can change the hearts and minds of anybody who thinks that it’s not a good investment at this point.”
Christian Urrutia holds a press conference in Manchester Aug. 18, 2026, where he argued he is the only candidate in New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District race truly in favor of Medicare for All. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Urrutia, who works as a lawyer and Army National Guardsman, said he’s “the credible progressive with a message of change.” Additionally, Urrutia has gone on the offensive, particularly against Sullivan and Shaheen, who have consistently been at the top of the polls.
“Maura Sullivan calls for Medicare for all who want it,” he said. “That’s just consultancy-speak for not-Medicare. It borrows the phrase Medicare for All, and then denies the single element that makes it important, which is a universal healthcare coverage that wraps in everyone together.”
Urrutia argued Sullivan’s proposal would create “a tiered system: the sick and the poor on the public rolls, the rich and the healthy on the private rolls.”
“Stefany Shaheen, look, I got to be frank with you,” Urrutia continued. “I spent a year on the campaign trail with Stefany Shaheen. I still don’t know her healthcare position. Her answers have been a word salad.”
Asked about those criticisms, Shaheen said, “I’d invite him to go back and think through the number of candidate forums starting on the very first day I launched this campaign, highlighting healthcare as the cause of the campaign and the cause of my life.”
Shaheen denies accusations she isn’t fervently pro-Medicare for All or that she recently changed her stance. However, previous statements she made appeared noncommittal.
“I support every option we need to fix this broken healthcare system, but that (single-payer) is not where we — we know we have to deliver change today with meaningful measures that happen today. We can’t wait for rebuilding the system to deliver relief for people,” she told NH Journal in June.
Criticism of senators’ caving in the ACA tax credits fight
Shaheen is the daughter of current U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. The elder Shaheen drew stinging criticism last year when she provided a key vote to end a Democratic-induced shutdown. Democrats had shut down the government in an effort to force Republicans to renew an expiring set of Affordable Care Act tax credits that Americans used to pay for healthcare. Eventually, however, Sen. Shaheen caved and, alongside a small group of Democrats, ended the shutdown before securing any definitive Republican promises on the tax credits.
Maura Sullivan fills out paperwork to file for her candidacy to represent New Hampshire’s 1st Congressional District in the State House on June 12, 2026.(Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
The younger Shaheen, at that point months into her own congressional campaign, was outspoken in criticizing her own mother for the vote.
“As a result of those tax credits not being extended, 12,000 New Hampshire people today are without health insurance who had it a year ago,” she said in an interview last week, “because it has gotten so expensive that families can’t afford to keep their health insurance. So when it was clear that Speaker (Mike) Johnson wasn’t going to guarantee a vote, I knew I couldn’t support the deal.”
Virtually the entire field echoed Shaheen in opposing the move. Sullivan, for her part, said she’d make restoring that tax credit a top priority should she be elected.
Other proposals
Chadzynski concedes she doesn’t believe enough members of Congress will sign on to pass Medicare for All.
“I am absolutely a single-payer system proponent,” she said. “However, I think one of the biggest things that we’ve done as Democrats is overpromise and underdeliver.”
Sarah E. Chadzynski
For that reason, Chadzynski wants to tackle something she thinks is more feasible: have the federal government take over what she calls “re-risk insurance,” a special type of insurance that insurers secure from other insurers to cover potentially high-cost patients. She thinks the government can do it cheaper.
“This is something we could get done in the next two years,” she said.
Chadzynski also wants to switch the entire healthcare system to a nonprofit model and put more guardrails on how insurance companies can dictate to providers how care is provided.
“If the whole system is moved over to a nonprofit model, then you level the playing field, and you don’t have the for-profit model as the reason for shutting down maternity wards,” she said.
Meanwhile, Beriont has emphasized antitrust laws as a tool to break up the corporate monopolies she argues have a harmful stranglehold on the U.S. healthcare system.
“I think that one of the reasons that our healthcare experience is so much of a nightmare and way too expensive is because we have like a handful of corporations that own our doctors and our pharmacies and our insurance companies and our hospitals,” she said. “They take a cut at every step of the way, and it’s so expensive for all of us.”
Carleigh Beriont, shown here surrounded by supporters in Concord on June 9, 2026, is the leading progressive in the 1st Congressional District race. She supports a single-payer Medicare for All system and has advocated to break up healthcare monopolies. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Emerson said he wants to focus on fighting Medicaid fraud. Asked for specifics on his plan to do so, Emerson said: “You need to have complete oversight, and that’s in the contracts we produce. That’s in making sure we severely limit no-bid contracts. That is looking at people who overbill Medicaid and Medicare.
“When you have a budget that’s in the trillions,” he said, “to think that there’s no one committing fraud, that’s almost like hyperbole.”
Conlin, who hasn’t polled above 1% in recent polls, did not respond to the Bulletin’s request for an interview.
Spinoza, the remaining candidate, told the Bulletin she doesn’t expect to win. She called her campaign “basically a messaging and accountability campaign this cycle” and in future cycles she’ll “double down and concentrate on electability.” She described herself as a “Democrat-Libertarian hybrid.”
The primary will take place Sept. 8. The Republican primary is also crowded. In November, the winner of the Democratic contest will face Portsmouth businessman Anthony DiLorenzo, Manchester state Rep. Brian Cole, Newfields businesswoman Hollie Noveletsky, Bedford finance professional Melissa Bailey, or Moultonborough businessman Lindsey Anderson.

name: National
title: Cheaper health insurance changed their lives. Then it went away.
description: Part 1 of an occasional series on how people are being affected by the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies. EDWARDS, Miss. — Every now and then a freight train rumbles through, creaking and groaning on the rusted tracks that run along the edge of the largely deserted downtown. On some days, that train is […]
text:
Derrick Clark, 51, stands in front of the Jackson-Hinds Comprehensive Health Center in Jackson, Mississippi, on June 6, 2026. Over the past few years, Clark and many other diabetes patients in Mississippi were getting regular care through subsidized Affordable Care Act health insurance plans. But Congress allowed so-called federal enhanced subsidies to expire at the end of last year, forcing Clark and more than 200,000 other Mississippians to give up their coverage. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline) Part 1 of an occasional series on how people are being affected by the expiration of Affordable Care Act subsidies.
EDWARDS, Miss. — Every now and then a freight train rumbles through, creaking and groaning on the rusted tracks that run along the edge of the largely deserted downtown. On some days, that train is just about the only thing moving.
Grandma’s Ice Cream Shoppe, an ice cream parlor owned by a retired preacher and his wife, gets only one or two customers per day. There is a small barber shop, and the empty ruins of a former thrift store. The sugary, smoky red meat at Lee’s Heavenly Barbecue and the fried shrimp and catfish at the M & L Fish Hut draw some folks. But the ellipticals and treadmills are silent, as usual, at the 4-year-old Kut-N-Fit Wellness Club on Vicksburg Street.
Derrick Clark, 51, has lived in Edwards his whole life.
Clark has always struggled with his weight and he readily describes himself as obese. About two decades ago, he was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes.
“My grandmother, my uncle, my dad are all diabetics, and I’ve had some relatives that have gotten some of their limbs cut off because of their diabetes,” Clark said. “When it’s a hereditary disease that runs in the family, it’s kind of hard.”
Last year, Clark was reelected as the at-large member of the Edwards Board of Aldermen. But the part-time job only pays about $500 a month. His family owns a small sports bar in town, but it’s only open for a few hours a day and doesn’t generate much additional income.
He has no health insurance.
As is the case with many chronic diseases, the worst consequences of diabetes — such as blindness and amputations — can be prevented with routine care. Clark and many other diabetes patients in Mississippi were getting that care over the past few years through subsidized Affordable Care Act insurance plans.
But Congress allowed the so-called enhanced subsidies to expire at the end of last year. Now the number of diabetic Mississippians without insurance, and thus regular care, is once again on the rise: According to state data, enrollment in ACA plans has fallen by nearly two-thirds in just eight months. The medical and financial consequences could be dire — for individual patients like Clark and for the state.
Mississippi maladies
Designed as a temporary pandemic-era measure, the enhanced subsidies were made available by the American Rescue Plan Act in 2021 and later extended through the end of 2025 by the Inflation Reduction Act.
 


 
In 49 states (all but New Mexico), the number of people enrolled in ACA plans, also known as Obamacare, has declined since the subsidies expired and coverage became more expensive. Nationwide, participation has declined this year by nearly 3 million people, to about 19.2 million from 21.8 million in 2025, according to the Trump administration. The 2025 figure was the highest ever recorded, after six years of steady increases.
But few if any states are feeling the absence of the subsidies as acutely as Mississippi.
By many measures, Mississippi is the poorest state, with more than 14% of its families living below the federal poverty line. Its traditional Medicaid program has strict income limits, and excludes nearly all non-disabled adults, including Clark. And it is among the 10 states that have not expanded Medicaid to single adults and higher-income parents under the Affordable Care Act.
A gas station in Edwards, Mississippi, is home to a small market that sells some basic groceries, such as sliced and canned meats, in addition to prepared fried foods. The only other store that sells groceries is a Dollar General. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)
Mississippi is also one of the unhealthiest states. The federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has identified a “diabetes belt,” where people are most likely to have the chronic disease. It includes 644 counties across 15 states, primarily in the South; Mississippi is the only state where every county made the list.
In addition to its high diabetes rate, Mississippi has the nation’s second-highest heart disease mortality rate, and it is one of only two states, along with West Virginia, with an obesity rate above 40%.
Black people make up more than 36% of Mississippi’s population — the highest percentage of any state — and Black Americans are more likely than other racial groups to have chronic diseases, including diabetes. That’s largely because Black people are more likely to live in poverty, to have trouble accessing healthcare, and to be exposed to pollution and chronic stress.
 


 
When the subsidies significantly lowered the cost of Obamacare coverage — making it free or nearly free for some people with low incomes — Mississippi state health officials made a concerted effort to get residents to enroll. Dr. Daniel Edney, Mississippi’s state health officer, said the state launched a public information campaign to encourage people to sign up at their local health departments.
It worked. The number of Mississippians enrolled in Obamacare plans more than tripled, from fewer than 99,000 people in 2020, the year before the subsidies went into effect, to more than 338,000 at the end of 2025, according to state data.
A freight train rumbles through downtown Edwards, Mississippi, a half dozen times a day. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)
“Our uninsured rate went down significantly, and I’m convinced it’s one of the reasons why our overall population health scoring has improved,” Edney said in an interview in his office in downtown Jackson.
In its 2025 public health report card, the Mississippi State Department of Health reported lower rates of opioid-related deaths, HIV, syphilis, congenital syphilis, teen births and accidental deaths. Health officials acknowledged that the state had made less progress on chronic conditions such as hypertension and obesity, but also noted that it went from dead last in overall national health rankings three years ago to 48th last year.
But when the subsidies expired at the end of last year, Mississippi’s Obamacare enrollment numbers plunged: Roughly 134,000 residents were still enrolled as of Aug. 21, about 40% of last year’s total. And the state projects that the number will fall to around 127,000 next year.
Obamacare enrollment declines in 49 states

Many of the Mississippians who dropped their coverage have diabetes or other chronic conditions. Without insurance, they are likely to put off routine care, Edney said.
“What’s gonna happen to them? Probably present to the emergency room, eventually showing up once their vision is blurry, or they start having chest pain, or they have a sore on their foot that won’t heal,” he said. “At that point, you’re scrambling to get them placed into care.”
The Obamacare subsidies made a huge difference for Clark, who is unmarried and does not have any children. With coverage, his insulin and medications to control his blood pressure and blood sugar cost him about $15 per month, he said. But he could no longer afford his insurance plan when the subsidies expired and his premiums went up by “hundreds of dollars.”
Without insurance, he says his medications now cost him about $200 per month — and that’s with discounts he gets from medical clinics. Sometimes, he said, family members give him insulin they don’t plan to use.
At some point, he said, he might have to choose between paying for medications and paying his other bills.
“I still have utilities and water and gas and food and still have to buy my medicine monthly out of pocket,” Clark said. “I’m just praying for a better day and trying to lose some weight so I can try to get my diabetes in control.”
Opening a gym 
Like Clark, 49-year-old hair stylist and salon owner Angie Myles-Griffin grew up in Edwards, and she never really wanted to leave. But the limitations of living in a small town hit home after she gave birth to her third child and she set out to lose some of the weight she had gained: She had to drive more than an hour round trip to Jackson to find a gym and a grocery store selling healthy food.
Frustrated by the back and forth, Myles-Griffin decided to do something about it: She became a certified personal trainer and opened her own gym in Edwards, the Kut-N-Fit Wellness Club, right down the street from Lee’s Heavenly Barbecue.
“I became very passionate about health and just fitness overall,” Myles-Griffin said. “So I wanted to bring that back to my community, so people wouldn’t have that excuse of having to drive.”
On most days, downtown Edwards, Mississippi, is practically deserted. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)
Myles-Griffin said that in 2024 she partnered with the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson to lead a yearlong diabetes prevention program for 20 Edwards-area women. Myles-Griffin gave participants fitness and nutrition coaching at her new gym and even brought in dieticians to show them how to prepare healthy meals. A dozen people stuck with it.
But since the  medical center concluded its sponsorship, most of Myles-Griffin’s clients have melted away. Even though Kut-N-Fit is conveniently located, she said most Edwards residents just don’t have the “mindset” to work out regularly. And Edwards residents still have to drive about a half hour to get to a grocery store with a wide selection of healthy offerings, she said.
Some states are helping to make Obamacare plans more affordable

Unfortunately, a lack of transportation is one of the many challenges that Edwards residents face.
“If you don’t have transportation, you can’t get to a job, and if you can’t get to a job, there’s no income,” Myles-Griffin said. “And so when there’s nothing going on, it’s like a lack of motivation.”
Poverty, a lack of exercise, obesity, diets high in sugar, unhealthy fats and processed ingredients — that confluence of factors exists in many Mississippi communities. It’s a recipe for diabetes, and it’s costing Mississippi billions of dollars.
Diagnosed cases of diabetes cost the state an estimated $5.1 billion annually — $3.4 billion from direct medical expenses and another $1.7 billion from lost productivity in 2022, according to the American Diabetes Association.
And when diabetics don’t get regular care, because they don’t have insurance or don’t have easy access to a doctor, the most extreme — and expensive — health outcomes become more likely. Mississippi’s lower extremity amputation rate is about twice the national rate, according to the American Heart Association.
Grandma’s Ice Cream Shoppe, in Edwards, Mississippi, gets only one or two customers per day. (Photo by Shalina Chatlani/Stateline)
Irena McClain, the executive director of the nonprofit Diabetes Foundation of Mississippi, said that since the subsidies expired, her organization has been receiving more calls from people asking for help. Without insurance, medical care for diabetes can cost people upward of $1,000 per month, according to a 2022 study.
“I had someone call me up last week, whose doctor wants her on an insulin pump to control her Type 1 diabetes, and she doesn’t have any insurance. She can’t get a pump unless someone donates a pump to us,” McClain said. “And there’s certainly a lot of people who need help much more than the amount that these charities have to give. I don’t know what’s going to happen.”
In Jackson, McClain said, charities, free clinics and community health centers are struggling to provide care to all the diabetes patients who have lost their Obamacare coverage.
Mississippi hospitals also are feeling the pinch, according to Richard Roberson, president and CEO of the Mississippi Hospital Association. In 2023, the most recent year for which numbers are available, Mississippi hospitals provided more than $600 million in “uncompensated care,” or care for which they received no payment from either the patient or an insurer.
“That trajectory of costs combined with the trajectory of uninsureds is just going to really exacerbate the challenges for hospitals,” Roberson said. He added that changes to hospital funding included the broad tax and spending law President Donald Trump signed last summer, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, will increase the financial strain.
“We’re just going to start seeing that decrease in revenue, increase in cost, and at some point on the axis, they’re going to cross, and it’s going to be bad,” he said.
No help coming
Meanwhile, the cost of Obamacare coverage keeps going up. Next year, the median proposed premium increase is expected to be close to 15%, the second consecutive year of a double-digit premium hike.
In addition to the expiration of the federal subsidies, prices have increased because of other factors, including labor shortages and the rising cost of prescription drugs, driven in part by the growing demand for GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy.



Quotation







It’s not that there’s a big money room in the basement where we can go get the money that we’re keeping from everyone. 


– Mississippi Republican state Rep. Lee Yancey


At least 10 states are using their own money to help people buy Obamacare health plans, partially replacing the expired subsidies. But Mississippi isn’t one of them.
“It’s not that there’s a big money room in the basement where we can go get the money that we’re keeping from everyone,” Mississippi Republican state Rep. Lee Yancey, who serves on the House’s public health and human services committee, told Stateline. “It’s just there’s a limited amount, and there’s only so much you can do.”
Yancey expressed sympathy for Mississippians who can’t afford Obamacare plans without the subsidies. However, he added, he doesn’t believe that “just because a problem exists the government is the one that has to fix it.”



Quotation







It’s not about a race thing. It’s just poor people — the working poor. 


– Derrick Clark, 51, of Edwards, Mississippi


Without the Obamacare plan he used to have, Clark said he has little choice but to drive to Jackson every month to get discounted medications at the Jackson-Hinds Comprehensive Health Center.
“Sometimes you got to do what you got to do, and with this high price of gas and food … it’s just rough,” Clark said as he stood outside the clinic.
“If you go in there, you see it’s not about a race thing,” he said. “It’s just poor people — the working poor.”
Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org.
This story is part of “Uninsured in America,” a project led by Public Health Watch, a nonprofit newsroom based in Texas. The project focuses on life in America’s health-coverage gaps and the impact of potential Medicaid cuts and other changes.

title: How the ‘Rule of 90’ became a campaign calculation for RI’s embattled incumbent governor
description: To many Rhode Islanders, the “Rule of 90” sounds like an obscure lesson from high school geometry. Not to Scott Conley. The 53-year-old special education teacher at Davies Career and Technical High School has had more than a decade of schooling on the rule proposed as an alternative to the 2011 pension reforms led by […]
text:
Scott Conley, 53, a McKee supporter and regional vice president for the National Education Association of Rhode Island, has been a special education teacher at Davies Career and Technical High School in Lincoln for 21 years. (Photo by Laura Paton/Rhode Island Current)To many Rhode Islanders, the “Rule of 90” sounds like an obscure lesson from high school geometry.
Not to Scott Conley. The 53-year-old special education teacher at Davies Career and Technical High School has had more than a decade of schooling on the rule proposed as an alternative to the 2011 pension reforms led by then-General Treasurer Gina Raimondo.
The Rule of 90 would offer retirement with full benefits to participants who reach at least 60 years old, and whose years in government service plus their age add up to 90. A 61-year-old with 29 years of service, or a 62-year-old with 28 years of service would also be eligible for retirement under the same formula — five years ahead of the current “Rule of 95” retirement policy that resulted from Raimondo’s pension changes. Before 2011, public employees could generally retire at age 60 with 10 years of service, or at any age with 28 years of service.
“I’m not someone who’s just counting down the clock, but it’s nice to know if I work 30 years, I have the option to leave when I would like to,” said Conley, who also serves as a regional vice president for the National Education Association of Rhode Island.
Unions have failed to win over legislative leaders on Smith Hill, who have stuck to Raimondo’s plan restricting cost-of-living increases and other benefit changes until the pension system reaches 75% funding.
Enter Gov. Dan McKee. Down 20 points in his reelection bid against Democratic primary challenger Helena Buonanno Foulkes, McKee announced on Aug. 20 — the first day of early voting — that he would include the Rule of 90 provision in his fiscal 2028 budget proposal. 
“Fifteen years ago, a promise was taken away from our workers,” McKee said in a statement following the Thursday afternoon press conference with union leaders. “They didn’t break that promise — they kept showing up and doing the job anyway. It’s past time to begin the process of making people whole, and one of the ways I can do that is by putting it in my budget. This will let veteran teachers retire with the respect they’ve earned, and open the door for the next generation coming up behind them. As long as I am Governor, this state will show up for working people.” 
Motives questioned 
The Foulkes campaign said the governor’s pledge was a political maneuver meant to win union support. 
“Dan McKee has been the governor for six years,” Angelika Pelligrino, a Foulkes campaign spokesperson said in an email Friday. “That means he has had six budget cycles to adopt the Rule of 90. He hasn’t done it. And now — two months after his most recent budget and on the first day of early voting — he’s making a cynical, empty promise that he has no plan to pay for.”
Joe Fleming, a political analyst for WPRI-TV 12, also acknowledged the political benefits for McKee’s reelection campaign. 
“He’s looking to grab more teacher support by doing this,” Fleming said. “This is probably something to motivate the rank and file members of the union, to give a reason why they should vote for the governor.”
The trio of unions leading the charge for the Rule of 90 — the Rhode Island Council 94 of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees, the National Education Association of Rhode Island and the Rhode Island Federation of Teachers and Health Professionals — have each endorsed the governor already. The three groups represent a combined 34,000 teachers and government workers.
The National Education Association asked both McKee and Foulkes about their stances on pension benefits, including retirement, during interviews prior to the endorsement decision, Stephanie Mandeville, an association spokesperson said.
Jim Cenerini, spokesperson for Council 94,  said McKee never discussed the Rule of 90 proposal with union leaders prior to its endorsement vote. 
A spokesperson for the Federation of Teachers and Health Professionals did not immediately return requests for comment.
Sophie Mestas, a McKee campaign spokesperson, also said the governor has expressed support for the issue previously.
But McKee’s own budget director warned about the implications for the state pension fund when Rule of 90 legislation was reviewed by Senate lawmakers in May. 
“Any bill that expands retirement benefits will increase State retirement costs over time and may slow the decline of the State’s unfunded liability,” Brian Daniels, director of the state Office of Management and Budget, wrote in the May 14 letter. “Further, as the State continues to face structural deficits in the coming years, any increased pension contributions may require cutting other programs or increasing revenues.”
At what cost?
As of June 30, 2025, the pension system stood at 66.3% funding, with a nearly $4.4 billion unfunded liability, according to the state’s actuarial valuation report. The state is expected to pay $405.2 million, or 6.8% of its general revenue, to cover its share of retirement contributions in the current fiscal year, Daniels wrote. 
A 10-member panel set up in 2023 under Rhode Island General Treasurer James Diossa’s office to consider the long-term impact of the 2011 pension reforms considered how the Rule of 90 would affect the health of the pension system in its final report in 2024.The Pension Advisory Working Group estimated the earlier retirement age would increase state and local contributions by $12.1 million in fiscal 2025, with annual contributions increasing in subsequent years. The measure would increase the unfunded liability by $106 million and decrease the funded ratio by half a percent, the report stated.
And it could diminish benefits for retirees, who by ending their careers five years earlier, lose out on the extra years of contributions.



Quotation







I’m not someone who's just counting down the clock, but it’s nice to know if I work 30 years, I have the option to leave when I would like to.


– Scott Conley, a special education teacher at Davies Career and Technical High School in Lincoln


Carla Rojo, a spokesperson for Diossa’s office, said the estimates included in the report reflect 2024 demographics, and would need to be updated based on present pension funding ratios and plan participants. 
Rojo did not directly answer when asked for Diossa’s stance on the proposal.
“Treasurer Diossa supports responsible and sustainable changes that do not jeopardize the long-term financial health and stability of the pension system,” Rojo wrote in an email Friday.
Senate President Valarie Lawson and House Speaker Christopher Blazejewski were similarly noncommittal, noting the legislation, if included in the fiscal 2028 budget, will be “thoroughly examined through the public committee review process.” Their spokespeople confirmed that McKee had not given them a heads up about his budget pledge beforehand.
Promises broken 
Supporters frame the proposal as a matter of fairness, resurrecting a promise to the 60,000 public employees that was “broken” through the 2011 pension reform.
It might also help rebalance the scales with Massachusetts, which has lured Rhode Island teachers with a more favorable benefits system, said Maribeth Calabro, president of the Rhode Island Federation of Teachers and Health Professionals. 
“We are effectively training our workforce only to watch them cross the border to a state that honors their service with a functional retirement contract,” Calabro wrote in a May 14 letter to lawmakers in support of the Rule of 90. “Rhode Island cannot continue to act as a ‘training ground’ for our neighbors while our own staffing levels reach a breaking point.”
Letting public employees and teachers retire earlier could heighten workforce challenges for cities and towns already plagued by vacancies and limited capacity, Ernie Almonte, president of The League of Cities and Towns, wrote in a letter to lawmakers. 
The bill, sponsored by Senate Majority Leader Frank Ciccone, a Providence Democrat, failed to advance out of the Senate Committee on Finance. The same fate came to the House companion, sponsored by Rep. Deborah Fellela, a Johnston Democrat and retired Providence public school teacher.
The measure does little for the 28,000 already retired state employees, whose pleas to restore the cost-of-living adjustments suspended in 2011 remain mostly unanswered.
But Conley sees it a sign of progress — small, but symbolic. He could retire at 62 rather than 65 if the rule is included in the fiscal 2028 budget.
 Will it sway his vote in the primary?
“I was already planning on voting for the governor,” Conley said, noting his appreciation for McKee’s signature on the charter school moratorium law.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Data centers unifying Hoosiers in opposition
description: While it often feels that there’s not much on which we can all agree, data centers are increasingly challenging that narrative. Seven in ten Americans now oppose the construction of AI data centers in their community, making it a rare topic of widespread consensus across age, political affiliation, and geography.  At Citizens Action Coalition, we’ve […]
text:
A sign opposing data centers is posted in Indianapolis on Wednesday, July 22, 2026. (Photo by Leslie Bonilla Muñiz/Indiana Capital Chronicle)  While it often feels that there’s not much on which we can all agree, data centers are increasingly challenging that narrative. Seven in ten Americans now oppose the construction of AI data centers in their community, making it a rare topic of widespread consensus across age, political affiliation, and geography. 
At Citizens Action Coalition, we’ve worked on many issues over more than five decades as Indiana’s leading consumer and environmental advocacy organization, yet none in recent memory have galvanized as much public attention — and opposition — as data centers. 
Unfortunately, sweeping data center opposition is being unfairly vilified and belittled by a small number of influential elites. These politicians, business leaders, and paid commentators seek to push their own agenda and further their own financial interests, which often coincides with doing Big Tech’s bidding.
Having lost control of the narrative, they are now lashing out with attacks seeking to divide and marginalize data center opponents. They condescendingly chide us about spreading “misinformation,” while they roll out the red carpet for Big Tech to operate in secrecy, mislead communities, and greenwash their products. They cherry-pick quotes and contort statistics to portray legitimate concerns as unreasonable hysteria. 
When all else fails, they try to smear the opposition through innuendo and invectives. Data center proponents derisively refer to community defenders as “NIMBYs,” and falsely claim we are against “growth,” “innovation,” and “progress.” As their social license has rapidly deteriorated, they have turned to unfounded and fantastical conspiracy theories that suggest China has tricked us into opposing data centers or is otherwise behind the opposition.
Temporarily banning data centers draws more interest from state, local officials

The truth is that ubiquitous resistance forming across Indiana communities has organically emerged in response to the onslaught of data center proposals that are sprouting next to residences and schools like a noxious, hard-to-kill weed. Each data center could use a city-size amount of electricity, millions of gallons of water every day, receive billions in state and local subsidies, generate dangerous levels of continuous loud noise, dump massive amounts of pollution into the environment, and further strain our aging electric grid. 
In October 2024, CAC became the first organization in the nation to call for a moratorium on large data centers, based on our analysis of the significant harms caused by these facilities. Since then, the projections have only gotten worse for Indiana, demonstrating our concerns were not only valid, but understated. We have since been joined by 26 Hoosier organizations and more than 500 organizations across the country in calling for a data center moratorium. 
Hoosiers are also rising to the occasion to defend their communities. Many thousands have attended public meetings and protests, contacted their elected officials, put up signs, knocked on doors, spoke at hearings, submitted written comments, and spread the word on social media. 
Local organizing is working in Indiana. Dozens of counties have passed moratoria or bans and nearly as many individual project proposals have been defeated or withdrawn in the past two years. 
We certainly need some data centers to enable the internet, cloud storage, social media, and other beneficial uses. But the process, pace, and purpose of the current AI-fueled data center frenzy are completely unsustainable, unaffordable, and a disaster for Indiana communities. It benefits a few to the considerable detriment of the many. 
We need stronger environmental safeguards, robust consumer protections, greater transparency, and meaningful opportunity for community input. But that’s just a start. Data centers are also highlighting the structural flaws underpinning our economic and political systems, which also deserve a broader conversation. 
It’s time for data center proponents to stop casting aspersions at concerned communities and Hoosier advocates who want the best for Indiana’s residents and come to the table with real solutions. Until then, the data center resistance will continue to grow stronger by the day.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: New Hampshire’s jail staffing challenge isn’t just about jails
description: One of the most important staffing decisions we’ve made at the Carroll County Department of Corrections had nothing to do with hiring. We have made it possible for our population to use secure tablets for calling and messaging 24 hours a day. Before that, people in our custody had to share a limited number of […]
text:
"People may take a job for a paycheck, and they stay because of how they're treated once they get there." Here, the Carroll County Department of Corrections in Ossipee. (Carroll County Department of Corrections photo)One of the most important staffing decisions we’ve made at the Carroll County Department of Corrections had nothing to do with hiring. We have made it possible for our population to use secure tablets for calling and messaging 24 hours a day.
Before that, people in our custody had to share a limited number of wall phones to call a spouse, child, attorney, or other important contact. Staff spent a surprising amount of time managing disputes over phone access. Once secure tablet communications were available around the clock, I’d estimate close to 80% of that friction disappeared.
What mattered wasn’t just the calmer housing unit; it was seeing my officers get out of the phone line business and back into the corrections business. Instead of managing disputes over access to a shared phone, they could focus on supervising the facility and supporting the people in it.
That matters because, like correctional facilities across New Hampshire, we’re solving a challenge shared by essential services around the state: How do you recruit good people for important jobs, and how do you keep them?
Most people don’t spend much time thinking about correctional officers. I get that. If we’re doing our jobs well, our work happens largely out of sight. But most people do understand what happens when schools can’t find teachers, hospitals can’t find nurses, or police departments struggle to fill vacancies. Communities feel it. Budgets feel it. The people doing the work certainly feel it.
Corrections departments face those same challenges. When I became superintendent, we had 16 vacancies and a starting wage of about $16 an hour. We were competing for employees with the McDonald’s and Dunkin’ down the street. For a small facility housing about 56 people and staffed by 36 officers, that wasn’t sustainable.
Several contracts later, starting pay is around $28 an hour, and we’re down to two openings. Pay was a critical part of that turnaround, yet it wasn’t the whole answer. People may take a job for a paycheck, and they stay because of how they’re treated once they get there.
Leadership sets the tone
My son is 17 and has played hockey most of his life. Several years ago, one of his coaches lost his composure every time a call didn’t go his team’s way. He let his frustration show by yelling at referees and throwing his hat. Before long, players did the same. The team’s attitude mirrored the coach’s, so tempers were shorter, and penalties grew.
Watching from the stands, I couldn’t help but think about leadership. The team plays with the coach’s attitude, and the same thing happens inside a correctional facility. Officers watch how leaders respond to pressure, setbacks, and mistakes. If leadership reacts with anger and frustration, that spreads. If leadership stays steady and accountable, so does the staff. 
Early in my time as superintendent, I stood in front of our staff and admitted something that wasn’t easy to say: I had been so close to the problems we were facing that I hadn’t realized I was contributing to some of them. You can’t expect employees to be honest about challenges or mistakes if leadership isn’t willing to go first.
Support starts with paying attention
The hardest moments in corrections are often the quiet ones that come after the emergency has passed.
Years ago, when I was a lieutenant, one of our newer officers responded to a serious incident involving a man going through alcohol withdrawal who was harming himself. It became an all-hands-on-deck effort to stabilize him while the rest of the facility continued operating around us. An hour later, that same officer was back on a food service assignment as if it were just another day.
I remember looking over and noticing she was standing by herself, so I went and asked how she was doing. She looked at me and said, “I’ve never seen anything like that before in my life.” That conversation has stayed with me because correctional officers are professionals. In difficult situations, they do what needs to be done and keep moving. But that doesn’t mean those experiences simply disappear when the shift ends. 
Like first responders, healthcare workers, and others in demanding professions, officers carry stress that people don’t always see. That’s one reason Carroll County will host Boulder Crest Foundation’s first full five-day Struggle Well program in New Hampshire this year.
I took the introductory course myself and in an exercise, I found myself responding more emotionally than I expected. The experience reinforced something important for me as a leader: if leadership treats vulnerability as weakness, employees will hide what they’re carrying. When that happens, we miss opportunities to support people before small struggles become larger ones.
Technology can help good people stay
Technology often gets discussed as a public safety issue or an operational issue, while it should also be talked about as a workforce issue. The tablet communication example is one reason.
Giving people better ways to stay connected with family and legal support reduces behavioral incidents, which makes housing units safer for incarcerated individuals and staff alike. The same holds true beyond calling and messaging. When people can access approved media and educational content on those tablets, they have constructive ways to spend their time, and we see fewer behavioral incidents across the unit as a whole. That benefit extends to everyone in the building, not just the people using the tablets. When officers don’t have to spend their shifts managing avoidable conflicts, they can focus on the parts of the job they signed up to do.
We’ve seen similar benefits with monitoring tools that help staff identify communications that warrant attention instead of manually reviewing hours of content. We’ve seen benefits from officer tablets that put schedules, reporting, and rounds on a single screen rather than requiring staff to bounce between systems and paperwork.
The tools do not replace people. They help people spend more of their time on work that matters. In a profession where every minute counts, that’s not a small thing. The test I apply to any technology is simple: Does it fit our facility? Does it support our staff? Does it make the work better?
If the answer is yes, it’s worth considering.
Creating a place where people want to stay
New Hampshire’s county superintendents talk often. Just like teachers across classrooms or nurses across hospitals, we sit on the same boards, compare notes, and learn from one another. We all understand the reality that we’re recruiting from many of the same talent pools, and so is the state.
Recruitment matters, yet retention is where the biggest opportunity exists. People stay when they trust their leaders. They stay when someone checks on them after a difficult day. They stay when they’re given tools that help them do their jobs effectively. They stay when they feel valued. 
So, when we find people who are willing to do hard work, the leaders’ responsibility is to create the kind of environment that makes them want to stay.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Pentagon fires Kansas journalist at Stars and Stripes in latest chapter of government censorship
description: When I read the headline, something told me that it referred to one of my former University of Kansas journalism students.  “Pentagon fires Stars and Stripes editor, publisher and reporter”  And so it did.  Lara Korte, a 2019 University of Kansas graduate of the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communications, was fired […]
text:
Lara Korte graduated from the University of Kansas' William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communications. She reported for Stars and Stripes and was fired on Friday. (Photo submitted by Lara Korte)When I read the headline, something told me that it referred to one of my former University of Kansas journalism students. 
“Pentagon fires Stars and Stripes editor, publisher and reporter” 
And so it did. 
Lara Korte, a 2019 University of Kansas graduate of the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communications, was fired Friday from the military publication “Stars and Stripes.” After she and her editor appeared on CBS News, the Pentagon fired both on the same day.
Korte said the notice she received labeled her broadcast comments as “insubordination.”
“Specifically, it singled out a phrase where I said I work for Stars and Stripes, not the Pentagon, not the administration and not any policy maker,” Korte wrote to me in an email from Germany after the firing. “My understanding in that context is that I was reaffirming Pentagon policy about Stars and Stripes’ editorial independence.”
In the process, one of Kansas’s best and brightest lost her job, another casualty in the Trump administration’s targeting of the press and facts. 
Korte grew up in Colwich, attended Bishop Carroll Catholic High School and worked for Kansas publications, including the University Daily Kansan and the Wichita Eagle.
During her time at KU, Korte was a juggernaut. Her investigative work for the student newspaper showed fellow students how to do watchdog reporting: articles about sexual assault, budgetary gambles, fraternity hazing and white nationalism on campus. 
“It’s very easy to look at the world and feel helpless when you see injustice,” Korte wrote to me, “and journalism, to me, was a chance to jump into the fray, dig into the facts, and make sure our public officials were being held to high standards. I never felt like any topic or subject was off limits — if it mattered to the public, it mattered to me.”
She wrote or contributed to more than 200 articles for the Daily Kansan — an extraordinary number in recent years — while advancing from reporter to news editor to editor-in-chief.   
“That training was indispensable for my career as a journalist,” Korte wrote. “It’s where I grew a spine.”
Having taught thousands of Jayhawks, I struggle to remember many individual students. Not so with Lara. Almost 10 years after she was in my classroom, I still use one of her projects as a classroom example.
From Germany, Korte has defended her work and confusion at being fired in interviews since Friday with National Public Radio and CBS News.  
Before her firing Friday, Korte said she “had received no complaints or concerns from Pentagon officials about my coverage.”
We’ve seen quite a bit of this during the last few years.
Public broadcasting was kneecapped when Trump resumed the presidency in 2025 by politicized cuts that threatened the very existence of PBS and NPR. On network TV, the credentialing power of the FCC hung over the heads of late-night comedians like Jimmy Kimmel and Stephen Colbert in an effort to make their bosses quake and retreat. Lawsuits from Trump cowed the ABC and CBS networks to settle cases that media lawyers saw as frivolous. 
The only sign of the Trump administration not getting what it wants: A court rebuffed the Department of Defense’s effort to restrict reporters within the Pentagon — but only after the policy was in effect for more than eight months.
During the past two years, the federal government repeatedly has aimed its BB gun at free expression. Ping. It knocks down independent journalists. Ping. It picks off responsible public media outlets. Ping. Ping.
Imagine if someone stepped in front of this petulant, armed child, wrenching back the BB gun. Even more fantastical, imagine if Congress — the ultimate absentee parent — was the one to act.
The Trumpian pattern of censorship and intimidation seems pulled from a playbook. Consider the particular media the Trump administration has challenged. Both public broadcasting and Stars and Stripes have complex, if not blurry, combinations of funding and editorial control.
The Corporation for Public Broadcasting was the independent, parent company for public television and public radio. 
But the CPB was partially funded by Congress. How does that work?
The Department of Defense explains that Stars and Stripes should provide military “personnel with an independent source of news and information through the Stars and Stripes Media Organization.”
But Korte and her editor could be fired. Why is that permitted?
If you need proof that the relationship between the Department of Defense and Stars and Stripes is confusing, see this 17-page instruction document with a table of contents and glossary. Two pages of references point to obscure and arcane manuals, such as “DoD Manual 8910.01, Volume 2, ‘DoD Information Collections Manual: Procedures for DoD Public Information Collections,’ June 30, 2014, as amended.”
For both public broadcasting and Stars and Stripes, there was and still is a hazy, refutable system of quasi-independence. Basically, press freedom was a norm waiting to be broken by an administration brazen enough to do so.
I am not sure that many Americans understand this narrow parsing of journalistic independence and funding. (I’m not sure that I do.) Our popular confusion makes it easier for the Trump administration to quash journalistic operations, fire employees and steer coverage. The Trump administration likely sees this nebulous region of public journalism as a place to wedge its crowbar and pry for leverage.
Korte sees something different. She sees virtue in public journalism.
“The United States has always viewed freedom of the press and freedom of speech as foundational rights for Americans,” Korte wrote, “and I believe public funding for various independent media outlets like PBS, Stars and Stripes and Voice of America is an expression of those values. To me, it’s a show to the American people that the government believes in their individual right to information.”
With free expression crises multiplying, free expression has become tenuous for journalists who rely on the government to do their job. We assumed that the First Amendment was a robust bulwark — a law that would protect responsible, publicly supported journalists. That’s what we were taught from elementary school on.
Instead, we find the Trump administration plinking down media outlets one by one with its mischievous, bullying BB gun of censorship.
Eric Thomas teaches visual journalism and photojournalism at the William Allen White School of Journalism and Mass Communication at the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Experts caution against complacency after slow start to this year’s hurricane season
description: It’s been a quiet Atlantic hurricane season so far – the season is nearly halfway through, and there hasn’t been a single hurricane. But a slow start doesn’t guarantee a slow finish, and peak storm season still lies ahead. 2026 has had the slowest start to the hurricane season of any year since 2022, said […]
text:
An Augusta residence avoided any serious damage from a large tree that was knocked over after Hurricane Helene made landfall in 2024. Stanley Dunlap/Georgia RecorderIt’s been a quiet Atlantic hurricane season so far – the season is nearly halfway through, and there hasn’t been a single hurricane. But a slow start doesn’t guarantee a slow finish, and peak storm season still lies ahead.
2026 has had the slowest start to the hurricane season of any year since 2022, said AccuWeather lead hurricane expert Alex DaSilva, when the Atlantic basin finished August without a single hurricane. That season went on to produce seven hurricanes between September and November, but AccuWeather does not predict another late season surge this year.
Any hurricane that would make landfall in the U.S. would be the first since October 2024 after going all of 2025 without a hurricane from the Atlantic coming ashore, according to AccuWeather.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The wind conditions in the Atlantic are not favorable to hurricanes, said National Weather Service meteorologist Sam Marlow.
“A couple of things that you need for hurricanes, you need really warm ocean waters and you need fairly calm winds aloft, so up in the atmosphere,” he said. “And right now the one thing that we don’t really have is those calm winds aloft.”
El Niño, a recurring climate pattern causing warm waters in the Pacific Ocean, is giving east coasters a hand by increasing wind shear in the Atlantic.
“These waters basically form a high pressure bubble that kind of guides the jet stream and the flow of the jet stream into a pattern that is not conducive to hurricanes,” Marlow said. “What it can lead to, at least for our area, is a slightly wetter pattern as we go into the winter months, but other than that, the biggest impact would be tamping down those tropical effects.”
Marlow stressed that Georgians should not become complacent just because there haven’t been any hurricanes in a while.
“Even though we are in an El Niño pattern, it doesn’t mean that we’re not going to get any kind of tropical systems,” he said. “So still stay aware of things as we go through September through October and November.”
Marlow added that Hurricane Andrew spawned during an El Niño year. That 1992 storm caused havoc when it made landfall as a Category 5 hurricane, leaving 65 dead and causing more than $28 billion in damages, according to the National Weather Service.
“It’s not something we can really put our guards down for,” he said.
DaSilva said historically, up to 70% of tropical storms form from late August through the end of November.
He added that a tropical wave coming off of Africa is moving into a pocket of low wind shear and high moisture. While many forecasting models predict a storm that curves into the open ocean, DaSilva said people on the Eastern Seaboard should keep their eyes on this wave as it progresses across the Atlantic.
AccuWeather has scaled back its predictions for the season from its July forecast. Their model now predicts nine named storms, down from 11. Three of those are expected to be hurricanes with one major hurricane, down from a predicted five hurricanes including two major hurricanes.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Medicaid changes to reduce payments for hospital services in at least 37 states, including Ohio
description: New research shows that at least 37 states, including Ohio, are facing billions in reduced federal payments for hospital services because of the Trump/Republican Medicaid funding changes. The limits imposed as part of the 2025 federal congressional budget reconciliation bill, championed by President Donald Trump as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, may mean bi[...]
text:
(Photo via Getty Images)New research shows that at least 37 states, including Ohio, are facing billions in reduced federal payments for hospital services because of the Trump/Republican Medicaid funding changes.
The limits imposed as part of the 2025 federal congressional budget reconciliation bill, championed by President Donald Trump as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, may mean billions less in federal funding and state-directed payments, which could include devastating effects, especially to rural and financially struggling hospitals.
The healthcare research group KFF released a new analysis estimating $60 billion in current federal spending for hospitals could be reduced when new limits from the reconciliation bill take full effect.
That number is a moving goalpost, as the changes aren’t all being implemented at the same time.
“It does not represent the amount by which federal payments would be reduced in any given year, since these limits will be phased in over time starting in January 2028, and will fully take effect at different times in different states,” KFF wrote in the analysis.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The group also estimated an overall federal Medicaid spending reduction of $911 billion based on the terms of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
The reduction in state-directed payments to hospitals will have varying impacts from state to state, and even from hospital to hospital, based on how much the states are spending for their individual Medicaid programs.
Hospitals operating on relatively high margins could see the changes land more softly on their bottom line.
“On the other hand, hospitals with relatively low operating margins (like rural hospitals and those serving relatively large shares of Medicaid patients) may adapt in ways that affect Medicaid enrollees’ access to care, such as by cutting service lines or closing,” KFF researchers stated.
Ohio’s Medicaid program serves more than a quarter of the state’s population, accounting for nearly 3 million residents, and is the second most common form of health insurance in the state, according to the Health Policy Institute of Ohio.
The institute noted the Medicaid budget in the state exceeded $43 billion in fiscal year 2025, with the federal government paying 68.5% of the total costs.
With the budget reconciliation bill restricting the ability for states to raise revenue through methods like provider taxes, along with placing caps on the amount states can reimburse providers through those state-directed payments, Ohio will have to account for the funding gap.
As part of the changes from the budget bill, Ohio has to change or eliminate a health insuring corporation franchise fee by July 1, 2027.
The fee is calculated using state Medicaid member counts, and is a provider tax overseen by the Ohio Department of Medicaid.
The health policy institute’s research showed the change or elimination of the fee could result in annual losses to state revenue of $640 million starting in 2028, along with $1.5 billion in lost federal matching dollars.
“States may pursue reducing Medicaid expenditures, however, doing so is likely to have negative health and economic consequences for Ohioans,” the institute said in a March analysis of the reconciliation bill’s changes to Medicaid.
The analysis also said Medicaid enrollees could see a loss of optional covered services, such as dental coverage, as a result of the changes, and Ohioans may have to pay more for things like prescription drugs.
Originally, the total funding losses to the state’s Medicaid program were estimated at $33 billion over the next decade.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio bill would create a limit on reimbursement rates for foster care placements
description: A newly proposed bipartisan bill would create a cap on reimbursement rates for Ohio foster care placements.  Ohio state Reps. Darnell Brewer, D-Cleveland, and Justin Pizzulli, R-Scioto County, recently introduced Ohio House Bill 984.  “This legislation aims to provide greater financial predictability for counties, fiscal responsibility for taxpayers, support[...]
text:
The Ohio Statehouse in Columbus. (Photo by David DeWitt, Ohio Capital Journal.)A newly proposed bipartisan bill would create a cap on reimbursement rates for Ohio foster care placements. 
Ohio state Reps. Darnell Brewer, D-Cleveland, and Justin Pizzulli, R-Scioto County, recently introduced Ohio House Bill 984. 
“This legislation aims to provide greater financial predictability for counties, fiscal responsibility for taxpayers, support providers, and most importantly, help ensure that Ohio’s foster youth have access to care and resources they need to thrive,” Brewer said at a recent press conference. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The bill would require the Ohio Department of Children and Youth to set reimbursement rates for the placement and care of children in foster care. 
“My goal with House Bill 984 is to ensure that the system safeguarding our children’s welfare remains viable by reigning in out of control rising placement costs,” Pizzulli said. 
Counties across Ohio are facing financial challenges due to rising placements and cost of care, the lawmakers said. 
Scioto County went from having 407 children in foster care in 2022 to having about 197 children in foster care today, but the county’s placement costs have increased, Pizzulli said. 
“We’re spending roughly three times as much per child as we were just five years ago,” he said. 
“Many of the children coming into care today have much more significant needs than we saw years ago. Providers are dealing with staffing shortages, wages have gone up, and the cost of providing this care has gone up.”
The costs in Scioto County surpassed $8 million last year, Pizzulli said. 
“What we are facing is an unsolvable math problem,” said Scioto County Commissioner Scottie Powell. 
“Counties pay nearly three quarters of all placement costs through levies and their general funds, with the federal reimbursement covering the remaining one quarter,” Powell said. 
The number of Ohio children placed in custody has dropped 9% since 2020, but costs have increased by 68% — a jump from $231 million to $389 million, he said. 
The average cost of care for a child in Ross County went from $59.64 per day to $151.55 per day and in Hocking County it went from $65.94 to $181.02 per day, Powell said. 
Scioto County Job and Family Services Director Tamela Moore Morton said they have a child in custody “who exhibits extreme behaviors” and has been placed in at least a dozen different placements around Ohio. 
“Because of behaviors, the facilities can decide to increase our daily rate to any amount they want, without necessarily increasing the level of care,” she said. 
“They know this child is hard to place, so they take advantage of the situation and charge the county unreasonably, or threaten discharge, or return the child to the lobby of the agency. There is no limit or cap on the amount they can ask for.” 
The child was on track to use nearly $1 million dollars of Scioto County’s funding in one year, Morton said. 
“That’s not the child’s fault,” she said. 
“But when you have 200 other children that need those same protections, how do you choose who gets the services with the limited funds? Every county either has or will have a similar situation with a high needs child that could bankrupt their county in the blink of an eye. Unfortunately, Scioto County is already there.” 
Pizzulli mentioned the 16 children from Vinton County who were found by law enforcement authorities in terrible conditions at the end of June and how the therapeutic foster care costs needed for each child (ranging from $150-250 each day) would have bankrupted the southeastern Ohio county. 
The Ohio Controlling Board recently approved $1 million in emergency funds to help the 16 children from Vinton County, whose ages range from 18 months to 18 years old. 
“It’s imperative, especially in circumstances like that, that counties have the resources that they need to make appropriate placements and ensure children receive the care and support they deserve,” Pizzulli said. 
“I don’t want to wait for another county to reach a breaking point.” 
There were more than 14,000 children in foster care in Ohio in 2025 while the state had more than 6,000 certified foster homes, Brewer said. 
“Every foster youth deserves a safe, loving, and stable home,” Brewer said.  
“Foster parents and providers deserve the support they need to provide. We are trying to create reasonable guardrails, not barriers, to appropriate care.”
The Ohio lawmakers are currently on break and will come back after the November election. Any bill that does not pass before the two-year General Assembly ends in December would have to be reintroduced. 
“What we know of the General Assembly is that if we really want to do something, we can do it, and we can do it very, very quickly if we want to,” Pizzulli said.
