name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Democrats don’t agree on how to talk about trans athletes. Just look at Ohio.
description: This story was originally reported by Amanda Becker of The 19th. Meet Amanda and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. It took mere minutes for the U.S. Supreme Court decision upholding state bans on trans athletes competing in women’s and girls’ sports to reverberate in Ohio’s competitive governor’s race — and […]
text:
Dr. Amy Acton, Ohio Democratic gubernatorial candidate and former director of the Ohio Department of Health, speaks to supporters during a rally on April 28, 2026 in Cincinnati, Ohio. (Jon Cherry/Getty Images).
This story was originally reported by Amanda Becker of The 19th.  Meet Amanda and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
It took mere minutes for the U.S. Supreme Court decision upholding state bans on trans athletes competing in women’s and girls’ sports to reverberate in Ohio’s competitive governor’s race — and the reactions from the Republican and Democratic nominees were all but indistinguishable.
“Ohio has barred men from competing with women in women’s sports and the Supreme Court now held that it’s constitutional,” Republican Vivek Ramaswamy told a Toledo newspaper.
Ramaswamy, a pharmaceutical entrepreneur, called the ruling “common sense” and pledged to enforce an Ohio law containing a ban on trans athletes in school-age sports. It was vetoed by the state’s current Republican Gov. Mike DeWine and opposed by every Democrat in the state legislature.
Then, Democrat Dr. Amy Acton weighed in.
“I do not support boys playing in girls sports. This is already settled law in Ohio, and as governor I will enforce and uphold the law,” the physician, who served as DeWine’s public health director, said in a statement to the same newspaper.
“As a doctor, public servant, and a mom, I will always stand up for fairness and protect kids’ health and safety,” she added.
Two candidates, from two different parties, taking the same public position, using the same language — wording favored by President Donald Trump’s MAGA movement that misgendered transgender athletes by referring to them as men instead of trans women. And in Acton’s case, language that misgendered trans children.
Democrats have been trying to figure out how to respond to Republicans’ anti-trans attacks since former Vice President Kamala Harris lost to Trump in the 2024 election. Republican campaigns and allied political groups spent more than $215 million that election cycle on ads targeting Democratic candidates’ past support for trans people and LGBTQ+ issues, according to data from AdImpact, which tracks political ad spending. In the final weeks of the campaign, tens of millions of dollars worth of these ads targeting Harris blanketed key suburbs in battleground states. They ended with the line: “Kamala is for they/them; President Trump is for you.” Harris never figured out how to respond. Internal research from the top super PAC supporting Harris showed that the “they/them” ads, on average, moved viewers 2.7 points in Trump’s favor.
The conversation among Democrats about how the party’s candidates should — or should not — respond to anti-trans attacks has since taken up a lot of oxygen in Washington as party strategists debate the best course forward.
Now, the conversation is consuming Democrats in Ohio.
Acton’s initial statement on the day of the Supreme Court ruling landed like a lead balloon with the state’s LGBTQ+ groups and leaders, the vast majority of whom were enthusiastic about her candidacy and the potential to beat Ramaswamy, who said during a GOP presidential primary debate in late 2023 that being trans was a “mental health disorder.”
Several Ohio-based LGBTQ+ leaders told The 19th that they expected to hear more from the candidate herself. They hoped she might clean up the inarticulate language she used misgendering trans children, or offer additional reassurances to LGBTQ+ Ohioans that she would have their backs.
But no public or private reassurances came.

Transgender rights advocates stood outside of the Ohio Statehouse to oppose and bring attention to participation in high school and college sports. (Stephen Zenner/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty Images)
Equality Ohio, one of the state’s largest groups working to protect the rights of LGBTQ+ people, updated Acton’s status on its 2026 Candidate Scorecard to “pending” from an “A” grade.
Ramaswamy’s “F” rating has remained unchanged.
“This reflects our belief that accountability is still possible, and that the door remains open at this time. Should Dr. Acton choose to take meaningful steps forward, we will update the status accordingly,” the group said in a statement.
The ratings change was announced during what was initially branded as a “conversation” between Acton’s campaign, the state party and LGBTQ+ stakeholders that only further inflamed the situation. The meeting — and its fallout — was first reported by the Buckeye Flame, a Cleveland-based news site focused on Ohio’s LGBTQ+ community.
The vice chair of the Ohio Democratic Party’s Pride Caucus, who is trans, was not admitted to the meeting and had to participate on speakerphone via the chair. It quickly became clear that it was less a conversation than a chance for participants to air concerns without any response from the campaign, attendees told The 19th. One described Acton’s campaign manager, Philip Stein, as “looking like someone who wanted to crawl under the table.”
Another participant said they went into the meeting thinking it could be a “teachable moment” that could repair relations between the campaign and Ohio’s LGBTQ+ community; they left feeling like the misgendering of trans children was intentional and a “cynical, consultant-driven play” to appeal to conservative voters.
“It felt like they were trying to throw trans people under the bus to provoke a backlash,” the person added.
Meeting participants who spoke to The 19th all asked to not be identified because the campaign has told them that talking to the press precludes future conversations.
Acton’s campaign wrote in an email to The 19th that she “will always stand up for Ohioans, including the LGBT community. As governor, she is committed to standing up to discrimination and ensuring all Ohioans receive equal protection under the law.”
More than 11 percent of Ohio’s adult population is LGBTQ+, according to an analysis released this month by the Human Rights Campaign, and research shows that queer people vote at higher rates than the overall adult public. While LGBTQ+ voters tend to favor Democrats, participants on the Zoom call told The 19th that the fallout would likely dampen queer voters’ willingness to support Acton by donating money, putting signs in their yards, going door-to-door in the final push or phonebanking.
Recent opinion polls show Acton and Ramaswamy nearly tied, trading single-digit leads well within polls’ margins of error.

Governors are uniquely positioned to defend or reject anti-trans bills: Congress remains deadlocked on all but the most pressing, must-pass legislation; the U.S. Supreme Court decided that state-legislature passed bans on trans athletes in sports can stand.
The law at issue in Ohio, H.B. 68, also prohibits minors from receiving gender-affirming care. DeWine vetoed it for that reason, but the GOP supermajority in the state legislature overrode his veto. The legality of the ban on gender-affirming care is a live question before the state Supreme Court.
Acton, in an interview with The 19th following the U.S. Supreme Court ruling but before the campaign’s Zoom meeting with LGBTQ+ leaders, offered a more nuanced position on the law than she has shared publicly:
“This is a political battle,” Acton said, “and sadly, people are using people’s healthcare and personal decisions and choices as a way to pit us intentionally against one another, and it has been a successful tactic politically to scare people and frighten everyday Ohioans.”
“I’m also here to fight for our common humanity,” she continued. “The governor vetoed pretty draconian legislation, and the way he did that is he took advice from folks: I, amongst many people, gave advice. He listened to families. As governor, I will always research issues, listen to the absolute best experts in the field, as he did, talk to families and understand their personal decisions and what’s going on with their healthcare, with their physicians.”
She added that Democrats needed to break the GOP supermajority in the statehouse so gubernatorial vetoes could not be overridden.
Acton’s campaign did not explain why she has not incorporated a more holistic approach to LGBTQ+ issues, like the one she described to The 19th, during campaign trail discussions. The campaign, as well as Acton herself, often point out that she is trying to become the first Democrat to lead Ohio in 15 years. A single Ohio Supreme Court justice is the only elected Democrat in statewide office; Ramaswamy is a billionaire self-funding his campaign with the backing of Peter Thiel, a tech billionaire and Trump ally.
Still, Acton’s public statement on trans athletes puts her at the conservative end of an array of approaches being taken by Democrats on issues impacting trans people in the country’s five most competitive gubernatorial races.
In Georgia, which has a ban on trans athletes competing in public school and college sports, Keisha Lance Bottoms is trying to flip the governor’s seat for Democrats in a race against Republican healthcare executive Rick Jackson. Shortly after the Supreme Court ruling, Bottoms’ campaign told a local news outlet that, as a mother, she “understands that there are important differences between male and female athletes in competitive sports. However, Keisha believes decisions about athletic participation should be made by appropriate athletic governing bodies — not by politicians.” Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, also told a local editorial board regarding gender-affirming care: “I do not believe the government should weigh in on medical decisions by Georgians and their physicians,” and that those decisions should not be “dictated by politicians looking to score political points.” Nearly every reliable poll has shown Bottoms ahead of Jackson since they won their respective primaries.
In Wisconsin, term-limited Democratic Gov. Tony Evers has repeatedly blocked bans related to trans athletes and gender-affirming care from taking effect. Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, the Democratic nominee for governor, has said that decisions regarding trans athletes should be left up to the state’s high school athletics association. He told HuffPost: “We don’t have to throw out our morals, our ethics … we don’t have to capitulate and get involved in these cultural wars Republicans try to throw out there because they don’t have anything to run on.” Polling conducted after the state’s Aug. 12 primaries shows Crowley with a slight lead over his Republican opponent, U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany, who is also a small business owner.
In Nevada, where sitting Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo tried but failed to get a “Protect Girls’ Sports” initiative onto 2026 ballots, Democratic Attorney General and gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford has differentiated between his own beliefs and how he would govern. “I personally do not support trans athletes competing in sports opposite their gender assigned at birth,” Ford told a Nevada newspaper, using language preferred by LGBTQ+ rights groups. “But let’s be clear, Lombardo doesn’t care about this issue; he’s only using it as a political ploy to drum up support for his flailing reelection campaign.” Polls show Lombardo with a lead in the race.
In Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand responded with a simple “no” when a conservative radio host asked him in May 2025 whether “biological males” should play women’s sports — another way to describe trans women that many in the LGBTQ+ community find offensive. But Sand, the state’s auditor, has also backed protections for trans people. He said at a town hall that it was “wrong” for Iowa Republicans to repeal state civil rights protections for trans people — Iowa was the first state in the country to do so. “You should not be fired from your job in the state of Iowa for being different. You should not be evicted from your apartment,” Sand said. Polls have for months shown Sand with a lead over Republican businessman Zach Lahn. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report last week moved the Iowa gubernatorial contest from the “toss up” category to “leans Democratic” in its competitiveness rankings.

John Neffinger, a Democratic strategist and past communications director for the Democratic National Committee, said Democrats should remember that, beyond sports, a majority of voters believe trans people should be protected from discrimination. Candidates shouldn’t be afraid to highlight their desire to support basic protections for LGBTQ+ people, he added.
Polling consistently shows, for example, that more than half of voters prefer the Democratic Party’s approach to handling issues impacting trans people over solutions offered by the Republican Party. That includes polls conducted by Fox News.
The political challenge for Democratic candidates is that nearly three-quarters of American adults say they are “uncomfortable” with trans athletes competing on sports teams that align with their gender identities, according to data from the nonpartisan Pew Research Center. Republicans have used Democrats’ past pro-LGBTQ+ stances to highlight this perceived vulnerability with voters in widespread attack ads. The dynamic has put many battleground Democratic candidates in between a voting populace not ready to largely embrace trans athletes in kids’ sports and many LGBTQ+ and progressive groups that want candidates to offer full-throated support for trans people as they face existential threats from the Trump administration.
In focus groups of a dozen or so undecided voters, Neffinger said, there might be one person who objects to LGBTQ+ protections on moral grounds, but the vast majority show a high level of empathy for the challenges trans people face in public life — especially trans children and their parents.
“When you talk about sports, what you get from people is, ‘Now, that’s not right,’” Neffinger said. “But even then, they don’t want politicians picking on kids, they get that that’s not cool.”
For several years now, Neffinger has been in a cohort of Democratic strategists trying to help and encourage the party’s candidates and lawmakers to figure out how to meet Republicans’ anti-trans attacks head on. There are ways for candidates to walk the line between where the average voter is and where LGBTQ+ and other progressive advocacy groups want them to be, he said. They just have to be willing to do it.
Neffinger pointed to a 2025 statement from Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto shortly after the Nevada Democrat voted against the Republican-offered “Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act,” as an effective example of messaging that resonates with middle-of-the-road voters.
Cortez Masto’s statement read: “I support fair play and safety and do not support transgender athletes competing in girls’ and women’s sports when it compromises those principles. I believe local schools, student athletes, coaches, and parents are much better equipped to implement fair, strong policies on this issue than politicians in Congress.”
Staking out a fairness-based position — for everyone — paves the way for politicians to offer different policy solutions as circumstances demand, Neffinger said. That could mean allowing prepubescent athletes to compete on teams that match their gender identities, or on a case-by-case basis permitting trans athletes who received gender-affirming care before going through puberty, he added.
“Saying ‘no boys in girls sports’ feels like the latest way to dodge — ‘don’t make me talk about this.’ It doesn’t look like leadership, it looks like a cop-out, and it actually feels like you’re picking on trans kids,” he added.
Democrats of all stripes — centrists, progressives and LGBTQ+ advocates — also point to the 2025 governor’s race in Virginia, when Democratic former Rep. Abigail Spanberger beat Republican Winsome Earle-Sears, the state’s former lieutenant governor who spent as much as $9 million attacking Spanberger’s support for trans rights. Spanberger beat Earle-Sears by more than 15 points, and by nearly 30 points in Loudoun County, an exurban area near Washington, D.C., where anti-trans ads were believed to have hurt Harris the year before. Harris won Virginia, but only by about 5 points.
The various Democratic factions agree that what made Spanberger’s approach successful was that she introduced voters to her values early on, then took on anti-trans attacks as a matter of discrimination. Spanberger also emphasized that parents and doctors should make decisions for children, and she took voters’ concerns about fairness in sports seriously.
“Leaders must take a joint approach: fiercely defending LGBTQI+ people from discrimination and advocating for policies that will lift up families across the country,” the Center for American Progress, a Democratic policy organization, concluded in a recent analysis that caused ripples in Washington by recommending the party’s base accept some restrictions on trans athletes in youth sports.
Nan Whaley, the former Democratic mayor of Dayton, Ohio, and the party’s gubernatorial nominee in 2022, acknowledged that the political landscape related to LGBTQ+ issues has shifted to the right since her unsuccessful bid. She is an enthusiastic supporter of Acton and believes that, despite the falling out between her campaign and LGBTQ+ groups, voters should trust her. Whaley said that trans Ohioans have shared fears with her about their safety; some have asked whether she thinks they should leave the state, given its politics.
“If Vivek Ramaswamy wins, I don’t know what I can say to them, but I know what I can say if Amy Acton is governor,” Whaley said.“That’s what’s at stake.”

title: Ohio lawmakers must prevent Kroger’s surveillance pricing scam
description: Kroger’s controversial customer surveillance scheme was recently the subject of harsh bipartisan criticism in Congress. Ohio lawmakers have an opportunity to join the nationwide effort to protect consumers from the Cincinnati company’s pricing program. Kroger was the literal poster child for bad corporate behavior at the U.S. Senate hearing called, “Your Dat[...]
text:
The Kroger Co. corporate headquarters is seen in downtown Cincinnati. (Photo by Scott Olson/Getty Images)Kroger’s controversial customer surveillance scheme was recently the subject of harsh bipartisan criticism in Congress. Ohio lawmakers have an opportunity to join the nationwide effort to protect consumers from the Cincinnati company’s pricing program.
Kroger was the literal poster child for bad corporate behavior at the U.S. Senate hearing called, “Your Data, Their Profit: The Consumer Cost of AI Surveillance Pricing.”
In front of a sign emblazoned with Kroger’s name, Republican U.S. Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Missouri, stated “Kroger is not just a grocery store … It is a data-selling mega-corporation” that earns “a third of its income … from selling the personal data of its own customers.”
The ire came from both sides of the aisle. Democratic U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Illinois, explained that, “Kroger’s loyalty program uses your data to predict exactly how much money you make.”
In short, surveillance pricing is a tool companies use to learn as much as they can about shoppers, including our income and education level, then leverage that information to charge each individual the maximum price they will pay. In Kroger’s case, it sells collected customer data to other companies, earning over $500 million last year.
Surveillance pricing may sound like science fiction, but it’s anything but. A former chief data officer of Visa testified before the Senate that it already costs the typical American household roughly $1,800 a year.
Hawley called surveillance pricing “the unholy trinity of everything Americans hate: spying on people, ripping them off, and taking away jobs.”
More than 2,000 shoppers have written to KrogerHurtsFamilies.com, a portal my organization opened this summer, to report how the company scams customers.
The spying: As one customer put it, “what at first seemed innocent … I now see as an absolute invasion of my privacy. They are tracking me! I feel like a bug under their corporate microscope.”
The ripping off: Hundreds of customers tell us they’re overcharged at the register, and a Consumer Reports exposé confirms it’s systemic: shoppers at Kroger stores nationwide paid nearly 20% more than the advertised sale price because of expired tags and other errors.
The jobs: As it turns out, Kroger cutting its workforce may be part of the pricing problem. “I work at Kroger and the problem with items ringing up wrong is because they cut hours,” a worker shared. “They don’t have enough people doing tags.”
Kroger is working to remedy this not by hiring more workers but by rolling out electronic shelf labels: AI-driven technology that could allow the grocer to change prices in an instant based on the weather or other temporary factors – or even what it knows about us and our families. Flu going around? Kroger could jack up the prices of cold medicine or tissues just when we need these products most.
Kroger says it doesn’t engage in this kind of surge or personalized pricing. But it won’t commit to not using these tools against us, and it has spent millions of dollars developing secret shopper profiles, digital price tags, facial recognition technology, and partnerships with big AI companies: the exact infrastructure it’d need to make each of us pay the most we’ll tolerate. Nobody spends that kind of money building a machine they don’t intend to use.
Kroger’s history gives us every reason to believe it intends to. A senior executive admitted under oath that Kroger raised milk and egg prices above inflation during the pandemic, raking in record profits. The company also admitted to charging higher prices in “no-competition” zones: places where shoppers have few other grocery options.
The machine is built, and the motive is on the record. Right now, the only thing standing between Ohio shoppers and the “on” switch is Kroger’s word.
Other statehouses are not waiting to find out what that word is worth. Lawmakers in at least 11 states introduced surveillance-pricing bills, and bipartisan bills are moving in Congress.
Ohio, the one state with the most at stake and the most leverage, has introduced nothing.
That’s why it’s time Ohio officials crack down on surveillance pricing before it’s too late.
Taylor Warren is the president of the Center for Responsible Food Business, a nonprofit dedicated to promoting corporate social responsibility to build a better food system. Through industry engagement, research, and consumer education efforts, the Center works to advance practices that benefit all stakeholders from the farm to the dinner table.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. skill games could disappear in October. Businesses that rely on them are worried.
description: A state Supreme Court ruling could force skill games out of businesses and nonprofits unless lawmakers agree on how to regulate and tax them.
text:
A skill games parlor in Williamsport, Pa. (Photo by Peter Hall/Capital-Star)This story was originally published by WITF.
The four machines at the Highspire VFW in Dauphin County don’t take up much space. They look like arcade games, and people sit to play them, sometimes for hours at a time.
With their flashing lights and chance to win money, they look a bit like casino slot machines. But unlike slot machines, they don’t make noise, and customers can play them in places such as laundry mats, gas stations and VFWs.
They’re called “skill games,” and they have become a fixture in some gathering places – and an important source of revenue for the businesses that host them.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
They have also been at the center of Pennsylvania’s state budget battles and political fights for years.
Now, the machines could disappear from those locations in October.
The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled in June that skill games are slot machines under state law and that unlicensed skill games are unlawful. The court stayed enforcement of its ruling for 120 days, giving lawmakers until October to decide whether to create a regulatory system.
Michael Barley demonstrates how to play skill games at the Highspire VFW in Dauphin County. (Photo by Hayley O’Brien/WITF)
For organizations such as the Highspire VFW, the stakes are high.
Sue McMurray is She says the nonprofit is raising funds for a new roof and can’t afford to lose a revenue source.
“Without those skills machines, it will set us back a lot,” she said. “We’ll never be able to do the things we need to do… to keep this nonprofit in business.”
It’s possible Republicans and Democrats could reach a deal when it comes to skill games when they return to Harrisburg in September. But lawmakers did not include a skill games measure in the state budget agreement reached this summer.
Industry advocates are urging lawmakers to regulate and tax the games rather than eliminate them.
There are about 70,000 skill games throughout Pennsylvania, and themachines have operated without a comprehensive statewide regulatory system for nearly 15 years. Supporters say they provide an additional source of income for small businesses, bars, taverns and nonprofit organizations. 
Shay’s Vending operates arcade and skill games in various locations including the Highspire VFW.
Manager Willie Shay says the new industry allowed his family business to evolve from its start, offering jukeboxes and pool tables.

“Shay’s Vending’s been around since 1938 and it saved our business… it’s savings a lot of nonprofits and bars and clubs,” he said. “If this ban comes through and nothing’s done, the fallout’s going to be really scary.”
Doug Sprankle is president of the Pennsylvania Taverns and Players Association (PATAP), a nonprofit that advocates for legislation further regulating and taxing the skill games industry.
His family’s business operates three grocery stores in Western Pennsylvania,and he says implementing skill games machines generated revenue that allowed the company to provide health insurance for their employees. 
According to a report from the Independent Fiscal Office, the machines each generate an estimated $47,000 in a year.
“Our story is a lot like a lot of the people you hear from that have skill games in small businesses,” he said.
Sprankle wants regulation to weed out “bad actors” that operate terminals that aren’t technically skill games or opened “pop-up casinos.”
“The idea originally was to supplement income for that organization or business, not to be the number one draw to the facility,” he said.
“Regulation will clear a lot of that up,” said Michael Barley, director of public affairs for Pace-O-Matic, which develops skill game software. “We’re not the only issue that Harrisburg has not figured out recently.”
 Laws proposed

Lawmakers failed to regulate the games as part of this year’s budget.
PATAP and other advocates are encouraging support for HB2213 and SB1079.
The bills would establish a $500 fee for each skill game terminal and set a statewide limit of 50,000.
The proposed laws would generate $300 million every year. A report from the Independent Fiscal Office estimates the games would eventually bring in more than $1 billion a year.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Guthrie exhausts appeals to regain council seat lost after a 2024 felony theft hearing
description: Former Harford County Councilman Dion Guthrie is not backing down from claims he was wrongfully removed from office after entering a no-contest plea to felony theft charges, even after the Maryland Supreme Court rejected his case, ending his two-year fight.
text:
Then-Harford County Councilman Dion Guthrie (D), who lost his seat after pleading no contest in 2024 to felony theft charges. The Supreme Court of Maryland on Friday declined to hear his appeal of his removal from office. (File photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)A former Harford County Councilman is not backing down from claims he was wrongfully removed from office after entering a no contest plea to felony theft charges, even after the Maryland Supreme Court rejected his case Friday.
The high court’s decision ends the nearly two-year effort by Dion Guthrie, a Democrat, to overturn his removal from office.
Guthrie was removed in 2024 after pleading nolo contendere to felony theft charges from the union where he was a longtime officer. The plea, under the Maryland Constitution, triggered his immediate removal from office “by operation of law.”
In a phone interview Monday, Guthrie said “it don’t apply to me. You know, it mandates removal from office upon entry and acceptance of the nolo contendere plea, and in the judge’s decision … he did not accept it.” He railed against the ruling, his lawyer in the 2024 case, and the president of the Harford County Council.
Guthrie also noted two other cases involving members of the Harford County Council — Jacob Bennet and Aaron Penman — who were either prevented from being sworn in or removed from office and later won appeals at the Supreme Court of Maryland.
“The Supreme Court overturned both of them, and they won’t hear mine,” Guthrie said. “It’s discrimination.”
Doug Gansler, a former Maryland attorney general who represented Guthrie on appeal, called the court’s refusal to hear the case “stunning.”
“The decision below is so clearly wrong,” Gansler said Monday. “There’s nobody that hears the facts of it that thinks that it was not wrongly decided, and to have the Supreme Court not even hear the case when the Constitution and 250 years of jurisprudence are exactly on the other side of it is just stunning.”
It only takes three of the seven justices on the high court to agree to hear an appeal. And while there could be a request for reconsideration, Gansler acknowledged “it’s the end of the case.”
Guthrie’s unsuccessful string of appeals followed his removal from office in 2024.
Guthrie, one of two Democrats on the seven-member council, was charged in October 2024 with one count of theft between $1,500 and $25,000 between 2017 and 2021 from the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 1501, where he was president and business manager.
Guthrie maintained his innocence and said he had made restitution to the union. But a month later, he appeared before Baltimore County Circuit Court Judge Dennis Robinson Jr. and entered a plea of nolo contendere.
A defendant who enters no contest plea does not accept responsibility for the charged crime and waives the right to a trial, agreeing to accept the punishment meted out by a judge.
Robinson during the hearing struck the “guilty verdict” and sentenced Guthrie to probation before judgment. Later that day, Guthrie was informed that his plea triggered his immediate removal.
In 2012, the Maryland General Assembly passed an amendment — approved later that year by voters — adding a provision to the law governing the removal of state and local officials. It  automatically removes any elected official who enters a plea of guilty or nolo contendere to any felony charge or misdemeanor crimes related to the official’s public duties and responsibilities.
Previously, the constitution required a “final conviction, after judicial review or otherwise,” which left open a potential for some officials to remain in office pending appeals or sentences of probation before judgment, a sentence that effectively strikes the finding of guilt.
Removal is automatic on entering the plea, and is not affected by any sentence that follows, according to Harford County officials, who said at the time that they were acting on advice from the Office of the Attorney General.
But on appeal, Gansler and Guthrie asserted that Robinson did not accept Guthrie’s no contest plea and he thus should not have been removed from office.
The Appellate Court reached a different conclusion saying the Robinson misspoke.
“As we read the transcript, Judge Robinson likely realized while sentencing Mr. Guthrie to probation before judgment that a guilty verdict could not stand alongside the nolo contendere plea, and therefore explained that he was ‘going to strike the guilty verdict’ to preserve the plea’s compliance with the Rule,” the Appellate Court wrote in its decision. “The broader record also supports Judge Robinson’s acceptance of the plea.”
Guthrie maintained his innocence in the underlying felony theft case Monday. When asked why he entered the nolo contendere plea, he said he was acting on the advice of his lawyer at the time.
“In all my years on this earth, I’m now 88 years old, I’ve never heard of that term,” Guthrie said. He said his original attorney “advised me of it, and he said, ‘Well, you put that in, it’ll put this case behind you. You can be done with this. You go back to Harford County.’… You can go back to your council seat and put all this behind you.”
While his appeal was pending, Guthrie ran for his old seat but lost the June primary by 29 points to Nolanda Robert, who had been picked by the county Democratic Central Committee to replace Guthrie in January 2025.
Harford County Council President Patrick Vincenti (R) said he welcomed the ruling and the resolution of the case.
“It’s sad that it takes this long to put something to rest when clearly he committed a felony. He pled nolo contendere … and he was removed by the constitution by matter of law, not by me,” Vincenti said. “I’m glad to see it’s over.”
Vincenti lamented the cost of defending against Guthrie’s appeals. Guthrie said “hundreds of thousands of dollars” were spent by the council. Vincenti said a final tally was not yet available but would be made public.
“It’s a shame that we have to tolerate frivolous lawsuits like this,” Vincenti said. “It’s overwhelmingly expensive and such a waste for the citizens of Harford County.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: We should measure Corrections by the lives we change
description: What is the purpose of our correctional system?
text:
In 2024, I first visited York Correctional Institution. It’s the state’s only women’s correctional institute; it’s down the street from where I live in Niantic, but I didn’t know much about the place or the 900 incarcerated people who lived there. 
When I went, I learned about life inside prison from the incarcerated women we spoke to. But I left thinking about what happens after prison.

Nick Menapace

 As I spoke with incarcerated women, I heard the same message again and again. They weren’t asking for sympathy or shorter sentences. They weren’t asking anyone to excuse the mistakes that had brought them there. They wanted something much simpler: the opportunity to learn skills that would help them build a life when they returned home. 
 That conversation has stayed with me because it raised a question we don’t ask often enough: What is the purpose of our correctional system? 
 Certainly, incarceration serves an important purpose. It protects the public, holds people accountable, and provides justice for victims. Those responsibilities are essential. 
 But if the overwhelming majority of incarcerated people will one day return to our communities, then public safety doesn’t end at the prison gate. We should also ask what happens next. 
 Do people leave prison prepared to support themselves, provide for their families, and become productive members of their communities? Or do they leave carrying the same barriers that contributed to their incarceration in the first place? Since becoming a Connecticut legislator, I have visited York a few times; it’s so close that I even ride my bike there. 
Recently, I returned to York for the graduation of the first class of Connecticut’s Building Trades Training Institute . Through a partnership involving the Department of Correction, the Department of Labor, Connecticut’s Building Trades, and other labor organizations, six women earned industry-recognized credentials and a direct pathway to apprenticeship opportunities upon release.
 One graduate said something I won’t forget: “My past doesn’t define my future.” 
 That single sentence captures what this program is really about. 
 It isn’t about being soft on crime. It isn’t about overlooking the harm that crime causes. It’s about recognizing that accountability and opportunity are not mutually exclusive. If someone has served their sentence and is returning to society, every one of us has a stake in whether they succeed. 
 That is why I believe we need to rethink how we measure success in corrections. 
 Too often, we focus on what happens inside prison: how many people are incarcerated, how facilities operate, or what programs are offered. Those things matter. But the true measure of success is what happens after someone walks out the front gate. 
Did they find stable employment?  Did they reunite with their family?  Did they become financially independent?  Most importantly, did they avoid returning to prison? 
 Those are the outcomes that make our communities safer. 
 They also make fiscal sense.   It costs tens of thousands of dollars each year to incarcerate one person.   Every individual who successfully rebuilds their life instead of returning to prison represents fewer victims, lower correctional costs, and another skilled worker contributing to our state’s economy. That is not simply compassion. It is sound public policy that everyone should be able to get behind. 
 The building trades program also arrives at an important moment. Connecticut employers are searching for electricians, pipefitters, carpenters, plumbers, and other skilled tradespeople. At the same time, many people leaving prison struggle to find employers willing to give them a chance. 
 Programs like this help bridge that gap. 
 I hope this first graduating class is only the beginning. Connecticut should continue investing in vocational education and workforce partnerships inside our correctional facilities, evaluate them rigorously, and expand those that demonstrate results. 
 When I first visited York Correctional Institute, I met women asking for an opportunity. This year, I watched six of them take the first step toward earning one. 
 That experience reinforced something I believe about government more broadly. We should judge public policy not simply by what it promises, but by what it accomplishes. 
 The success of our correctional system should not be measured by how many people pass through it. It should be measured by how many people leave it prepared to build a better life and never have to come back. 
Nick Menapace is a teacher and Democratic State Representative of the 37th House District serving East Lyme, Salem, and Montville.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Chronic conditions persist in Alaska, but there are bright spots in latest health report
description: Alaskans face chronic health problems that are not yet easing and, in some cases, getting worse, according to a new status report released by the Alaska Department of Health. At the same time, there are signs of improvement in health, health care and the socioeconomic conditions that support well-being, particularly among youth, according to the […]
text:
Partipants in the Alaska Run For Women are seen at the race finish line at the University of Alaska Anchorage campus on June 11, 2022. The Healthy Alaskans program tracks a variety of indicators, including rates of obesity and exercise among adults and youth. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Alaskans face chronic health problems that are not yet easing and, in some cases, getting worse, according to a new status report released by the Alaska Department of Health. At the same time, there are signs of improvement in health, health care and the socioeconomic conditions that support well-being, particularly among youth, according to the report.
The 2026 update is part of the long-term Healthy Alaskans program, a collaboration between the state Department of Health and the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium.
The program sets 10-year goals and uses a holistic approach that considers factors like food security, housing security, public safety, education and other indicators. The new report comes at about the midpoint of the period covered by the Healthy Alaskans 2030 State Health Improvement Plan.
“The State Health Assessment is a comprehensive health checkup for the whole state; it represents the health of all of us,” Dr. Robert Lawrence, the Department of Health’s chief medical officer, said in a statement. “Like any checkup, knowing where we are on target and where we can improve helps us be strategic on where we focus our time and attention to the benefit of all Alaskans.”  
The report includes some bad news, some of which concerns obesity, poor diets and related ailments.
In 2024, 185,000 Alaska adults were identified as suffering from high blood pressure and 167,00 from high cholesterol, health conditions often tied to excessive weight, the report said.
Those totals represent significant proportions of the state population. As of 2025, Alaska’s population was estimated at 738,737, about three quarters of whom were adults.
Among high school students, 33% were overweight or obese in 2023, the report said. And the vast majority of Alaskans, whether adults or students, failed to consume the recommended daily amounts of fruits and vegetables and failed to engage in the recommended daily levels of exercise, the report said.
Alaskans’ life expectancy has not increased since 2014 and actually showed a slight downward trend through 2024, though there has been recovery since the dip caused by the COVID-19 pandemic. Broken down into demographic groups, Alaska’s Asian and Pacific Islander residents had the highest life expectancy in 2024, at 81.0 years, and Indigenous residents the lowest, at 67.6 years. The Alaska Native life expectancy in 2024 was 10 years shorter than the overall U.S. average, the report said.
The statistics on life expectancy are among several examples of health disparities resulting in poorer health for Alaska Natives. Those are related in part to unequal access to health care and other services, the report said. “The current and historical conditions, policies, rules, and power structures in communities underlie whether individuals have the best chance at living a healthy life, including practicing healthy behaviors,” it said.
Rates of infant mortality showed no improvement over the past decade, and a big disparity persists for Alaska Native people. The rate of infant deaths was 13 per 1,000 births among Alaska Native people in the years from 2020 to 2024 — about twice the rate for the state as a whole, according to the report. 
Childhood vaccination rates in Alaska continue to lag national rates, the report said.
 

Bernadette Hartley and other volunteers assemble opioid-reversal kits at an Aug. 29, 2025, event in Anchorage. The kits contain naloxone. The event held at Anchorage’s Fairview Community Recreation Center was organized by the Alaska Department of Health’s Project HOPE and the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium. State officials recorded a reduction in overdose deaths in 2024, and that downward trend appears to have continued into 2025. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	There is good news in the report, though.
Among those positive signs is a significant increase over time in prenatal care. In 2008, only 39% of women who gave birth in Alaska had received adequate prenatal care starting in the first trimester; by 2024, that measure had risen to 67%
High school graduation rates are up as well. In the 2010-11 school year, 68% of Alaska students graduated high school within four years; by the 2023-24 school year, that rate has risen to 78%. Graduation rates for Alaska Native students lagged the state average, but they also improved during the period, from 51% to 65%, the report said.
That is important because education is linked to better health, the report said.
“In Alaska, 35% of adults without a high school degree reported five or more poor physical health days in the last 30 days, compared with 22% of adults with at least some college education,” it said.
Alaska teens are less likely to be exposed to secondhand tobacco smoke, part of an overall trend toward establishment of tobacco-free zones and similar policies, the report said. In 2011, 36% of high school students were exposed to tobacco smoke; the rate fell to 25% in 2024, the report said.
Some health-related metrics showed mixed signals as of 2024, according to the report.
Drug overdoses that spiked amid the national opioid crisis are showing signs of abatement. Alaska’s rate of fatal overdoses more than doubled from 2019 to 2024, from 18.1 per 100,000 people to 45.6 per 100,000 people, the report said. But the 2024 rate represented a 5% decrease from the peak rate hit the year prior. That was not as dramatic as the national drop of nearly 27% from 2023 to 2024, but indications are that the downward trend will continue into 2025, according to Department of Health records.
Climate change poses numerous health challenges, the report said. In rural areas, changes to fish runs, wildlife populations and berry crops have interfered with traditional harvests of wild foods and diminished food security. In various parts of the state, wildfire smoke is a health hazard. Risks of certain diseases have increased with the changing climate, the report added.
As those challenges mount, there are new programs and systems aimed at mitigating those threats, the report said.
Alaska’s extensive and continually improving trail system, which helps people reach sources of wild food, and also supports exercise. Contributes to overall health, the report said. More Alaska-grown food has become available over time. Organizations like the Food Bank of Alaska are reaching residents in need, including the state’s growing population of elderly residents.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Yurts, campsites open for reservation at new Western Maryland state park
description: The yurts are open for business. Gates will officially open this Friday at Maryland’s newest state park, Savage Highlands, with rooms -- and yurts -- for rent, unlocking some 55,000 acres of Western Maryland woodlands outside of Frostburg for public use.
text:
Four of the eight yurts at the new Savage Highlands State Park will be available to rent through October, after which they will likely close for the season and reopen in 2027. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)The yurts are open for business.
This Friday, the gates will officially open at Maryland’s newest state park, Savage Highlands, unlocking some 55,000 acres of Western Maryland woodlands outside of Frostburg for public use, free of charge.
But already, online bookings are open for overnight stays at four small but luxurious yurts — at a cost of about $200 per night — as well as $20-a-night primitive campsites along the property’s hiking trails, complete with a fire ring, picnic table and bear-proof storage container.
Once a privately held vacation resort called Savage River Lodge, anchored by a rustic ski lodge with its own restaurant, the facility used to be geared toward adults, advertising romantic getaways for couples and even charging added fees for children to tag along.
Maryland Park Service staff applaud during an opening ceremony Saturday at Savage Highlands State Park. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
But the state park service is determined to welcome families. In other words, out with the loveseats and in with the sofa beds.
“Under state ownership, children and families will experience this remarkable property together at a price point in line with what our Maryland state park visitors can afford,” said Angela Crenshaw, director of the Maryland Park Service, during an opening event for the state park on Saturday. “That represents a meaningful shift from a private past.”
For now, the yurts and campsites are open for bookings through the end of October. The state plans to close them over the winter due to the bumpy condition of the steep gravel road entering the property, which the state is hoping to repair.
State parks officials say even more improvements are in the works at Savage Highlands, which they hope will become a hub for visitors to other nearby state lands, including nearby Savage River State Forest, New Germany State Park and Dan’s Mountain Wildlife Management Area.
The property also features 18 quaint cabins — which, like the yurts, have electricity, indoor plumbing and other amenities — but several need new roofs, so the state has opted against opening them to reservations, likely until next spring. Those facilities will likely come at a similar nightly cost to the yurts, officials said.
Other things also still remain unfinished. The lodge will be open to any visitors — both day hikers and overnight campers — come Friday, with its plush armchairs beneath the taxidermied head of an antlered buck, and its sprawling deck with Adirondack chairs and benches aplenty, overlooking the park’s forested surroundings.
But state officials are still puzzling through how they might utilize the old restaurant space in the lodge. Maybe it could be a wedding venue. Maybe a contractor could serve food of some sort.
The jury is still out, but one thing is for sure: “Park rangers are not the kind of cooks you want in the lodge,” joked Jonas Williams, director of planning for the park service.
A deck overlooks the grounds of the former Savage River Lodge, a private vacation resort turned into Maryland's newest state park, which opens officially on Aug. 28, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)A small gift shop inside the lodge at the Savage Highlands State Park features Maryland-themed memorabilia. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)A seating area inside the former Savage River Lodge, which will be open to the public Aug. 28. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Julia Musselwhite,a park ranger at New Germany State Park, gives tours of a yurt at Savage River Highlands State Park on August 22, 2026. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)The Maryland Park Service plans to replace the moss-covered roofs on many of the cabins at the new Savage Highlands State Park, so the cabins are not currently available for booking. State officials say they could be open in 2027. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Cabins at Maryland's new Savage Highlands State Park feature a wood stove, seating areas, lofted bedroom, small kitchen and bathroom. But they are not yet open to the public due to required roof repairs. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Cabins at Maryland's new Savage Highlands State Park feature a wood stove, seating areas, lofted bedroom, small kitchen and bathroom. But they are not yet open to the public due to required roof repairs. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)A sign advertises the new Savage Highlands State Park, which features more than 5 miles of hiking trails, in addition to campsites, yurts and cabins (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)A sign advertises the new Savage Highlands State Park, which features more than 5 miles of hiking trails, in addition to campsites, yurts and cabins (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)A gravel road leads into the new Savage Highlands State Park outside of Frostburg (Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
The state purchased the property for $8.7 million in 2024, an eyebrow-raising figure to some critics, especially given that it does not include the investments the state must make to modernize the facility and add new features.
But state officials consider it a worthy investment, especially considering high visitorship, which reached a peak of 21 million visitors at all state parks in 2020, forcing the state to temporarily close a small group of the most popular parks 292 times because they had reached capacity. And even amid budget crunches, the state has the cash set aside.
The money to purchase the Savage property came from Program Open Space special funds, derived from a portion of the state’s transfer tax.
Seating areas overlook the grounds of the former Savage River Lodge, a private vacation resort turned into Maryland’s newest state park. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
At Savage Highlands, in addition to the new cabin roofs, the park service plans to build ADA-accessible additions to two cabins, so that they each have a private bedroom on the ground floor, Williams said. Currently, the cabins have loft bedrooms reached by climbing a small staircase. The state also wants to add stoves to the cabins, which only have a microwave, sink and miniature fridge, Williams said.
The yurts, of which there are eight on the property, currently have heated floors and a woodstove but no other heating or cooling, the state has already added small air conditioning units, and is considering enhanced window HVAC units.
The state also evaluated the park’s roughly 5.75 miles of hiking trails, implementing new trail designs to replace routes deemed unsuitable for long-term public use.
Despite the price tag, at least one of the three members of the Maryland Board of Public Works, who must approve land purchases and other infrastructure costs incurred by the state government, thought it was an easy sell.
Maryland Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D), a former Baltimore City delegate, said she began traveling to the property with her family while it was still in private hands, during the coronavirus pandemic.
“When the secretary came to me and said, ‘Hey, we have this idea about bringing this into the state park system,’ I did not need a lot of convincing,” Lierman said.
Lierman made a return trip on Saturday to attend the park’s opening ceremony.
“My son, who’s now 13, actually remembers the cabin that we stayed in, remarked on, ‘Oh, we had s’mores down there by the campfire,’ and remembered the hike that we went on,” Lierman said.
The state is eyeing additional park openings following the uniquely high popularity of the state park system during the coronavirus pandemic.
Maggie Weathers-Smith and her husband Matt Smith won a contest to be the first members of the public to stay at Savage Highlands State Park, a week before its official opening.
In May, the state opened Freedman’s State Park in Montgomery County. The state is currently in the planning phase for Wicomico County’s first state park, a 445-acre property called Wetipquin Creek State Park, and is soon to open a new natural resources management area at Holly Beach Farm in Anne Arundel County, a 293-acre waterfront parcel donated by the Chesapeake Bay Foundation in 2024. The state also accepted the donation earlier this year of Catoctin Furnace Cemetery at Cunningham Falls State Park.
Over the last year, the state has also implemented — and then expanded — a new online registration requirement for daytime visitors to some of its most popular parks, including Sandy Point, Rocky Gap Swallow Falls and parts of Gunpowder Falls.
Department of Natural Resources Secretary Josh Kurtz, who oversees the Park Service, hears it all from state park visitors.
“People either tell you what bathrooms were dirty when they went to the park, or some wild story or adventure that they had in our parks,” Kurtz said on Saturday.
“Moving forward, there will be marriages here. There will be proposals here. There will be first hikes here. There will be first campsites here. There will be first s’mores here,” Kurtz said. “And I think those are the kind of things that leave a lasting indelible mark on people.”
For one Maryland couple, the memories began this past weekend. Newly married Matt Smith and his wife, Maggie Leathers-Smith, of Pikesville, were hiking on their honeymoon in West Virginia when they learned that they had won a free stay at Savage Highlands, and would become the first members of the general public to stay at the newly minted state park.
The couple were participating in the Miles for Maryland challenge for 2026, which pushes participants to hike 250 miles in honor of the nation’s 250th anniversary this year, and received the free stay after a random draw for program participants.
Maryland Park Service Director Angela Crenshaw, right, speaks with Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) at Saturday’s opening for Savage Highlands State Park. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)
“We’re very fortunate in Maryland to have this now for the public,” Smith said. “I didn’t know this existed privately, and just learning about it recently, it’s like: Wow.”
Maryland Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) also made the trek from Charm City, and stayed in a yurt at the new park Friday night.
He told the small crowd on Saturday how he and his family turned to an Eastern Shore state park after a contentious General Assembly session this year, marked by Ferguson’s feud with Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) over middecade congressional redistricting, and a trying primary election, during which Ferguson defeated the most formidable challenger of his political career.
The family’s trip to a cabin at the state park brought far quieter moments beside the campfire, Ferguson said, including a heart-to-heart with his son about his plans for the beginning of high school.
“It was that moment of connection between a father and a son that was unbelievably powerful in the middle of Tuckahoe State Park. To me, that is what these investments do,” Ferguson said.
In 2022, in the wake of record park visitorship during the pandemic, the General Assembly passed the Great Maryland Outdoors Act, which set aside tens of millions for park acquisitions and improvements.
On Saturday morning, Ferguson said he texted a picture from Savage Highlands to Rep. Sarah Elfreth (D-3rd), who was the lead sponsor of the Great Outdoors bill as a state senator.
I said, “This is everything you imagined,’” Ferguson told the crowd.
The rustic main lodge at Savage Highlands State Park features plush seating for campers and daytime guests alike. State officials say it could soon become a wedding venue, or offer an eatery like in days’ past. (Photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)

name: Maryland Matters
title: Tom Hendershot, former Prince George’s school board, council member dies at 82
description: Thomas Hendershot, a former Prince George’s County school board member, county council member and basketball coach, died Aug. 18. He was 82. Hendershot, a Democrat, served on the school board from 1984 to 1987 and on the council from 1997 to 2006.
text:
The Prince George's County Administration Building in Upper Marlboro. (Photo courtesy Prince George's County)Former Prince George’s County school board member, county council member and high school basketball coach Thomas Hendershot died Aug. 18. He was 82.
Hendershot, a Democrat, served on the school board from 1984 to 1987. During his time on the school board, he was a basketball coach at Bowie High School that won the county title during the 1992-93 season.
Hendershot was elected a member of County Council in 1997 where for nine years he represented council’s District 3, which includes Berwyn Heights, College Park and New Carrollton.
Hendershot’s son-in-law, Del. Andrew Pruski (D-Anne Arundel), said in an interview Monday that Hendershot dedicated his life to public service, off and on the basketball court.
“I’m only aware of [Hendershot being] the only school board member in the state that was the chairman of the board of education while also coaching a high school basketball team,” Pruski said. “There’s been a lot of former players who reached out. He encouraged a lot of people to get involved in public service. He was one of the happiest people you could ever meet.”
Council Vice Chair Eric Olson (D), who currently represents District 3, served on College Park City Council from 1997 to 2006, the same years Hendershot was on the county council. Hendershot was term-limited after two terms, and Olson won the election to succeed him. Olson served until 2014, and was returned to council in 2022.
Former Prince George’s County Council member Thomas Hendershot. (Photo courtesy Hendershot family)
“Tom was dedicated to Prince George’s County and its residents. He was a strong supporter of public education and county workers,” said Olson, who learned of the death from a reporter Monday. “He was a strong supporter of labor. His legacy lives on in his children, who are also public servants. My heart goes out to [Hendershot’s wife] Flo and his entire family.”
Born in March 1944 in Baltimore, Hendershot spent part of his childhood in Morgantown, West Virginia. The family moved to Philadelphia, where he graduated high school, but he went to college at West Virginia University, where he met his wife. Both graduated in 1966 with degrees in education.
Hendershot moved back to Pennsylvania to attend Villanova University Law School, and served as an aide to former Rep. William Green (D-Penn.).
According to the Washington Post, Hendershot became involved in Democratic politics, that included passing out fliers for John F. Kennedy’s presidential campaign in 1960 and for Robert F. Kennedy’s campaign in 1968.
Hendershot was a delegate to several Democratic National Conventions, including 1988 when he was a delegate for by Illinois Sen. Paul Simon.
During his time on county council in 2000, the Washington Post said that Hendershot’s law license in Maryland was suspended indefinitely after clients complained that he failed to represent them properly. Despite that, Hendershot remains viewed by former colleagues as somone who supported union workers, educators and who pushed for better healthcare in Prince George’s as a member of the Dimensions Oversight Committee. Eventually, the state-of-the-art University of Maryland Capital Region Medical Center in Largo that opened in June 2021 replaced the much-older Prince George’s Hospital Center in Cheverly.
“Tom Hendershot was a champion for Prince George’s County Schools and a leading advocate for labor. For years he had a major positive impact on the Prince George’s County Council,” County Councilmember Tom Dernoga (D), who served on council with Hendershot between 2002-06, said in an email Monday afternoon.
Hendershot is survived by his wife of 60 years and their four children – Thomas Jr., Emmett, Nathan and Roxanne – and 13 grandchildren. His obituary says a Celebration of Life service will be held Sept. 20 at the Greenbriar Terrace Community Room at 7600 Hanover Parkway, #101, in Greenbelt.
