name: Alaska Beacon
title: Dismantling the Roadless Rule threatens to disrupt wildlife, water and peace
description: Pause for a moment and listen. What do you hear? Chances are, somewhere in the background, is the ever-present hum of a road. More than 4.2 million miles of public roads crisscross the lower 48 states – enough to reach the Moon and back almost nine times. This vast network of roads spiderwebs its way […]
text:
Tongass National Forest (Photo by U.S. Forest Service)
Pause for a moment and listen. What do you hear? Chances are, somewhere in the background, is the ever-present hum of a road.
More than 4.2 million miles of public roads crisscross the lower 48 states – enough to reach the Moon and back almost nine times. This vast network of roads spiderwebs its way across the contiguous U.S., leaving only about 5% as an inventoried roadless area or wilderness.
Now, some of those last remaining lands free of roads are under threat from the Trump administration’s proposed rollback of the 2001 Roadless Rule. That includes southeast Alaska’s Tongass National Forest, where eagles, bears, salmon and many other species thrive in old-growth coastal forest along the Inside Passage.
In announcing its plan, the administration said rescinding the rule would remove prohibitions on road construction and logging on nearly 59 million acres of national forest, arguing that the rule slowed economic development. A 30-day public comment period on the formal proposal ends on Sept. 21, 2026. Instructions on how to submit comments are included in the proposal.
In Congress, another effort is underway to try to change the law through an amendment to the Wildfire Prevention Act. That change, if approved, would both remove the Roadless Rule and prevent the U.S. Forest Service from reinstituting it in the future, despite overwhelming public support for the rule.
As ecologists who have spent decades studying wilderness and the animals and ecological functions that depend on undisturbed habitats, we believe it’s important to understand that preserving roadless areas has value for environmental health, clean water, wildlife survival and people’s own well-being.
 What is the Roadless Rule?

The National Forest Roadless Area Conservation Policy, better known as the Roadless Rule, was issued in January 2001 by President Bill Clinton. It has had overwhelming public support and received more public comments than any other rule in history.
The rule prohibits road construction, maintenance and commercial timber harvest in inventoried roadless areas within the National Forest System. It applies to over 58 million acres across the country, excluding Idaho and Colorado, which have their own state-specific roadless rules. While most of these roadless areas are in the western states and Alaska, 38 total states as well as Puerto Rico host roadless areas.

The nation’s inventoried roadless areas are primarily in the western U.S. and include large parts of southeast Alaska, where 14,779,000 acres of roadless areas are within National Forest System land. (US Forest Service Enterprise Map Services Program)
The primary goal of the Roadless Rule is to maintain forest health and productivity for future generations. It also helps avoid exacerbating the U.S. Forest Service’s road maintenance backlog by not making new roads.
The Roadless Rule prohibits new road construction, with very limited exceptions, as well as commercial logging in designated roadless areas. It does not restrict other uses that are compatible with the management plan, such as hiking and mountain biking, or resource uses such as grazing livestock and working existing mining claims.
Beyond providing vital habitat for species and enabling healthy forests, the rule protects drinking water for the millions of Americans whose water flows from national forests. It also preserves high-quality recreation opportunities – hiking, camping, hunting and fishing – that Americans cherish.
 The problem with roads in national forests

While roads can provide benefits, such as access to forests, they can also do ecological harm.
Roads enable invasive weeds to spread by being carried on vehicle tires and deposited in exposed soils, erode sediments into streams and fragment habitat that wildlife rely on. Vehicles directly kill and injure animals through collisions. They occasionally start fires, too. A recent study found that fires are more likely to start in areas with roads than in areas without.
Studies show that road noise displaces wildlife, increases stress and can affect wildlife behavior patterns at distances of over a mile from the road.
And roads don’t just cause problems for species on land. Most roads cross streams and rivers, which requires building a way for those waters to keep flowing under the road (structures called culverts). While culverts can be designed to allow fish to pass through and maintain ecological connections, they are rarely built to do so. This leads to declines in the health of fish populations and can leave some species locally extinct.
 The benefits of roadless areas

Inventoried roadless areas are among the most ecologically intact and wildest places left in the United States, yet – unlike Wilderness Areas and National Parks – there are no signs acknowledging their boundaries when you enter one.
Most are part of larger ecosystems, directly adjacent or ecologically connected to better known national parks and wilderness areas. Removing Roadless Rule protections would erode ecological buffers to these more famous protected lands.
For some species, roadless areas protect critical core habitat. For instance, over half the suitable habitat for relictual slender salamander, a critically imperiled species native to the Sierra Mountains of California, occurs in a roadless area. Nearly 40% of Mount Pinos, lodgepole chipmunk, an imperiled subspecies of the lodgepole chipmunk, also live in roadless areas in California.
Research shows that every formal roadless area provides habitat for at least two wildlife species of conservation concern – those facing risks to their long-term survival – with the median roadless area supporting 10 of these imperiled species. Some Arizona roadless areas contain habitat for up to 62 of these species.
Roadless areas also protect watersheds that supply drinking water to 47 million Americans.
Without this protection, these watersheds would still provide water, but their long-term health and hydrological sustainability could be compromised if roads block stream flow and increase sediments flowing into waterways. The result can be higher costs for water purification.
The Forest Service’s own watershed health assessment, known as the Watershed Condition Framework, uses road density as a key indicator of conditions that can disrupt water quantity and quality.
 What is at risk in rescinding the Roadless Rule?

The Trump administration’s proposed rollback, expected to be formalized in 2026, would open these last wild places to development, fragmenting habitats that can never be restored.
The American public spoke loudly in 2001 when they supported the Roadless Rule. Two decades later, the public comments submitted on the recission notice overwhelming opposed rolling back the rules, a Center for Western Priorities review found, reaffirming that U.S. roadless forests remain as vital and valued as ever.
Protecting these areas is about promoting healthy ecosystems on public lands so they can provide hiking, hunting and fishing opportunities for generations to come to enjoy the tranquility of being in nature.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Feud escalates between NJ governor, GOP over voter registration gaffe
description: Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) and Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R) are sparring over Sherrill's recent revelation that the state registered noncitizens to vote.
text:
Gov. Mikie Sherrill (D) and Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R) are sparring over Sherrill's recent revelation that the state registered noncitizens to vote. (Photos by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The war of words between Gov. Mikie Sherrill and congressional Republicans escalated Monday when Rep. Jeff Van Drew accused Sherrill of personally attacking him and his colleagues for investigating the state’s voter registration debacle.
Van Drew, a Republican seeking reelection in November, called a letter Sherrill sent him and a group of House Republicans on Friday a “political hit piece” that was beneath her office. He and Sherrill have been trading barbs over last month’s revelation that state officials registered thousands of noncitizens to vote.
“This was never about Governor Sherrill or any one political party. It is about New Jersey and the integrity of our country’s elections. Our mutual constituents deserve fair and secure elections, and they deserve the truth about how something this serious was allowed to happen,” Van Drew said in a statement from his office.
Republicans have used the voter registration blunder, which Sherrill has said was the result of a software error at the state Motor Vehicle Commission that started in 2023 and was caught in 2024, to criticize Democratic policies like automatic voter registration and driver’s licenses for undocumented immigrants. Van Drew and 18 of his colleagues wrote a letter to Sherrill on July 24 demanding she answer a host of questions about the matter by Aug. 21.
Sherrill’s response, which came Friday, blasted Republicans in Congress as seeming “much more concerned with using the issue for political gain than they are with protecting our elections.”
“Seven of you attempted to overturn the 2020 elections and voted to challenge the electoral votes of states,” she wrote. “And notably, one of the signatories to your letter employed an operative convicted of voter fraud, bribery and blackmail.”
That last sentence is a reference to Craig Callaway, a former Atlantic City council president and Democratic operative who pleaded guilty in federal court last year to a 2022 mail ballot fraud scheme. In 2022, Callaway was working for Van Drew’s reelection campaign. Van Drew has denied any knowledge of the scheme.
Politico New Jersey reported last week that an attorney representing Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell, who as secretary of state oversees state elections, told Van Drew and other House Republicans that the state would cooperate with their probe by sending them certain documents related to the voter registration gaffe starting this week. Sherrill had previously said the state would not release “personally identifying information” of the voters involved to the federal government because the Trump administration would “weaponize it against people.”
It’s unclear what documents Caldwell intends to share. Sherrill indicated to the New Jersey Monitor after an unrelated press conference last week that the state will share public documents with the Trump administration.
“We have seen again and again and again the Trump administration going on a fishing expedition here in New Jersey, and so they’ve attempted on numerous occasions to get all access to our voter rolls, the private information on those voter rolls. They provided no reason why they need that,” she said.
A federal judge recently dismissed a lawsuit the Trump administration filed against Caldwell seeking private data of all New Jersey voters.
Micah Rasmussen testifying at a Senate budget hearing on March 9, 2024, at the Statehouse in Trenton. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Micah Rasmussen, director of Rider University’s Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics, said Republicans “do deserve some credit for raising this issue all along,” pointing to state Sen. Kristin Corrado (R-Passaic), who had criticized automatic voter registration at motor vehicle locations long before Sherrill’s revelation about noncitizens voting. But he pushed back on Van Drew’s framing that the scrutiny of Sherrill isn’t political, noting that GOP-led states like Iowa and Florida have also found noncitizens on their voter rolls.
“There are definitely politics that are being played on both sides of the aisle,” he said. “I feel largely that the Republicans are handling this with a partisan advantage. I also think that Democrats are responding with politics of their own, and Gov. Sherrill is taking a good faith approach at trying to fix this.”
Sherrill said last week that state officials have deleted 5,100 registered voters from state voter rolls and have asked county election officials to review another 1,650 names. She said that roughly 340 of the 6,600 erroneously registered voters cast ballots.

title: North Dakotans receiving developmental disability services affected by phishing attack on state
description: A data breach made public Monday by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services may have exposed health information of people receiving developmental disability services. A phishing email attack targeted the Department of Health and Human Services in July. The Information Technology Department investigated and determined that three Developmental[...]
text:
The state flag of North Dakota waves in the wind outside of the Capitol in Bismarck on Feb. 27, 2025. (Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A data breach made public Monday by the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services may have exposed health information of people receiving developmental disability services.
A phishing email attack targeted the Department of Health and Human Services in July. The Information Technology Department investigated and determined that three Developmental Disabilities Division employees interacted with the phishing email, which led to unauthorized access of their email accounts, according to the agency. 
The Information Technology Department promptly secured the accounts, but some personal health information may have been accessed. The information exposed may include name, contact information, date of birth, age, developmental disabilities service information, name of health plan and identification number, medical information and guardian information.
The department said it is providing written notification to those affected by the breach and encourages them to monitor their medical and financial accounts for potential fraud.
“HHS takes the privacy and security of protected health information seriously,” the Health and Human Services Department said in a statement. “We are working closely with NDIT to strengthen safeguards, enhance cybersecurity awareness training, and prevent similar incidents.”  
Those affected by the breach should be cautious of unexpected communications through email, text messages, phone calls, or requests for personal information, the department said.
Free fraud alerts can be placed with the three credit reporting agencies at:

Equifax: (877) 478-7625 or www.equifax.com
Experian: (888) 397-3742 or www.experian.com
TransUnion: (800) 680-7289 or www.transunion.com

Additional information on reporting identity theft can be found on the North Dakota Attorney General’s website or through the Federal Trade Commission website.
The department notified the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights and the North Dakota Attorney General’s Office about the unauthorized access of protected health information.
Those affected by the data breach should contact Kristen Vander Vorst, Developmental Disabilities Field Services Administrator for HHS, at (800) 755-8529.

name: Source New Mexico
title: US Rep. Stansbury calls on New Mexico agencies to provide Project Jupiter water information
description: U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) sent a letter to several New Mexico state agencies Monday afternoon asking them to provide a “clear public accounting” of the various water sources that will support the Project Jupiter data center under construction in southern New Mexico.
text:
U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.), pictured at a 2025 Rio Rancho town hall, on Aug. 24, 2026, said she was demanding answers from several state leaders about Project Jupiter’s water sources. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)U.S. Rep. Melanie Stansbury (D-N.M.) sent a letter to several New Mexico state agencies Monday afternoon asking them to provide a “clear public accounting” of the various water sources that will support the Project Jupiter data center under construction in southern New Mexico.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In addition to the amount of water the project needs, Stansbury said she is asking for details about the water rights and permits behind each source of water Project Jupiter plans to use.
Stansbury sent the letter to New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, state Environment Secretary James Kenney, State Engineer Elizabeth Anderson and the chair and director of the Interstate Stream Commission. Stansbury requested their responses in writing by the close of business Friday. Source has pending requests with all agencies and will update this story as needed.
Stansbury’s letter comes on the heels of two Sunday night orders from the New Mexico Supreme Court, which ordered the temporary end to some water use for Project Jupiter’s construction and paused the development’s pending air quality permit hearing.
Both Supreme Court orders were unanimous.
One came after the Center for Biological Diversity alleged that the Office of the State Engineer violated state law by approving the emergency drilling of a well for Project Jupiter without first providing public notice or holding a hearing.
The other came after the Santa Fe-based clean energy group New Energy Economy alleged that the air quality permit hearing, which was scheduled to begin in September, appeared to be premature, considering that the pipeline needed to feed Project Jupiter’s power system is still stuck in the federal regulatory process.
Since Project Jupiter’s plans became public last year, Stansbury said she has noticed that many southern New Mexico residents feel as if their county government approved the development without adequately informing the public about it.
“For over a year, New Mexicans have been asking basic questions about this project — about its viability because of water, about land use, about the use of public taxpayer dollars,” Stansbury said on a call with reporters Monday afternoon. “The huge outrage that New Mexicans have issued in this case as it has moved forward…is not only warranted, we believe that our state agencies need to be providing more answers to the public.”
Stansbury said she is concerned that developments like Project Jupiter will deplete the Rio Grande and make it difficult for the state to comply with the terms of the recent settlement agreement in the long-running Texas v. New Mexico and Colorado case.
“In New Mexico, water is life, water is culture, water is place and water is essential to everything that our people do,” Stansbury said. “We cannot allow an industrial water user that might threaten our state’s ability to meet the needs of our own farmers and ranchers, our own communities, our own acequias, our own tribal communities…to threaten our ability to meet our own needs without a transparent process that is open to the public.”
Regarding the state Supreme Court’s orders, an Oracle spokesperson in a Monday afternoon statement said company leaders were “deeply saddened” that the order to temporarily stop using water, which the company has long said comes from a local sod farm, would impact a local business.
“The immediate impact of this order falls on the region’s only commercial sod farm and the 14 Santa Teresa residents whose jobs depend on its operations,” the statement said. “We will of course comply with the order and remain focused on long-term water stewardship. This includes a responsible, carefully developed plan that protects water as a valuable resource through closed-loop cooling, minimal ongoing use of non-potable water, and a recently announced partnership with Arable to conserve more water in the Rio Grande-Bravo watershed than Project Jupiter uses.”
As for the court’s other order, which temporarily halted the development’s air quality permit hearing, the spokesperson wrote that Oracle and its partners “remain committed to developing Project Jupiter responsibly.”
“The New Mexico Environment Department’s air-permitting process includes a thorough technical review, with many opportunities for public input at every stage in the process. Project Jupiter is meeting applicable permitting requirements, stands ready to proceed with the department’s public hearing process, and is engaging with the community as that review moves forward,” the statement said. “The effort to bypass the department’s established procedural deadlines is unwarranted, but we will continue to share facts about the project transparently and are confident the regulatory process will prevail.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Nevada officials face reckoning as residents and tourists compete for lodging, cell service, roads
description: The Hawk Fire northwest of Reno and north of Lake Tahoe ignited dry fuel mid-day on August 22 amid red flag warnings with wind gusts up to 40 mph. Within hours the wildfire exploded to thousands of acres with ash, smoke, and flames encompassing sage-covered hills in northern Nevada’s densely populated areas. This is the […]
text:
Nevada National Guard personnel block a closed road during the Hawk Fire on August 23, 2026 in Reno, Nevada. (Photo by Trevor Bexon/Getty Images)The Hawk Fire northwest of Reno and north of Lake Tahoe ignited dry fuel mid-day on August 22 amid red flag warnings with wind gusts up to 40 mph. Within hours the wildfire exploded to thousands of acres with ash, smoke, and flames encompassing sage-covered hills in northern Nevada’s densely populated areas. This is the third of several major wildfires in northern Nevada in the past weeks. The Bug and Stallion wildfires had already strained resources.
Meanwhile, tourists and day visitors to the Reno-Tahoe area continued to enjoy their weekend with some making their way on ebike rentals to Tahoe’s East Shore Trail and to nearby beaches. Columns of smoke appeared above dense pine-covered forests from the Tahoe Rim Trail, which lies 20-30 miles south of Reno.
Wary residents around Reno and Tahoe, familiar with summer wildfires, instinctively packed go-bags and kept a watchful eye on the Perimeter Map app that Washoe County officials recommend for updates. New evacuation zones spread north, east, west, and south of the fire’s start. For subscribers, the Watch Duty app pinged cellphones with warning of the Hawk fire progress nearby. 
Early emergency management systems prove inadequate
Just after 6:00 pm on Saturday, with dinner preparations under way, more than 60,000 lost power. Cell services quickly overloaded. Alerts stopped arriving. An eerie quiet settled over the region. Pine trees danced in the strong winds. The only sound was the spotty distant firing of a few generators launching. Neighbors in Washoe Tahoe’s Mill Creek subdivision walked outside to compare notes as the sun set with no power and no understanding of how the winds would shift in the coming hours. Most people in neighborhoods around the greater Reno-Tahoe area were in the dark without a good understanding of which direction might be safest to evacuate if the fire embers made their way into surrounding forests. The posted red flag warning wasn’t due to expire until 11:00 pm. 
Just after midnight the power lurched back on for a portion of the Reno-Tahoe area. NV Energy sent out an email warning of additional “pro-active Emergency De-Energization” noting that “because wildfire conditions are dynamic, we are unable to provide a reliable restoration time during emergency de-energization.” It suggested that customers look to Washoe County for information.
As experience proved on Saturday, that ability is highly compromised and could prove impossible with intermittent power outages and if cell service overloads again. 
Coincidentally, two days earlier, on August 20, the Nevada Legislative Committee for the Review and Oversight of the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency and the Marlette Lake Water System met for its final 2026 meeting to discuss bill draft recommendations (BDRs) for the 2027 legislative session. Wildfire evacuation was on the agenda.
This item followed consistent public pleas at county and state meetings to update and reinforce emergency evacuation plans and models to reflect increasingly erratic wildfire starts, huge visitor surges, expanding tourism amenities, and proposals for new high-density developments along constrained two-lane evacuation routes. Ultimately, the oversight committee addressed evacuation with a vaguely worded call for an “evacuation study” in its work session document. 
A Tahoe first: Include peak visitation in evacuation planning
In a welcome move, state Sen. Robin Titus underscored resident requests with a specific ask after the evacuation study recommendation was read into the record. In a first for the Tahoe basin, Titus stated: “what we hear time and time again from the people who live there year-round at Lake Tahoe is that the evacuation plans that are being developed, and have been done by these agencies, don’t take into consideration the full transient population at any one time. I want to make sure when these evacuation plans are done that truly the real picture of Lake Tahoe during the peak seasons, or in ski seasons, all of this, the home rentals and all the folks that really are there at the time are taken into consideration.”
Including visitors along with the increasing local population makes sense as peak fire and summer tourist seasons coincide.
The Nevada Current first reported on retired Fire Battalion Chief Doug Flaherty’s self-funded independent wildfire evacuation study in 2024. He reiterated on Thursday that comprehensive analysis is needed, noting: “Unfortunately, as long as TRPA relies on an initial Environmental Checklist for approving projects without substantial evidence that those projects do not impact wildfire evacuation, there is simply going to be more lawsuits. Personally, I can’t stand by and watch people being jeopardized as far as their safety is concerned.”
His supporting evidence on tourism visitation and wildfire unpredictability was prescient. 
By Sunday, news reports noted “the fire moved exceptionally fast Saturday night, jumping over fire trucks and making it difficult for responders to get to hot spots while residents were trying to get out, sheriff [Darin Balaam] said.”
Competition for infrastructure
Reno-Tahoe and the upcoming annual Burning Man Project (which has a permit population cap of 80,000) are heavily promoted by county and state tourism boards so it’s no wonder that Reno area residents who evacuated their homes have faced added difficulties for a place to stay. The Reno Gazette Journal reported that when one local resident with children in tow went in search of an advertised discounted hotel room at one of many casino resorts, she was told no rooms were available. 
She noted that roads in and around her home were “jammed” with much longer than expected times to reach safer parts of town. Another resident described his escape as “the gnarliest 24 hours of my life.”
As of Monday there remained a number of roadway closures.
Burning Man attracts visitors from around the world who extend their stays in and around Reno, Lake Tahoe and north towards the Black Rock Desert. As with other high profile tourism destinations around the world, tourists present a complicating factor for resources, infrastructure, and lodging even in the best of times. 
As of Monday morning, 42,000 residents around Reno in “go now” zones were ordered to evacuate, with an additional 45,000 people in adjacent areas asked to “get set.”
Fire officials on Monday said the Hawk Fire was 27% contained and expected to make moderate to high intensity runs over possibly the next 48 hours. From incident command: “conditions remain dynamic and subject to rapid change.”
With climate-driven disasters taxing locations in apocalyptic ways, Nevada officials are overdue in acknowledging that the state’s addiction to tourism needs a serious reset to ensure that resident taxpayers don’t take a backseat to tourists’ needs. Residents are the ones who fund the state’s first responders and infrastructure year in and year out.  
The state’s top disaster chief’s comments in May to another legislative committee have never been more accurate and in need of attention: “if you go home and sleep well tonight after I’m done talking to you, I have done you a disservice.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Interior’s oil rule changes silence landowners, put land at risk, groups say
description: A North Dakota landowner is among those protesting oil and gas rule changes proposed by the federal government.  The changes affect people such as Donald Nelson of Keene in northwest North Dakota. Nelson is a farmer and rancher who owns surface land but the Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Land Management owns the mineral […]
text:
A Bureau of Land Management office in Billings, Montana. (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick/Daily Montanan)A North Dakota landowner is among those protesting oil and gas rule changes proposed by the federal government. 
The changes affect people such as Donald Nelson of Keene in northwest North Dakota. Nelson is a farmer and rancher who owns surface land but the Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Land Management owns the mineral rights. That ownership situation is known as a split estate. 
The changes would reduce bonds from $500,000 down to $25,000 for all wells a company drills in a state. The money is expected to cover the costs of plugging a well when it is done producing and returning the land to its original state. 
“The bonds would not even cover the plugging,” Nelson said. 
Trump, Burgum out to undo Roosevelt’s legacy, conservation advocates say

The rule changes would eliminate the requirement that the BLM notify split-estate landowners when the agency offers oil and gas leases under their property. 
The changes would also reduce the amount of time for comment on potential oil and gas development on a split estate from 90 days down to 10. 
“No notice, no voice, no future,” said Don Schreiber, a New Mexico landowner who joined Nelson and others Monday on a video press conference about the changes. The press conference was organized by the Western Organization of Resource Councils, which includes North Dakota-based Dakota Resource Council. 
Schreiber said bonding is about planning for the future, and he agreed with Nelson that proposed requirements are too low. 
Nelson said oil and gas companies need to be held accountable.
“They are able to charge what they need to make money, whereas we end up as taxpayers paying it from both ends — we pay for the fuel, and then we pay for the reclamation because they walk away,” he said.
Schreiber criticized Interior Secretary and former North Dakota Gov. Doug Burgum and the department for the changes. 
“They just want the landowners out of the way,” Schreiber said. 
The Department of the Interior announced the changes on June 22. Burgum and President Donald Trump’s administration have advocated for oil and gas development on public lands and where the federal government holds mineral rights as part of its goal for American energy dominance.
A news release touted updates to a waste prevention rule that the Interior Department said would cut compliance costs for oil and gas companies by nearly $17 million annually.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum speaks during the 2026 Williston Basin Petroleum Conference in Bismarck on May 21, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
“Energy dominance requires regulatory clarity,” Burgum said in the release. “These targeted updates cut through the red tape that has historically deterred investment, ensuring our public lands remain a reliable engine for economic growth and innovation.” 
The announcement kicked off a 60-day comment period, which ended Monday. 
The Western Organization of Resource Councils submitted formal comments from more than 300 people who support keeping the Biden-era rule.A letter signed by 16 split-estate landowners in Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Wyoming, Colorado, and New Mexico also called on Burgum and Pearce to keep changes made in 2024 intact.
BLM staff will review the public comments and then release a final rule, likely later this year or next year.
The BLM manages about 245 million acres of public land primarily in 12 western states. The BLM also administers 700 million acres of mineral rights, according to the agency.
There are 58 million acres of split-estate land across the United States, most of which are in the West and occupied by ranches and farms, according to the Western Organization of Resource Councils.
Nelson noted in a press release that oil drilling can bring heavy truck traffic, dust, noise, impacts to water, and disruptions that affect ranching. “Those aren’t inconveniences; they are costs to our livelihood and changes to the places we call home,” Nelson said. 
Reach North Dakota Monitor deputy editor Jeff Beach at jbeach@northdakotamonitor.com

name: VTDigger
title: A Vermonter is running for treasurer as a Progressive. The party says he’s not their candidate.
description:
“Most of my dearest friends were astounded to discover my choice of party when I decided to run for office,” Zachary Hampl said earlier this year.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  A Vermonter is running for treasurer as a Progressive. The party says he’s not their candidate..
text:
Zachary Hampl, the Vermont Progressive Party’s nominee for state treasurer, speaks during a candidate forum in June. Screenshot

Typically, the political party labels on a ballot can give voters a sense of where each candidate stands on the biggest issues. But in at least one case in this fall’s election in Vermont, it won’t be that simple.
Zachary Hampl, an author and financial account manager from Rutland Town, won the Vermont Progressive Party primary for state treasurer earlier this month. He was the only candidate on the party’s ballot for that office and got 289 votes. In all, just 474 voters pulled a Progressive ballot this year.
He will appear on the general election ballot alongside the incumbent state treasurer, Democrat Mike Pieciak, and Lynn LaFleur, the Republican Party’s nominee. GOP leaders put LaFleur on the ballot after a different Republican — perennial candidate H. Brooke Paige — won the Republican primary but withdrew afterward to run for one of three other offices he sought this year. 
Hampl’s situation is even more unusual: The party whose primary he won has so far refused to support him.
At a meeting in May, Progressive Party leaders voted against formally endorsing Hampl’s campaign, according to Bill Hunsinger, the party chair. Hampl was one of just two statewide candidates on the party’s primary ballot. The other, Rachel Shaw, got the party’s endorsement in her bid for secretary of state at the same leadership meeting, Hunsinger said.
It’s common for the Progressive Party to have its own candidates for only some statewide offices. The Progs often pick some of the Democratic Party’s nominees to endorse as well, as party leaders did in May for governor and state auditor, according to Hunsinger.
Hunsinger said in an interview that many details about Hampl’s views were unclear to him but that “he certainly does not appear to have the progressive credentials” party leaders are looking for. 
By Hampl’s own admission, it isn’t hard to see why.
“Most of my dearest friends were astounded to discover my choice of party when I decided to run for office,” Hampl wrote in a post on his campaign Facebook page in June, in which he also described the Progressives as a party he would not normally identify with.
In an interview last week, the 32-year-old described his politics as a mixed bag of left- and right-wing ideas that have evolved and do not fully align with the Progressive Party’s platform, or those of Vermont’s other two major parties. 
After securing enough signatures — at least 500 — to get on the ballot, Hampl said he settled on running as a Progressive because he sees too many faults in the traditional two-party system of Democrats and Republicans. The only way to seriously enter the statewide political conversation otherwise is to run as a third-party candidate — and the Progressives have by far the biggest platform of that kind, he said.
Hampl long called himself a libertarian and conservative, he said. As a student at Castleton University, he founded a chapter of Young Americans for Liberty, a prominent nationwide organization supporting libertarian causes on college campuses, including free speech and gun rights. His views led him to support the 2016 presidential campaign of U.S. Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., a staunch libertarian, he said.
He said his views started changing when he worked as an emergency medical technician during the Covid-19 pandemic. He said he got a firsthand view of how difficult it is for many people to find affordable housing and get healthcare. That led him to the conclusion that housing and healthcare should be treated as human rights, he said. 
In that sense, he sees eye-to-eye with many in the Progressive Party, he said. But he suggested he also remains skeptical of major government intervention in society, citing a quote from former Republican President Ronald Reagan that “when government expands, liberty contracts.”
He acknowledged it will probably confuse voters to learn there is a Progressive candidate who does not have the party’s support. But he made the case that there could be benefits to having a treasurer who is not backed by any political party, since the duties of the job — managing state coffers and public employees’ pensions — are nonpartisan. 
“That’s good news for both Republicans and Democrats,” he said. “We have a candidate who’s actually more independent than anything else — but just so happens to be running as a Progressive.”
Hunsinger, the Progressive chair, said he would not rule out his party endorsing Hampl. He pointed to a message from Hampl stating that he would promote “equal access to economic opportunities for all Vermonter’s (sic) based on championing the power of teamwork.” That embodies the spirit of the Progressive Party, Hunsinger said.
At the same time, the party has not discussed throwing its weight behind a different candidate, including Pieciak. Asked whom people should vote for this fall if they want the most progressive treasurer possible, Hunsinger declined to say. 
“I don’t really quite have the answer for you — and I think that might be indicative enough,” he said.
A key proposal of Hampl’s campaign is to increase collaboration between the government and financial institutions around the state. He suggested Vermont set up an institution that is similar to the Bank of North Dakota, which is the only government-run bank in the U.S. and provides banking services to government agencies along with supporting loans for farms, businesses and students.
He has also argued that his experience as an account manager, along with a brief stint selling insurance, gives him the know-how to oversee the state’s investments.
In addition to that financial work, Hampl has written two novels. Both focus on relatively dark themes, titled “The Mortician’s Curse” and “Slaughter Scheme.”
According to a description online, the latter, published in 2024, tells the story of “a killing spree in the trenches of morbidly corrupt academia.”
Hampl said he is working on a third book, though his political ambitions have taken center stage over writing lately.
“I’ve been campaigning all over the state,” he said.

title: Crop report: Nearly half of Iowa corn in dent stage
description: With 47% of Iowa corn acres in the dent stage, according to the latest crop progress and condition report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the crop is nearing harvest season.  Soybean acres setting pods reached 88% during the period, which is slightly behind last year’s crop. Soybean condition was 77% good to excellent during […]
text:
Nearly half of Iowa's corn crop has reached the dent stage. (Photo by Jared Strong/Iowa Capital Dispatch)With 47% of Iowa corn acres in the dent stage, according to the latest crop progress and condition report from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the crop is nearing harvest season. 

Crop phenological stages:
— Corn in dough stage: a thick or dough-like substance is present in all kernels.
— Corn in dent stage: all the kernels have dented, ear is firm and no milk is present in the kernels.
— Soybeans setting pods: pods are developing on lower portions of the plant, with some blooming still on top of plant.
The 2026 crop is 5 percentage points ahead of last year’s crop in terms of the share in the dent stage. Corn acres in the dough stage reached 90% during the Aug. 17 through Aug. 23 reporting period, which is 3 percentage points ahead of last year’s crop. One percent of corn acres had reached maturity as of the reporting period.

Soybean acres setting pods reached 88% during the period, which is slightly behind last year’s crop. Soybean condition was 77% good to excellent during the period and corn condition was 78% good to excellent, according to the report. 
Iowa subsoil and topsoil had mostly adequate moisture conditions, according to the report which put subsoil moisture at 66% adequate and topsoil moisture at 70% adequate. 
Iowa had “unseasonably” dry weather during the reporting period, according to State Climatologist Justin Glisan, who reported the statewide average precipitation was just over two-tenths of an inch, while the normal is more than nine-tenths of an inch. 
The dry weather, however, followed a particularly wet week where Iowa’s statewide average, at 2.60 inches, was nearly triple the normal for the Aug. 10 through Aug. 16 reporting period. 
Glisan reported a “shift to more seasonal weather” for the most recent reporting period, when the statewide average temperature was 71.1 degrees Fahrenheit – less than 1 degree above the normal for the period. 
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig said the weather conditions were “beautiful” throughout the last week of the Iowa State Fair, which he said had “fairgoers turning out in record numbers.” 
According to the Iowa State Fair, 1,218,834 people attended the event in Des Moines over its 11-day run, beating the previous attendance record from 2024 by more than 36,000 people.
“As students and families settle into the routines of a new school year, farmers are keeping an eye on the forecast as crops continue to mature,” Naig said. “Warmer temperatures and near-normal rainfall into early September should help keep the crops moving along as we inch closer to the busy fall harvest season.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas State Police director cancels appearance before Black lawmakers to discuss traffic stop
description: The head of Arkansas State Police said Monday he would be unable to appear before the Arkansas Legislative Black Caucus to discuss a state trooper punching an 18-year-old during a traffic stop because of pending litigation.  Col. Mike Hagar had been scheduled to appear before the caucus Tuesday to discuss the Aug. 1 traffic stop […]
text:
Arkansas State Police Director Col. Mike Hagar speaks during a legislative subcommittee meeting on Jan. 21, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)The head of Arkansas State Police said Monday he would be unable to appear before the Arkansas Legislative Black Caucus to discuss a state trooper punching an 18-year-old during a traffic stop because of pending litigation. 
Col. Mike Hagar had been scheduled to appear before the caucus Tuesday to discuss the Aug. 1 traffic stop of Alisa Hackett of Osceola that has drawn national attention and sparked a civil rights lawsuit. 
“I offered to meet privately with the Caucus to have an open and candid conversation about any public safety concerns they would like to discuss,” Hagar said in a statement released late Monday afternoon. “That offer stands, and I’d be very happy to talk individually with any legislator. Unfortunately, because of pending litigation, it would be irresponsible and impossible for me to have an open discussion in a public setting.” 
Rep. Jay Richardson, a Fort Smith Democrat and caucus chairman, said Monday that lawmakers would still meet at the scheduled time Tuesday.
According to a federal lawsuit filed earlier this month, Hackett was stopped near Manila for speeding by Moisses Arellano, an Arkansas State Police officer. 
Dash camera footage obtained through a public records request shows Arellano throwing Hackett, who is Black, to the ground while trying to handcuff her and then punching her in the face. 

The Arkansas Legislative Black Caucus and NAACP Arkansas State Conference have called for answers over the traffic stop. A rally was planned in response to the meeting.
The NAACP Arkansas State Conference expressed its disappointment in Hagar’s decision in an emailed statement Monday. The meeting was “an important opportunity” for elected officials and the public to hear directly from Arkansas State Police and receive clarity regarding the traffic stop, the statement said. 
Barry Jefferson, president of the NAACP Arkansas State Conference, said this meeting is not about asking for special treatment, but rather “equal treatment, transparency, and accountability.”
“Alisa Hackett and her family deserve answers, and the taxpayers and elected officials of Arkansas deserve to know whether the policies and training of the Arkansas State Police were followed,” Jefferson said. “When a citizen has questions about an encounter with law enforcement, the answer cannot simply be silence.” 
Hagar “respectively communicated” to Richardson that he would be unable to appear before lawmakers as scheduled tomorrow, according to the release. Hagar said he hoped legislators would call on him, and he wanted to thank them in advance for understanding the position he’s in. 
“I understand and appreciate that our lawmakers have a duty to represent their constituents, and I know we share a common mission to keep Arkansans safe,” Hagar said.
Reporter Ainsley Platt contributed to this story.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Board of State Canvassers deadlocks on citizens-only voting measure, setting up court fight
description: After nearly seven hours of discussion, the Michigan Board of State Canvassers deadlocked 2-2 on a ballot measure that would enact strict voter ID laws, meaning the proposal was not certified for the November ballot. However, the measure is likely to go to the Michigan Supreme Court for a final decision.  The board’s four members, […]
text:
All four members of the Board of State Canvassers gather with Bureau of Elections staff to review signatures on the citizens-only ballot petition on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)After nearly seven hours of discussion, the Michigan Board of State Canvassers deadlocked 2-2 on a ballot measure that would enact strict voter ID laws, meaning the proposal was not certified for the November ballot. However, the measure is likely to go to the Michigan Supreme Court for a final decision. 
The board’s four members, along with leadership and staff from the state Bureau of Elections, spent hours looking at specific affidavits of signatures that had been challenged by those opposed to the petition and analyzing handwriting on sheets of signatures to verify the validity of addresses and signatures. Among the issues examined were procedural questions about the timeliness of turning in those challenges and responses to the Bureau of Elections and the Board of State Canvassers. 
Many of the decisions came to a deadlock — the board is made up of two Democrats and two Republicans, and many decisions split along those partisan lines. In the case of a 2-2 vote on a given signature, that signature is not counted as valid.



Quotation







We’re aware of the gravity of this. We are aware of the seriousness of considering this one.


– Richard Houskamp, chair of the Michigan Board of State Canvassers. 


The Bureau of Elections staff had recommended against certifying the ballot measure based on a standard random sample of 1,000 signatures. Based on the more than 709,000 signatures submitted, compared with the required 446,198, at least 629 signatures in the sample needed to be valid.
“Practically speaking, the board’s view for decades is that it’s not really practical to review, in this case, over 700,000 signatures individually,” Jonathan Brater, director of the Bureau of Elections explained about the sampling process. 
Based on the staff report from the bureau, which counted 612 valid signatures, lawyers for both the sponsors of the ballot measure and the opposition to it brought new challenges and additional information to try to make their respective cases about whether or not the measure should make the ballot. 
Sean Dutton, a lawyer supporting the citizens-only voting ballot petition, provides information to Jonathan Brater, the director of the Bureau of Elections, at a Board of State Canvassers meeting on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
After reviewing information and voting on a number of individual signatures, the Board of State Canvassers had identified 626 valid signatures — just three signatures below the needed threshold. A number of those decisions were contentious, with Paul Cordes, a Republican on the board, saying just before the vote that he believed there were more than enough valid signatures to put the petition on the ballot. 
Paul Jacob, chairman of Americans for Citizens Voting, the group behind the initiative, has indicated that the group will sue and would take the case to the Michigan Supreme Court and, if necessary, the U.S. Supreme Court. 
Meanwhile, Mark Brewer, a lawyer for opponents of the measure, said that it had been a “very sloppy petition drive from the very beginning.”
“Sponsors and the challengers have had ample opportunity to make arguments and present evidence. There are hundreds, if not thousands, of pages of arguments and evidence before you that your staff has thoroughly reviewed and produced two reports, and they recommend that based on strict compliance with those legal requirements, that this petition drive is short of signatures,” Brewer said. 
Cordes also compared the process of Monday’s meeting to last month’s approval of the Michiganders for Money Out of Politics ballot measure. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“My math says that we would have a greater buffer than on that one,” he said. “I’m not saying this was done well, obviously, but we would have more than that one did, and during that back and forth that we did a month ago, we went through bureau approved signatures and removed a fair amount of them, a very good amount of them.”
Eric Doster, a lawyer for petition’s sponsors, similarly said, “We’re just asking for the same treatment as MMOP,” referring to that measure, in early remarks to the board.
Richard Houskamp, the board chair and one of the Republicans on the board, opened the meeting by noting the level of interest and concern that the petition — which voting rights activists said could disenfranchise legal voters. 
“This petition has generated an enormous amount of emotion, of concern. The fact that we have all of you folks here this morning indicates there’s a lot of interest in it,” Houskamp said. “We’re aware of the gravity of this. We are aware of the seriousness of considering this one.”
Throughout the hearing, both Republican members of the board and lawyers for the proposal emphasized the importance of allowing voters to put a measure on the ballot.
“Please remember what’s at stake and which way the law leans. This board must decide and must always lean towards counting the voter signature,” Doster told board members. “These are the signatures of real registered Michigan voters who have now come forward under oath to confirm their own participation. The settled policy of Michigan election law is to favor the participation of qualified voters, not to disenfranchise them on subjective technicalities.”
Meanwhile, opponents of the measure celebrated the outcome. 
“Michiganders do not want out-of-state billionaires to take away their right to the ballot box, which is why these restrictive voting initiatives failed,” said Shannon Abbott, the Michigan program manager for Common Cause, which launched a “decline-to-sign” campaign against the initiative. “Our Michigan members told us that these initiatives would have prevented eligible U.S. citizens from voting by putting restrictive red tape in front of access to the ballot box.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Zach Lahn calls for state regulation of data centers, surveillance cameras
description: Zach Lahn, the GOP nominee for Iowa governor in 2026, said Monday many of the major concerns about new technologies like data center power use and Flock cameras are issues that need to be regulated at a state level. Lahn, a businessman, spoke about his gubernatorial campaign and answered questions at an Iowa Association of […]
text:
Iowa Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn gave a speech and answered questions at a candidate forum Aug. 24, 2026 hosted by the Iowa Association of Business and Industry in West Des Moines. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Zach Lahn, the GOP nominee for Iowa governor in 2026, said Monday many of the major concerns about new technologies like data center power use and Flock cameras are issues that need to be regulated at a state level.
Lahn, a businessman, spoke about his gubernatorial campaign and answered questions at an Iowa Association of Business and Industry candidate forum in West Des Moines. His general election opponent, Democrat Rob Sand, spoke to ABI members in June at the organization’s conference.  ABI staff said Lahn was invited to speak at that event, but could not attend.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Republican candidate said Monday he came into the race as an “outsider” and first-time candidate. Lahn said his “Iowa first” vision, which focuses on improving quality of life and encouraging young people to stay and live in the state, was a message that has resonated with GOP primary voters and Iowans overall.
Prioritizing Iowa would also be a staple of his economic policy if elected, Lahn said at the forum. For example, he criticized a multinational company, which he did not identify but said has been “given a tremendous amount of refundable tax credits by the government,” then went onto sue a “third generation Iowa company.” Though the Iowa company eventually won the lawsuit, he said the government subsidized the larger company.
“If you look at some of these tax incentives we’ve been giving as a state, oftentimes we’re incentivizing companies that are competing against Iowa’s homegrown businesses,” Lahn said. “… It doesn’t make sense. We have scarce resources we’re trying to allocate as a state. If we want to build a culture, we’ll invest in Iowa’s homegrown businesses first.”
Lahn has also made previous comments saying he would place new restrictions on foreign workers with certain nonimmigrant U.S. work visas, and called in a campaign ad for H-1B visa holders to be banned from employment by Iowa state government and universities. Sand has cited this ad from Lahn in his own campaign events, quoting “Iowa jobs are for Iowans,” as he and other Democrats have criticized Lahn for having lived in and registered to vote in Kansas, and for continuing to make trips to the state using his personal airplane.
At the ABI event, Lahn was asked about his approach to energy policies specifically related to data centers. The candidate has said he would support a temporary moratorium on data centers, and said he believes the focus needs to be on how a data center will improve the Iowa communities where they’re located.
“I’m not someone who’s saying we should ban (data centers) outright, I don’t think that’s the case. I’m trying to bridge this gap of saying that a temporary pause, a moratorium, to get the rules of the game in play, to be able to say that if you’re going to come to Iowa, the question you need to answer for Iowa citizens is, ‘how are you going to benefit all Iowa?'”
In April, Lahn told the Des Moines Register he would support raising taxes on Iowa data centers by five times to lower property taxes.
Lahn said at the ABI conference his approach to data centers would involve no tax incentives for data center companies, requiring the companies to pay for their electricity use, and requiring the companies “make sure that the environmental concerns are addressed and taken care of.” He also said he believed environmental concerns could be an area where data centers could find inroads with Iowa communities by taking steps to improve water infrastructure.
He said he met with a company that didn’t know Iowa faced water quality issues, and told them, “You really want to make a difference when you go to a community, offer to build a nitrate removal system on the water supply, and then deliver the water to the municipality.”
“And it’s like a light bulb went off with their engineer,” Lahn said. “And now I’ve had a couple different conversations about this directly, where they say, ‘we think we can actually do this.’ You do that, you’d be a totally different story in our communities. People would actually be saying, ‘Wow, you’re here to benefit me and my kids.'”
Sand has also introduced a data center policy plan which includes several of the same priorities as Lahn has discussed, including limiting tax incentives and having data centers pay for utility costs, as well as calling for “accountability and transparency over new data centers” through public disclosures on energy and water use, as well as the permanent and construction jobs created through the center.
Lahn said the discussion on data centers — as well as about the use of Flock cameras, AI-powered automatic license plate readers which photograph vehicles — are spaces where technology has been implemented in communities before people have had a chance to decide whether the technology is operating legally and fairly. Several Iowa localities have challenged both Flock cameras and data centers through local government actions.
“Tech is way ahead of ‘how do we properly use the tech,’ and you don’t need to go any further than listen to Elon Musk for a little bit of time talk about what’s going to happen with AI,” Lahn said. “… We have real concerns here. So, the state level is where we should adjudicate these things. This is not a federal decision, in my opinion.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Single-subject complaint filed against ‘Respect Nebraska Voters’ ballot measure
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s top elections official will decide whether a ballot measure seeking to make it harder for Nebraska legislators to amend voter-approved laws is too broad for the November ballot. Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen confirmed Monday he has been asked to weigh the fate of the Respect Nebraska Voters measure. State Sen. Machaela […]
text:
Signs for the new Respect Nebraska Voters ballot measure campaign. Jan. 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s top elections official will decide whether a ballot measure seeking to make it harder for Nebraska legislators to amend voter-approved laws is too broad for the November ballot.
Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen confirmed Monday he has been asked to weigh the fate of the Respect Nebraska Voters measure. State Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha, a Democrat, and former state Sen. Curt Friesen of Henderson, a Republican, filed the objection. They served together in the Legislature for four years, between 2019 and 2023.
Then-state Sen. Curt Friesen of Henderson, a former chair of the Legislature’s Transportation and Telecommunications Committee, in his Legislative District 34 office in November 2022. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska News Service)
The pair argue the measure contains at least two subjects and violates a Nebraska Constitution limit that any voter-passed laws or constitutional amendments be on one related subject.
“I just feel that it’s not right and that the Legislature always has to retain some authority to make changes, even on things I don’t like them changing,” Friesen said Monday.
Proposal specifics
The proposal seeks to amend the Nebraska Constitution to increase the threshold for lawmakers to amend or overturn voter-approved laws from 33 of 49 state lawmakers (66%) to 40 of 49 (80%). Additionally, only laws that facilitate and “safeguard” voter-approved statutes and “advance a compelling state interest by the least restrictive means” would be valid.
The change applies to any voter-approved law dating to 2004 — minimum wage, Medicaid expansion, caps on payday loans, casino gambling, medical cannabis and paid sick leave.
Advocates for a proposed amendment to the Nebraska Constitution hope to make it harder for legislators to tweak ballot measures approved by voters. Advocates, including ballot co-sponsor Jo Giles, at the podium, host a launch event in Omaha. Jan. 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The campaign launched after lawmakers scaled back voter-approved paid sick leave promised for most workers and just before legislators slowed voter-approved increases to the state minimum wage. Lawmakers supporting the laws cited economic reasons for their action.
Laws making it harder to run statewide initiative and referendum petitions would be invalid, too. Those powers are reserved in the Nebraska Constitution.
County election officials have not yet finished validating petition signatures for the measure, but if election officials confirm at least 138,473 valid signatures, the measure qualifies for the ballot. Evnen gets the initial determination of whether the Cavanaugh-Friesen objection has merit. 
The secretary noted the deadline to certify the ballot, Sept. 11, “is rapidly approaching.”
“I will likely be announcing my decision on whether the petition meets the single-subject requirements before the validation is entirely complete in order to ensure that deadline can be met,” Evnen said in a statement.
‘Cut both ways’
Friesen, on Monday, and Cavanaugh in the past have said lawmakers have a hard enough time getting 33 votes, the same number needed to overcome filibusters. Friesen served in the Legislature for eight years. Cavanaugh is in her eighth year and will be term-limited come January. Friesen said it makes sense to leave the rules about ballot measures the same because the single-subject requirement for ballot measures also complicates what language can go before voters.
State Sens. John Arch of La Vista, Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha and Ben Hansen of Blair, from left, meet on the floor of the Nebraska Legislature. Arch is speaker of the Legislature. Jan. 15, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Most ballot measures, he said, likely need tweaking after passage.
“Whether it’s a rural or urban issue, I mean, it’s going to cut both ways someday,” Friesen said.
He noted that he would love to see a ballot measure about property taxes, for instance, but the rule requires ballot language to be compact. If it can’t be refined by lawmakers, that complicates future legislation.
“If you’re forbidding them from going in and dealing with this issue, I just don’t see how you could have passed something good enough in a ballot initiative to satisfy the need to fix the problem,” Friesen said.
Nebraska Secretary of State Bob Evnen. June 6, 2025. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln had said in December 2025 that she was unsure whether the Respect Nebraska Voters petition was a single subject, according to reporting from 10/11 in Lincoln.
Jo Giles, executive director of the Women’s Fund of Omaha and a sponsor of the group, said then that she believed the group’s petition was OK because the focus was increasing the votes needed for any changes involving ballot initiatives.
“We wouldn’t be here today if lawmakers were actually working together to support the will of the people,” Giles said July 2 when supporters turned in signatures.
The Examiner reached out to the campaign Monday for comment on the Cavanaugh-Friesen complaint.
No matter Evnen’s decision, the final say could come from the Nebraska Supreme Court. The general election is Nov. 3.

name: VTDigger
title: 15 years after Irene, plucky business owners recall the monster storm and its aftermath
description:
Residents remembered the destructive power of the storm as it drove the North Branch of the Deerfield River well over its banks and into homes and businesses.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  15 years after Irene, plucky business owners recall the monster storm and its aftermath.
text:
After the floodwaters receded, the extent of the damage to the Wilmington business community became apparent. File photo by Mike Eldred/Deerfield Valley News

This story by John Hurdle was first published in The Deerfield Valley News on Aug. 20, 2026.
WILMINGTON — Lisa Sullivan recalled the morning of Sunday, Aug. 28, 2011, when raging floodwaters from Tropical Storm Irene threatened to destroy the building that houses Bartleby’s Books.
Water pressure on the building was so great from the “river” flowing down Route 9 that Sullivan’s husband, a builder, decided to open the front door to help the water drain away, albeit through their bookshop.
As soon as they did, a large blue flower tub washed in. Then the smell of propane coming from tanks dislodged from buildings drove them out, for fear of an explosion. The bookstore owner and her husband escaped by climbing to the second floor, then down the back stairs and up the hill behind the shop in Wilmington village.
Just before the 15th anniversary of the worst flood in Wilmington in decades, residents remembered the destructive power of the storm as it drove the North Branch of the Deerfield River well over its banks, and into homes and businesses that were closed for months as the owners cleaned out feet of stinking mud and tried to rebuild their lives.
“We were in the store about up to our knees in water,” said Sullivan. “At that point, the smell of propane became really intense because large propane tanks were being pulled off buildings.
That’s when we said we have to get out because we said we didn’t know what could happen.”
Sullivan lost about 85% of her books in the flood, which rose to about 3.5 feet in her store. Her overall losses totaled about $400,000, only $160,000 of which was covered by insurance, she said.
At the Village Pub on South Main Street, owner Ginny Blake said she first looked through the windows of her bar and thought the water damage wasn’t too bad. But then she got inside and found her second-floor bar 2 inches deep in “stinky mud.”
Still, the damage was indeed minor compared with a downstairs jazz club that had been so badly flooded that freezers and bars had been knocked off their stands and were floating in the muddy water, she said. “The whole downstairs was destroyed and had to be gutted out,” said Blake, whose bar is along the east side of the river, just downstream from the bridge at the intersection of routes 9 and 100.
Blake also recalled watching the severe damage done to Dot’s diner on the west bank of the river.
Despite the shocking scale of Irene’s destruction, residents and business people also recall the resilience of people who live and do business in Wilmington, and their success in rebuilding from a ferocious act of nature.
“What we remember just as much as the destruction is how quickly everyone came together,” said Christian Engel and Jen Betit-Engel, owners of Ratu’s liquor and cannabis stores, in remarks gathered by local writer Rachel Olstein, who has collected a number of Irene stories. “It wasn’t just about rebuilding homes and businesses. People needed driveways repaired so they could get to work, help making a car payment or money for whatever was going to keep their heads above water.”
“Irene showed us how vulnerable a small town can be but it also showed us just how strong Wilmington is when people take care of each other,” the Engels wrote.
Even businesses that weren’t operating when Irene hit recognize that the storm has had a lasting effect on Wilmington.
“Irene is always in the backdrop as we continue to exist,” said Susan Motyl, owner of the five-year-old Alpenglow Bistro, in remarks to Olstein. “There is the reminder of the toll it took and the floods that devastated this area by looking at the height of the flood water clearly delineated on the siding of our town hall offices.”
The flood height of Irene is vividly marked on the outside wall of Wilmington Town Hall, exceeding by a few inches the previous record dating to 1938.
“Thankfully, this little town manages to skirt severe weather patterns, and perhaps it’s because it withstood and recovered from one not too long ago,” Motyl said.
At the Village Pub, customer Eileen Lombardo said she first underestimated Irene, assuming the storm would cause just another nuisance flood on the low-lying sports field near the bar. “We never thought anything of it — it was just another rainstorm,” she said.
But it quickly became clear that Irene was no ordinary rainstorm, as shown by Lombardo’s mandatory evacuation from the top floor of the Village Pub building, where she has lived for some 20 years.
And after first heading toward Bennington on Route 9, she and a friend turned around because the quantity of water cascading down from the hills during the storm showed that continuing to head west was, to put it mildly, unsafe. “We’re headed up the mountain and we saw all this water rushing down. We said, ‘Let’s go home.’ It’s a good thing we did,” she said.
For Sullivan, who also owns the Pickwell’s Barn women’s boutique in Wilmington village, reopening the bookstore about three months after losing most of her stock was an important way of showing the town that the business was invested in the community.
But the rebuilt inventory — some of which is now on the second floor — has been accompanied by contingency planning for any new monster storm. There are now empty boxes on the third floor that would hopefully enable Sullivan to move her inventory out of harm’s way on the first floor if a storm of Irene’s magnitude ever comes again.
“We’re more prepared in that we know it can happen,” she said.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Ex-vendor sues Oklahoma ethics board over ethics system replacement, seeks $6M in damages
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — A Texas company countersued the state Ethics Commission on Tuesday, alleging it suffered $6 million in losses after the agency ended a contract to replace the state’s campaign finance system.  RFD and Associates filed a counterclaim against the Oklahoma Ethics Commission, claiming the agency unnecessarily terminated its contract and that dela[...]
text:
Lee Anne Bruce Boone, executive director of the Oklahoma Ethics Commission, speaks with a reporter following a meeting of the board at the state Capitol April 10, 2025. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A Texas company countersued the state Ethics Commission on Tuesday, alleging it suffered $6 million in losses after the agency ended a contract to replace the state’s campaign finance system. 
RFD and Associates filed a counterclaim against the Oklahoma Ethics Commission, claiming the agency unnecessarily terminated its contract and that delays in the project were due to issues with provided datasets and unclear and changing expectations. 
The company delivered the project before the provided deadline despite problems they say were caused by the Ethics Commission, the “Guardian 2.0” system was delivered before the provided deadline, according to their filing in Oklahoma County District Court. 
“You cannot separate the project timeline from incomplete data, delayed approvals and changing requirements,” said Scott Glover, chief operating officer of RFD, in a statement. “Despite those challenges, we worked through the issues, completed testing and delivered a system that was accurate and available for active filers by Dec. 12, 2025.”
The Ethics Commission voted to terminate its contract with RFD and Associates and pursue legal action against it in December, alleging it had failed to fulfill the terms of its contract and replace the system on schedule. The Oklahoma Ethics Commission, represented by Attorney General Gentner Drummond, sued RFD and Associates in January.
The state’s lawsuit asserts multiple claims, including breach of contract, fraud, unjust enrichment, negligent misrepresentation, breach of warranties and violations of the Oklahoma Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Drummond has said the failures have cost the state over $800,000. 
The Guardian System was not fully functional for three months, leaving the public and those running for public office unable to access campaign filings. Among other things, the finance system allows the public to examine lobbyist and candidate expenditures and track campaign donations. 
The Attorney General’s Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Lee Anne Bruce Boone, executive director of the Ethics Commission, said the contract was appropriately terminated. 
“We categorically disagree with these self-serving misrepresentations and unfounded allegations,” she said in a statement. “Make no mistake, RFD knew what this project required — it described the work in its proposal before it was ever awarded the contract.”
The expectations were outlined in writing that services would be timely and the delivered system would run uninterrupted and error-free, Bruce Boone said. The Ethics Commission paid over $800,000 based on these promises. 
“By the end, RFD acknowledged it could not deliver on its promises, admitting it had overpromised and underdelivered,” she said. 
The company’s lawsuit alleges that on Dec. 15, the Ethics Commission described the new system’s status as “good” but then ended the contract and immediately entered into a new one with the company that hosted the original Guardian System four days later at a board meeting. 
“The Ethics Commission solicited a replacement for the Guardian system, induced RFD to build that replacement on a compressed timeline, and then exploited RFD’s performance as a bargaining chip to extract a drastically reduced price from its legacy vendor, Civix, while concealing its intent to return to the old system,” the lawsuit alleges. 
Data provided by the Ethics Commission was also “riddled with defects,” including format changes, thousands of missing document files and troublesome formatting, and RFD had to correct datasets, according to the company’s counterclaim. The Ethics Commission was also sometimes months late in signing off on various deliverables. 
RFD invested over 25,000 hours into the project in less than a year and is seeking more than $1 million in unpaid labor and $5.1 million in damages from “lost profits and business opportunities as a result of the Ethics Commission’s actions,” according to a news release.
