title: Trump, McMahon promote school voucher program as students return to class
text: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump and U.S. Education Secretary Linda McMahon on Monday touted a national private school voucher program set to launch in early 2027.During a White House Rose Garden event celebrating the back-to-school season, Trump and McMahon lauded the incoming federal school choice effort along with many of the education policies the administration has pursued, including ongoing efforts to dismantle the 46-year old Education Department.At least 30 states have already opted in to the school voucher program, which allocates up to $1,700 in federal tax credits for people donating to organizations that provide private and religious school scholarships.The program, known as the Education Freedom Tax Credit, was created in the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut bill Trump signed into law in July 2025. “One year ago, as part of the great, big, beautiful bill, we passed the Education Freedom Tax Credit — the largest ever expansion of school choice — and we want every parent to have the power to send their child to a high-quality school that shares their values,” Trump told the crowd of educators, parents and students. Monday’s event highlighted Trump and congressional Republicans’ continued focus on school choice as a central point of their education agenda, with the upcoming voucher program marking a pillar of that effort. The umbrella term “school choice” centers on alternative programs to a student’s assigned public school. While opponents argue these efforts drain critical funds and resources from school districts, advocates say the initiatives are necessary for parents dissatisfied with their local public schools.Attendees at the Rose Garden also included Republican Govs. Jim Pillen of Nebraska and Sarah Huckabee Sanders of Arkansas, as well as GOP Rep. Tim Walberg of Michigan, who chairs the House Committee on Education and Workforce.  McMahon echoed the president, saying the federal program gives parents “unprecedented freedom to choose the path that is best for their child.” She added that “it’s no surprise that over half of our nation’s states — both red and blue — have raced to this historic choice option, benefiting families whether their child attends public or private school.”  Dems working to reverse programMeanwhile, congressional Democrats are already attempting to axe the program. Sens. Mark Kelly of Arizona and Mazie Hirono of Hawaii in April introduced a bill in the Senate, alongside nearly 30 of their colleagues, that would repeal the program. Rep. Gwen Moore of Wisconsin introduced a companion bill in the House in June with Reps. Suzanne Bonamici of Oregon, Maxwell Frost of Florida, Adelita Grijalva of Arizona, Mark Pocan of Wisconsin and dozens more original co-sponsors. The legislation faces a dismal fate in the GOP-controlled House and Senate.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Friction emerges as K-12 school funding commission weighs solutions
description: CT's Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding must report recommendations by January. An expert presentation Thursday drew pushback.
text:
Gov. Ned Lamont’s Blue Ribbon Commission on K-12 Education Funding and Affordability has a daunting task: Reinvent Connecticut’s school funding system and produce a report with recommendations by the end of the calendar year. 
Those recommendations are likely to play a major role in what the General Assembly does after it reconvenes in January, and they could reshape the state’s public school system for decades.
As a first order of business, members of the commission set out to learn what other states are doing. 
On Thursday, they heard from Marguerite Roza, director of the Edunomics Lab at Georgetown University and expert in the many problems now afflicting public schools across the country. Not everyone was thrilled at what she had to say.
Roza broke her presentation into four sections: uneven access to funds, poor financial management, rising costs and a weak return on investment for educational expenses. 
She invited commissioners to interrupt with questions and comments, and interrupt they did, particularly during the first two sections. Organizers eventually told members to hold their input until the end to ensure the meeting didn’t run over.
For some time now, advocates and leaders across Connecticut have had a strikingly consistent diagnosis for what ails the state’s public schools: The state’s funding formula hasn’t been adjusted for inflation since 2013, and districts have lost hundreds of millions of dollars in unrealized revenue as a result. Spurred to action, the General Assembly approved a roughly $180 million boost for public schools earlier this year, but advocates say more is needed. 
Roza did not dismiss or outright challenge that argument. In fact, one of the first slides in her presentation illustrated how inequitable Connecticut’s system is: On average, schools in wealthy towns spend (and by implication receive) more money per pupil than poorer districts. In California, which directs state dollars more aggressively to lower-income districts, the pattern is reversed. California’s wealthiest districts get about $2,000 per pupil from state tax dollars; in Connecticut, that number is closer to $4,000.
But Roza also observed that there are wide disparities in how districts with the same level of wealth perform. She said that suggests some schools are using their dollars more effectively than others and are worth learning from.
“That data is going to be really important when we start to say … beyond just distributing money, what kinds of policies can work to make sure, when the money lands in the district, that it’s driving strong value for the kids in that district,” Roza said.
That drew pushback from commission member Lisa Hammersley, chief executive of the School and State Finance Project and one of Connecticut’s leading voices on education.
“I think it’s just more of a nuanced conversation than just looking at these spots on the graph, right?” Hammersley said.
Say there are two schools with the same level of student poverty, but one has a much higher number of multilingual learners. “The ability for those students to achieve at the same level is going to look different,” Hammersley said. That might be why outcomes are worse in one district even though it spends more money per pupil.
Roza acknowledged the importance of comparing like districts to one another. But she maintained that Hammersley’s example isn’t the norm.
“I wish that were the explanation for most of them. It’s generally not,” Roza told Hammersley.
Roza touched another nerve when she suggested there’s another reason schools are finding themselves strapped for cash — one that has nothing to do with the choices made in the state Capitol.
“A lot of times, people look heavily to choice programs or other variables to find out who’s to blame. But I am here to tell you that there is a villain, and it is young people. They’re not having enough kids,” Roza said.
That matters because most school funding is based on enrollment. Fewer kids means fewer students, which means less money. Roza said some districts aren’t reacting appropriately to that reality. 
“Assuming this is going to flip in the next couple years, I think, is shortsighted. Districts are going to probably have to downsize and it’s going to be difficult. And some are going to drag their feet, and then they’re going to get themselves in financial trouble,” Roza said.
Roza offered a few examples of how states can push schools to manage their money more responsibly:

Requiring districts hold minimum budget reserves
Requiring standardized 5-year budget projections 
Force labor contract renegotiations if reserves drop below 5%
Staged interventions based on financial triggers, from support and mandatory budget plans to full-blown state takeover of a district

“We didn’t see much in the way of financial crises in the last five years because so much federal came [through the ESSER program]. That’s gone,” Roza said. “And now a lot of districts … they have a whole team that might be used to spending, not cutting.”
Windsor Board of Education Vice President Leonard Lockhart pushed back.
“ESSER funds actually highlighted the fact that the districts need more funding and support,” he said, adding, “I’m of the belief that local communities should not have to pay for something they truly have no control over.”
Lockhart expressed unease at putting more requirements and restrictions on schools at a time when so much attention is now on whether the state needs to do more.
“We have to be careful what the state is asking local districts to do, ‘cause all it’s going to do is complicate the situation and possibly make it worse,” Lockhart said.
New Haven Mayor Justin Elicker chimed in not long after. He told Roza that most financially distressed districts in Connecticut — including his — are in that position because of uneven state funding, not financial mismanagement. 
“And the list of recommendations for districts in financial distress that you have are more related to districts that are not making the right decisions, rather than helping districts that are simply not able to raise money,” Elicker said.
Roza responded, “All over the country, we’re seeing a mix of districts fall into financial distress. So it’s not just high-poverty districts that do it.” And she reiterated that equitable funding is important.
“I think it can be both [inequity and poor management], but I think you want to keep your eye on it,” she said.
Elicker wasn’t entirely satisfied.
“I think we just should be careful not to assume that districts in financial distress are districts that are making bad decisions. In New Haven, we’ve closed four schools, we’ve reduced our staff when we actually should increase our staff because our students need more,” he said.
“Then you’re not one of the ones” in this category, Roza interjected.
On the topic of equitable funding, Roza offered a range of approaches all centered on one core problem: Funding schools with local wealth is inherently inequitable, but voters are much more likely to support raising local taxes over state ones. If the state limits local school funding, that could end up leaving money on the table, Roza said.
Sen. Jeff Gordon, R-Woodstock, questioned whether that’s still true.
“I can tell you in my part of the state … there really isn’t any appetite to keep raising local taxes, including one town that just, for the fourth time, voted its board of ed budget down,” Gordon said.
Roza said her impression nationwide is that many districts are still voting the same way on local taxes as they always do, whether that’s in favor or against.
“The ones in the middle really want to know, incrementally, what any sort of increase is going to deliver locally,” Roza said.
Roza said states that want more equitable funding should adopt some kind of “tap and tame” approach — tapping into those local tax dollars voters will more regularly approve while taming the inequities that result. For example: The state sets an overall per-pupil spending target, then decides how much of that the local community should raise itself, based on the community’s wealth. The state pays the difference.
For example: The state decides a district should spend $20,000 per pupil. If it determines the town can raise $15,000 per pupil itself, then the state would provide the remaining $5,000 per pupil.
That prompted a comment from Rep. Tina Courpas, R-Greenwich.
“These [strategies] … assume a level of state familiarity and expertise with the particular needs and concerns of every municipal budget. Because it says things like, ‘You all can afford to put in $15,000 per pupil,’” Courpas said. 
“So can I just ask — what would distinguish different needs in one municipal budget versus another?” Roza interjected.
“I guess that’s my point. A million things that the state can’t possibly be privy to,” Courpas said.
After a brief back-and-forth, Roza explained that a typical tap-and-tame strategy “doesn’t assume that you have to know about each municipality’s budget. It assumes that each municipality has a range of things that are complicated for that community.”
In other words, Roza said, “You’re a local community, you guys have local priorities … you have a level of local resources, you’ve gotta manage your local obligations locally.”
At the end of the day’s meeting, Elicker offered some pointed reflections to Roza.
“A lot of the recommendations you have are about, how do we force, require, mandate municipalities to get their acts together … and that doesn’t feel very collaborative to me,” Elicker said. He asked if Roza had examples of states holding themselves accountable for their part in school funding, rather than being “condescending and accusatory.”
“I don’t think that I brought these ideas in the spirit of being accusatory. I think states are trying to figure out what levers they have and not wanting to overstep,” Roza replied. 
She said there are examples of states like Louisiana and Mississippi that collaborate extensively with schools to improve academic outcomes. 
“The point here is to say, well, if we’re putting this money in, and we’re not happy with this outcome that we’re getting, where do we — what levers do we have to create that focus again,” Roza said.
Rep. Toni Walker, a New Haven Democrat and co-chair of the Appropriations Committee, was also at the meeting, filling in for Sen. Gary Winfield. She pushed back on her mayor’s remarks.
“I take a little back on the idea of its being accusatory, as opposed to, these are things that people have seen and want to work on,” Walker said. “And I feel like all of us here have done that. Not in a political way, but in a very earnest way of trying to understand, how do we … improve things that we see.”
A survey for members of the public to share their thoughts with the Blue Ribbon Commission is open until the end of August and can be accessed here. The next commission meeting is Sep. 17. Its final report is due Jan. 15.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: 31 charged with drug smuggling after SC nightclub investigations
description: Law enforcement officers seized large quantities of narcotics and guns from nightclubs operating without permits, the state's top prosecutor said.
text:
State Law Enforcement Division Chief Mark Keel, along with fellow law enforcement and prosecutors, talks about a series of nightclub raids that led to more than 31 arrests at the state grand jury office in Columbia, S.C., on Monday, Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Skylar Laird/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — A series of Lowcountry nightclub raids led to drug trafficking charges for 31 people believed to be associated with Mexican drug cartels, state law enforcement officials said Monday.
A state grand jury indictment announced Monday was part of a widespread investigation into unlicensed nightclubs where officials have found evidence of illegal activity, including trafficking narcotics, prostitution and gang violence, according to the state attorney general’s office.
Three of those charged with drug smuggling also face gun charges, and one faces charges of prostitution and operating a brothel, according to the attorney general’s office. Investigators found large amounts of narcotics, such as cocaine, fentanyl and methamphetamine, as well as 33 guns, including machine guns.
Charleston immigrant community decries police, ICE raid of SC nightclub

“Families across South Carolina fell victim to these vast, illicit networks that put many South Carolina communities at risk,” Mark Keel, chief of the State Law Enforcement Division, said during a Monday news conference.
The widespread investigation began last year with a raid on a Summerville nightclub called Alamo, said Attorney General Alan Wilson. Officers arrested 80 people and seized guns, cocaine and cash, Charleston County Sheriff Carl Ritchie said at the time.
Five of those arrested faced criminal charges. The remaining 75 were taken into custody on civil immigration charges, officials said.
Community members pushed back soon after the raid, saying many of the people arrested for immigration charges had no idea what criminal enterprises were taking place at the club and that many people didn’t know where their family members ended up. Law enforcement officials on Monday gave no update on their status.
But Wilson said the investigation, dubbed Operation Last Stand, continued after that raid. Law enforcement wanted to know where the drugs came from, he said.
“We began looking into who was behind nightclubs like the Alamo, so we began to conduct other raids,” Wilson said.
That led to a raid in February on another unlicensed nightclub called La Fogata, this time in North Charleston. There, law enforcement arrested 86 people, including 79 on civil immigration charges, according to the attorney general’s office.
SC police, ICE arrest 80 people in raid of unlicensed Charleston County nightclub

Officers also seized cocaine, fentanyl, methamphetamine and marijuana, according to the attorney general’s office. Continued investigation into the source of the drugs led law enforcement to conclude that “international narco-terrorist cartels and gangs were involved in large-scale trafficking of narcotics, predominantly in the Charleston area,” Wilson said.
“This trafficking pipeline was historically responsible for hundreds of kilos of cocaine coming into our state across the southern border from Mexico,” Wilson said.
Among those cartels were Los Zestas, also known as Cartel de Noreste, and Jalisco New Generation Cartel, both of which are considered terrorist organizations under a 2025 executive order.
Affiliates of the cartels then smuggled the drugs through Texas, Florida and Georgia, officials said. Federal Homeland Security Investigations officers and South Carolina law enforcement, including statewide investigators and local sheriffs, worked with those other states to track the illicit substances, Wilson said.
“No single agency can face this alone,” Ritchie said Monday. “But we share information, coordinate operations and train side by side. We close gaps the dangerous criminals try to exploit and deliver a significant blow to these criminal organizations and cartels.”
All 31 people charged are in jail and awaiting initial hearings in front of a judge. The investigation is ongoing and could lead to more charges, Wilson said.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Report finds bacteria from fecal matter affecting Pennsylvania rivers and streams
description: E. coli can cause gastrointestinal illness, respiratory disease and infections of the skin, ears and eyes. It's harmful for swimmers and people engaging in recreational activities like fishing, boating or paddling.
text:
Bridges across the Monongahela River in Pittsburgh (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)A report found rivers and streams across Pennsylvania are testing positive for harmful levels of the bacteria E. coli, which spreads through fecal matter.
The nonprofit PennEnvironment found that at 55% of 653 monitoring sites, levels of E. coli reached potentially unsafe levels for swimmers in 2024 and 2025. Nearly 40% of testing sites tested positive for unsafe levels of the bacteria on at least one-quarter of the days they were tested.
E. coli is especially harmful for swimmers. It can cause gastrointestinal illness, respiratory disease and infections of the skin, ears and eyes. But the report notes that bacteria can be harmful for people engaging in other recreational activities like fishing, boating or paddling.
The report released earlier this month highlighted particularly unsafe conditions in the Philadelphia section of the Delaware River, the Brandywine Creek in Delaware County, the Pittsburgh section of the Monongahela River and Allegheny River in Venango County.
The group created an interactive map to see test results across the state.
In the Philadelphia section of the Delaware River, E. coli levels tested exceeded what’s known as the Beach Action Value — meaning they were high enough to cause closures or advisories —  at 37 out of 43 testing locations on at least one day. At 12 locations, E. coli levels exceeded Beach Action Values on all days they were tested.
Nearly 90% of samples taken from Pittsburgh’s Saw Mill Run had unsafe levels of fecal bacteria. 
And parts of the Allegheny River and Brandywine Creek also tested positive for potentially unsafe levels of bacteria every day samples were taken in 2025.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Pennsylvanians love our state’s rivers and streams as popular destinations to paddle, swim and fish, but sometimes the water isn’t as safe as it should be,” said David Masur, executive director of the PennEnvironment Research & Policy Center.  “We ought to have access to clean, healthy water when we visit our great waterways in any part of Pennsylvania.”
High levels of pathogen pollution can be caused by outdated sewage systems and private septic systems, sprawling development and factory farming. 
The report urges state, local and federal leaders to invest in repairing and modernizing wastewater and stormwater infrastructure to prevent spills, leaks and overflow; protecting and restoring wetlands, floodplains and streamside buffers that act as natural filters for pollution; and expanding water quality monitoring.
According to PennEnvironment, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has estimated it will cost nearly $640 million a year to repair and improve Pennsylvania wastewater and stormwater infrastructure over a 20 year period. In the 2026 Fiscal Year, Congress appropriated $135 million to the state through the Clean Water State Revolving Fund.
“Other communities swim in their waterways, but Philly’s rivers are so polluted that most of us forget that this is something we should be able to do here,” said Jamie Gauthier, chair of the Philadelphia city council’s Committee on the Environment. “I’ll keep working with the Philadelphia Water Department to make our rivers safe for recreation, and advocate for the federal and state investments we need to accomplish this.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado Sen. Cathy Kipp submits first complaint under state’s deepfake disclosure law
description: The Colorado secretary of state’s office will investigate whether a video from a libertarian think tank generated with artificial intelligence violates a state law against undisclosed deepfake videos of candidates. Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat, filed a complaint with the office on Aug. 5 against the Independence Institute, as first reported by CB[...]
text:
Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat, speaks on the Colorado Senate floor about a bill to ask voters for more public education funding on April 24, 2026. (Screenshot from Colorado Channel YouTube)The Colorado secretary of state’s office will investigate whether a video from a libertarian think tank generated with artificial intelligence violates a state law against undisclosed deepfake videos of candidates.
Sen. Cathy Kipp, a Fort Collins Democrat, filed a complaint with the office on Aug. 5 against the Independence Institute, as first reported by CBS Colorado. She alleges that a video posted to multiple Independence Institute social media accounts violates a 2024 law that requires disclosure on deepfake videos of candidates within 90 days of a general election. A deepfake is a realistic-looking photo or video created with AI that makes it seem like a person is saying or doing things they never did.
The Independence Institute is a leading opponent of Proposition NN, a tax-related measure placed on this November’s ballot by Democratic lawmakers. In the 45-second video, Kipp is portrayed as a grocery store clerk refusing to give a customer their change, saying in a harsh tone that management decided to keep all change in order to fund education.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A narrator’s voice then says, “Proposition NN wants to keep your tax refund forever. How is that fair?” as the same words show up in large font. There is a small disclosure visible for about three seconds that reads, “AI generated content because who gets a human cashier these days?”
Kipp sponsored the bill that referred Proposition NN to the ballot. If approved by voters, the measure would let the state keep more tax revenue than currently allowed under the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights and then redirect the funding to public education. TABOR is a constitutional amendment that, among other things, requires the state to return tax money that exceeds an annual limit.
In the complaint, Kipp wrote that there are no disclosures on the video as required by law. The law requires disclosure in a text around the same size as any other text in the content, as well as information about the AI tool used in the video or photo’s metadata. That disclosure must be “This (image/audio/video/multimedia) has been edited and depicts speech or conduct that falsely appears to be authentic or truthful.” The law includes a carve-out for satire.
It is the first complaint “filed within the statutory timeframe required for consideration,” according to Jack Todd, a spokesperson for the secretary of state’s office.
Representatives from the Independence Institute did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The complaint comes amid an increase in AI-generated campaign content, including event flyers, photo posts and deepfake videos. Colorado is one of 31 states that regulate deepfakes in election messaging, according to the National Conference of State Legislators. Kipp, who is running for reelection, filed the complaint exactly 90 days before the November election. As of the afternoon of Aug. 24, the video was still live on the Independence Institute’s public social media pages.
“The bottom line is simple: it is disturbing and wrong to use a deepfake, AI-generated video of someone without their consent,” Kipp said in a statement. “We should not allow the rampant misuse of AI and the spread of false information to become normalized in our elections. While this millionaire-backed group uses bad-faith tactics, I’m focused on what matters: funding our schools and making sure every Colorado kid has access to a quality eduction.”
The Secretary of State’s office decided to investigate the allegations on Aug. 19 and has a deadline of Sept. 18.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Contested New Mexico hearing officer for Project Jupiter air quality permit hearing recuses himself
description: The hearing officer presiding over the New Mexico Environment Department’s air quality permit hearing for the Project Jupiter data center has recused himself from the case, according to newly filed documents.
text:
The New Mexico Environment Department on Aug. 24, 2026, announced that Max Shepherd, the hearing officer presiding over Project Jupiter's air quality permit hearing, pictured above at a July virtual meeting, had recused himself from the matter. (Screenshot) The hearing officer presiding over the New Mexico Environment Department’s air quality permit hearing for the Project Jupiter data center has recused himself from the case, according to newly filed documents.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
An NMED paralegal emailed several interested parties in the ongoing permitting process minutes before 12:30 p.m. Monday with an attached document that showed Hearing Officer Max Shepherd had recused himself.
Attorneys with the New Mexico Environmental Law Center and the Center for Biological Diversity in a filing last week sought to disqualify Shepherd, arguing that he “has failed in his duty to ‘conduct a fair and impartial proceeding.’”
Their complaint came after Shepherd rankled project opponents in late July by rescheduling the hearing for Project Jupiter’s pending air quality permit application. The data center’s developers are seeking a permit from the New Mexico Environment Department to operate a gas pipeline-fed fuel cell system as an on-site power source.
Shepherd initially scheduled the hearing for mid-October. When attorneys representing Project Jupiter developer Yucca Growth Infrastructure argued that it would leave NMED officials inadequate time to make their final decision on the permit by their Nov. 23 deadline, Shepherd responded that the case was highly technical and complex and said he would rather look into extending the November deadline.
Days later, however, he filed a scheduling order showing that he was moving the hearing up, consistent with the developer’s request.
The New Mexico Supreme Court on Sunday night issued an order that temporarily delays the hearing, after the Santa Fe-based clean energy organization New Energy Economy questioned whether the proceeding was premature, given that the pipeline needed to power the fuel cell system has yet to clear its own regulatory hurdles.
Opponents argued that Shepherd deprived involved parties of due process and left them with too little time to adequately prepare for the hearing.
Shepherd did not respond to Source NM’s request for comment. Typically, the New Mexico Environment Department secretary or leaders on the Environmental Improvement Board or Water Quality Control Commission appoint hearing officers to preside over public hearings. An environment department spokesperson did not respond to Source NM request for information on next steps.
New Mexico Environmental Law Center Senior Attorney Maslyn Locke, who signed the August filing seeking Shepherd’s ouster, on Monday told Source NM that she was encouraged by Shepherd’s departure.
“It’s pretty remarkable to see him disqualify himself, finally. It’s been such a fight to get any sort of due process in this hearing,” she said. “With the broader Project Jupiter fight, it’s been so hard to get transparency and community involvement in a way that is meaningful and actually impacts the decision-making.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC failed to protect coastal fisheries, court says
description: None of North Carolina’s 13 state-managed coastal fish stocks is currently viable for the long term, according to the court’s 190-page ruling.
text:
None of North Carolina’s 13 state-managed coastal fish stocks is currently viable for the long term, according to the court’s 190-page ruling. (Photo of NC coast: Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline)North Carolina’s coastal fisheries are in danger. The state failed to protect them, according to a landmark Superior Court ruling.
Following a six-year lawsuit, Judge Bryan Collins ruled last week in favor of the Coastal Conservation Association of North Carolina, saying the state’s mishandling has led to depleted fish stocks along the coast. 
None of North Carolina’s 13 state-managed coastal fish stocks is currently viable for the long term, according to the court’s 190-page ruling. These include southern flounder, shrimp, and speckled trout. 
“The court affirmed what we have said for years: the state has a responsibility to protect and manage our fisheries for the benefit of all citizens and future generations, and our current system has failed to meet that responsibility,” CCA NC Executive Director David Sneed told NC Newsline in an email. 
Endangered red wolves rebound in NC with four litters of pups born this year

CCA NC and 86 citizen plaintiffs, including five former members of North Carolina’s Marine Fisheries Commission, filed the lawsuit in 2020.
They claimed the state has a legal responsibility to keep fisheries healthy and available to the public over the long term, which it failed to do. 
In particular, plaintiffs say shrimp trawling and overfishing contributed to the lower quantities of aquatic animals along the coast. 
The General Assembly introduced legislation last year to ban inland shrimp trawling. Hundreds of fishermen left their boats for Raleigh to oppose the bill, leading House Republicans to drop it. No action was taken on that bill in the short session. 
While the court ruled in favor of CCA NC, Sneed said it isn’t a moment for celebration. 
“There is no real victory when our fisheries are depleted,” he said. “The important thing now is that the magnitude of the problem has been recognized.”
Collins said in the ruling it will take “drastic management changes” for North Carolina to rebuild its fisheries.
“We look forward to a day when our fisheries management is not the laughingstock of the country,” North Carolina Wildlife Federation CEO Tim Gestwicki told NC Newsline. 
Sneed said moving forward, there needs to be collaboration between the general public, scientists, fisheries managers, and policymakers to protect and restore North Carolina’s fisheries.
It’s also a time for unity between commercial fishermen, recreational anglers, charter captains, seafood businesses, and coastal communities, which all depend on the same resource.
“The opportunity we have now is to bring those groups together and focus on practical solutions that rebuild our fisheries,” Sneed said. 
Rep. Pricey Harrison, a Democrat from Guilford County who has served on the Coastal Resources and Marine Fisheries Commissions, said the ruling seemed very one-sided in favor of CCA. 
She said she isn’t sure the judge took other impacts on fisheries into account. These include issues like climate change, habitat degradation, and coastal development, all of which affect water quality and aquatic life. 
“It’s a very nuanced, complicated situation that the judge’s opinion didn’t take into consideration all sides,” Harrison told NC Newsline. “Each species needs to be considered individually.”
A spokesperson for the North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality said the Division of Marine Fisheries is reviewing the judge’s findings, but the division will not comment further, as the case is ongoing. 
Collins ordered attorneys representing both sides to meet and submit a joint report with any future considerations. That will determine a timeline for the remedy phase, which could dictate if certain waters are closed to fishing or if changes are made to fisheries policies.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis uncertain Florida’s redistricted congressional map can save House Republicans this fall
description: TAMPA — Although Gov. Ron DeSantis and the Republican-led Florida Legislature have always insisted constitutional obligations compelled their mid-decade congressional redistricting, the map was designed to add as many as four Florida Republicans to the U.S. House of Representatives. But with Donald Trump’s approval ratings tanking and images of a Democratic[...]
text:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis speaking at Feeding Tampa Bay's headquarters in Tampa on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Mitch Perry/Florida Phoenix)TAMPA — Although Gov. Ron DeSantis and the Republican-led Florida Legislature have always insisted constitutional obligations compelled their mid-decade congressional redistricting, the map was designed to add as many as four Florida Republicans to the U.S. House of Representatives.
But with Donald Trump’s approval ratings tanking and images of a Democratic blue wave emerging, DeSantis acknowledged Monday that the GOP may not net all four seats.
“This year they’re winnable, but I think that it’s going to require some effort,” the governor said Monday during a press conference in Tampa.
Florida’s redistricting was set in motion in July 2025, when the governor initially said it would be “appropriate” for the Florida Legislature to redraw the state’s 28 congressional districts because it had been “malapportioned” following the 2020 U.S. Census.
Those comments came a week after President Donald Trump, concerned House Republicans could lose their slim majority, urged Texas to redraw its congressional map to add GOP seats to Congress, and that he’d like other states to do so as well.
Later in the year, DeSantis said the state would be “forced” to redistrict because of an expected ruling by the U.S. Supreme Court regarding the constitutionality of a part of the Voting Rights Act, and he and the Legislature would not use “partisan data” in composing a new map.
The U.S. Supreme Court did ultimately strike down that portion of the Voting Rights Act. It happened the same day the Florida House approved the new map, which left four Democratic incumbents — Tampa Bay’s Kathy Castor, Central Florida’s Darren Soto, and South Florida’s Debbie Wasserman Shultz and Jared Moskowitz — residing in heavily Republican-leaning districts.
DeSantis has previously boasted that his own redistricting map following the decennial Census saved the Republican majority in the House in 2022. That map added four Republican seats to Congress that year.
“That was partially the map but partially you know, me winning the biggest victory that Republicans had ever won in the history of governor’s races. That had a lot to do with it, too,” he said Monday.
He was less certain Florida’s new map could save the GOP this fall.
“Now in this election, obviously I’m not on the ballot,” he said. “But the political environment’s a little bit different. You’re seeing it. You’re seeing it in numbers, and when you do these midterms, it’s not necessarily just about local. It can be, but a lot of times it can be nationalized. And if there’s a certain mood in the country, that can be something that you have to combat.”
Embattled Democrats
Two of those targeted Democrats, Wasserman Schultz and Moskowitz, opted to run in different districts this year, and both won big in their primary elections last week.
Soto and Castor are running for re-election in their same districts. For Soto, his CD 9 seat went from 3.5%-plus for Kamala Harris in 2024 to one Trump won by nearly 18 points that year.
Castor has served in Congress for 20 years in a district that always leaned strongly Democratic. Now it’s Trump +10, but some political observers believe she has a chance to defeat Republican former Florida House member Mike Beltran.
DeSantis said he had spoken with the all of the Republicans now running.
“We’re helping them out in different ways, but I think that they’re all going to be competitive races for sure,” the governor said, adding that “absent major events” most voters  will know for whom they will vote by Labor Day.
Voting rights advocates and Democrats argue the map violates the Florida Constitution.
The Elias Law Group, on behalf of the Equal Ground Education Fund, filed a lawsuit the day DeSantis signed the new congressional map into law in May, contending violation of Florida’s 2010 Fair District Amendments, which prohibits drawing congressional (and state legislative) districts that favor incumbents of a political party.
The Florida Supreme Court in June rejected an emergency petition to stop the new map from taking effect. However, the underlying legal challenge remains pending.
Republicans represent 20 of the state’s 28 congressional districts. Democrats represent seven districts. They had represented eight districts, but Democrat Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick resigned in Congressional District 20 earlier this year amid allegations of stealing federal disaster money.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: A Democratic Socialist could cost Peltola votes in November. But he says he’d actually boost her.
description: This story was originally published in the Anchorage Press. Subscribe here.  Leading up to Alaska’s high-profile U.S. Senate primary, political groups spent millions of dollars to boost not only the leading Republicans and Democrats, but also fringe candidates who could tip the balance of a tight race in November. Most of those efforts fell flat […]
text:
David Leslie, who's currently sitting in fourth place in preliminary results in Alaska's U.S. Senate race, says he's not a "perennial candidate." (Photo courtesy David Leslie)This story was originally published in the Anchorage Press. Subscribe here. 
Leading up to Alaska’s high-profile U.S. Senate primary, political groups spent millions of dollars to boost not only the leading Republicans and Democrats, but also fringe candidates who could tip the balance of a tight race in November.
Most of those efforts fell flat — namely, those that tried to boost spoiler candidates who don’t even live in Alaska, like Arizona resident and Green Party candidate Richard Grayson, who garnered just 343 votes in preliminary counts.
One novice candidate who did crack the top four, though, and is now poised to appear on the general election ballot is David Leslie — a Democrat, Democratic Socialist and Fairbanks resident who, unlike some of the other longshot candidates, has spent years in Alaska politics.
If preliminary results hold, Leslie’s presence on the general election ballot, as a Democratic candidate, could represent a win for conservatives who want to see as few Republicans as possible in the race, to avoid competition for votes for incumbent GOP U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan.
But if Leslie were to drop out before an Aug. 31 withdrawal deadline, it could bump the fifth-placed finisher, Republican Gerald Heikes, onto the ballot — which some politically operatives say would boost the chances of Democratic challenger Mary Peltola.
We wanted to know what Leslie was thinking: why he’s in the race, and whether he might drop out. So, on Thursday, the Anchorage Press called him.
Below is a transcript of the interview, edited for clarity and length.
Nathaniel Herz: For people who don’t know David Leslie, who is he?
David Leslie: I am Iñupiaq. My mom was born in Kotzebue. She was sent to Nome for school when she was four or five, and she was raised in Fairbanks by my white adoptive grandparents, Chuck and Carol Leslie. Chuck was really high up in the plumber pipefitters union, Local 375. I grew up going to all of the union holiday parties. And I was born in Louisiana — my mom finished high school there. My mom was in a terrible car accident when she was pregnant with me — she survived, but that’s why, as soon as I could get on a plane when I was a few weeks old, we moved from Louisiana back to Fairbanks so my grandparents could raise me.
My biological grandfather was John Schaeffer, the first president and CEO of NANA.
Herz: What’s your history in politics?
Leslie: I first really got involved in activism when I was 16 years old, a junior in high school at Lathrop High School (in Fairbanks). I became the vice president of the Gay-Straight Alliance, especially because I was the only openly queer guy in my class. As an Iñupiaq person, raised by my white family, I’ve been on a journey of reconnecting and rediscovering my Iñupiaq family. I actually met a lot of my aunts and uncles through organizing around NANA’s ICE detention contracts, and that has been a silver lining — to realize that I’m not just against these contracts, but my family, who I’ve never met before, we all share these same values.
I was involved with Occupy Fairbanks when that went down in 2011, 2012. I was out there protesting for, like, six months at 50 below. I also was the union steward for the Fairbanks Pioneer Home, and for biographical purposes, I’m still on the board of the Northern Alaska Environmental Center.
If you follow politics, you know that I have been involved. I’m not this weird outsider person, a perennial candidate. I am someone who cares deeply about the community, and I’m deeply involved in many different facets of Alaska politics, and this is just the obvious next step.
Herz: How do your values differ from Mary Peltola’s, and why did you feel the need to run against her?
Leslie: There are three main issues why I decided to primary Mary Peltola. There also was ranked choice voting, which is an important part of why I made this decision. If we did not have ranked choice voting, I would not be running, because it is so important that we get Dan Sullivan and Republicans out of power.
But the biggest issue was the genocide in Palestine. Alaska Native people are still enduring a genocide here in Alaska. And if you can deny that blowing up children, blowing up grandparents, starving tens of thousands of people is a genocide — if you can deny that, you can deny the genocide of Alaska Native people happening in front of us here.
Herz: What do you mean by ongoing genocide of Native people?
Leslie: You talk to our elders, they remind us that this genocide never ended.
Our languages are still dying off, and the state and federal government are not ensuring that we don’t lose these languages. We have an epidemic of murdered and missing Indigenous women, two-spirit people, and just people in general. The cops still kill Alaska Native people at higher rates. And also we see our land being continually encroached upon by industry in ways that harm not only our people, but also make us less able to live off the land in our traditional ways — which is both harming us physically, but also harming us culturally. And we still have not seen a proper reckoning of the boarding school era, which didn’t end until the 1990s.
All of these things compound to show that there is still a genocide. There has not been reparations for boarding schools. There has not been a full-on attempt to stop the dying of our languages, and there has not been an investment in investigating all the murdered and missing Indigenous people in the state.
Herz: When it comes to Israel and Palestine, you’re critical of Mary Peltola’s position there?
Leslie: I really wanted to see Mary Peltola explain why she took AIPAC money, and then commit to not taking it, to saying that there are allegations of human rights abuses and crimes against humanity and genocide, and address that. But her Alaska-centric campaign is better fit for a gubernatorial candidate, and the fact that she has not answered these yet is such a huge issue.

Democrat Mary Peltola is leading in preliminary results in Alaska’s U.S. Senate election. (Nathaniel Herz/Northern Journal)
Another issue I decided to primary her on is the environment. Her support for the Willow project, as climate change is destroying our actual villages. You know, Kotzebue, my people’s ancestral homeland, damn near eroded into the ocean from one of the typhoon remnants. We saw how those typhoons destroyed other villages. We cannot continue to ignore how the oil companies are causing climate change, which is destroying our homelands and making them unlivable.
And then, third, when the U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents, ICE, murdered Alex Pretti and Renée Good, we need someone who’s going to say, ‘These ICE agents are murdering people. They are tools of violence. They’re equivalent to brown shirts, and that their camps are concentration camps that are crimes against humanity and must be shut down.’
( Peltola’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment on Leslie’s statements.)
Herz: What’s your take on Peltola, generally?
Leslie: Mary Peltola is obviously better than Dan Sullivan in so many ways, but we can’t be running campaigns on not being as bad as the other person. We need someone with strong vision and a strong value that actually aligns with our Alaska Native values to be the leaders in our country. And running concentration camps, continuing this rhetoric that borders are not under control — which has led to the murder and rape of immigrants — is not our Alaskan Native values. Native people don’t know borders. The borders crossed us.
Herz: Obviously, there is a concern among liberals, progressives — I think even among some folks who are very closely aligned with you politically — that your presence in the race, assuming the results hold, risks making you a spoiler to Peltola.  I’m wondering what your response is to that contention.
Leslie: I have met so many people who will not vote for Mary Peltola because of her stance on the genocide in Gaza.
By having someone who will take a strong stance on Palestine and Gaza, I am encouraging people to show up to the ballot who normally wouldn’t, and will rank her second. These people have strong moral convictions, which is good — but they need someone to get them to the polls in the first place. I am that candidate that will allow these people to vote their values, and then they will rank Mary Peltola second. If I was not in this race, they would not be there at all.
Herz: Do you encourage them to rank Mary second?
Leslie: I do. When I first announced my declaration of candidacy, I said, ‘I will ask people to rank Mary Peltola second, because Dan Sullivan and the Republicans are the party of white supremacy, Christian nationalism, and genocide on our own lands. We must remove them from office, no matter what.’ (A Sullivan spokesman, Nate Adams, said in a statement: “Alaskans can come to their own conclusions about David Leslie’s radically liberal worldview, but at least he has principles.”)
I am running so that more progressives, liberals, and Democrats show up — so they will at least rank me and Peltola, so we can get Dan Sullivan out of office.
Herz: There are clearly, though, some Republicans that see you and your presence on the general election ballot as advantageous to them. How confident are you that your participation won’t hurt Peltola?
Leslie: I have had people express concern that people will only vote for who they believe in the most, and ultimately end up submitting an exhausted ballot. I really, truly believe we are still fully understanding the importance of ranked choice voting, as we continue to relitigate it.
There is so much power in ranked choice voting. It has been so important for us to have that in Alaska. We are setting the path for so many other states to join us. We have to believe that ranked choice voting operates as it should.
There are some people who are only going to vote for one person, and that is their right. But we must exercise our rights and tools of democracy to make sure that we get the best candidates we can. And I believe ranked choice voting is that way, and again, I am only running because we have it. It is so important that we maintain it and we use it to its fullest extent.
Herz: What consideration will you give to dropping out before the Aug. 31 deadline, if you do end up being the fourth-placed candidate in the primary?
Leslie: The things that I am running on, the values I hold, are strong. I am not here to waver in my beliefs. I think it’s good that we have two progressives in the race. I believe that by dropping out, I would be platforming dangerous Republicans who are white supremacists and Christian nationalists, and we must not allow their rhetoric to take hold. That is also dangerous.
Herz: Have you heard from Peltola or the Alaska Democratic Party since Tuesday?
Leslie: I’ll be meeting with someone from the leadership of the Alaska Democrats later today.
Herz: Is there a world in which, if there was a commitment from Peltola or others on the issues that matter to you, you would entertain the idea of dropping out?
Leslie: A lot can happen between now and Aug. 31. I don’t want to take any options off the table. But at this point in time, there’s so many huge issues that are important, and these issues will determine whether or not tens of thousands of people will die.
Max Graham contributed reporting.

name: VTDigger
title: Vermont cannot spend its way into affordability
description:
New taxes and revenue proposals won't fix what's driving up costs for Vermonters.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont cannot spend its way into affordability.
text:
This commentary is by Elizabeth Brown, who is a state director at the Fiscal Alliance Foundation.
Despite six years of skyrocketing state spending, with increases at twice the rate of inflation, for many the answer to Vermont’s affordability crisis continues to be more revenue, higher taxes and an expansion of government programs. With the third-highest total tax burden in the nation, why should taxpayers believe spending even more will make Vermont more affordable?
New revenue proposals have been focused on a new income-tax surcharge, a new tax on investment proceeds and a higher property tax rate on certain non-homestead residential properties. Income tax proposals would elevate our highest marginal tax bracket to the top in the nation. 
Vermont already has among the most progressive systems in the country. By proposing more taxes on higher-income earners in Vermont, you are also putting more tax burdens on our small business owners. Vermont is already losing private-sector businesses and jobs at one of the highest rates in the country. 
While we are talking about expanding taxes, let’s not forget that 50 towns have now implemented the 1% local option tax, with 25% of those proceeds going back to the state. An extra bonus for shopping locally. 
Another popular proposal, a bill also debated this past legislative biennium, is a state-funded primary care system that paves the way for universal healthcare paid for with another payroll tax, in addition to our first-in-the-nation childcare tax. Vermont has been pursuing a single-payer healthcare system for decades. We decided back in 2014 that single-payer was not affordable, and ultimately pursuing that put us on a disastrous path. It has been overregulation driving out competition that has created the healthcare mess we are in. A single-payer primary care system does not solve the real issue: a shortage of primary care doctors, especially in more rural parts of our state.
It’s time to examine proposals based on their impact on affordability, taxpayers, economic opportunity and the long-term fiscal health of the state, not just hitting emotional high points with voters. 

READ MORE

Simply put, Vermont has a spending problem, not a revenue problem, and it is time to understand where all the money is going and who will be left to foot the bill. Vermont is now the fastest-shrinking state in the country per capita, with one of the oldest populations and a workforce that contracted by roughly 10,000 workers last year. The warning signs are increasingly difficult to ignore: Workers are leaving the workforce, private-sector jobs are being lost at one of the highest rates in the country, and too many businesses are struggling to stay open.
Vermonters deserve time-tested, practical solutions that recognize there is a limit to what taxpayers can afford. It is time to stop being a petri dish for policies brought to our state from outside influences that cost taxpayers real dollars. We’ve created our own inflationary pressures with ineffective government spending. The solution means looking at the cumulative costs of our existing policies that are driving up everyday expenses for Vermonters, where fees, regulations and taxes are death by a thousand cuts. 
You can debate whether you like another state’s politics, but you cannot debate the fact that states that put a high tax burden on their citizens are on the losing end, and in Vermont’s case, substantially so. Maybe it is time that more Vermonters admit to themselves that they don’t like our politics, because it does not add up. 
There is a reason we have the lowest economic growth and the fastest-shrinking population. Before we ask for more money or continue to shift around who pays, let’s ask the question: Why are we spending so much? And can we do better? Because the answer is a resounding yes. More taxes don’t solve problems, and in Vermont, they’re contributing to them.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Did school vaccines just become a campaign issue?
description: Mandated vaccines for school attendance—and a parent’s ability to reject those vaccines— may have been injected into the race for Florida governor. With five months left before he’s term limited out of office, the administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis Monday released a proposed regulation that would eliminate a number of vaccines required for public and […]
text:
A health care worker places a bandage on a child after giving a vaccination shot. New federal guidance to reduce the number of recommended childhood vaccines from 17 to 11 comes as states are already charting their own course on vaccine policy. (Photo by Scott Housley/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)Mandated vaccines for school attendance—and a parent’s ability to reject those vaccines— may have been injected into the race for Florida governor.
With five months left before he’s term limited out of office, the administration of Gov. Ron DeSantis Monday released a proposed regulation that would eliminate a number of vaccines required for public and private school students and make it easier for parents to opt out if vaccines conflict with “sincerely held moral or ethical belief(s).”
The proposed rule was released one day after Republican gubernatorial hopeful Byron Donalds, appearing on Face the Nation, said he’d like to “study and really engage it” before making a decision about whether to repeal statutory vaccine requirements for schools. 
During that same interview, Donalds suggested a measles outbreak in southwest Florida may be happening in part because “people have come into the country illegally” and “have not had that vaccination schedule.” 
Donalds’ position differs from that of Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo, who earlier suggested the outbreak is tied to abortion opposition. 
Florida has 142 reported measles cases, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That ranks Florida fifth in the number of cases behind South Carolina (670), Utah (526), Pennsylvania (321), and Virginia (176).
Meanwhile, Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Jolly’s camp said if elected Jolly would fire Ladapo.
“Floridians are done with people playing politics with our children’s health. As governor David Jolly will fire the Surgeon General and follow the guidance of a new Surgeon General who embraces science and evidence-based public health,” Mark Riddle, senior adviser to Jolly, said in a text to the Phoenix.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The debate comes after a number of Florida legislative Democrats sent a letter to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Acting Director Jay Bhattacharya, and Ladapo.
In the letter, the legislators said they were concerned about communication and coordination problems surrounding infectious disease threats. 
“In recent years, our public health partners, hospitals, and doctor’s offices in our legislative districts have experienced lapses in the timely and consistent communication, guidance, and coordination needed to support effective responses to infectious disease threats,” the letter, sent by Rep. Yvonne Hinson of Gainesville and signed by 14 other state House Democrats, reads.
“A renewed federal and state effort is needed to restore confidence in core public health responsibilities, including disease surveillance, clinician alerts, outbreak reporting, technical assistance, laboratory coordination, and clear public-facing risk communication. These functions are essential when new threats arise and when familiar diseases re-emerge in communities.”
The new regulation isn’t a new idea. Ladapo first rolled out the proposed change about a year ago, equating vaccine mandates with slavery, calling them wrong and immoral, and declaring, “Your body is a gift from God. What you put into your body is because of your relationship with your body and your God.”
DeSantis administration pushes to eliminate all vaccine mandates in Florida

The changes
Florida law contains a number of immunization requirements for the young and the old. The DeSantis administration has taken aim only at the mandates for children.
The state allows exemptions for valid medical reasons and religious and certain belief systems, and, in some cases, allows personal exemptions for philosophical beliefs.
For entry and attendance in Florida schools, childcare facilities, and family daycare homes, state law requires children to be immunized for poliomyelitis, diphtheria, rubeola, rubella, pertussis, mumps, tetanus and “other communicable diseases as determined by rules of the Department of Health.”
Under that authority, the DOH has required through regulation that children also be immunized for haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), hepatitis B, varicella (chickenpox) and pneumococcal conjugate.
The proposed new rule released Monday contains a trio of changes:

It first eliminates vaccine mandates that aren’t required by law; 
It proposes changes to the religious exemption form to allow opt-outs for parents and guardians who maintain immunizations conflict with their “sincerely held moral or ethical belief(s).”
It allows parents to opt out of their children’s information being input into SHOTS, the State Health Online Tracking System, a free statewide online immunization registry used to track and manage vaccine records. 

The administrative process
DeSantis leaves office in about five months, which is not a long time when it comes to the rulemaking process.
Last year, when the administration announced it wanted to eliminate vaccine mandates, it published notice of what it called “rule development,” the first step in the rulemaking process.
During rule development, the public can request a public workshop, an opportunities to provide insights on a proposal. 
There were requests for public hearings and DOH complied by holding one meeting in December. 
The agency didn’t continue down the rulemaking path following the meeting, however, instead lobbying the Legislature to change the policy via statute, thereby negating the need for administrative changes.
But the Legislature didn’t pass the governor’s proposal during the 2026 regular session or any subsequent special sessions.
Without the help of the Legislature, the DeSantis administration was forced to go back through the rulemaking process. Now it’s doing that.
But it didn’t begin the process with the traditional first step, notice of rulemaking development. This time, the administration released notice of a proposed rule change, typically the second step in the process.
Following publication of a proposed new regulation, the public has 21 days to request a public hearing.
Hearings, according to Jacksonville healthcare attorney and lobbyist Christopher Nuland, are more formal than workshops. Hearings give the public the opportunity to comment on specifics of a proposal and what they like or don’t like about it.
If following the hearing the agency makes no changes to the proposed regulation, the public has 21 days to file a challenge in the state Division of Administrative Hearings. 
During such a dispute, the rule wouldn’t go into effect.
And these challenges can take months to resolve.
Still, Nuland said, that could change if the governor pushes hard enough.
“What’s going to be interesting is, does DeSantis make this his going-away shot and push this to get this in before he leaves office,” he said.

title: Ex-delegate Pritt pleads not guilty to federal charges of alleged child sexual exploitation
description: Former Fayette County lawmaker Elliott Pritt pleaded not guilty to three federal charges in connection with an alleged inappropriate sexual relationship he forced with a minor girl.  Pritt, 36, appeared in federal court in Charleston, West Virginia, on Monday morning.  He was indicted on federal charges last week after federal prosecutors described how Pritt[...]
text:
Del. Elliott Pritt, R-Fayette, was arrested July 22, 2026, and faces one count of enticement of a minor. (Photo courtesy of Carter County Detention Center)Former Fayette County lawmaker Elliott Pritt pleaded not guilty to three federal charges in connection with an alleged inappropriate sexual relationship he forced with a minor girl. 
Pritt, 36, appeared in federal court in Charleston, West Virginia, on Monday morning. 
He was indicted on federal charges last week after federal prosecutors described how Pritt, a public school teacher, groomed an underage girl through online communication before beginning an inappropriate physical relationship with the minor.
In both the indictment and the criminal complaint, Pritt is accused of trying to intimidate the girl not to contact authorities. According to a criminal complaint, Pritt allegedly told her not to tell anyone because it would “open up hell in our lives” because it would be in the news. 
Pritt pleaded not guilty before U.S. Magistrate Judge Omar Aboulhosn to sexual exploitation of children, coercion of a child under 18 for sex and intimidating a witness.
A trial is scheduled for Oct. 5.
Wesley Page, Pritt’s court-appointed attorney, said in court that Pritt would not challenge his continued detention. He has been held in a correctional facility in Kentucky. Pritt may seek a bond in the future if he is placed in a residential program overseen by the Veterans Administration since he is a veteran. 
Pritt resigned from the House of Delegates on July 27; he was first elected as a Democrat to the House in 2022 then switched to the Republican Party in 2023. He also removed himself from the ballot in Fayette County, where he was seeking reelection in the November election. 
An investigation began on July 9 after the family of a 15-year-old girl reported to local law enforcement that Pritt had allegedly sexually assaulted her, according to the criminal complaint. 
The complaint said that Pritt allegedly began communicating with the girl when she was in eighth grade in 2024 through the online game Roblox then later on Snapchat. Pritt later allegedly initiated a physical relationship with the minor and requested that she meet him in his classroom at Oak Hill High School to engage in sexual activity at least five to 10 times.
Pritt was arrested in Oak Hill, West Virginia, on July 22. 
State Schools Superintendent Michele Blatt suspended Pritt’s teacher certification as a result of the charge brought against him. Blatt said that if Pritt is ultimately convicted or pleads guilty to these charges, the state superintendent will permanently revoke his teaching certification.

title: Hogue named Arkansas’ new state fire marshal
description: Longtime investigator John Hogue has been appointed the next state fire marshal, the Arkansas Division of Emergency Management announced Monday.  Hogue is a certified investigator of fire and explosions, and a licensed private investigator, according to a press release from the agency. Hogue, who has 32 years of experience in fire, explosion and hazardous ma[...]
text:
The Arkansas Division of Emergency Management announced John Hogue had been appointed the new state fire marshal on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo courtesy of ADEM)Longtime investigator John Hogue has been appointed the next state fire marshal, the Arkansas Division of Emergency Management announced Monday. 
Hogue is a certified investigator of fire and explosions, and a licensed private investigator, according to a press release from the agency. Hogue, who has 32 years of experience in fire, explosion and hazardous materials investigations, is “uniquely qualified” to lead the state’s fire prevention and investigative efforts, the release said.
“John’s depth of experience and proven leadership in complex fire and explosive investigations make him an outstanding choice for State Fire Marshal,” ADEM Director A.J. Gary said. “His commitment to public safety, professionalism, and interagency coordination reflects exactly what this role requires to best serve Arkansans.”
Hogue has conducted more than 1,500 fire and explosive investigations across the country, according to the release. Additionally, he’s taught courses for the Arkansas Fire Academy and local emergency medical technician associations, and holds multiple nationally recognized certifications.
Hogue will begin transitioning into his new role immediately “to ensure continuity of statewide fire prevention, investigation, and public safety operations,” according to the release. 
The State Fire Marshal’s office is responsible for enforcing, periodically revising and updating the Arkansas Fire Prevention Code, according to its website. 
The office also conducts inspections of state buildings, licenses companies and individuals involved with the fireworks industry, and issues permits for above ground storage tanks used for combustible, flammable and hazardous substances.  
Hogue succeeds Dennis Free who retired July 1. Hogue assumed the role of Acting State Fire Marshal while the state conducted a statewide search for a permanent successor, according to a press release.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: 33 apply to be Rhode Island’s first inspector general. Few may qualify.
description: Nearly three dozen people want to be Rhode Island’s first inspector general to root out waste and improve government efficiency. But the pool of qualified candidates may be much smaller. The five-member Inspector General Independent Advisory Commission received resumes from 33 applicants by Friday’s deadline for the position created in the fiscal 2027 state[...]
text:
Will Fletcher, president of the Association of Inspectors Generals, says he expects the number of qualified applicants for Rhode Island's first-ever inspector general to be in the single digits. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current) Nearly three dozen people want to be Rhode Island’s first inspector general to root out waste and improve government efficiency. But the pool of qualified candidates may be much smaller.
The five-member Inspector General Independent Advisory Commission received resumes from 33 applicants by Friday’s deadline for the position created in the fiscal 2027 state budget, the Secretary of State’s office confirmed to Rhode Island Current. 
But the Secretary of State’s office did not comment on how many hold the certification required for the job.
“The final review and assessment of application materials is the responsibility of the commission,” LeeAnn Byrne, chief of staff for Secretary of State Gregg Amore, wrote in an email Monday. “As that process is still ongoing, we cannot share any details about applicants or applications at this time.”
The commission is made up of the attorney general, secretary of state, general treasurer, Ethics Commission executive director, and the president of the Association of Inspectors General. They are scheduled to meet at 2:30 p.m. Wednesday in the State House and have a Sept. 28 deadline to interview and recommend three finalists to Gov. Dan McKee. 
Will Fletcher, president of the New York-based Association of Inspectors General, said he expects the number of qualified applicants to be in the single digits. But he saw no problem with that small pool amid what he described as a “fairly robust response” to the job posting. 
“The number gives me confidence that the commission will have enough of a pool to work with to narrow down three candidates for the governor’s consideration,” he said.
Once chosen, the inaugural officeholder may serve for five years and be eligible for reappointment for one term of the same duration. The position will pay between $175,000 and $225,000 annually, a range the commission settled on during its July 29 meeting.
With a tight timeline looming, inspector general search panel agrees to open applications Monday

Applications for Rhode Island’s inspector general opened on Monday, Aug. 3, leaving a short window to conduct a nationwide search. The job posting crafted by the commission calls for a candidate with at least 10 years of experience in areas including investigations, law enforcement, auditing or government oversight, along with other qualifications.
The state’s top government watchdog must also have professional certification from the Association of Inspectors General, a requirement set in the state budget. Rhode Island Attorney General Peter Neronha repeatedly warned that the certification requirement could significantly limit the application pool. 
Tim Rondeau, a spokesperson for Neronha’s office, said in an email Monday the AG “is currently reviewing the applications received that are complete and meet the qualification requirements of the General Assembly.”
During the commission’s July 29 meeting, Fletcher noted that his organization has a current record of 1,129 certified inspectors general and 2,141 certified inspector general investigators.
Still, Fletcher said Monday that it was to be expected that more people would apply than meet the position’s certification and other requirements.
“So long as there are enough candidates for us to have meaningful discussions and interview candidates who want to serve in this role, then I think we’re in good shape,” he said.
The job posting states interviews will be held during a public meeting either in open or a closed executive session. A decision on the interview process is on the agenda for Wednesday’s commission meeting.
Interviews may be held in person or via video conference, according to the posting. Candidates who travel to attend an in-person interview may be eligible for reimbursement of reasonable travel expenses. 
Following advice from the Department of Administration in a July 21 letter, commissioners agreed on July 29 to cover the commission’s search-related costs with the $1.3 million allocated for the office in the state budget. That reimbursement also applies to Fletcher’s travel, as he takes the train from New York to attend the meetings and returns home afterward.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Pressed on Biddeford shooting investigation, Vance shifts focus to drug overdoses
description: Vice President JD Vance said the federal government is investigating the fatal U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shooting in Biddeford, but quickly shifted focus to drug overdoses when pressed about updates Monday.  “What I see from Democrats is people who are far more worried about a shooting involving an illegal alien than they are about […]
text:
Bypassers stop by a memorial to Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, the Biddeford resident and father who was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on July 13, 2026. (Photo by Lauren McCauley/ Maine Morning Star)Vice President JD Vance said the federal government is investigating the fatal U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement shooting in Biddeford, but quickly shifted focus to drug overdoses when pressed about updates Monday. 
“What I see from Democrats is people who are far more worried about a shooting involving an illegal alien than they are about the fact that tens of thousands of Mainers died from fentanyl overdoses,” Vance told a crowd at Compotech in Brewer.
“My message to the Democrats who are so worried about that situation is to say: Have a little bit of perspective.”
Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who ICE agents shot and killed in Biddeford on July 13, was not the target of the operation that had brought the agents to the area, ICE has confirmed. Guerrero had a pending asylum case and a valid work permit, according to his family and the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project. 
At least 22 people have been shot by federal agents since January 2025, when President Donald Trump began his second term and immigration crackdown. Guerrero is at least the fourth person federal agents killed this year. 
Meanwhile, fentanyl seizures decreased by 39% during the first year of the second Trump administration after ICE shifted the Department of Homeland Security’s criminal investigations arm to conducting immigration enforcement, according to a report government investigators published Friday. 
The report found that the hours dedicated to fentanyl investigations for fiscal year 2025 declined by more than 250,000 hours, or 31%, compared to fiscal year 2024. On the other hand, immigration enforcement saw the largest increase across all investigative categories, rising more than 1.7 million hours, or over 800%, according to the report. 
Vance’s comments came after national Democrats and the attorney for the Guerrero family criticized the federal government’s silence on the fatal ICE shooting during a “shadow” hearing in Biddeford last week.
Every Democratic member of Congress requested information about the shooting in a letter to the Department of Homeland Security on July 15, but they have not received a response, Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, ranking member of the Homeland Security Committee, told reporters in Maine.
Ben Gideon, legal representation for the Guerrero family, said that no federal agency has reached out to the family — including his wife, Karolina Rojas Alvarez, who heard the shots and soon after saw her husband’s body — which would be typical when such an investigation occurs. The state Attorney General’s Office has interviewed Rojas Alvarez.
Vance said on Monday that the federal government is investigating but did not provide any further insight. 
“I’m not going to prejudge the case because I think everybody is entitled to their case, not in the court of public opinion but a court trial by their juries, an actual real investigation, if that’s what ultimately happens,” he said. 
Vance also reiterated some of the agency’s contradictory explanations of the shooting.  
“When you have a law enforcement action, when you have somebody who is committing a crime in the United States of America, and you go and arrest that person — now I believe the person who was shot was not part of the underlying investigation, but when the officers approached the person they were trying to arrest, that person like drove away from the scene,” Vance said. “And what at least the law enforcement officers argue is that that person posed a danger to the community.”
At first, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told independent U.S. Sen. Angus King that Guerrero “weaponized” his vehicle before being shot by an ICE agent, an explanation the agency has frequently used in other shootings. But ICE later said he attempted to flee and “fearing for public safety” an agent shot him.
States Newsroom reporter Ariana Figueroa contributed reporting to this story.
