name: Nevada Current
title: Nevada sues feds over Colorado River cuts
description: Nevada officials have filed the first lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s Colorado River plan, a plan that would require Nevada to cut water use by about 17% over the next two years and authorizes even larger cuts during dry years.  The lawsuit filed Monday, comes three days after the Trump administration released its 10-year plan […]
text:
Nevada already has the smallest allocation of Colorado River water among the three Lower Basin states. (Lake Mead photo by Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current)Nevada officials have filed the first lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s Colorado River plan, a plan that would require Nevada to cut water use by about 17% over the next two years and authorizes even larger cuts during dry years. 
The lawsuit filed Monday, comes three days after the Trump administration released its 10-year plan for managing the Colorado River, and the nation’s two largest reservoirs, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, amid ongoing drought and record low water storage.
Under the plan, Nevada will have to give up 50,000 acre-feet of its Colorado River allocation over the next two years. An acre-foot is equal to 325,851 gallons — the amount of water needed to cover an acre of land a foot deep or enough water to supply two to three households for a year.
Additionally, Arizona will be required to reduce its water use by 760,000 acre-feet, while California will have to cut about 440,000 acre-feet under the plan.
But if conditions worsen, Nevada could have its 300,000 acre-foot Colorado River entitlement cut by more than 213,000 acre-feet or about 71% of its allocation. Nevada already has the smallest allocation of Colorado River water among the three Lower Basin states. 
Upper Basin states – Colorado, New Mexico, Wyoming and Utah – are not subject to mandatory water cutbacks under the plan.
Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo said challenging the federal plan was “a matter of survival” for Southern Nevada, which “represents about two-thirds of our state’s citizens and the lion’s share of its economy.”
“Nevada could lose more than 70 percent of its already meager Colorado River allocation while the Upper Basin states of Colorado, Utah, New Mexico, and Wyoming are not required to contribute a drop,” Lombardo said in a statement Monday.
“The Department of the Interior can’t roll Nevada and solve the entire Colorado River shortage on the backs of the Lower Basin states,” Lombardo continued.
Neither the Interior Department nor the Bureau of Reclamation responded to requests for comment early Monday.
 John Entsminger – the Southern Nevada Water Authority General Manager and Nevada’s lead negotiator on the Colorado River – called the additional reduction proposed by the Interior Department “entirely unrealistic.”
Southern Nevada used about 212,500 acre-feet of water in 2024, however, the steepest cuts under the longer-term federal plan would leave the region with less than 86,500 acre-feet of Colorado River water per year.
“This shortfall will cause devastating environmental, socioeconomic, and health and human safety impacts to southern Nevada and its citizens,” the lawsuit reads. 
Entsminger emphasized the state’s success in water conservation over the last two decades, cutting water use by about 40% as the region added more than 800,000 residents. 
“However, conservation has its limits, and there is just no way to meet even the basic needs of this community with the volume of water Interior has proposed,” Entsminger said in a statement Monday.
Lower Basin states have sought mandatory cuts to Upper Basin states, asking that cuts be shared among all states. Upper Basin states have argued they are already limited in their water use due to obligations to release water to Lower Basin states. 
The lawsuit – filed by the State of Nevada, in conjunction with the Colorado River Commission of Nevada and Southern Nevada Water Authority, and through the Nevada attorney general’s office – requests an injunction to stop the federal plan from being implemented. 
It alleges the federal government’s plan violates the Administrative Procedure Act, the National Environmental Policy Act, and the Law of the River. 
In the complaint, Nevada officials say the federal government failed to consider a reasonable range of alternative plans, failed to adequately consider environmental and socioeconomic effects of the plan, and failed to respond to comments from Nevada.
Specifically, the lawsuit says the federal government did not properly analyze the potential economic cost of water cuts on Southern Nevada’s $180 billion economy in the Interior’s final environmental analysis. 
According to the lawsuit, the federal government’s environmental analysis largely focused on the potential economic losses in agriculture and river-based recreation due to cuts rather than urban and industrial impacts. 
Analysis of socioeconomic impacts to Nevada were limited to Clark County, the state’s largest metropolitan area, which drives the state’s tourism economy. 
“There is no acknowledgment that contraction of Clark County’s economy has implications for the economy of the state as a whole, including the functioning of state government services on a broad scale,” the lawsuit says. 
The lawsuit said the federal government’s analysis did not consider how a 71% cut in the state’s Colorado River allocations would affect the state’s bond ratings, borrowing costs, reductions in tree canopy that could increase urban temperatures, and the increased rate pressure on water users. 
Lower Basin states have repeatedly stated they would prefer to avoid a drawn-out legal battle over the Colorado River. However, for the last three years, Upper Basin states and the Lower Basin states have blown through deadline after deadline in attempts to come to a seven-state consensus plan.
Earlier this month, Entsminger said Nevada preferred negotiation over litigation during an annual water summit and still had hoped states could reach an agreement, but said Nevada “fight to protect our community’s water supply.”
On Friday, Tom Buschatzke, the director of the Arizona Department of Water Resources and the state’s top water negotiator, said he welcomed the two-year operating agreement released by the federal government which would allow Lower Basin states to focus on a “longer-term, equitable, basin-wide outcome that includes shared sacrifices along with our Upper Basin partners in an effort to avoid protracted litigation.”

name: Maine Morning Star
title: With focus on fraud and ‘socialism,’ Vance returns to Maine to rally for Republican candidates
description: During his second visit to Maine this year, Vice President JD Vance rallied for Maine Republicans and against “socialism” ahead of the midterm elections.  At defense manufacturer Compotech on Monday, Vance cast Republicans U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and congressional candidate Paul LePage as independent voices, aiding their efforts to distance themselves from P[...]
text:
Vice President JD Vance speaks to a crowd at defense manufacturer Compotech in Brewer, Maine on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo via White House livestream screenshot) During his second visit to Maine this year, Vice President JD Vance rallied for Maine Republicans and against “socialism” ahead of the midterm elections. 
At defense manufacturer Compotech on Monday, Vance cast Republicans U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and congressional candidate Paul LePage as independent voices, aiding their efforts to distance themselves from President Donald Trump’s administration as they campaign. 
But the vice president ultimately touted them both, as well as Republican gubernatorial nominee Bobby Charles, as friends of the administration. Mostly, his praise went toward LePage, who is running to replace Democratic U.S. Rep. Jared Golden in the 2nd District. 
“I’m going to say very simply, my friends, everything that we’ve accomplished over the past couple of years, it could be undone if you send a lot of crazy people to Congress to fight against us,” Vance told the crowd gathered in Brewer. “What I’m asking is that you send an independent voice, a voice for Maine, you send somebody who’s going to fight for you and against the fraud. Send Paul LePage to Congress, and let’s get to work to save our country.”
Like other previous visits from Trump administration officials, Vance spent a portion of his speech focused on allegations of fraud in Maine’s Medicaid system.
He said he doesn’t want anti-fraud work to become partisan and that “some people” in the administration of Gov. Janet Mills have been responsive to the White House’s efforts to crack down on abuse.
“But I hate to say it, that after a few months of working with these guys, I don’t have a great amount of confidence that they’re going to lean into this anti-fraud effort,” Vance said. “And I think the problem is that their incompetence — or their something worse — is one of the reasons why Maine has become such a capital of fraud, and particularly it’s a lot of healthcare fraud.”
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services has disputed claims that the agency is not cracking down on fraud, announcing earlier this month that it suspended payments to five providers and terminated two providers’ contracts for subjecting residents to serious health risks and unsafe conditions. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Mehmet Oz, administrator of the U.S. Centers of Medicare and Medicaid Services, also visited Maine earlier this month, during which he did not meet with state officials but instead appeared in a video alongside LePage criticizing the state for its handling of the issue.
Vance also tied the issue of fraud directly to LePage’s campaign, and said during his time as governor, LePage came down hard on fraud, and would continue to do so in Congress. 
“Paul LePage has been the biggest advocate in state or federal government anywhere in the state of Maine at protecting your tax dollars and protecting these programs,” Vance said. “It’s one of the reasons why we’ve got to get Paul LePage to Congress. I need the help, ladies and gentlemen. You got to send Paul to help me.” 
While in office, LePage oversaw an overhaul of the state’s income taxes as well as dramatic cuts to the state’s healthcare programs, significantly reducing coverage for low-come adults. 
He vetoed five bills that would have expanded MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program. And after voters in 2017 approved a referendum to expand MaineCare with 59% support, LePage refused to implement it. 
Vance also took the opportunity to criticize LePage’s Democratic opponent, state auditor Matt Dunlap. The vice president criticized Dunlap for “failing the auditor exam.”
In 2021, Dunlap stepped down as state auditor after he failed to pass two accounting tests, preventing him from securing a key certification within the eligibility window. Jacob Norton filled the position, but also resigned shortly after he failed to get his auditing certification. Dunlap passed the exams after his 2021 resignation, and returned as state auditor in 2022. 
Fate of Medicare, Medicaid emerge as key issue in 2nd District race

“And for Matt Dunlap, if you’ve got a guy who cannot protect your tax dollars from fraudsters who has turned your state into one of the fraud capitals of the United States of America, maybe you should be saying to Matt Dunlap, ‘You’re fired,’ not promoted to the United States Congress,” Vance said. 
Vance also repeatedly hit Democrats for their embrace of what he referred to as “socialism,” likely a reference to more progressive candidates — some with connections to the Democratic Socialists of America — winning Democratic primaries in Maine and elsewhere.
“The Democrats are running a very corrupt game, which is they’re trying to tear down this country, tear down our young people, tear down our military, and what’s left over with the ashes of what they’ve torn down is socialism,” Vance said. 
“But I got to say that what we’re doing, it’s not just a two-year or even a four-year process,” Vance said. “Think about this: this country was plundered over a generation. Our goal is to reverse a consensus that has screwed over communities like this one for decades.”
Collins has also made similar pitches as to why Mainers shouldn’t support her rival, Democratic nominee Troy Jackson, calling him a “Bernie bro”, referring to independent U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont. 
While Collins did not get as much airtime in Vance’s speech, the vice president called her “our very independent friend” — echoing how she’s pitching herself on the campaign trail, even though she did not attend Monday’s event. 
The word “bipartisan” appears 2,651 times on her website. However, the senior senator has voted with Trump about 95% of the time. 
But, that is one of the lowest ratings among Republican senators, which Vance alluded to in his remarks on Monday. He said Collins “sometimes makes my job just a little bit harder” because “she is coming to work every single day and fighting not for a political party or not for any abstraction. She comes to work every single day and she fights for the great people of Maine.”
Collins’ Democratic critics often argue she only breaks with her party when her vote isn’t consequential. 
A Bangor Daily News analysis of Collins’ votes confirmed that she rarely casts deciding votes against Republicans. At the same time, it found that she has cast more of those votes than anyone else in the chamber.
Charles did not attend Monday’s event either, but received a brief shoutout from the vice president for his previous work in numerous federal government positions, such as at the Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs, though the effectiveness of that work has been disputed. 
“He has been an amazing fighter for the state of Maine,” Vance said. “He’s going to make a more amazing governor for the state of Maine.”

title: US House Speaker Mike Johnson to campaign in Albuquerque for GOP congressional challenger Cunningham
description: Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson will visit Albuquerque Wednesday to campaign for fellow Republican Greg Cunningham, a retired Marine and Albuquerque Police Department detective who’s challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) in the Nov. 3 general election.
text:
U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson, (R-La.), left, will visit Albuquerque on Aug. 26, 2026, to campaign for Greg Cunningham, a Republican challenging U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez for New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District. (Johnson photo at U.S. Capitol on March 3, 2026 by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom; Cunningham photo by Danielle Prokop/Source NM)Republican U.S. House Speaker Mike Johnson will visit Albuquerque Wednesday to campaign for fellow Republican Greg Cunningham, a retired Marine and Albuquerque Police Department detective who’s challenging incumbent U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez (D-N.M.) in the Nov. 3 general election.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Cunningham’s campaign announced the visit Monday morning and said the pair will join “New Mexico law enforcement leaders to discuss public safety, border security, and the cost of crime on New Mexico families and small businesses.”
Johnson joined President Donald Trump in endorsing Cunningham in April.
At the time, Trump posted on his social media platform, Truth Social, to say that Cunningham has the “Wisdom and Courage required to Defend our Country, Support our Brave Military, Veterans, and Law Enforcement and Ensure PEACE THROUGH STRENGTH.”
In a joint statement at the time, Johnson, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, Majority Whip Tom Emmer and House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain said Cunningham “is a patriot who will help us continue to deliver safe streets, secure borders, lower costs, and peace through strength.”
New Mexico’s Congressional District 2, which includes much of southern New Mexico and stretches up to Albuquerque’s South Valley, is expected to be among New Mexico’s more competitive federal races.

name: Michigan Advance
title: El-Sayed says Hasan Piker does not speak for his campaign amid comments about Jewish candidate
description: In response to comments made by online influencer Hasan Piker, a controversial left-wing streamer, in which he tied his criticisms of support for Israel by the American Jewish community to state Sen. Jeremy Moss of Bloomfield Township, Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said that “nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.” Piker w[...]
text:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, left, and political influencer Hasan Piker, right, take questions from the media before an event on the campus of Michigan State University in East Lansing, Mich on April 7, 2026 (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)In response to comments made by online influencer Hasan Piker, a controversial left-wing streamer, in which he tied his criticisms of support for Israel by the American Jewish community to state Sen. Jeremy Moss of Bloomfield Township, Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said that “nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople.”
Piker was a staunch supporter of El-Sayed in his primary campaign against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham), appearing with him at a pair of campus rallies in April and at a primary night party in Detroit. In the general election thus far, his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed by tying him to Piker’s past comments — even calling him El-Sayed’s “running mate” at the state Republican Party’s nominating convention on Saturday. 
“While politicians and pundits try to make this race about a Twitch streamer, we’re going to be talking about gas, groceries, good schools, and healthcare,” El-Sayed said in a statement on Monday. “Because that’s what Michiganders keep asking about. It’s why I’m fighting to get money out of politics, money in your pocket, and Medicare for All.”
Streamer and political influencer Hasan Piker speaks at an event with Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on the campus of Michigan State University in East Lansing, Mich. on April 7, 2026 (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
During a Twitch stream, Piker’s screen showed a social media post with a graphic and a photo of Moss while he said, “If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews. I don’t know how people don’t recognize how dangerous this predicament is, how dangerous this is for Jews.”
Moss, who is Jewish, is the Democratic nominee for Michigan’s 11th Congressional District, which was vacated by Stevens in her bid for U.S. Senate. Earlier in August, an audio clip that purported to be of Moss circulated on social media claiming he said the entire purpose of his campaign for the U.S. House is to ensure America continues to support Israel. Moss, in a post on the X social media platform, called the clip fake, stating that it uses “manipulated and unsourced audio.”
“It peddles in offensive tropes and lies – especially the lie of dual loyalty suggesting that Jews are never fully citizens of or loyal to their home countries,” he continued. 
State Sen. Jeremy Moss (D-Bloomfield) addresses supporters after clinching the Democratic nomination for the 11th Congressional District on Aug. 4, 2026. (Campaign photo provided)
Moss did not respond to a request for comment on Piker’s statements or El-Sayed’s response. This story will be updated when a response is received.
U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten — who was a strong supporter of Stevens in the primary and has yet to endorse El-Sayed following his primary win — also responded to Piker’s comments in a statement on social media, calling them “unacceptable.” 
“Piker is a hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe because he lacks substance. It’s dangerous for everyone,” Scholten said in a post on X. “We should all be calling out this disgusting rhetoric so it loses its grip on our politics once and for all. It has no place in Michigan, and no place in our country.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While El-Sayed’s statement did not directly call Piker’s statements themselves antisemitic or condemn them specifically, he called antisemitism a “scourge.”
“I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past,” he said. “My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters.”
His statement also comes as El-Sayed has seemed to distance himself from Piker since the primary election.
Rogers, meanwhile, called Piker’s statements “absolutely disgusting” in a post on Sunday, saying that “If Abdul El-Sayed had any courage at all, he would call this out and disavow Hasan Piker once and for all.”
Rogers has come under similar criticism for his connection to last week’s Christian nationalist rally in Dearborn that featured anti-Muslim rhetoric and led to the arrest of nearly two dozen individuals. The event was organized in part by Detroit Pastor Lorenzo Sewell, a member of Rogers’ Faith Coalition Leadership Team. 
Rogers’ campaign declined to answer questions from Michigan Advance about whether he supported Sewell’s role in the Dearborn rally.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: USC governing board elects first chairwoman
description: The University of South Carolina's governing board elected is first ever chairwoman, Rose Newton, a banker and spouse of an SC House member.
text:
The University of South Carolina's governing board elected is first ever chairwoman. Rose Newton, wife of Republican state House Judiciary Chariman Weston Newton, on Friday, Aug. 21, 2026, became the first woman to lead the 20-member board. (Photo courtesy of USC)COLUMBIA — The University of South Carolina’s governing board elected is first ever chairwoman.
Rose Newton, wife of Republican state House Judiciary Chariman Weston Newton, on Friday became the first woman to lead the 20-member board.
Newton succeeds Thad Westbrook, who was chairman from 2022 through 2026.
Other elected female members sitting on the board include Dr. Coleman Floyd Buckhouse of Florence, the daughter of former longtime board member Dr. Eddie Floyd; Leah Moody, a Rock Hill lawyer and daughter of the late Rep. Bessie Moody-Lawrence; and Emma Morris, a lawyer in Seneca.
While Newton is USC’s first chairwoman, she’s far from the only woman leading a college board in the state.
The governing boards of Clemson University, College of Charleston and Coastal Carolina University are all led by women.
Kim Wilkerson became Clemson’s first female board chair in 2021.
Renee Buyck Romberg is College of Charleston’s second female chair. She was elected to lead the board in 2023. Before Romberg, Marie Land in 2009 became the first female chair at the college founded in 1770.
At Winthrop University in Rock Hill, Kathy Bigham, mother-in law of former state Sen. Scott Talley, was the last woman to lead the board. First appointed to the board in 2003, she was elected chairwoman in 2008. She remains vice chair.
And at Lander University, Linda Dolny, elected in 2018, was the last female board chair. She still sits on the Greenwood college’s board.
“We have a lot of women doing a lot of great things in the state so just glad to be a part of that team moving higher ed forward in the state of South Carolina,” Newton told reporters Friday.
Newton, a third-generation banker who chairs the board at the Bank of Clarendon, holds degrees in finance and economics from Converse College and a Master of Business Administration from USC. She’s been on the board since 2018.
Her husband, Rep. Weston Newton, has a law degree from USC. He’s led the House Judiciary Committee since 2022.
Their daughter, Reedy Newton, was USC’s student body president before graduating in 2023. Their son, William Newton, is a 2025 graduate and first-year USC law school student, and their younger daughter Eliza Rose is a senior at USC.
Rose Newton said she hopes to maintain the momentum the university has enjoyed in recent years in terms of student growth and investments.
Before rising to the chairmanship, Newton was vice chair for four years.
Reid Sherard, a Greenville attorney who has been on the board since 2023, will succeed Newton as vice chair.
They are among USC’s 17 voting board members; 16 of those are selected by the Legislature to represent geographic regions and one is selected by the governor.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: How Georgia farms’ fame (and favor) outpace their place in the economy
description: Gov. Brian Kemp says it. Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper says it. Congressman Sanford Bishop has said it, as did his late colleague U.S. Rep. David Scott. The phrase “Agriculture is Georgia’s No. 1 industry” infiltrates Georgia politics like pollen in the spring air. Folks wearing business casual evoke sweat-stained hats and dirty boots, putting romant[...]
text:
Linda Smith, owner of Heritage Hill Farm, inspects and picks blueberries during the summer harvest in Ludowici on June 24, 2026. Blueberries outpace peaches in Georgia. Credit: Justin Taylor/The Current GA/CatchLight/Report for AmericaGov. Brian Kemp says it. Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper says it. Congressman Sanford Bishop has said it, as did his late colleague U.S. Rep. David Scott.
The phrase “Agriculture is Georgia’s No. 1 industry” infiltrates Georgia politics like pollen in the spring air.
Folks wearing business casual evoke sweat-stained hats and dirty boots, putting romanticized rural life at the heart of the state and high on its policy priority list. Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson, an Atlanta native, posted on social media that not only is agriculture the state’s No. 1 industry, it’s “part of who we are.”
Under the Gold Dome, the slogan pairs with policies that benefit Georgia’s tiny number of farmers and timber-growers, favorable property tax treatment, and allowing heavier trucks that damage public roads as long as the cargo is agricultural.
But the bucolic ideal of the family farm is nowhere near how the vast majority of Georgians make a living.
Cultivation and harvesting make up less than one percent of the state’s output and few Georgians own or work on a profitable farm.
To put agriculture anywhere near the top of Georgia’s economy requires stretching the definition to include restaurants and grocery stores — any workplace that uses food, fiber or timber — according to Kemp’s former top economic advisor, agricultural economics professor Jeffrey Dorfman.
The state’s most valuable work products come from people providing services like health care, government and real estate management and rental; or from manufacturing higher-value things like airplanes and cars.
Of course farming is incredibly important — we all need to eat. But politicians mislead the public when they imply that it’s a large part of the economy.
 Old saying, new publication

In print, the claim that agriculture is Georgia’s No. 1 industry goes back to at least the 1960s when the Georgia Farm Bureau Federation president, a former state legislator, repeated it in his 1968 lobbying to promote the interests of farmers.  In 1974, the line appeared in a poultry industry lament about trucker strikes, which was delivered by one of Georgia’s legendary lobbyists, Abit Massey, who stayed at work in the state capitol until 2009.
Some newspapers and magazines copy and paste the claim, without attribution.
But in months of searching, The Current GA could not find anyone claiming to be the source of the saying or anyone with backup for it.
The search included calls and emails with the most well-connected sources in Georgia agriculture and politics, including the Georgia Farm Bureau, the Georgia Agribusiness Council, the state Department of Agriculture and the University of Georgia’s school of agriculture.
Both the governor’s office and the office of the Georgia Secretary of Agriculture referred The Current to the University of Georgia’s Ag Impact Report, an unsigned, undated public relations website created by the school’s College of Agriculture and Environmental Sciences in 2025 to build public and legislative support for the agriculture industry.
The top of the site proclaims that Georgia’s No. 1 industry is agriculture, but it doesn’t include any source or any comparison to other industries. Instead, the website showcases farmers’ harvest values by crop and by county, data that the school has collected and published annually for more than a decade. CAES Professor Ben Campbell is among the team who work on those benchmark county statistics, but he had no documentation for the promotional line at the top of the website.
Neither Kemp’s nor Tyler’s office could cite a source for claims made about the agriculture industry before UGA published the website.
 What statistics say

There are three ways economists might look at an industry’s size compared to others, according to Economist David Sjoquist, an emeritus professor at Georgia State University who specializes in public policy and Georgia’s economy.
Freshly cut pine trees sit on trailers waiting to be transported to a timber mill. Near Folkston on Oct. 2, 2025. (Justin Taylor/The Current GA/Catchlight Local/Report for America)
“Most economists, if asked to measure the relative size of an industry, would use the federal Bureau of Economic Analysis’ gross domestic product data. Alternatively, they might use employment or wages and earnings,” Sjoquist wrote to The Current GA via email.
Georgia’s livestock, crop and timber farms’ output was about $6.7 billion, or 0.7% of Georgia’s $925 billion gross state product in 2025, according to the BEA, placing it well behind other categories such as financial services, government and manufacturing.
But that small number is a narrow definition of agriculture, according to Dorfman, Kemp’s former economics advisor who is now a professor of agricultural and resource economics at North Carolina State University.
“If by agriculture you mean ‘farming,’ then there’s no chance it’s the No. 1 industry anywhere,” Dorfman told The Current GA.

Georgia’s biggest industries by share of economy
Finance and services, not farming and growing timber, are the biggest industries in Georgia, measured by their share of the $925 billion in goods and services produced by Georgia industries in 2025.


He’s among the economists who include more businesses, like slaughterhouses, to calculate the size of “agribusiness” in their states.
But “agribusiness” would still have to stretch deep into suburbs and cities and include everyone who works in a restaurant or grocery store to be anywhere near the top of industry by GDP in Georgia.
Counting any workplace that touches any food, fiber or timber that comes from anywhere in the world, around 11% to 13% of the economy in Deep South and Midwestern states would go in the “agribusiness” category,  Dorfman said.
But there’s one last hiccup to the BEA and its definitions. There’s no category just called “healthcare.”  If there were, that would be a lot.
“We know the national average on healthcare spending is about 18% of the economy … Georgia has a lot of big hospitals,” Dorfman said.  Given the state’s hospitals and medical schools, “I really doubt we are much under the national average.”
 Few farmworkers, profitable farms

The decline of the tough and low-margin work of raising commodities has been evident for decades.
Parts of farm work are so tough that few will choose it at the wages offered if they have any other option. Farms and slaughterhouses sometimes turn to the people most desperate for work: guest workers or undocumented workers.
And many farms seek to bypass human labor with ever-developing machinery and devices, like drones to spot-spray herbicides and health-tracker collars for cows. Some farmers have diversified toward crops hardly known two generations ago, like pine trees and blueberries that require years of waiting for a payoff but no annual planting.
About 57,000 Georgians worked on a farm either as owner or employee in 2022, according to the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis.  About five times as many people work for local school systems.
Agriculture side-hustles or farms that lose money are far more common than full-time family farming. The Census of Agriculture counts all of them — its tally of farms includes any place that normally sells $1,000 or more of farm products a year.
Only about 6,100 farms in all of Georgia netted more than $50,000 in 2022, according to the U.S. Census of Agriculture.
The other 33,000 farms are a mix of tiny farms, new farms, farms that experienced a bad year, or they’re run by “five o’clock farmers:” People who earn their living elsewhere but who also have a few acres of u-pick blueberries, a handful of chicken houses or some cows around the house.
 Role in the state

But even as some political leaders keep repeating an unfounded talking point, state Republicans — and sometimes Democrats — agree on aid to the industry.  Given natural disasters, paper mill closures, the cost of fuel, machinery, fertilizer and labor, it’s so hard to make money without help that few do.
In 2025, at the urging of some of the state legislature’s biggest farmers, Georgia became the second state to shield pesticide manufacturers from some lawsuits that blame the companies for illness caused by glyphosate.
When the Trump administration cut wages for short-term farm workers on H-2A visas in 2025 to as little as $10.52 an hour, some top Georgia Republican politicians celebrated.
Yet the state has made no major changes in regulation and oversight of worker conditions in response to a major federal farm labor trafficking case that opened in 2016.
The state grants favorable property tax treatment to timber farms and to land in conservation use, which includes farms. Georgia extends sales tax breaks on inputs and equipment to farmers who expect as little as $5,000 in annual revenue.
The Berry family packs freshly picked collards at their family farm in Long County on Oct. 28, 2023
The politicians and lobbies who support protections for the industry have a variety of reasons like food security and the health of rural economies.
Part of the official rosy tint around agriculture might be also attributed to constituency, or even history.
Most of the people in state and legislative elected leadership come from places where they and their constituents are most likely to see farming and related businesses, or even take part in it as a landowner or actual farmer.
The ruling GOP is more dependent on voters around places like Newington, Dublin, Vidalia or Bonaire for its thinning majority than it was even 10 years ago. Since President Donald Trump introduced MAGA into the discourse, Atlanta’s closer suburbs have nearly stopped voting for Republicans. That means there are fewer suburban voices in leadership, much less urban ones.
“As the blue dot has grown larger around Atlanta … the Republican vote has become very much a rural vote in Georgia,” said Charles Bullock, a political science professor at the University of Georgia who specializes in Deep South politics.
But even city folks may hold an idealized idea of the country; rural-to-urban migration is part of many Georgians’ stories.
“There may still be grandparents who are living in parts of rural Georgia, this may go along with childhood memories of going to visit grandparents in a rural area and how different that was than growing up in suburbia and how much more fun it was,” Bullock said.
Maggie Lee, The Current’s data reporter, is a first-generation, part-time farmer in Fulton County.
 METHODOLOGY

The BEA GDP numbers for Georgia for calendar year 2025 used in this story come from the agency’s April 9, 2026 publication of Annual Gross Domestic Product by State, table SAGDP2. To see this data, start with BEA’s Regional Data page and choose “Annual Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by State,” then choose “GDP by industry in current dollars.” On the next screen, set filters for “Georgia”, “all statistics in table,” then “2025.” 
The BEA’s definitions of each industry are linked in the resulting table. Other technical terms are explained in the agency’s documentation. 
These GDP figures omit unpaid labor, such as caregiving.
The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis data on employment by county and by industry from 1969 and 2022 captures farm workers and farm proprietors engaged in the direct production of agricultural commodities.  Data comes from tables CAEMP25S (1969-2000) and CAEMP25N (2001-2022). The BEA discontinued this data series in 2024. For discussion of these trends, see “Changes in Farm Employment, 1969 to 2021” by Mark White and Andrew VanLeuven in farmdoc daily, Department of Agricultural and Consumer Economics, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, July 14, 2023. 
 The 2022 U.S. Census of Agriculture statistics used in this story come from state-level data for Georgia, see Table 5. The USDA does that census every five years. 
For a discussion of different ways to count farmers and farmworkers, see “How many people work in agriculture in the United States,” by the Congressional Research Service, April 8, 2025.
Peach and blueberry statistics come from the USDA’s 2024 summary of crops, published in May 2025. Download the report here.

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Additional Amtrak passenger train service to and from Pittsburgh to begin in mid-November
description: Amtrak anticipates beginning ticket sales for the second Pittsburgh to New York passenger train in October, the administration said.
text:
Passengers board Amtrak's Keystone service to Philadelphia at the Harrisburg station on Wednesday, Dec. 6, 2023. (Photo by Peter Hall/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)Amtrak will operate a second daily passenger train between Pittsburgh and New York via Harrisburg and Philadelphia starting in mid-November, Gov. Josh Shapiro’s office announced Monday. 
The expanded service is the result of nearly three years of planning and more than $80 million invested in the project, in cooperation with Amtrak and freight railroad Norfolk Southern Corp., which owns the tracks between Pittsburgh and Harrisburg.
The second daily trip will give Pennsylvanians better access “to modern, safe, reliable passenger rail service,” connecting the commonwealth’s communities and creating jobs, economic development and infrastructure investment, the Shapiro administration said in a statement.
“Railroads transformed our commonwealth into a powerhouse of the industrial age and my administration is focused on continuing that legacy while responding to our communities’ needs and helping them grow,” Shapiro said. “The people of western Pennsylvania have waited a long time for more passenger rail service and my administration has chased every opportunity to get this done.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Amtrak anticipates beginning ticket sales for the second Pennsylvanian train in October, the administration said. The trip from Pittsburgh to New York currently takes more than nine hours.
The administration announced in September 2023 that PennDOT and Norfolk Southern had reached an agreement that would allow Amtrak to operate a second Pennsylvanian passenger service.
The Pennsylvanian carried about 212,000 passengers in 2019 before ridership dropped sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2024, ridership exceeded pre-pandemic levels for the first time with nearly 234,000 passengers, according to the Rail Passengers Association.
Norfolk Southern had determined in a 2020 study that adding a second daily Pennsylvanian service on its Pittsburgh line would result in unacceptable delays for freight and intermodal trains. It said, however, a second passenger train could be supported with the construction of a new mainline track, passing sidings, switches and other infrastructure.
The commonwealth put the cost of the project at $200 million. In December 2023, former U.S. Sen. Bob Casey (D-Pa.) and U.S. Sen John Fetterman (D-Pa.) announced a $144 million Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) grant under the Biden-era Bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. 
The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) was responsible for about 20% of the project’s cost, Casey’s office said at the time.
“This momentous milestone was made possible by the department successfully securing federal infrastructure funding and this Administration’s nonstop coordination with Amtrak and Norfolk Southern,” PennDOT Secretary Mike Carroll said. “Combined with the relentless advocacy of elected officials and community members along this corridor, this tireless work is making this long-awaited service expansion a reality.”
The administration noted PennDOT has been a national leader in using funds from the bipartisan infrastructure act, including FRA grants to study the resumption of passenger rail service from Scranton to New York and from Reading to Philadelphia.

While Amtrak’s service between Harrisburg and Pittsburgh now runs only once a day, the national passenger rail company operates 13 weekday Keystone Service trains in each direction between New York and Harrisburg via Philadelphia’s 30th Street Station. That’s because Amtrak owns the Keystone Corridor line between Philadelphia and Harrisburg and controls which trains operate on it and when.
Amtrak Board Member Robert Gleason said the expanded Pennsylvanian service highlights the strong partnership between Amtrak, PennDOT and Norfolk Southern.
“The expansion of Pennsylvanian service demonstrates what is possible when public and private partners work together toward a shared vision for rail transportation,” said Norfolk Southern Senior Vice President and Chief Strategy Officer Mike McClellan, according to the release.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Gov. Morrisey, Kanawha delegate call for roads review after numerous vehicles fall off interstate
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey and a Kanawha County delegate are each calling for a close review of recent crashes at an interstate spot in Charleston after multiple vehicles recently fell off of the road or dangled off of the edge.
text:
Multiple vehicles have fallen off the interstate near the Interstate 64/77 split in Charleston, West Virginia, in recent months. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Division of Highways)Gov. Patrick Morrisey and a Kanawha County delegate are each calling for a close review of recent crashes at an interstate spot in Charleston after multiple vehicles recently fell off of the road or dangled off of the edge.
The latest accident occurred Friday night, when four young men died after their vehicle left the roadway on Interstate 77 near the Interstate 64 split. Their vehicle tumbled off the interstate into the Martin Marietta Charleston Yard below, according to Charleston police.  
The fatal incident occurred just days after two people were injured from a tractor trailer going off the interstate in the same area. There was an additional accident in the area in the last week.
On Monday, Morrisey said he’d directed the West Virginia Division of Highways to work with law enforcement and highway safety officials to examine the circumstances surrounding each of these crashes. 
“My heart goes out to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in Friday night’s tragic crash in Charleston, as well as to those who have been injured in other recent crashes along our interstate system,” Morrisey said in a statement to WSAZ.
“While we should not draw conclusions about their causes before those investigations are complete, we need to understand what happened in each instance and determine whether there are additional steps we can take to improve safety,” the governor said.
Del. Dana Ferrell, R-Kanawha, has called for a closer look at the problematic interstate area as well as other Charleston interstate spots where roadway barriers may not be sufficient. 
Del. Dana Ferrell, R-Kanawha, has called for a closer look at the problematic interstate area as well as other Charleston interstate spots where roadway barriers may not be sufficient. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Ferrell’s daughter and her boyfriend were involved in an auto accident last week that left their vehicle hanging over the barrier of the Fort Hill Bridge. Their vehicle was bumped by another driver.
“This is an interstate system that was designed in the 1960s, probably, then constructed in the ’70s. There’s been a fourfold increase in semi-truck traffic since then, and a 140-some percent increase in SUVs and pickups traveling,” Ferrell said. “These barriers were just not designed to properly retain that impact, they’re more for sedans… They’re 32-inch barriers.”
Ferrell plans to ask the West Virginia Division of Highways about adding additional guardrails.
“​​I think you have to take an offensive and a defensive approach to this. You go on offense by putting the flashing lights up, like you do on some of the curves … and you put the rumble strips to you know get people’s attention if they’re on their phones,” Ferrell said. “The defensive side comes down to the barriers.”
Ferrell said he also plans to ask WVDOT about the potential of working with federal authorities to create a bypass system in Kanawha County for semi-trucks. 
The West Virginia Division of Highways was already working to install high friction surface treatment on several of the elevated portions of the interstate prior to the recent crashes.
“We anticipate having those treatments installed later this fall. We are closely coordinating with the Charleston Police Department to monitor crashes in this area and will determine additional countermeasures that may be implemented as they complete their crash investigations,” State Transportation Secretary Stephen Todd Rumbaugh said in a statement.

name: Source New Mexico
title: Democratic governor candidate Haaland says ‘transparency’ the lesson of Project Jupiter
description: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland talks affordability, data centers and more during statewide tour.
text:
Democratic New Mexico gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland speaks with Abbey Gallegos, a Mesilla market vendor, during a campaign visit to southern New Mexico on Aug. 23, 2026. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Southern New Mexico residents deserve a voice in decisions that are being made for the rest of the state, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Deb Haaland told Source NM during a visit to the area over the weekend.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
She added that people bring up Project Jupiter, the Oracle and OpenAI data center underway in southern Doña Ana County, each time she visits the area. She told Source that transparency is “the lesson to be learned” from how the project has been handled by government officials and agencies. 
“The community deserves to know what industry is coming into their community,” Haaland said.  “They deserve to know exactly how much water they want to use, how they’re going to get their electric power, what they plan to do with respect to moving our renewable energy goals forward. That’s not too much to ask…In talking with legislators, they want to put guardrails on data centers, but I’m feeling like it should be any industry that comes to New Mexico.”
NM Supreme Court temporarily halts Project Jupiter air quality permit hearing

Haaland spoke with residents in Las Cruces and Mesilla Sunday during a visit on her latest statewide tour leading up to the Nov. 3 general election, in which Haaland faces Republican Gregg Hull, the former mayor of Rio Rancho. Haaland’s tour started in Rio Rancho last week, with stops in Grants, Silver City, Deming and Lordsburg, and was scheduled to stop in Truth or Consequences and Socorro on Monday. She touched on major topics of focus for her campaign such as education, economic development, access to health care, public safety and affordability. 
“There’s this overarching umbrella over every single thing that New Mexicans do every day and that’s the affordability crisis,” Haaland said to a crowd of supporters, pointing to the Trump Administration’s tariffs and various program cuts. “Under this president, New Mexicans are sicker, poorer and hungrier and so we need to ensure that New Mexicans can have a little bit more money in their pockets every single month.”
Haaland said she wants to enhance the state’s child tax credit and working families tax credit to give New Mexicans “a raise” to help make ends meet. She recalled her experience worrying about paying rent and buying groceries while raising her daughter as a single mother, and not qualifying for emergency food stamps. 
“I cried right there in the food stamp office. I just understand what it’s like for so many New Mexicans,” she said. “We just need to make sure that we are acting like a real community, that all of us are working to lift up the people who need help the most.”
She said she also believes the film industry is a sustainable industry for the state and an area that she wants to help modernize through updated tax credits and reviewing how they are applied.
Abbey Gallegos, a Las Cruces resident and area farmer, told Source that she has followed Haaland since she served as the U.S. Secretary of the Interior and hopes if elected governor Haaland will put “New Mexicans first over corporate” and foster more opportunities for New Mexico students to continue their education and careers in the state. 
“We have so much to improve on, but for New Mexicans, not corporations,” Gallegos said, adding that she wants to see plans in writing, not just discussed. “I want to know a first-year plan, third-year plan, fifth-year plan.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: New coalition aims to sharpen Nebraska’s competitive edge, has single focus: child care policy
description: LINCOLN — Carrying and delivering twins didn’t take nearly the toll on Jessica Pallas as what came after: finding suitable childcare so she and husband Cale could hold onto their jobs and health insurance. “Figuring out the childcare puzzle was more stressful than the pregnancy and the twins in the beginning,” said the first-time mom […]
text:
A new statewide campaign and coalition, Child Care Can, launched Monday in Lincoln with an announcement and gathering of about 200 people. The coalition, started with 65 member entities, will be focused solely on improving child care policy through recurring public investment. Organizers say next steps are developing specific strategies. (Photo courtesy of Child Care Can)LINCOLN — Carrying and delivering twins didn’t take nearly the toll on Jessica Pallas as what came after: finding suitable childcare so she and husband Cale could hold onto their jobs and health insurance.
“Figuring out the childcare puzzle was more stressful than the pregnancy and the twins in the beginning,” said the first-time mom who lives in the small Nebraska town of Stromsburg with husband Cale and their daughters Merrick and Rowan.
Cale and Jessica Pallas of Stromsburg with twin daughters Merrick and Rowan. (Photo courtesy of Erin Dickey)
The girls are now 3 years old, and their jigsaw puzzle of care looks different depending on the day and hour. Sometimes the twins are with a nanny at home. Some days they’re in York with Mom shifting them between a private preschool and a day care as she works remotely from a nearby coffee shop. One day a week they attend public preschool in Stromsburg.
“It’s wonky,” Jessica said.
But the wonky set the Pallases on a mission. They’ve done research. They’ve talked to many families. They said they recognize that childcare challenges date back decades, and they’re determined not to leave their daughters or grandkids with the same or worse difficulties.
So the couple has jumped into a new statewide campaign, Child Care Can, that launched Monday. Organizers describe the coalition as the largest ever formed – 65 entities so far — to focus solely on childcare policy in Nebraska.
The campaign defines its long-term goal: to secure recurring, robust public investment that increases access to affordable and quality child care so working parents can help grow economies in rural, urban and all areas of the state. 
“Nebraska’s competitiveness depends on affordable, quality child care,” says the Child Care Can website. 
 Ranked 38th 

The campaign is funded by Voices for Healthy Kids, an initiative of the American Heart Association, and the Alliance for Early Success. Early Futures Partnership, which includes Communities for Kids, is the organizational backbone.
Coalition members are led by a 13-person steering committee and range from child learning centers, colleges and YMCAs to economic development councils. Membership is diverse, including I Be Black Girl, Nebraska Indian Community College, the Nebraska Commission on Latino-Americans and the Center for Rural Affairs.
Specific strategies are to come later. Monday’s kickoff drew about 200 people and featured talks from business and childcare industry leaders, including the Aksarben Foundation, which has been focusing on how to turn around a lag in Omaha and Lincoln job growth compared with peer cities in other states. 
Child Care Can organizers say child care should be viewed as infrastructure — foundational systems like roads, public safety and hospitals that allow communities and economies to function.  
Elizabeth Everett serves as the campaign’s manager and says advocates in past years have done “tremendous” legwork to shine light and understanding on the child care challenge.
‘It’s a workforce issue,’ Nebraska lawmakers say of child care subsidy bill they advanced

This past legislative session, for instance, advocates pushed and state lawmakers adopted Legislative Bill 304 to permanently set household eligibility caps for childcare public assistance at 185% of the federal poverty level, rather than lowering back to 130%, as was the situation prior to 2021. That means eligibility for a family of four tops out at about $61,000 a year, compared with about $43,000 previously.
Nebraska’s childcare subsidy program is funded by federal and state funds, and early-childcare advocates say that as of the 2025 fiscal year, the state directs roughly $128 million a year in assistance. Families with a household gross income over 100% of the federal poverty level pay 7% of their gross income for childcare.
Everett said Nebraska currently ranks No. 38 among states for investment in childcare assistance.
Everett shared data points to reinforce the need for action. Among them: 

The statewide median cost for center-based childcare is between $9,000 and $15,000 per child annually. 
Since 2019, the number of center-based and family-based programs has declined by 4.7% and 22.6%, respectively. About two-thirds of young Nebraska children live in households where all available parents are working. 
Affordability and access difficulties annually lead to an estimated statewide loss of $64 million in state income tax revenue and roughly 6,800 jobs. 
Childcare workers make 52% of the average annual salary of all occupations in Nebraska, and annual turnover in the child care industry is about 20%.

 What other states do 

While Nebraska has made certain strides, Child Care Can leaders note that other states such as Montana, Iowa, New Mexico and Louisiana are going farther with “intentional” public investments in childcare strategies to grow their economies and to compete for workers, businesses and families.
Everett said states that are finding success in the childcare arena have in common coordinated and sustained advocacy efforts to help sway childcare policy.
Children from the KU Kids Deanwood Child Care Center complete a mural celebrating the launch of a local child tax credit in 2021 in Washington, D.C. (Photo courtesy of Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Community Change)
“Nebraska will now have that,” she said of the Child Care Can campaign. Everett also is vice president of Early Futures Partnership, which oversees Communities for Kids and First Five Nebraska. She said creating the new campaign “makes an important shift from awareness to action.” 
Montana, for example, recently created a state-driven trust fund to support early childhood education programs. New Mexico lawmakers established a similar fund in 2020, with about $300 million in seed money. That state designates a portion of surplus oil and gas revenues to help sustain the trust fund. 
Iowa lawmakers recently passed a law making childcare assistance permanently available to childcare workers regardless of their income. Everett called the move a “huge workforce recruitment tool.” Nebraska failed to pass a similar bill.
State Sen. Eliot Bostar of Lincoln will work with the campaign as it explores ways for public investment. 
“Nebraska has a role to play in building a stronger, more sustainable childcare system, but this is work we have to do together,” Bostar said. “By partnering with parents, childcare providers, businesses and communities, we can find practical solutions that help families afford quality care, help providers build sustainable businesses and help employers maintain the workforce they need.”
Everett said childcare providers are working long hours in businesses that can be difficult to sustain. She said quality childcare has become harder to find, afford and keep for too many families. 
The Pallases said their search began early, when their pregnancy was about two months in. Jessica said she’d tell providers of her need and then it would come: a “big sigh” and “no space for two infants.”
When the girls were born, the Pallases hired college students as nannies. The cost essentially wiped out Jessica’s salary, but the family’s health insurance was provided through her job as an estimator for a Grand Island-based manufacturing company. She is able to work remotely. Cale works at his family’s agricultural feed sales company.
The couple, who met as students at the University of Nebraska at Lincoln — he’s 33 and she’s 31, knew they wanted to live in Stromsburg, where Cale grew up. But limited child care providers had them searching outside the town of about 1,100 population.
Eventually they landed spots in a nonprofit childcare center in York. Jessica estimated that 15 to 20 kids leave Stromsburg for York each day for childcare, about a 20-minute drive one way. She said her family loved their service provider there, but it shut down with only a two-week notice to families.
“We were really distraught to say the least,” Jessica said in an interview. The couple also spoke Monday at the campaign kickoff. They said sickness and health issues that required frequent attention were an added stress.
The couple found another York provider and more recently added preschool to the girls’ routines. Now two days a week, Jessica stays in York, performing work duties via computer at a local coffee shop, so she can tote the girls back and forth between daycare and preschool.
But the Pallases wanted their daughters to get to know Stromsburg kids as well, since that’s where they’ll go to kindergarten. On Wednesdays, Merrick and Rowan attend a preschool in their hometown.
They “make it work with a patchwork of solutions,” Jessica said. “Those are our babies. We love them to death. To put them in someone else’s care, especially when they are so little … it’s a lot.” 
 Childcare matters to business growth

Cale said improving childcare options matters to the growth of his family business. Currently he, his dad and another young man handle the operation, but plans include expanding by one or two workers as early as next year.
A 2025 poll from advocacy group First Five Years Fund found that 4 out of 5 rural Americans “say the ability of working parents to find and afford quality child care is either in a ‘state of crisis’ or ‘a major problem.’” (Photo courtesy of Sue Barr/Getty Images)
An area’s lack of childcare for young families can be a deterrent to recruitment and retention, he said. 
“That can become such an insurmountable issue,” Cale said. “We as a business would never be able to attract the best employees to our community.” 
The Pallases love their life in Stromsburg and are working to help strengthen the town’s long-term viability via their local community foundation. A listening session identified childcare as the top issue, they said. The pair plugged into the Communities for Kids network, which is key to the new Child Care Can campaign.
They pointed to reports from decades past that laid out daycare challenges. Jessica said she didn’t want her kids to inherit the “horror stories of worrying about childcare.”
“At some point we can’t just keep kicking the can down the road,” said Cale. “We wanted to be part of the solution.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Kentucky mom advocates for more social media regulations as state leads court case against Meta
description: This story discusses suicide.  If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. A Kentucky mom is closely watching a court case against Meta that could determine if the social media company knowingly designed addictive products that are harmful to children.  Shannon Heacock, […]
text:
OAKLAND, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 18: Shannon Heacock holds a photo of her son, 16-year-old Elijah, who allegedly died from impacts of social media, outside the Ronald V. Dellums Federal Building and U.S. Courthouse on August 18, 2026 in Oakland, California. State attorneys general are alleging that Meta attempted to deceive the public by allowing features on their platforms, Facebook and Instagram, that harm children's mental health and are intended to be addictive. (Photo by Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images)This story discusses suicide.  If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988. 
A Kentucky mom is closely watching a court case against Meta that could determine if the social media company knowingly designed addictive products that are harmful to children. 
Shannon Heacock, from Glasgow, told the Kentucky Lantern social media platforms should face more accountability and regulations. Last year, her teenage son, Elijah, died by suicide after receiving a barrage of messages seeking money or face the release of AI-generated photos of himself, she said. 
Through social media and school websites, the person that sent Elijah the messages knew personal details about his life, Heacock said. Before that, she had open dialogue with her children, particularly about using social media, she added. 
Heacock said an FBI agent said Elijah was the victim of sextortion. Kentucky legislators passed a law in 2025 making that a felony. 
“Talk to your children,” Heacock said. “The internet is a war for them that we’re not invited to. They’re on the front lines of an open cesspool of harassment.”
Kentucky is one of four states leading the case in court against Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram. The states allege the social media company used harmful features to drive compulsive use by children and teens while also claiming the platforms were safe for young users, the Kentucky Attorney General’s office said. Kentucky is joined by California, Colorado, and New Jersey in court. The lawsuit also includes attorneys general from 25 other states. 
Heacock traveled to California for the trial last week with other advocates from the Heat Initiative, which calls for Big Tech companies to have better protections for children online. Heacock said she hoped the group’s presence showed those inside the courtroom that they “want big tech as an industry to be accountable for their own products,” and noted that other industries, such as tobacco and alcohol, are regulated to prevent minors from using those products. 
Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman, a Republican, said in a statement last week this is the “largest consumer protection lawsuit in American history.” 
“We’ll show a jury that Meta concealed what it knew about the harm its products cause young people because looking away was more profitable,” Coleman said. “AGs are in the perfect position to get this done. We did it with the Tobacco Settlement in the 1990s. We did it with the companies behind the opioid crisis. We’ll do it again with Meta and kids will be safer as a result.”
Earlier this year, a Republican-backed bill that sought to regulate social media use for minors in Kentucky, including to restrict those under 15 from using social meda without parental consent, passed the House. However, the bill did not move out of the Senate. Meta lobbied against the bill. 
Heacock said while she wants to see lawmakers pass more regulations for social media companies, she also encourages parents to have conversations with their children about using it. 
“Don’t leave them alone with the internet. It’s not safe,” Heacock said. “Don’t get upset if they come to you. Talk to them. Talk to them. Talk to them.”

text:
State Rep. Charlie St. Clair died on Saturday from injuries he suffered in a motorcycle crash. (Photo courtesy of the New Hampshire Democratic Party)State Rep. Charlie St. Clair, 76, who represented Laconia and served as executive director for the Laconia Motorcycle Week Association, died Saturday from injuries he sustained in a motorcycle crash earlier this month, the Laconia Motorcycle Week Association announced.
The accident occurred Aug. 4, the association said in a statement Saturday, and “despite every effort, his injuries were too severe, and he ultimately passed away from heart failure.”
St. Clair headed the Laconia Motorcycle Week Association for 35 years. The association has been hosting an annual motorcycle festival for over 100 years and boasts that it’s the “World’s Oldest Motorcycle Rally.”
“Charlie was a beloved member of our caucus family,” House Minority Leader Alexis Simpson wrote on social media, “and his loss will be deeply felt by everyone who knew and loved him. Please keep his loved ones in your thoughts.”
Gov. Kelly Ayotte put out a statement Saturday: “Rep. Charlie St. Clair dedicated his life to serving the people of Laconia — from serving on the Planning Board to representing the city at the State House. Charlie loved our state and was proud to welcome visitors from around the world to New Hampshire during his 35 years as head of the Laconia Motorcycle Week Association. Joe and I are praying for Charlie’s family, friends, and fellow riders as they mourn his loss.”

title: U.S. Supreme Court lifts pause on Trump mail-ballot order
text: WASHINGTON — With just over two months until the November midterms, the U.S. Supreme Court gave way Monday for President Donald Trump to have a hand in regulating mail-in ballots nationwide, a voting method he has falsely claimed is rife with corruption since he lost the 2020 presidential election.In an unsigned emergency docket opinion, the court’s conservative majority wrote the Trump administration is likely to prevail on its argument that 23 Democratic-led states do not have standing to stop his executive order to change how the U.S. Postal Service processes mail-in ballots. The majority justices also wrote that a lower court’s injunction is “causing irreparable harm,” but left open the possibility that the executive order could still be considered unconstitutional.“The Court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the majority wrote. The legality of a Massachusetts federal district court order, which paused the executive order to overhaul vote-by-mail systems before the Nov. 3 midterms, will now be decided by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.In a lengthy dissent, Jackson wrote the ruling “needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections.”The principle of courts not altering voting systems too close to the election has been eroded, she said, amounting to a “Kafkaesque nightmare.”“States administering elections and the voting public that relies on them to do so deserve clarity, not caginess or confusion,” she wrote.Final rule issuedThe March 31 executive order at the heart of the case in part directs USPS to direct the redesign of mail-in ballot envelopes, including adding a unique barcode. It also asks USPS to collect voters’ names and addresses from state elections officials and directs the U.S. Justice Department to investigate and prosecute state officials who violate the order.The Postal Service issued a final rule Friday detailing how the process would be carried out.Whether an overhaul of mail-in ballots for each state could be completed in time for the Nov. 3 election remains to be seen, as vote-by-mail documents are sent to voters well in advance of Election Day.A federal district judge in Massachusetts chastised the Trump administration for sowing confusion and “creating” an emergency by noticing a rule Friday that the U.S. Postal Service will eventually require federally regulated mail-in ballot voting envelopes and state data.A 95-page notice alerting that the final rule would appear in the Federal Register on Aug. 26 outlined justifications for federal requirements on states to redesign ballot envelopes and provide a list of recipient names and addresses to USPS. The final rule became effective Friday, according to the document.The final rule runs contrary to U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani’s Aug. 11 preliminary injunction barring the federal government from changing states’ mail-in voting rules prior to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, the judge wrote in a brief order on the docket Sunday. “Defendants did not file an appeal and did not seek, let alone obtain, a stay of the preliminary injunction,” Talwani wrote. “Nonetheless, on August 21, 2026, USPS issued its Final Rule, with an anticipated publication date in the Federal Register of August 26, 2026.” Talwani was appointed to the bench by President Barack Obama in 2013 and unanimously confirmed by the Senate the following year. Effective date delayedThe rule includes a provision that it will not be in effect for this year’s midterm elections if Talwani’s injunction is still in place, but the judge said it would still create significant confusion for voters.The Trump administration asserted the rule would “have no effect on the rules themselves while the injunctions are in place, while ignoring the confusion that the publication will engender,” Talwani wrote.It’s unclear what effect the final rule will have on the active litigation on the issue.The federal government had appealed Talwani’s injunction because, it argued, Trump’s order could not be challenged until an agency published a final rule.Groups want quick order The voting rights advocacy groups, led by the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts, who sued President Donald Trump and administration officials over a March executive order overhauling mail-in voting procedures swiftly filed an emergency motion Saturday. They urged Talwani to quickly enforce her injunction, and to order expedited responses from the administration, citing “immediate, ongoing, irreparable harm caused by Defendants’ violation of the preliminary injunction, and in light of these fast-approaching dates.”“There are now only 73 days before the November 2026 election, and far fewer before mail ballots begin to go out,” they wrote.The Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court in late July a similar district court ruling against its mail-in voting restrictions order in a case brought by nearly two dozen Democrat-led states.The states argued that the federal government has no constitutional role in election administration, that the executive order unfairly limited vote-by-mail, which some states use exclusively, and that an overhaul of ballot requirements this close to an election was unworkable. High court appealIn a supplemental brief filed to the Supreme Court justices Monday, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer said the USPS’s rule issuance “underscores the need for relief from the district court’s improper, unripe injunction.”“The Postal Service’s final rule imposes only modest requirements for preparation and envelope design for federal ballot mail — requirements that fall well within its traditional authorities to impose mailing standards for particularly sensitive types of mail,” wrote Sauer, who formerly worked as Trump’s personal defense attorney. Democratic officials in 23 states — California, Massachusetts, Nevada, Washington, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania — and the District of Columbia brought the suit challenging the executive order. Twelve states with Republican attorneys general — Alabama, Missouri, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas — joined the appeal to the Supreme Court on the federal government’s side.

published a final rule.Groups want quick order The voting rights advocacy groups, led by the League of Women Voters of Massachusetts, who sued President Donald Trump and administration officials over a March executive order overhauling mail-in voting procedures swiftly filed an emergency motion Saturday. They urged Talwani to quickly enforce her injunction, and to order expedited responses from the administration, citing “immediate, ongoing, irreparable harm caused by Defendants’ violation of the preliminary injunction, and in light of these fast-approaching dates.”“There are now only 73 days before the November 2026 election, and far fewer before mail ballots begin to go out,” they wrote.The Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court in late July a similar district court ruling against its mail-in voting restrictions order in a case brought by nearly two dozen Democrat-led states.The states argued that the federal government has no constitutional role in election administration, that the executive order unfairly limited vote-by-mail, which some states use exclusively, and that an overhaul of ballot requirements this close to an election was unworkable. High court appealIn a supplemental brief filed to the Supreme Court justices Monday, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer said the USPS’s rule issuance “underscores the need for relief from the district court’s improper, unripe injunction.”“The Postal Service’s final rule imposes only modest requirements for preparation and envelope design for federal ballot mail — requirements that fall well within its traditional authorities to impose mailing standards for particularly sensitive types of mail,” wrote Sauer, who formerly worked as Trump’s personal defense attorney. Democratic officials in 23 states — California, Massachusetts, Nevada, Washington, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania — and the District of Columbia brought the suit challenging the executive order. Twelve states with Republican attorneys general — Alabama, Missouri, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas — joined the appeal to the Supreme Court on the federal government’s side.

title: Frijoles Fire officials report crew death as fire reaches 45% containment
description: The team fighting the 15,200-acre Frijoles Fire in the Pecos Wilderness announced Sunday that a crew member had died from a medical emergency.
text:
The Frijoles Fire burning in the Pecos Wilderness is 45% contained and has stayed at roughly 15,200 for more than 48 hours, officials announced Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo courtesy Inciweb)The team fighting the 15,200-acre Frijoles Fire in the Pecos Wilderness announced Sunday that a crew member had died from a medical emergency. 
A news release from the California incident command team overseeing fire suppression efforts described the person who died as an incident support crew member. Leaders said the crew member was transported to a local hospital due to an unspecified medical emergency and died despite the efforts of emergency medical responders. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We are grieving alongside our fire family and will do everything we can to support those impacted,” Mike Page, the incident commander leading California Interagency Management Team 8, said in a statement. The team is overseeing Frijoles Fire suppression efforts. Page asked for privacy for the person’s family, as well as crew members. 
Two other personnel have suffered unspecified injuries in fighting the blaze, internal reports show. 
The announcement of the death comes as incident command reports that the fire’s growth has slowed over the last 48 hours and firefighters have achieved 45% containment. The blaze’s footprint has remained at roughly 15,200 acres since Saturday morning. 
The lighting-caused wildfire has threatened structures and prompted evacuations in the Santa Fe National Forest since it first ignited Aug. 4, but the command team in charge of the fire has reported steady progress in recent days. 
The internal report the team produced notes that the next 24 to 48 hours present the best opportunity over the next seven days to make significant progress on building containment lines, so long as the team has access to additional helicopters. If the helicopters arrive promptly, commanders wrote in a Monday morning situational report, crews have a 70% to 75% chance of containing the most prominent wildfire spread. 
The fire has recently emitted large amounts of smoke that have prompted multiple state health advisories, though the forecast Monday predicts good air quality from Taos to Santa Fe and Española to Nambe. 
Santa Fe National Forest officials on Sunday also announced that a new wildfire, the Osha Medio Fire, started near Pecos Canyon in the Pecos-Las Vegas Ranger District. The fire, which officials say may have started due to lightning, had reached approximately five acres as of Sunday morning, though it presents “moderate to high” potential for significant growth.
The national forest officials said they would share updates going forward on the Osha Medio Fire.
